sets.title: Newborn with an abnormal T-cell screen
Peanut anaphylaxis in the emergency department
Extended CMV prophylaxis after kidney transplant
sets.introHtml: Study summary (fictional). A randomized, open-label trial at 24 transplant centers enrolled 400 adult kidney recipients who were CMV IgG negative and received a kidney from a CMV-seropositive donor (D+/R−). Patients received either standard-duration oral antiviral prophylaxis (100 days) or an extended 200-day course of the same study drug. The primary outcome was CMV disease within 12 months. CMV disease occurred in 20% of the standard group and 10% of the extended group (P = .004). Leukopenia requiring dose interruption occurred in 8% and 15%, respectively. All-cause mortality at 12 months was 2% in each group. The trial was not powered to detect differences in mortality.

sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). A multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 2,400 adults with a first unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism who had completed 6 to 12 months of anticoagulation without recurrence. Exclusion criteria were active cancer, known antiphospholipid syndrome, a mechanical heart valve, need for antiplatelet therapy, creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min and pregnancy. Participants were randomly assigned to a reduced dose of drug Q, an oral direct factor Xa inhibitor, or to placebo for 12 months.

sets.title: A toddler with pallor after bloody diarrhea

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy is evaluated for 4 months of headaches, intermittent low-grade fever, loss of previously acquired words and an unsteady gait. Since 9 months of age he has had five episodes of otitis media and two of pneumococcal pneumonia. Examination shows no palpable tonsils or cervical lymph nodes. Cerebrospinal fluid shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis with mildly raised protein and normal glucose; reverse-transcriptase PCR of the fluid is positive for echovirus. Serum IgG, IgA and IgM are markedly decreased. CD19+ cells are 0.5% of lymphocytes; CD3+ T-cell count and mitogen response are normal. Which of the following best explains his susceptibility to this central nervous system infection?

options.label: B
options.html: Absent neutralizing antibody to the virus

items.explanationHtml:
Near-absent B cells with panhypogammaglobulinemia in a boy, onset after maternal IgG waned and absent lymphoid tissue indicate X-linked agammaglobulinemia. Enteroviruses are controlled mainly by neutralizing antibody, which blocks viremia and spread; without it, patients develop chronic enteroviral meningoencephalitis, a slowly progressive illness with regression and ataxia. His T cells, which handle most other viruses, are normal.

Takeaway: chronic enteroviral meningoencephalitis is a signature infection of B-cell absence because enterovirus clearance depends on neutralizing antibody.

whyNot.A: Complement deficiency predisposes to encapsulated bacteria and Neisseria, and his complement-dependent killing would be intact if antibody were present; it does not explain chronic enteroviral infection with absent B cells.
whyNot.C: His T-cell count and function are normal; CD8 defects present with severe herpesvirus infections rather than isolated enteroviral disease with agammaglobulinemia.
whyNot.D: Type I interferon defects cause severe viral disease such as HSV encephalitis or life-threatening influenza, not recurrent pneumococcal infection with absent B cells.
whyNot.E: Defects of the IL-12/IFN-γ axis cause mycobacterial and Salmonella disease, not sinopulmonary bacterial and enteroviral infections.

items.objective: Explain why absent B cells predispose to chronic enteroviral meningoencephalitis.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of her fourth episode of radiologically confirmed pneumonia in 3 years and chronic sinusitis. At age 24 she was treated for immune thrombocytopenia. She takes no medications. Serum studies show IgG 310 mg/dL (reference range, 700–1,600 mg/dL), IgA 12 mg/dL (reference range, 70–400 mg/dL) and IgM 25 mg/dL (reference range, 40–230 mg/dL); albumin and urine protein are normal. Antibody titers to tetanus and to pneumococcal serotypes fail to rise after vaccination. Flow cytometry shows a normal number of CD19+ cells with a reduced proportion of class-switched memory B cells. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?

options.label: A
options.html: Arrest of B-cell development at the pre-B stage

options.label: C
options.html: Loss of CD40 ligand on activated T cells

options.label: D
options.html: Mutation of the common γ chain of cytokine receptors

items.explanationHtml:
Adult-onset hypogammaglobulinemia of IgG with low IgA and IgM, poor vaccine responses, no secondary cause, and autoimmunity (ITP) is common variable immunodeficiency. B cells are present, but they fail to complete terminal differentiation into antibody-secreting plasma cells, and switched memory B cells are reduced.

Takeaway: CVID has B cells but not enough plasma cells; X-linked agammaglobulinemia lacks the B cells themselves.

whyNot.A: A pre-B block (BTK deficiency) leaves almost no circulating CD19+ cells and presents in infancy; her B-cell count is normal.
whyNot.B: Thymic aplasia (22q11.2 deletion) reduces T cells and presents with cardiac and parathyroid disease in infancy, not adult antibody failure.
whyNot.C: CD40 ligand deficiency gives normal or high IgM with absent IgG and IgA and opportunistic infections from early childhood; her IgM is low.
whyNot.D: Common γ chain mutation causes X-linked SCID in male infants, with absent T and NK cells.

items.objective: Identify the cellular defect in common variable immunodeficiency from immunoglobulin, vaccine and B-cell findings.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old girl is found to have serum IgA below 5 mg/dL (reference range, 70–400 mg/dL) during evaluation for celiac disease. Serum IgG and IgM are normal, and her antibody response to tetanus toxoid is protective. She has had two uncomplicated sinus infections in her life and no gastrointestinal infections. Intestinal secretions from such individuals contain increased amounts of another immunoglobulin that protects the mucosa. Transport of this compensating immunoglobulin into the gut lumen depends on which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Binding to the neonatal Fc receptor on enterocytes

options.label: B
options.html: Binding to the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor

options.label: C
options.html: Fc-γ receptor–mediated transcytosis by M cells

options.label: D
options.html: IgE receptors on intestinal mast cells

items.explanationHtml:
Most people with selective IgA deficiency stay healthy, partly because pentameric IgM, which carries a J chain like dimeric IgA, binds the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor on the basolateral surface of epithelial cells, is transcytosed and released with secretory component as secretory IgM.

Takeaway: J-chain–containing IgM uses the same pIgR transport route as IgA, which helps compensate mucosal defence in IgA deficiency.

whyNot.A: The neonatal Fc receptor transports and recycles IgG and does not move J-chain polymers into secretions.
whyNot.C: M cells sample luminal antigens and deliver them to Peyer patches; they do not secrete immunoglobulin into the lumen.
whyNot.D: Mast-cell IgE receptors bind IgE for degranulation; IgE is not the compensating mucosal antibody and is not transported this way.
whyNot.E: Intact epithelium does not let large immunoglobulin polymers diffuse between cells in useful amounts.

items.objective: Describe how secretory IgM, transported by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor, compensates for selective IgA deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl is evaluated for recurrent sinusitis, two episodes of pneumonia due to Haemophilus influenzae and recurrent diarrhea. Her parents are first cousins. She has had no opportunistic infections. Examination shows enlarged tonsils and diffuse, nontender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. Serum IgM is 580 mg/dL (reference range, 40–230 mg/dL); IgG, IgA and IgE are markedly decreased. CD40 ligand expression on her activated T cells and CD40 expression on her B cells are normal. A lymph node biopsy shows giant germinal centres. The enzyme most likely deficient in this patient normally performs which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Cleavage of DNA at recombination signal sequences

options.label: B
options.html: Deamination of cytidine in immunoglobulin genes

options.label: D
options.html: Phosphorylation of signal proteins of the pre-B receptor

options.label: E
options.html: Purine salvage by removal of an amino group from adenosine

items.explanationHtml:
Hyper-IgM with normal CD40L and CD40, autosomal recessive inheritance, lymphoid hyperplasia with giant germinal centres and no opportunistic infections indicates deficiency of activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID). AID deaminates cytidine to uridine in switch and variable regions, starting class-switch recombination and somatic hypermutation. Germinal-centre B cells proliferate but cannot switch, so they accumulate.

Takeaway: AID deficiency is the B-intrinsic hyper-IgM: large germinal centres, pyogenic infections only, normal CD40L.

whyNot.A: RAG enzymes cut DNA at recombination signal sequences during V(D)J recombination; their loss abolishes B and T cells (SCID).
whyNot.C: Superoxide generation is the role of NADPH oxidase; its loss causes chronic granulomatous disease with normal immunoglobulins.
whyNot.D: Bruton tyrosine kinase signals downstream of the pre-B receptor; its loss removes B cells and all immunoglobulin, including IgM.
whyNot.E: Adenosine deaminase loss causes T−B−NK− SCID through dATP toxicity, not isolated class-switch failure.

items.objective: Relate activation-induced cytidine deaminase deficiency to hyper-IgM with lymphoid hyperplasia.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for 2 months of watery diarrhea and weight loss. He has had recurrent otitis media since infancy and was treated for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia at 11 months of age. Stool testing shows Cryptosporidium oocysts. Serum alkaline phosphatase and GGT are elevated, and magnetic resonance cholangiography shows beading of the intrahepatic bile ducts. Serum IgM is elevated, and IgG and IgA are very low. Lymph nodes lack germinal centres. A maternal uncle died in childhood of liver disease. The defective protein in this patient is normally expressed most prominently on which of the following cell types?
items.explanationHtml:
X-linked hyper-IgM with Pneumocystis, cryptosporidial diarrhea and sclerosing cholangitis is CD40 ligand deficiency. CD40L (CD154) is expressed transiently on activated CD4+ T cells. It engages CD40 on B cells for class switching and germinal-centre formation, and CD40 on macrophages and dendritic cells for IL-12 production and killing of intracellular organisms, which explains the opportunistic infections.

Takeaway: CD40L is a T-cell molecule, so its loss impairs both B-cell switching and macrophage activation.

whyNot.B: Follicular dendritic cells hold antigen in follicles; they are not the source of the CD40 signal, and the X-linked pattern fits a T-cell gene.
whyNot.C: B cells express CD40, the receptor; CD40 deficiency is autosomal recessive, whereas this boy's maternal-uncle history indicates an X-linked gene.
whyNot.D: NK cells are not the main source of CD40L, and NK defects present with severe herpesvirus infections.
whyNot.E: Macrophages express CD40 and respond to the signal; they do not supply the missing ligand.

items.objective: Identify the cell type that expresses CD40 ligand and link its loss to opportunistic infection in X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 9-month-old girl is evaluated after her third episode of acute otitis media, each of which resolved with oral antibiotics. She was born at term, is growing along the 50th percentile and has received all routine vaccines. Examination is normal and tonsillar tissue is visible. Serum IgG is below the age-specific reference range, with IgM and IgA at the low end of normal. CD19+ B-cell and CD3+ T-cell counts are normal, and antibody titers to tetanus and to H. influenzae type b conjugate vaccine are protective. Repeat testing at age 30 months shows normal IgG. Which of the following best explains the low IgG level at 9 months?

options.label: A
options.html: Arrest of B-cell maturation in the bone marrow

options.label: B
options.html: Delayed onset of the infant's own IgG synthesis

options.label: C
options.html: Excessive loss of IgG through the gastrointestinal tract

options.label: D
options.html: Failure of isotype switching in germinal centres

items.explanationHtml:
Maternal IgG wanes during the first months, and the infant's IgG synthesis normally rises to fill the gap. In transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy, the infant's own production starts late, so the physiological nadir is deeper and longer. B cells are normal, protein-vaccine responses are intact, and IgG normalises in early childhood.

Takeaway: low IgG with normal B cells and normal vaccine responses in an infant that later normalises is delayed maturation, not a fixed defect.

whyNot.A: A marrow maturation arrest (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) leaves almost no B cells and does not resolve.
whyNot.C: Protein-losing enteropathy lowers albumin as well and needs diarrhea or edema; she is thriving with normal examination.
whyNot.D: Class-switch failure produces very low IgG with normal or high IgM and poor IgG vaccine responses, and it persists.
whyNot.E: Thymic hypoplasia lowers T cells; her T-cell count is normal.

items.objective: Explain the physiological basis of transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy has had three episodes of pneumococcal pneumonia in 2 years. Serum IgG, IgA, IgM and IgG subclasses are within reference ranges. Antibody titers to tetanus and diphtheria toxoids are protective. Four weeks after vaccination with a 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine, protective titers are present to 4 of 14 serotypes tested. After vaccination with a pneumococcal protein–conjugate vaccine, he develops protective titers to most serotypes in that vaccine. Which of the following immune processes is most likely impaired in this patient?

options.label: A
options.html: Antigen presentation on MHC class I molecules

options.label: B
options.html: C3b opsonization of bacteria in the classical pathway

options.label: C
options.html: Clonal expansion of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells

options.label: D
options.html: Responses to antigens that require T-cell help

options.label: E
options.html: Responses to antigens that do not require T-cell help

items.explanationHtml:
Normal immunoglobulins and protein-vaccine responses with poor response to pure polysaccharide antigens in a child older than 2 years is specific antibody deficiency. Polysaccharides are T-cell–independent type 2 antigens that cross-link B-cell receptors on marginal-zone and B1 B cells. Conjugate vaccines couple the polysaccharide to a carrier protein, recruit T-cell help and bypass the defect, which is why he responds to them.

Takeaway: specific antibody deficiency is a failure of T-independent polysaccharide responses; conjugate vaccines work because they make the response T-dependent.

whyNot.A: MHC class I presentation drives CD8 responses to intracellular pathogens, not antibody to bacterial capsules.
whyNot.B: Complement defects would not explain a selective failure to make anticapsular antibody with normal protein responses.
whyNot.C: CD8 expansion is needed against viruses; his problem is anticapsular antibody.
whyNot.D: His protective titers to tetanus, diphtheria and conjugate vaccine show that T-cell–dependent antibody responses are intact.

items.objective: Distinguish T-independent polysaccharide responses from T-dependent conjugate responses in specific antibody deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 4-month-old boy is hospitalized with hypoxemia and bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows Pneumocystis jirovecii. Since 6 weeks of age he has had persistent oral thrush and chronic diarrhea, and his weight has fallen from the 50th to below the 3rd percentile. Chest x-ray shows no thymic shadow. Flow cytometry shows absent CD3+ T cells and CD16/56+ NK cells, with a normal number of CD19+ B cells. His mother's brother died of infection in infancy. Loss of signalling through the receptor for which of the following cytokines best explains the absence of his T cells?
items.explanationHtml:
T−B+NK− SCID in a boy with an affected maternal uncle is X-linked SCID from IL2RG mutation. The common γ chain is shared by the receptors for IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15 and IL-21. Thymocyte development depends on IL-7 receptor signalling; loss of IL-15 signalling explains the missing NK cells.

Takeaway: in γc deficiency, absent IL-7 signalling removes T cells and absent IL-15 signalling removes NK cells.

whyNot.A: IL-2 supports proliferation and regulatory T-cell survival; IL-2 or CD25 deficiency causes autoimmunity with T cells present, not absent thymopoiesis.
whyNot.B: IL-4 drives Th2 differentiation and IgE switching; its loss does not prevent T-cell development.
whyNot.D: IL-15 is required for NK-cell development, which explains his missing NK cells but not the missing T cells.
whyNot.E: IL-21 supports B-cell differentiation and germinal centres; its loss contributes to poor antibody production, not absent T cells.

items.objective: Link loss of IL-7 signalling through the common γ chain to T-cell absence in X-linked SCID.

items.stemHtml: A 3-month-old girl has persistent thrush, chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive and severe RSV pneumonia. Her parents are first cousins. Chest x-ray shows no thymic shadow and flaring and cupping of the anterior rib ends. She did not pass her newborn hearing screen. Absolute lymphocyte count is 180/mm3, with very low T, B and NK cells. Accumulation of which of the following substances is most directly responsible for her lymphocyte depletion?
items.explanationHtml:
Autosomal recessive T−B−NK− SCID with rib-end cupping and sensorineural hearing loss indicates adenosine deaminase deficiency. Without ADA, deoxyadenosine is phosphorylated to dATP, which inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and blocks DNA synthesis; dividing lymphocytes, which have high kinase activity, are killed. The defect is systemic, which explains the skeletal and auditory findings.

Takeaway: ADA-SCID is a purine metabolic disease in which dATP is toxic to lymphocytes.

whyNot.B: Deoxyguanosine triphosphate accumulates in purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency, which spares B cells relatively and causes neurologic disease, not this picture with skeletal changes.
whyNot.C: Orotic acid accumulates in hereditary orotic aciduria or OTC deficiency, which cause megaloblastic anemia or hyperammonemia, not SCID.
whyNot.D: Raised phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate occurs in HGPRT deficiency and PRPP synthetase overactivity, which cause gout and neurologic disease.
whyNot.E: Uric acid is the end product of purine degradation and is low, not high, when ADA is missing.

items.objective: Explain how adenosine deaminase deficiency causes lymphocyte death through dATP accumulation.

items.stemHtml: A 10-week-old boy is evaluated for a generalized red, scaly rash that began at 3 weeks of age, loss of scalp hair and eyebrows, chronic diarrhea and poor weight gain. Examination shows diffuse lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Leukocyte count is 19,000/mm3 with 30% eosinophils (reference range, 0–6%). Serum IgE is markedly elevated. Flow cytometry shows no CD19+ B cells and a moderate number of T cells that are almost all activated memory cells with a restricted T-cell receptor repertoire; T-cell receptor excision circles are absent. A defect in which of the following processes is the most likely cause?

options.label: B
options.html: Negative selection of thymocytes by AIRE

options.label: E
options.html: V(D)J recombination of antigen receptor genes

items.explanationHtml:
Erythroderma, alopecia, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, eosinophilia, high IgE, absent B cells and oligoclonal activated T cells with absent TRECs make up Omenn syndrome. It is caused by hypomorphic mutations, most often in RAG1 or RAG2, that allow a little V(D)J recombination: a few T-cell clones form, expand and infiltrate skin, gut and liver.

Takeaway: Omenn syndrome is leaky SCID: residual V(D)J recombination yields a few autoreactive T-cell clones and no B cells.

whyNot.A: Class-switch defects (hyper-IgM) leave B cells present and do not cause T-cell oligoclonality or absent TRECs.
whyNot.B: AIRE deficiency causes APECED with candidiasis and endocrine autoimmunity in later childhood, with a normal T-cell repertoire and B cells.
whyNot.C: Oxidative burst defects cause CGD with bacterial and fungal infections and normal lymphocyte development.
whyNot.D: Somatic hypermutation occurs in mature B cells; its loss does not remove B cells or restrict the T-cell repertoire.

items.objective: Recognize Omenn syndrome as leaky SCID from hypomorphic defects in V(D)J recombination.

items.stemHtml: A 3-day-old boy has a generalized seizure. He was found on fetal echocardiography to have an interrupted aortic arch. Serum calcium is 6.4 mg/dL and PTH is undetectable. Chest x-ray shows no thymic shadow. Chromosomal microarray shows a 3-Mb deletion of chromosome 22q11.2. Flow cytometry shows a CD3+ T-cell count of 40/mm3 with absent naive T cells; B-cell and NK-cell counts are normal. A biopsy of a lymph node from this infant would most likely show depletion of which of the following regions?
items.explanationHtml:
Complete 22q11.2 deletion phenotype with athymia leaves almost no T cells. In lymph nodes, T cells occupy the paracortex, which is therefore depleted, while B-cell primary follicles in the cortex are preserved because B-cell development is normal.

Takeaway: T-cell deficiency empties the paracortex; B-cell deficiency empties follicles and germinal centres.

whyNot.A: Mantle zones are rims of naive B cells around follicles, and his B-cell count is normal.
whyNot.B: Medullary cords contain plasma cells and macrophages; they are not the T-cell compartment.
whyNot.D: Primary follicles are B-cell areas, and his B-cell count is normal.
whyNot.E: The subcapsular sinus is lined by macrophages and is unaffected by T-cell aplasia.

items.objective: Locate the lymph node compartment depleted in T-cell aplasia.

items.stemHtml: An 18-month-old boy is evaluated for eczema of the face and flexures since 2 months of age, recurrent otitis media and intermittent bloody stools. Examination shows petechiae on the trunk. Platelet count is 32,000/mm3 with a low mean platelet volume; the peripheral smear shows small platelets. Serum IgM is low, IgA and IgE are high, and IgG is normal. A maternal cousin had similar problems. The protein encoded by the mutated gene in this patient normally has which of the following functions?
items.explanationHtml:
Microthrombocytopenia, eczema and recurrent infection in a boy with X-linked inheritance is Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. WAS protein links receptor signalling to actin polymerisation through the Arp2/3 complex. Lymphocytes cannot form an effective immune synapse or migrate, and platelets are small and short-lived.

Takeaway: WAS protein is a hematopoietic actin regulator; its loss gives small platelets, eczema and poor polysaccharide antibody responses.

whyNot.A: Double-strand break sensing is the job of ATM, lost in ataxia-telangiectasia, which presents with ataxia and telangiectasias and normal platelets.
whyNot.B: Superoxide generation by NADPH oxidase is lost in CGD, which does not cause thrombocytopenia or eczema.
whyNot.C: Integrin binding to ICAM-1 depends on CD18, lost in leukocyte adhesion deficiency with neutrophilia and absent pus.
whyNot.D: Lysosomal trafficking defects (LYST) cause Chédiak-Higashi syndrome with albinism and giant granules, not small platelets.

items.objective: Identify the actin-regulating function of WAS protein from the Wiskott-Aldrich triad.

items.stemHtml: A 5-year-old girl is evaluated for clumsiness that began when she started walking and has steadily worsened, slurred speech and recurrent sinusitis. Examination shows a wide-based gait, dysmetria, difficulty initiating saccades and dilated, tortuous vessels on the bulbar conjunctivae. Serum α-fetoprotein is elevated; serum IgA is very low. Cultured lymphocytes from this patient are most likely to show increased chromosome breakage after exposure to which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
Progressive cerebellar ataxia from toddlerhood, oculomotor apraxia, conjunctival telangiectasias, raised AFP and low IgA indicate ataxia-telangiectasia. The ATM kinase senses double-strand DNA breaks, which ionizing radiation produces, and activates cell-cycle checkpoints and repair. Without it, cells show radiosensitivity and chromosomal translocations (often involving T-cell receptor and immunoglobulin loci), and patients have a high risk of lymphoma and leukemia.

Takeaway: ATM loss means radiosensitivity; minimise diagnostic radiation in ataxia-telangiectasia.

whyNot.A: Cold-induced effects are features of cold agglutinin or cryoglobulin disorders, not of a DNA repair defect.
whyNot.B: Hypersensitivity to crosslinking agents (mitomycin C, diepoxybutane) defines Fanconi anemia, which presents with marrow failure and limb anomalies.
whyNot.D: Oxidative stress sensitivity of red cells is a feature of G6PD deficiency, not ATM loss.
whyNot.E: Ultraviolet hypersensitivity defines xeroderma pigmentosum, a nucleotide excision repair defect with skin cancers.

items.objective: Relate ATM deficiency to hypersensitivity to ionizing radiation in ataxia-telangiectasia.

items.stemHtml: A 2-year-old boy is hospitalized with fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly and lytic bone lesions. Biopsy of a lesion shows poorly formed granulomas with abundant acid-fast bacilli, and cultures grow Mycobacterium avium complex. His parents are first cousins. Lymphocyte counts, immunoglobulins and the dihydrorhodamine test are normal. HIV testing is negative. His serum IFN-γ concentration is markedly elevated. Which of the following is the most likely defect?
items.explanationHtml:
Disseminated nontuberculous mycobacterial infection with normal lymphocytes, immunoglobulins and oxidative burst is Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease. A high serum IFN-γ means the cytokine is made but not used, which points to complete IFN-γ receptor deficiency. Defects upstream (IL-12 or its receptor) reduce IFN-γ production. The distinction matters: recombinant IFN-γ helps upstream defects but cannot act without a receptor, so complete receptor deficiency needs hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

Takeaway: in mycobacterial susceptibility, raised IFN-γ localises the defect to the IFN-γ receptor.

whyNot.A: IL-12 p40 deficiency reduces IL-12 production, so IFN-γ secretion would be low, not elevated.
whyNot.B: IL-12 receptor β1 deficiency impairs IFN-γ production by T and NK cells, so serum IFN-γ would be low.
whyNot.D: NADPH oxidase deficiency (CGD) would give an abnormal dihydrorhodamine test, and his test is normal.
whyNot.E: STAT3 dominant-negative disease causes staphylococcal abscesses, pneumatoceles and high IgE, not isolated disseminated mycobacterial infection.

items.objective: Use serum IFN-γ level to localize a defect in the IL-12/IFN-γ axis.

items.stemHtml: A 12-year-old girl is evaluated for recurrent skin abscesses caused by Staphylococcus aureus; the abscesses are fluctuant but cause little warmth, redness or pain. She has had eczema since the newborn period and two staphylococcal pneumonias, the second of which left a thin-walled cyst in the right lower lobe. Her primary teeth were extracted because they did not fall out, and she sustained a femur fracture after a minor fall. Serum IgE is 5,200 IU/mL (reference, below 100 IU/mL) with eosinophilia. Impaired differentiation of which of the following T-cell subsets best explains her susceptibility to staphylococcal infection?
items.explanationHtml:
Cold staphylococcal abscesses, pneumatoceles, newborn eczema, retained primary teeth, low-trauma fracture and very high IgE indicate autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome from dominant-negative STAT3 mutation. STAT3 transmits IL-6 and IL-23 signals that drive Th17 differentiation. Without IL-17 and IL-22, keratinocytes and airway epithelium make fewer neutrophil chemokines and antimicrobial peptides, so staphylococci and Candida flourish at barriers.

Takeaway: STAT3 hyper-IgE is a Th17 failure; the barrier, not the bloodstream, is undefended.

whyNot.A: Follicular helper T-cell defects reduce germinal-centre antibody responses; they do not explain cold abscesses, pneumatoceles or skeletal features.
whyNot.B: Regulatory T-cell loss (FOXP3) causes IPEX with enteropathy, diabetes and eczema, not recurrent staphylococcal abscesses with pneumatoceles.
whyNot.C: Th1 defects (IL-12/IFN-γ axis) predispose to mycobacteria and Salmonella, not staphylococcal skin and lung infection.
whyNot.D: Th2 activity is not reduced in this disorder; the high IgE reflects dysregulation, and Th2 loss would not cause infection.

items.objective: Link STAT3 dominant-negative hyper-IgE syndrome to failed Th17 differentiation.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old girl has a photosensitive rash over her cheeks and forearms, oral ulcers and proteinuria. Renal biopsy shows immune-complex glomerulonephritis. She has had two episodes of pneumococcal pneumonia. Her parents are second cousins, and an older brother died of an illness diagnosed as lupus at 12 years of age. Antinuclear antibody is positive. Serum C3 and C4 are normal, CH50 is undetectable and AH50 is normal. The most likely mechanism of autoimmunity in this patient is impaired clearance of which of the following?

options.label: C
options.html: Autoreactive B cells by regulatory T cells

items.explanationHtml:
Childhood lupus with recurrent pneumococcal infection, consanguinity, normal C3 and C4, an absent CH50 and a normal AH50 indicates deficiency of an early classical component other than C4, most likely C1q, the deficiency with the highest lupus risk. C1q binds apoptotic cells and immune complexes and, with C4b and C3b, directs their quiet removal. When clearance fails, nuclear autoantigens persist and drive anti-nuclear autoimmunity.

Takeaway: early classical complement deficiency causes lupus because apoptotic debris and immune complexes are not cleared.

whyNot.A: C5a is a chemotactic anaphylatoxin generated downstream; failure to clear it is not a cause of lupus, and early-component loss reduces C5a.
whyNot.C: Regulatory T-cell failure (FOXP3) causes IPEX, not complement-associated lupus with an absent CH50.
whyNot.D: Excess bradykinin causes angioedema in C1 inhibitor deficiency, not lupus with an absent CH50.
whyNot.E: Failure of thymic negative selection (AIRE) causes APECED, with candidiasis and endocrine autoimmunity rather than lupus.

items.objective: Explain why early classical complement deficiency predisposes to systemic lupus erythematosus.

items.stemHtml:
A 22-year-old woman has had episodes of nonpruritic swelling of the hands and face lasting 3 days since age 13, and two hospital admissions for severe abdominal pain with bowel-wall edema on CT. She has had no hives at any time. Her mother has a similar history. Laboratory studies obtained between attacks:

TestResult
C4Low
C1qNormal
C1 inhibitor protein (antigen)Normal
C1 inhibitor function22% of normal

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: E
options.html: Hereditary angioedema with normal C1 inhibitor

items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent swelling without urticaria, abdominal attacks and autosomal dominant inheritance indicate hereditary angioedema. A low C4 with low C1-INH function but a normal amount of C1-INH protein is type II, in which the mutant protein is made but is dysfunctional. A normal C1q argues against acquired deficiency.

Takeaway: HAE type I has low C1-INH level and function; type II has normal level and low function; both have low C4 and normal C1q.

whyNot.A: ACE inhibitor angioedema occurs in patients taking the drug and has normal C4 and C1-INH; she takes no drugs and has a family history.
whyNot.B: Acquired C1-INH deficiency begins in older adults, often with lymphoproliferative disease, and lowers C1q.
whyNot.C: Type I has a low C1-INH protein level, whereas hers is normal.
whyNot.E: HAE with normal C1-INH has normal C4 and normal C1-INH function.

items.objective: Classify hereditary angioedema from C4, C1q and C1 inhibitor level and function.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy is admitted to intensive care with fever, purpura fulminans and hypotension, and blood cultures grow Neisseria meningitidis serogroup Y. He recovers after a prolonged admission. A maternal uncle died of meningococcal sepsis at 17 years of age. He has had no other serious infections. Three months later, CH50 is normal and AH50 is markedly decreased; C3 is normal. Which of the following proteins is most likely deficient?
items.explanationHtml:
Fulminant meningococcal disease in a boy with an affected maternal uncle, with a normal CH50 and low AH50, indicates X-linked properdin deficiency. Properdin stabilises the alternative-pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb). Without it, the alternative pathway amplifies poorly on the meningococcal surface, and the classical pathway (CH50) is unaffected.

Takeaway: normal CH50 with low AH50 means factor B, factor D or properdin; X-linked meningococcal disease points to properdin.

whyNot.A: C2 deficiency lowers CH50 and leaves AH50 normal, the opposite pattern, and is autosomal.
whyNot.B: C3 deficiency lowers both CH50 and AH50 and lowers measured C3; his C3 and CH50 are normal.
whyNot.C: Terminal component deficiency (C8) abolishes both CH50 and AH50.
whyNot.D: Factor H loss consumes C3, so C3, CH50 and AH50 would all be low.

items.objective: Identify properdin deficiency from X-linked inheritance and a low AH50 with normal CH50.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy has 3 days of pallor, decreased urine output and periorbital edema. He has had no diarrhea. Blood pressure is 128/84 mm Hg. Hemoglobin is 7.4 g/dL, platelet count is 38,000/mm3, LDH is elevated and haptoglobin is undetectable; the smear shows schistocytes. Creatinine is 2.9 mg/dL. Direct antiglobulin test is negative, stool testing for Shiga toxin is negative and ADAMTS13 activity is normal. Serum C3 is low and C4 is normal. Genetic testing shows a heterozygous variant in the C-terminal region of the gene for complement factor H. Which of the following best explains the endothelial injury?

options.label: E
options.html: Unregulated alternative pathway activation on host cells

items.explanationHtml:
Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury without diarrhea, with negative Shiga toxin testing, normal ADAMTS13 and low C3, is atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome. The C-terminal domains of factor H bind host-cell surfaces (glycosaminoglycans and sialic acid) and inactivate C3b there. With that binding lost, the alternative pathway runs unchecked on endothelium, forming membrane attack complexes and driving thrombotic microangiopathy, mostly in the kidney.

Takeaway: atypical HUS is complement-mediated endothelial injury from failed surface regulation of the alternative pathway; C5 blockade is the treatment.

whyNot.A: Severely reduced ADAMTS13 activity defines TTP; his ADAMTS13 activity is normal.
whyNot.B: Antibodies to platelet factor 4–heparin complexes cause heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with thrombosis, not hemolysis with schistocytes and low C3 after no heparin exposure.
whyNot.C: Bradykinin excess causes angioedema without hemolysis or thrombocytopenia.
whyNot.D: Toxin-mediated HUS follows Shiga toxin–producing E. coli diarrhea; he has had no diarrhea and toxin testing is negative.

items.objective: Explain how factor H dysfunction causes atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 5-year-old girl has had recurrent pneumonia, otitis media and two episodes of bacteremia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae since infancy. Urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria, and renal biopsy shows membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. Serum immunoglobulins are normal. Both CH50 and AH50 are undetectable. Serum C3 is undetectable and C4 is normal. Factor H and factor I levels are normal. The loss of which immune function best explains her pyogenic infections?
items.explanationHtml:
Absent C3 with abolished CH50 and AH50 and normal regulators means primary C3 deficiency. C3b is the main complement opsonin: deposited on encapsulated bacteria, it is recognised by CR1 and CR3 on phagocytes. Without it, opsonophagocytosis of pneumococci and H. influenzae fails, and immune complexes are cleared poorly, which explains the glomerulonephritis.

Takeaway: C3 is the hub of complement; its loss removes C3b opsonization and causes severe pyogenic infection.

whyNot.A: Her immunoglobulins are normal, so class switching is intact.
whyNot.B: Granuloma formation depends on Th1 cytokines and macrophages; its failure predisposes to mycobacteria.
whyNot.C: Superoxide generation is lost in chronic granulomatous disease, which has normal complement.
whyNot.E: NK-cell cytotoxicity defends against herpesviruses; it is not reduced by complement loss.

items.objective: Relate C3 deficiency to failed opsonization of encapsulated bacteria.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and recurrent hemolytic episodes is to begin treatment with a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds complement component C5 and prevents its cleavage. Before the first dose, she must receive vaccines because the drug substantially increases her risk of serious infection by which of the following organisms?
items.explanationHtml:
Eculizumab and ravulizumab block C5 cleavage, preventing C5a and the membrane attack complex. MAC-mediated lysis is the critical defence against Neisseria, so the drugs reproduce terminal complement deficiency and carry a boxed warning for meningococcal disease. MenACWY and MenB vaccination is required before the first dose when possible.

Takeaway: anti-C5 therapy means meningococcal risk; vaccinate and educate.

whyNot.A: Invasive aspergillosis follows neutropenia, glucocorticoids or CGD; terminal complement is not the main defence.
whyNot.B: Listeria is controlled by T cells and is a risk with TNF inhibitors, glucocorticoids and pregnancy.
whyNot.C: Tuberculosis reactivation is the main infectious risk of TNF-α inhibitors.
whyNot.E: Pneumocystis risk follows CD4 lymphopenia or high-dose glucocorticoids, not C5 blockade.

items.objective: Identify the infectious risk of C5 inhibition by eculizumab.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman is evaluated after her second episode of bacteremic pneumococcal pneumonia in 4 years. She has had a photosensitive rash on her upper back and arms for 2 years, and ANA is positive at a low titer. She has a normal spleen on ultrasound, and serum immunoglobulins are normal. CH50 is 5% of normal and AH50 is normal. Serum C3, C4 and C1q concentrations are normal. Which of the following components is most likely deficient?
items.explanationHtml:
A very low CH50 with a normal AH50 localises the defect to the early classical pathway: C1q, C1r/s, C4 or C2. Normal measured C4 and C1q leave C2, the most frequent inherited complement deficiency in people of European ancestry. It presents with invasive encapsulated-bacterial infection in adulthood and an SLE-like illness with prominent skin disease.

Takeaway: low CH50 with normal AH50, normal C4 and normal C1q points to C2 deficiency.

whyNot.A: C1q deficiency also lowers CH50 with normal AH50, but her measured C1q is normal.
whyNot.C: C3 deficiency lowers both CH50 and AH50 and the C3 level; her AH50 and C3 are normal.
whyNot.D: C5 deficiency abolishes both CH50 and AH50 and presents with Neisseria rather than pneumococcus and lupus.
whyNot.E: Factor B deficiency lowers AH50 with a normal CH50, the opposite pattern.

items.objective: Localize a complement deficiency using CH50, AH50 and individual component levels.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy is hospitalized with pneumonia due to Burkholderia cepacia. At 18 months he had suppurative cervical lymphadenitis caused by Staphylococcus aureus, and at 2 years osteomyelitis caused by Serratia marcescens. Neutrophil count is normal, and flow cytometry shows that his neutrophils fail to oxidize dihydrorhodamine after stimulation. According to the classic explanation for this patient's narrow range of pathogens, which property of these organisms allows them to survive in his phagocytes?

options.label: A
options.html: Capsular polysaccharide that blocks complement deposition

options.label: C
options.html: Production of catalase that degrades hydrogen peroxide

options.label: D
options.html: Secretion of coagulase that forms a fibrin shield

options.label: E
options.html: Secretion of superoxide dismutase that consumes superoxide

items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent staphylococcal, Serratia and Burkholderia infections with an absent oxidative burst indicate chronic granulomatous disease. His phagocytes cannot make superoxide or H2O2, but myeloperoxidase is intact. Catalase-negative bacteria release their own H2O2 into the phagosome, which myeloperoxidase uses to make hypochlorous acid, killing them. Catalase-positive organisms break down that H2O2 and survive.

Takeaway: CGD infections are classically catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, Burkholderia, Serratia, Nocardia, Aspergillus).

whyNot.A: Capsules matter in antibody, complement and splenic defects; his pathogens are not mainly encapsulated, and opsonization is intact in CGD.
whyNot.B: IgA protease helps mucosal colonisation by Neisseria, H. influenzae and pneumococcus and does not explain survival inside oxidase-deficient phagocytes.
whyNot.D: Coagulase is specific to S. aureus and does not explain Serratia or Burkholderia infection.
whyNot.E: In CGD there is no superoxide to consume, so bacterial superoxide dismutase confers no added advantage.

items.objective: Explain the classic catalase hypothesis for the organisms that infect patients with chronic granulomatous disease.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old girl is evaluated for recurrent pneumonia, periodontitis and skin infections without pus formation. She has short stature and developmental delay. Her parents are first cousins. Leukocyte count between infections is 31,000/mm3 with 80% neutrophils. During blood typing she is found to lack H antigen on her red cells (Bombay phenotype). Flow cytometry shows normal CD18 expression on neutrophils and absent sialyl Lewis X (CD15s). Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?

options.label: C
options.html: Defective GDP-fucose transport into the Golgi

items.explanationHtml:
Neutrophilia with pus-poor infections, intellectual disability, short stature, Bombay red cells and absent sialyl Lewis X with normal CD18 is leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 2. A defective Golgi GDP-fucose transporter (SLC35C1) prevents fucosylation of glycoproteins: sialyl Lewis X, the selectin ligand required for rolling, and the H blood-group antigen are both fucosylated. Some patients improve with oral fucose.

Takeaway: LAD-2 is a fucosylation defect: no selectin-mediated rolling and Bombay phenotype.

whyNot.A: Kindlin-3 deficiency (LAD-3) causes LAD-1–like infection with bleeding from impaired platelet integrin activation, without Bombay phenotype or absent CD15s.
whyNot.B: Absent β2 integrin (CD18) defines LAD-1, but her CD18 expression is normal.
whyNot.D: LYST defects cause Chédiak-Higashi syndrome with albinism and giant granules, not absent selectin ligands.
whyNot.E: NADPH oxidase deficiency (CGD) does not cause neutrophilia from failed adhesion or abnormal blood-group antigens.

items.objective: Identify leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 2 as a fucosylation defect affecting selectin ligands.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy is evaluated for recurrent skin infections and pneumonia caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes. He bruises easily. Examination shows light skin, silvery-grey hair, nystagmus and photophobia. His parents are first cousins. Neutrophil count is 1,100/mm3. The peripheral blood smear is shown. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?
items.explanationHtml:
Partial oculocutaneous albinism with silvery hair, nystagmus, pyogenic infections, mild bleeding and neutropenia, with large cytoplasmic granules in neutrophils, is Chédiak-Higashi syndrome. Mutations in LYST disturb the size and trafficking of lysosome-related organelles: granules fuse into giant inclusions, phagolysosome formation and chemotaxis are poor, melanosomes are abnormal, and platelet dense granules are deficient.

Takeaway: giant granules plus partial albinism means a lysosomal trafficking defect (LYST).

whyNot.A: Actin regulation defects (WAS) cause small platelets, eczema and infections, without albinism or giant granules.
whyNot.C: Myeloperoxidase deficiency is mostly silent and causes no albinism, bleeding or giant granules.
whyNot.D: NADPH oxidase defects (CGD) cause catalase-positive and fungal infections with normal pigment and granules.
whyNot.E: β2 integrin loss (LAD-1) causes neutrophilia, delayed cord separation and pus-poor infections, not neutropenia with albinism.

items.objective: Recognize Chédiak-Higashi syndrome from albinism and giant neutrophil granules.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus is hospitalized with Candida albicans endophthalmitis and candidemia. He has had no unusual bacterial infections. An automated analyser that classifies leukocytes by peroxidase staining could not identify his neutrophils, which appear normal on Wright stain. Neutrophil count is normal, and nitroblue tetrazolium reduction by his stimulated neutrophils is normal. Which of the following reactions is most likely deficient in his neutrophils?

options.label: A
options.html: Conversion of hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid

options.label: C
options.html: Conversion of superoxide to hydrogen peroxide

options.label: D
options.html: Fusion of granules with the phagosome

items.explanationHtml:
Absent peroxidase staining with normal neutrophil morphology and a normal NBT test indicates myeloperoxidase deficiency, the most frequent inherited phagocyte defect. MPO uses H2O2 and chloride to make hypochlorous acid. Most affected people are healthy because superoxide and H2O2 still kill bacteria, but Candida killing depends more on MPO, and diabetes adds a second defect.

Takeaway: MPO deficiency: normal NBT, absent peroxidase staining, invasive Candida mostly in diabetes.

whyNot.B: Conversion of oxygen to superoxide is the NADPH oxidase reaction; its loss (CGD) gives an abnormal NBT test, and his is normal.
whyNot.C: Superoxide dismutase activity is not a recognised cause of an inherited phagocyte defect and would not abolish peroxidase staining.
whyNot.D: Defective granule–phagosome fusion occurs in Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, which has giant granules and albinism.
whyNot.E: Defective NET formation is not the explanation for absent peroxidase staining with normal morphology.

items.objective: Identify myeloperoxidase deficiency and the reaction it impairs.

items.stemHtml: An 8-month-old girl is hospitalized with a perirectal abscess. She had omphalitis in the newborn period, recurrent oral ulcers and gingivitis, and a skin abscess at 4 months. Absolute neutrophil counts on six occasions since birth have been 80–200/mm3. Hemoglobin, platelet count and monocyte count are normal. Maternal serum tested at birth showed no antineutrophil antibodies. Bone marrow aspirate shows arrest of granulocyte maturation at the promyelocyte stage. Genetic testing shows a heterozygous missense variant in the gene for neutrophil elastase. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of her neutropenia?

options.label: B
options.html: Apoptosis of myeloid precursors from protein misfolding

options.label: D
options.html: Sequestration of neutrophils in the spleen

items.explanationHtml:
Persistent profound neutropenia from birth with promyelocyte maturation arrest and a dominant ELANE variant is severe congenital neutropenia. Mutant neutrophil elastase misfolds in the endoplasmic reticulum, triggering the unfolded protein response and apoptosis of developing myeloid cells at the stage when elastase is made (promyelocyte). The condition responds to G-CSF and carries a risk of MDS and AML.

Takeaway: ELANE-related congenital neutropenia is an intrinsic marrow defect: misfolded elastase kills precursors.

whyNot.A: Alloimmune or autoimmune neutropenia destroys mature circulating cells and leaves normal or late-stage marrow maturation; maternal antibodies were absent and the arrest is early.
whyNot.C: Margination (pseudoneutropenia) gives normal marrow and no infections.
whyNot.D: Splenic sequestration requires splenomegaly and usually lowers platelets and hemoglobin as well.
whyNot.E: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency causes megaloblastic changes in all lineages and hypersegmented neutrophils.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of ELANE-related severe congenital neutropenia.

items.stemHtml: A 4-month-old boy has had fever for 12 days despite broad-spectrum antibiotics. His parents are first cousins, and a sister died at 5 months of age of an undiagnosed febrile illness. Examination shows hepatosplenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL, platelet count is 41,000/mm3, absolute neutrophil count is 600/mm3, ferritin is 22,000 ng/mL, fasting triglycerides are 420 mg/dL and fibrinogen is 90 mg/dL. Bone marrow shows macrophages that have engulfed erythrocytes and platelets. NK-cell cytotoxicity is absent, and flow cytometry shows no perforin in his NK and CD8+ T cells. Which of the following best explains the uncontrolled inflammation?

options.label: B
options.html: Failure of cytotoxic cells to kill target cells

options.label: C
options.html: Loss of FOXP3-expressing regulatory T cells

options.label: D
options.html: Unregulated activation of the alternative complement pathway

items.explanationHtml:
Fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias, very high ferritin, hypertriglyceridemia, hypofibrinogenemia and hemophagocytosis in an infant with an affected sibling indicate familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis; absent perforin defines FHL2. Cytotoxic T and NK cells recognise infected or antigen-presenting targets but cannot kill them. The targets persist and keep stimulating the lymphocytes, which release large amounts of IFN-γ, activating macrophages and producing a cytokine storm.

Takeaway: familial HLH is failed cytotoxicity: the stimulus is never removed, so activation never stops.

whyNot.A: IL-10 autoantibodies are not a cause of HLH and would not explain absent perforin.
whyNot.C: FOXP3 loss causes IPEX with enteropathy, diabetes and dermatitis, not perforin-negative HLH.
whyNot.D: Alternative pathway dysregulation causes atypical HUS or C3 glomerulopathy, not hemophagocytosis with hyperferritinemia.
whyNot.E: Mast-cell degranulation causes anaphylaxis or mastocytosis symptoms, not cytopenias with hemophagocytosis.

items.objective: Explain how failed lymphocyte cytotoxicity drives familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because he has had two radiologically confirmed pneumonias and three episodes of acute sinusitis in the past 12 months, each needing antibiotics. He was born at term, is growing along the 40th percentile and has no chronic cough, diarrhea or skin infections. Vaccinations are up to date. Sweat chloride testing last year was normal. Examination shows small but visible tonsils and is otherwise normal. CBC with differential is normal, and HIV testing is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.label: D
options.html: Serum IgG, IgA and IgM levels

items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent sinopulmonary infection with encapsulated bacteria is the antibody-deficiency pattern. After a CBC and HIV test, the best initial immunologic test is quantitative IgG, IgA and IgM, interpreted against age-specific ranges, followed by specific antibody titers to vaccines.

Takeaway: recurrent sinopulmonary infection: quantitative immunoglobulins first, then vaccine responses.

whyNot.A: Chest CT looks for bronchiectasis or structural disease; it does not identify the cause of recurrent infection in a child with normal growth and no chronic cough.
whyNot.B: DHR testing evaluates CGD, which presents with abscesses and catalase-positive or fungal infections rather than sinopulmonary infections.
whyNot.C: Lymphocyte subsets come after immunoglobulins, or first when opportunistic or severe viral infections suggest a T-cell defect.
whyNot.E: CH50 is the test for recurrent Neisseria or lupus-like disease; antibody defects are far more frequent and are tested first.

items.objective: Choose quantitative immunoglobulins as the first immunologic test for recurrent sinopulmonary infection.

items.stemHtml:
A 33-year-old woman comes to the clinic for evaluation of recurrent respiratory infections. In the past 2 years she has had three episodes of pneumonia and four of sinusitis. She takes no medications. Laboratory results:

TestResultReference range
Leukocytes6,800/mm34,500–11,000/mm3
Albumin4.2 g/dL3.5–5.5 g/dL
IgG480 mg/dL700–1,600 mg/dL
IgA45 mg/dL70–400 mg/dL
IgM30 mg/dL40–230 mg/dL
Urine proteinNegativeNegative
HIV antigen/antibodyNegativeNegative

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
She has a moderately low IgG with low IgA and IgM, and secondary causes (protein loss, drugs, HIV) are excluded. A diagnosis of CVID, and the decision to replace IgG, require evidence of impaired specific antibody production: measure titers to protein (tetanus, diphtheria) and polysaccharide (pneumococcal) antigens, immunising and retesting 4–8 weeks later if needed. This must be done before IgG replacement, which would mask the result.

Takeaway: test vaccine responses before starting IgG replacement for moderate hypogammaglobulinemia.

whyNot.A: Starting IgG first would make vaccine titers uninterpretable and commits her to lifelong therapy before antibody failure is proven.
whyNot.B: Marrow biopsy is not needed unless cytopenias or another feature suggest a lymphoid malignancy; her blood count is normal.
whyNot.D: Waiting a year leaves a woman with recurrent pneumonia unevaluated and at risk of bronchiectasis.
whyNot.E: Antibiotic prophylaxis may help some patients but does not establish the diagnosis or replace evaluation of antibody function.

items.objective: Order specific antibody testing before immunoglobulin replacement in suspected CVID.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man with common variable immunodeficiency has received IV immunoglobulin every 4 weeks for 2 years, with far fewer infections. After the last three infusions he developed severe headache, neck stiffness and photophobia 24 hours later; CSF after one episode showed a neutrophilic pleocytosis with negative cultures. Slower infusion rates, hydration and premedication did not prevent recurrence. He prefers treatment at home. Which of the following is the most appropriate change in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Discontinue immunoglobulin and give prophylactic antibiotics

options.label: B
options.html: Give fresh frozen plasma every 4 weeks

options.label: D
options.html: Increase the IV dose and extend the interval to 6 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent aseptic meningitis after IVIG is a known, dose- and rate-related adverse effect. Subcutaneous immunoglobulin, given weekly or every other week in smaller doses, produces steadier IgG levels without high peaks, has much lower rates of systemic reactions and can be self-administered at home.

Takeaway: systemic IVIG reactions that persist despite rate changes and premedication are an indication to switch to SCIG.

whyNot.A: He has proven antibody failure with a good response to replacement; stopping it would expose him to recurrent pneumonia and bronchiectasis.
whyNot.B: Plasma contains too little IgG to provide replacement and carries transfusion risks.
whyNot.C: Intramuscular immune globulin cannot deliver adequate replacement doses and is painful.
whyNot.D: Larger, less frequent IV doses raise peak IgG and the risk of aseptic meningitis while producing low troughs.

items.objective: Switch to subcutaneous immunoglobulin after recurrent systemic reactions to IVIG.

items.stemHtml: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because of 6 months of intermittent loose stools, abdominal bloating and poor weight gain. She has iron-deficiency anemia despite a normal diet. Serum tissue transglutaminase IgA is negative. Total serum IgA is below 5 mg/dL, far below the age-specific reference range, with normal IgG and IgM. Stool testing for Giardia antigen is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat tissue transglutaminase IgA in 6 months

items.explanationHtml:
Her symptoms suggest celiac disease, but IgA-based serology is uninterpretable because she has selective IgA deficiency, which is itself associated with celiac disease. Use an IgG-based test: tissue transglutaminase IgG or deamidated gliadin peptide IgG, followed by duodenal biopsy if positive or if suspicion remains high.

Takeaway: in IgA deficiency, test for celiac disease with IgG-based serology.

whyNot.A: Endomysial antibodies measured are IgA class, so they are falsely negative in IgA deficiency.
whyNot.B: HLA typing is useful for ruling celiac disease out, but a positive result is common in the general population and does not establish the diagnosis.
whyNot.C: Repeating an IgA-based test will remain negative and delays diagnosis.
whyNot.D: Stool elastase evaluates exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, which does not explain iron deficiency with this presentation as well as celiac disease does.

items.objective: Choose IgG-based celiac serology in a patient with selective IgA deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman is scheduled for elective hip arthroplasty, and transfusion may be needed. Two years ago, during her first transfusion, she developed hypotension, wheezing and urticaria within minutes and was treated with epinephrine. Subsequent testing showed serum IgA below 5 mg/dL with normal IgG and IgM, and anti-IgA antibodies were detected. If red cells are required during surgery, which of the following products is most appropriate?
items.explanationHtml:
Anaphylaxis to transfusion in a patient with selective IgA deficiency and anti-IgA antibodies is caused by IgA in donor plasma. Cellular products should be washed to remove residual plasma proteins, or obtained from IgA-deficient donors; plasma products must come from IgA-deficient donors. Autologous donation before elective surgery is another option.

Takeaway: anti-IgA anaphylaxis history: washed cellular products or IgA-deficient donor blood.

whyNot.A: CMV-seronegative products prevent CMV transmission and leave donor plasma IgA in the unit.
whyNot.B: Irradiation inactivates donor lymphocytes to prevent transfusion-associated GVHD and does not remove IgA.
whyNot.C: Leukoreduction removes leukocytes to reduce febrile reactions and CMV transmission; plasma IgA remains.
whyNot.E: Whole blood contains the most plasma, and a relative is not known to be IgA deficient.

items.objective: Select washed or IgA-deficient blood products for a patient with prior anti-IgA transfusion anaphylaxis.

items.stemHtml: An 11-month-old boy is brought to the clinic after three episodes of otitis media in 4 months, each of which resolved with oral amoxicillin. He was born at 36 weeks of gestation, is growing well and attends daycare. Examination is normal, with visible tonsils. Serum IgG is below the age-specific reference range, and IgA and IgM are at the low end of normal. CD19+ B-cell and T-cell counts are normal. Antibody titers to tetanus and diphtheria after his primary series are protective. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Refer for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation

items.explanationHtml:
Low IgG for age with normal B and T cells and protective responses to protein vaccines, in a well-growing infant with mild infections, fits transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy. Management is observation, treatment of infections as they occur, continued routine vaccination and repeat immunoglobulin levels in 6–12 months; levels typically normalise by early childhood.

Takeaway: low IgG with normal vaccine responses in an infant warrants follow-up testing, not replacement.

whyNot.A: IgG replacement is reserved for proven antibody failure or severe infections; his vaccine responses are protective and infections are mild.
whyNot.B: Routine vaccines, including live vaccines, are safe and appropriate in transient hypogammaglobulinemia.
whyNot.C: Transplantation is for SCID and other severe combined defects; his T cells are normal.
whyNot.E: Prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated for three uncomplicated otitis episodes in a child with normal antibody responses.

items.objective: Manage transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy with observation and repeat testing.

items.stemHtml: An 8-year-old girl is evaluated for three episodes of pneumonia and recurrent sinusitis over 2 years. She was born at term, is growing normally and has no diarrhea or skin infections. Sweat chloride testing is normal. Serum IgG, IgA, IgM and IgG subclasses are within age-specific reference ranges, and titers to tetanus and diphtheria are protective. Six weeks after a 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine, she has protective titers to 3 of 23 serotypes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Normal immunoglobulin levels and protein-vaccine responses with a poor response to pneumococcal polysaccharides in a child older than 2 years define specific antibody deficiency. Management starts with conjugate pneumococcal vaccination and prompt or prophylactic antibiotics; IgG replacement is reserved for persistent infection despite these measures.

Takeaway: recurrent pneumonia with normal immunoglobulins does not exclude antibody deficiency: test polysaccharide responses.

whyNot.A: CVID requires low IgG with low IgA and/or IgM; her immunoglobulins are normal.
whyNot.B: Selective IgA deficiency requires a very low IgA, and her IgA is normal.
whyNot.D: Transient hypogammaglobulinemia involves low IgG in infancy; she is 8 years old with normal IgG.
whyNot.E: X-linked agammaglobulinemia causes very low levels of all isotypes, mostly in boys.

items.objective: Diagnose specific antibody deficiency from a poor polysaccharide response with normal immunoglobulin levels.

items.stemHtml: A 9-day-old boy is seen in the clinic because his newborn screening result shows undetectable T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs). He was born at 39 weeks of gestation after an uncomplicated pregnancy, is breastfeeding well and has regained his birth weight. Examination is normal. He has not yet received any vaccines other than hepatitis B. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.label: A
options.html: Chest x-ray for a thymic shadow

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat TREC assay at 2 months of age

items.explanationHtml:
An undetectable TREC result on newborn screening means very low thymic output and must be followed promptly by lymphocyte flow cytometry (CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19 or CD20, CD16/56 and naive CD45RA T cells), which confirms or excludes SCID and other T-cell lymphopenias. Until results return, avoid live vaccines and use only irradiated, CMV-safe cellular blood products.

Takeaway: abnormal TREC newborn screen: flow cytometry next, without delay.

whyNot.A: The thymic shadow is unreliable in newborns, as stress shrinks it, and it does not quantify or classify lymphocytes.
whyNot.B: HIV testing may be part of a later workup of lymphopenia, but nothing suggests maternal HIV, and it does not characterize which lymphocyte lineages are missing.
whyNot.D: Immunoglobulin levels in a newborn reflect maternal IgG and do not assess his T cells.
whyNot.E: Waiting 2 months delays diagnosis while the infant is exposed to infections and to the 2-month live rotavirus vaccine.

items.objective: Order lymphocyte flow cytometry after an abnormal TREC newborn screen.

items.stemHtml: A 5-week-old boy was referred after an undetectable TREC result on newborn screening. Lymphocyte flow cytometry shows CD3+ T cells 25/mm3, CD19+ B cells 900/mm3 and CD16/56+ NK cells 5/mm3. Genetic testing shows a pathogenic IL2RG variant. He is afebrile and thriving. His mother is CMV seropositive. Transplant planning has begun. Which of the following is the most appropriate measure while he awaits transplantation?

options.label: A
options.html: Administer rotavirus vaccine at 2 months of age

options.label: C
options.html: Defer transplantation until after 1 year of age

options.label: E
options.html: Use nonirradiated blood if transfusion is needed

items.explanationHtml:
An infant with X-linked SCID needs protection from opportunistic infection until transplantation: Pneumocystis prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (from about 4 weeks of age), IgG replacement, protective isolation, no live vaccines and only irradiated, CMV-safe cellular blood products.

Takeaway: before transplant in SCID: Pneumocystis prophylaxis, IgG, no live vaccines, irradiated CMV-safe blood.

whyNot.A: Rotavirus vaccine is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in SCID, in which it causes chronic diarrhea and shedding.
whyNot.B: Breast milk from a CMV-seropositive mother can transmit CMV, which is dangerous before transplant; breastfeeding is withheld.
whyNot.C: Transplant outcomes are best when it is done in the first 3.5 months and before infection; delay worsens survival.
whyNot.E: Nonirradiated cellular products can cause fatal transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease in SCID.

items.objective: Choose appropriate protective measures for an infant with SCID awaiting transplantation.

items.stemHtml: A 7-week-old boy with X-linked SCID diagnosed through newborn screening is receiving trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis and IgG replacement in protective isolation. He has had no infections. His 4-year-old brother is a full HLA match. His parents ask about the treatment most likely to provide a lasting cure. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?
items.explanationHtml:
Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation cures most forms of SCID, with the best results from a matched sibling donor, early in infancy and before infection. Donor stem cells give rise to functional T cells; B-cell function may also be restored, depending on conditioning and engraftment.

Takeaway: SCID is a paediatric emergency treated definitively by early HSCT.

whyNot.B: IgG replacement does not supply T cells, and children with SCID die of infection in infancy without immune reconstitution.
whyNot.C: PEG-ADA treats ADA-deficient SCID as a bridge; he has an IL2RG defect.
whyNot.D: Interferon-γ is used for CGD prophylaxis and has no role in reconstituting T cells.
whyNot.E: Thymus implantation treats athymia (complete 22q11.2 deletion), in which stem cells are normal; in IL2RG SCID the defect lies in the hematopoietic cells.

items.objective: Recommend hematopoietic stem cell transplantation as definitive therapy for SCID.

items.stemHtml: A 6-day-old girl with truncus arteriosus is scheduled for cardiac repair this week. She had hypocalcemia on day 2, and chromosomal microarray shows a 22q11.2 deletion. Lymphocyte flow cytometry has been sent, and results are pending. Red cells and platelets are likely to be needed during surgery. Her father offers to donate blood for her. Which of the following blood-product modifications is most important for this patient?
items.explanationHtml:
Infants with 22q11.2 deletion may have severe T-cell deficiency, and until T-cell counts are known they must receive irradiated (and CMV-safe) cellular products. Irradiation stops donor lymphocytes from proliferating and causing transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease, which is nearly always fatal.

Takeaway: suspected or possible T-cell deficiency: irradiate all cellular blood products.

whyNot.A: Directed donation from a first-degree relative raises the risk of transfusion-associated GVHD because of shared HLA haplotypes, and such units must be irradiated anyway.
whyNot.C: Volume reduction limits fluid load and does not prevent GVHD.
whyNot.D: Washing removes plasma proteins to prevent allergic reactions and does not inactivate lymphocytes reliably.
whyNot.E: Fresh whole blood contains the most viable lymphocytes and carries the greatest GVHD risk.

items.objective: Order irradiated blood products for an infant with 22q11.2 deletion before T-cell status is known.

items.stemHtml: A 14-month-old boy has had eczema since 3 months of age, bloody diarrhea in infancy, three episodes of otitis media and pneumococcal bacteremia. Platelet count is 28,000/mm3 with a mean platelet volume of 5.8 fL (reference range, 7.5–11.5 fL). Sequencing shows a pathogenic WAS variant. He receives IgG replacement and antibiotic prophylaxis. A matched unrelated donor has been identified. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management?
items.explanationHtml:
Classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome causes life-threatening bleeding, infection, autoimmunity and lymphoma. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, ideally early in childhood, corrects the immune defect and the thrombocytopenia.

Takeaway: classic WAS is treated definitively with early HSCT.

whyNot.B: Glucocorticoids do not correct the WAS platelet defect and worsen infection risk.
whyNot.C: Thrombopoietin receptor agonists may serve as a bridge but do not treat the immunodeficiency or malignancy risk.
whyNot.D: Splenectomy raises the platelet count but greatly increases the risk of overwhelming sepsis and is avoided when transplantation is possible.
whyNot.E: Treating eczema alone ignores the bleeding, infection and lymphoma risks.

items.objective: Recommend hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because of an unsteady gait that has worsened since he began walking at 13 months. He falls many times a day, has slurred speech and turns his head rather than his eyes to look at objects. He has had four episodes of sinusitis in the past year. Examination shows truncal ataxia and dysmetria; the conjunctivae and skin are normal. Brain MRI is normal. Which of the following laboratory studies is the most appropriate next step to support the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Ataxia from the onset of walking with oculomotor apraxia and recurrent sinopulmonary infection suggests ataxia-telangiectasia, even before telangiectasias appear (usually a few years later). A raised serum α-fetoprotein after infancy is present in nearly all patients and is the best initial supporting test; ATM testing confirms it. Immunoglobulins should also be measured.

Takeaway: toddler-onset ataxia with sinopulmonary infections: check AFP for ataxia-telangiectasia.

whyNot.A: Friedreich ataxia begins later in childhood or adolescence with areflexia and cardiomyopathy, not toddler-onset ataxia with infections.
whyNot.C: Ceruloplasmin evaluates Wilson disease, which presents with liver or neuropsychiatric disease after early childhood.
whyNot.D: Vitamin E deficiency causes ataxia with neuropathy, usually with fat malabsorption, and does not explain recurrent sinusitis.
whyNot.E: Very-long-chain fatty acids screen for peroxisomal disorders such as adrenoleukodystrophy, which have abnormal MRI and later onset.

items.objective: Order serum α-fetoprotein to support suspected ataxia-telangiectasia.

items.stemHtml: A 12-year-old girl is evaluated for chronic oral thrush and thickened, discolored fingernails that have persisted since age 4 despite repeated courses of topical and oral antifungals. Last month she was hospitalized for tetany; serum calcium was 6.8 mg/dL with low PTH, and she now takes calcitriol and calcium. She has pitted tooth enamel. Her brother had similar candidiasis. Which of the following is the most important additional evaluation now?
items.explanationHtml:
Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and enamel dysplasia in a sibling pair indicate APECED (autoimmune polyendocrinopathy–candidiasis–ectodermal dystrophy) from AIRE mutations. The third classic component, adrenal insufficiency, typically follows hypoparathyroidism and can present as a fatal adrenal crisis, so morning cortisol and ACTH should be checked now and at intervals.

Takeaway: candidiasis plus hypoparathyroidism means APECED: screen for adrenal insufficiency.

whyNot.B: IgE is elevated in hyper-IgE syndromes, which do not cause hypoparathyroidism; it does not address the life-threatening risk in APECED.
whyNot.C: Sweat chloride testing is for cystic fibrosis, which does not cause candidiasis with endocrine autoimmunity.
whyNot.D: Celiac disease can occur with autoimmune disease, but screening for it is less urgent than detecting adrenal insufficiency.
whyNot.E: Endoscopy is for symptoms of esophageal candidiasis or GI disease, which she does not report.

items.objective: Screen for adrenal insufficiency in a patient with APECED.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy with autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome confirmed by a STAT3 variant is seen after drainage of his fourth staphylococcal skin abscess in a year. He had staphylococcal pneumonia at age 6 that left a pneumatocele. He has eczema treated with emollients. Serum IgE is 6,800 IU/mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his long-term management?

options.label: C
options.html: Oral prednisone at a low daily dose

options.label: E
options.html: Weekly IV immunoglobulin at high dose

items.explanationHtml:
In STAT3 hyper-IgE syndrome, the main threat is recurrent S. aureus infection of skin and lung. Daily anti-staphylococcal prophylaxis, usually trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, plus skin care (emollients, dilute bleach baths) reduces abscesses and pneumonias. Pneumonias need prompt, aggressive treatment to limit further pneumatoceles.

Takeaway: STAT3 hyper-IgE: daily anti-staphylococcal prophylaxis and barrier care.

whyNot.B: The high IgE is a marker of dysregulation, not the cause of infection; lowering IgE with omalizumab does not prevent staphylococcal abscesses.
whyNot.C: Glucocorticoids increase infection risk and are not part of prophylaxis.
whyNot.D: Surgery on pneumatoceles has a high complication rate and is reserved for those with persistent infection or other specific problems.
whyNot.E: IgG replacement may help some patients with poor antibody responses, but weekly high-dose IV dosing is not a standard regimen, and anti-staphylococcal prophylaxis is the key step.

items.objective: Prescribe anti-staphylococcal prophylaxis in STAT3 hyper-IgE syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man with hereditary angioedema type I comes to the emergency department 4 hours after a dental extraction because of progressive swelling of his lower face, a hoarse voice and difficulty swallowing. He has no hives or itching. Pulse is 104/min, respirations are 20/min and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. He has received IM epinephrine, IV diphenhydramine and IV methylprednisolone without improvement. Fibreoptic laryngoscopy shows supraglottic edema. The anesthesia team is at the bedside. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Laryngeal attacks of HAE are bradykinin-mediated and do not respond to epinephrine, antihistamines or glucocorticoids. While the airway team prepares, give an on-demand HAE therapy: IV C1 inhibitor concentrate (plasma-derived or recombinant), subcutaneous icatibant or ecallantide. C1 inhibitor concentrate replaces the missing regulator and halts kallikrein activity.

Takeaway: HAE laryngeal attack: secure the airway and give C1-INH concentrate, icatibant or ecallantide.

whyNot.A: Fresh frozen plasma contains C1 inhibitor but also kininogen substrate and is a fallback only when specific therapy is unavailable.
whyNot.C: Tranexamic acid is a weak prophylactic option with no role in an acute laryngeal attack.
whyNot.D: Epinephrine has already failed and does not act on bradykinin-mediated edema.
whyNot.E: Lanadelumab is a long-term prophylactic antibody against kallikrein; it is not used to treat an acute attack.

items.objective: Treat an acute laryngeal attack of hereditary angioedema with C1 inhibitor concentrate.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman with hereditary angioedema type I is 18 weeks pregnant. She has had two facial attacks in the past year, each treated with on-demand therapy, and has not used long-term prophylaxis. She needs extraction of an infected molar under local anesthesia next week. Which of the following is the most appropriate preprocedural prophylaxis?

options.label: A
options.html: Danazol for 5 days before the procedure

options.label: B
options.html: Ecallantide on the morning of the procedure

options.label: C
options.html: Plasma-derived C1 inhibitor before the procedure

options.label: D
options.html: Prednisone for 3 days before the procedure

options.label: E
options.html: Tranexamic acid for 5 days before the procedure

items.explanationHtml:
Dental procedures are a classic trigger of laryngeal attacks. Short-term prophylaxis with plasma-derived C1 inhibitor concentrate, given 1–6 hours before the procedure, is first-line and is the preferred agent in pregnancy. On-demand therapy should be available during and after the procedure.

Takeaway: preprocedural HAE prophylaxis is plasma-derived C1-INH, which is also the agent of choice in pregnancy.

whyNot.A: Attenuated androgens were once used for short-term prophylaxis but are contraindicated in pregnancy because they virilize a female fetus.
whyNot.B: Ecallantide is an on-demand treatment with an anaphylaxis risk; it is not used as preprocedural prophylaxis, and pregnancy data are limited.
whyNot.D: Glucocorticoids do not prevent bradykinin-mediated attacks.
whyNot.E: Tranexamic acid is less effective than C1-INH and is not the preferred option before a high-risk procedure.

items.objective: Select plasma-derived C1 inhibitor for preprocedural prophylaxis in a pregnant patient with hereditary angioedema.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man is observed in the emergency department for swelling of the tongue and lower lip that began 3 hours ago. He has no urticaria, itching or wheezing. He has taken lisinopril for hypertension for 4 years and takes no other drugs. Blood pressure is 152/90 mm Hg. The swelling resolves over 36 hours without airway intervention. Serum C4 measured during the episode was normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate antihypertensive regimen at discharge?
items.explanationHtml:
