Angioedema of the tongue and lips without urticaria in a patient taking an ACE inhibitor, with normal C4, is ACE-inhibitor angioedema, which is mediated by bradykinin that ACE would normally degrade. It can begin after years of use. The ACE inhibitor must be stopped permanently, and all ACE inhibitors avoided. A drug from another class, such as the calcium-channel blocker amlodipine, is appropriate.

Takeaway: ACE-inhibitor angioedema: stop the class for good; avoid neprilysin inhibitors; switch to another drug class.

whyNot.B: Enalapril is another ACE inhibitor and carries the same bradykinin-mediated risk.
whyNot.C: A lower dose does not remove the risk, and recurrence can be fatal.
whyNot.D: Antihistamines do not prevent bradykinin-mediated angioedema.
whyNot.E: Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin, which also degrades bradykinin, and is contraindicated after ACE-inhibitor angioedema.

items.objective: Manage ACE-inhibitor angioedema by stopping the ACE inhibitor and choosing another antihypertensive class.

items.stemHtml:
A 61-year-old woman has had four episodes of nonpruritic swelling of the face and hands and one of severe abdominal pain with ascites over the past 8 months. She had no swelling before this year, and no relatives are affected. She takes no medications. Examination shows small, nontender lymph nodes in both axillae and a palpable spleen tip. Laboratory results obtained between attacks:

TestResult
Hemoglobin12.6 g/dL
Leukocytes9,800/mm3, 58% lymphocytes
C4Low
C1 inhibitor antigenLow
C1 inhibitor functionLow
C1qLow

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
items.explanationHtml:
New angioedema after age 40 without a family history, with low C4, low C1-INH level and function and a low C1q, indicates acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency. It is associated with B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders and monoclonal gammopathy, which consume C1-INH or produce autoantibodies against it. Her lymphocytosis, lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly raise concern for lymphoma or CLL; begin with serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and free light chains, then flow cytometry of blood and imaging.

Takeaway: late-onset angioedema with low C1q: look for a B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder.

whyNot.A: Echocardiography does not address the cause of acquired C1-INH deficiency.
whyNot.B: Acquired C1-INH deficiency is not inherited, so testing her children is not indicated.
whyNot.D: Thyroid disease does not explain low C1q and C1-INH with lymphadenopathy.
whyNot.E: The abdominal attack was angioedema of the bowel wall; endoscopy does not identify the underlying lymphoproliferative disease.

items.objective: Evaluate for a B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder in acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and transfusion-dependent hemolysis is to begin eculizumab in 3 weeks. Her vaccination history includes childhood vaccines and a Tdap booster 4 years ago; she has received no meningococcal vaccines. She is clinically stable. Which of the following vaccination plans is most appropriate before the first dose?
items.explanationHtml:
C5 inhibitors raise the risk of meningococcal disease from serogroups A, C, W, Y and B. Patients should receive both MenACWY and MenB series, starting at least 2 weeks before the first dose, with boosters while therapy continues. Patients who must start urgently receive antibiotic prophylaxis until 2 weeks after vaccination. Pneumococcal and other routine vaccines are also brought up to date.

Takeaway: before C5 inhibition: MenACWY plus MenB, at least 2 weeks ahead, and teach the patient to seek care for fever.

whyNot.A: MenACWY alone leaves her unprotected against serogroup B, a leading cause of meningococcal disease in the United States.
whyNot.C: MenB alone leaves her unprotected against serogroups A, C, W and Y.
whyNot.D: Pneumococcal vaccination is reasonable for her but does not address the meningococcal risk created by C5 blockade.
whyNot.E: Her start date allows vaccination 2 weeks ahead; giving vaccines after the first dose leaves an avoidable window of high risk.

items.objective: Plan meningococcal vaccination before starting a C5 inhibitor.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy is recovering from meningococcal meningitis caused by serogroup W. He had meningococcal bacteremia caused by serogroup Y at age 13. Two months after discharge, CH50 and AH50 are both undetectable, C3 and C4 are normal, and C7 is undetectable. He received one dose of MenACWY vaccine at age 11. He has a 14-year-old sister. Which of the following is the most appropriate measure to reduce his risk of recurrence?
items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent meningococcal disease with unusual serogroups and absent CH50 and AH50 with undetectable C7 indicates terminal complement deficiency. Prevention relies on MenACWY and MenB vaccination with regular boosters, which work through opsonophagocytosis rather than lysis; patient education to seek care promptly with fever; and testing of siblings. Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis may be added in selected patients.

Takeaway: terminal complement deficiency: vaccinate against all meningococcal serogroups, keep boosting, and screen siblings.

whyNot.A: Plasma supplies C7 only transiently and is not used for prevention.
whyNot.B: His immunoglobulins are not deficient, and IVIG does not replace the missing lytic pathway.
whyNot.D: A 2-week course covers only the immediate post-infection period and does not provide lasting protection.
whyNot.E: Splenectomy would raise his infection risk.

items.objective: Prevent recurrent meningococcal disease in terminal complement deficiency with meningococcal vaccination.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl is evaluated after her second episode of pneumococcal bacteremia in 18 months. For 3 months she has had a photosensitive rash on her cheeks and oral ulcers, and ANA is positive at 1:640. Serum IgG, IgA and IgM and titers to pneumococcal serotypes are normal. Abdominal ultrasonography shows a normal spleen, and the smear shows no Howell-Jolly bodies. HIV testing is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next test?
items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent invasive pneumococcal disease with normal antibodies and spleen, combined with lupus in early childhood, suggests an early classical complement deficiency (C1q, C1r/s, C4 or C2). The screening test is CH50 (with AH50); an absent CH50 is followed by measurement of individual components.

Takeaway: childhood lupus with recurrent encapsulated-bacterial infection: screen complement with CH50.

whyNot.A: DHR testing evaluates CGD, which causes abscesses with catalase-positive organisms rather than pneumococcal bacteremia and lupus.
whyNot.B: Lymphocyte subsets suit opportunistic or viral infection patterns, not pneumococcal bacteremia with lupus.
whyNot.C: Repeating the ANA adds nothing; it is already strongly positive.
whyNot.D: Cystic fibrosis causes chronic sinopulmonary disease, not bacteremia and lupus.

items.objective: Screen with CH50 for early classical complement deficiency in childhood lupus with recurrent bacteremia.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy is discharged after 6 weeks of IV antibiotics for Serratia marcescens osteomyelitis. He had a staphylococcal liver abscess at age 2. The dihydrorhodamine test shows absent oxidative burst, and genetic testing shows a pathogenic CYBB variant. His mother has a bimodal dihydrorhodamine pattern. No matched sibling donor is available, and transplant evaluation is ongoing. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term prophylaxis?
items.explanationHtml:
Standard prophylaxis in chronic granulomatous disease is daily trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole against bacteria and daily itraconazole against Aspergillus, which is the leading cause of death; many centres add subcutaneous interferon-γ three times weekly. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is curative.

Takeaway: CGD prophylaxis is TMP-SMX plus a mold-active azole (itraconazole), with optional IFN-γ.

whyNot.A: Filgrastim raises neutrophil counts, but his neutrophils are present and normal in number; they lack oxidase activity.
whyNot.B: His antibody production is normal; IVIG does not correct defective intracellular killing.
whyNot.C: Benzathine penicillin does not cover S. aureus, Serratia or Burkholderia well and has no antifungal activity.
whyNot.E: Fluconazole has no activity against Aspergillus, the most dangerous pathogen in CGD.

items.objective: Prescribe trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and itraconazole prophylaxis in chronic granulomatous disease.

items.stemHtml: A 13-month-old girl with autosomal recessive chronic granulomatous disease (NCF1) is brought for a well-child visit. She takes trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and itraconazole prophylaxis and is well. The family will move next month to a country where tuberculosis is common, and they ask about vaccines recommended there in addition to the routine schedule. Which of the following vaccines is contraindicated for her?
items.explanationHtml:
In chronic granulomatous disease, live bacterial vaccines such as BCG (and oral typhoid) are contraindicated because phagocytes cannot kill the vaccine organisms, which can cause disseminated infection. Live viral vaccines (MMR, varicella, rotavirus) are safe because T-cell and antibody responses are intact, and all inactivated vaccines are given routinely.

Takeaway: CGD: no live bacterial vaccines; live viral and inactivated vaccines are fine.

whyNot.B: Inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended yearly for children with CGD.
whyNot.C: MMR is a live viral vaccine, which is safe in CGD because its control depends on T cells and antibody.
whyNot.D: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine is inactivated and part of routine care.
whyNot.E: Varicella vaccine is a live viral vaccine and is safe in CGD for the same reason as MMR.

items.objective: Identify live bacterial vaccines as contraindicated in chronic granulomatous disease.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because of recurring episodes of fever to 39.0°C (102.2°F), painful mouth ulcers, sore throat and tender cervical lymph nodes. Each episode lasts 4–6 days, and his parents' diary shows that episodes begin about every 3 weeks. He had a perianal abscess last year. His father had similar episodes as a child. Between episodes he is well. A CBC taken 10 days after the last episode is normal, with an absolute neutrophil count of 2,900/mm3. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: D
options.html: Serial CBCs two or three times weekly for 6 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Trial of a single oral prednisone dose during the next episode

items.explanationHtml:
Regularly recurring fever, aphthous ulcers, pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy every 3 weeks, a perianal abscess and an affected parent suggest cyclic neutropenia (autosomal dominant ELANE). A single normal count between episodes does not exclude it. Serial CBCs two or three times a week for about 6 weeks document the roughly 21-day cycle and nadirs; genetic testing confirms it. G-CSF reduces nadir severity.

Takeaway: periodic fever with mouth ulcers: serial neutrophil counts to look for cyclic neutropenia.

whyNot.A: Antineutrophil antibodies cause persistent, not cyclic, neutropenia, and would not explain the family history.
whyNot.B: Marrow examination is not needed to diagnose cyclic neutropenia and, done at a random time, may be uninformative.
whyNot.C: DHR evaluates oxidative burst in CGD, which does not cause periodic fever and mouth ulcers.
whyNot.E: A steroid response suggests PFAPA, but PFAPA does not cause abscesses or run in families, and the diagnosis of cyclic neutropenia must be excluded first by counts.

items.objective: Document cyclic neutropenia with serial CBCs over 6 weeks.

items.stemHtml: A 7-month-old girl has had omphalitis, two skin abscesses and a pneumonia. Absolute neutrophil counts on repeated testing since birth have been 100–300/mm3, with normal hemoglobin and platelets. Bone marrow aspirate shows maturation arrest at the promyelocyte stage, and genetic testing shows a pathogenic ELANE variant. She is now afebrile and well after completing treatment for pneumonia. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Severe congenital neutropenia is treated with G-CSF (filgrastim), titrated to the lowest dose that keeps the neutrophil count high enough to prevent infection. Most patients respond. Because the disease carries a risk of myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukemia, annual marrow examination with cytogenetics is recommended; transplantation is for nonresponders or transformation.

Takeaway: severe congenital neutropenia: G-CSF plus marrow surveillance for MDS/AML.

whyNot.B: Her antibody production is not deficient, and IVIG does not raise neutrophil counts in congenital neutropenia.
whyNot.C: Glucocorticoids may raise counts in autoimmune neutropenia but do not correct an intrinsic marrow defect and increase infection risk.
whyNot.D: Splenectomy treats hypersplenism; her neutropenia arises in the marrow.
whyNot.E: Granulocyte transfusions are a short-term measure for refractory infection, not maintenance therapy.

items.objective: Treat severe congenital neutropenia with G-CSF and arrange marrow surveillance.

items.stemHtml:
A 7-month-old boy has had fever for 2 weeks despite broad-spectrum antibiotics. His parents are first cousins, and his older sister died at 4 months of age of an unexplained febrile illness. Examination shows hepatosplenomegaly and irritability. Cultures are negative. Laboratory results:

TestResult
Hemoglobin7.6 g/dL
Platelets36,000/mm3
Absolute neutrophil count700/mm3
Ferritin18,500 ng/mL
Triglycerides, fasting410 mg/dL
Fibrinogen95 mg/dL (reference range, 200–400 mg/dL)
Soluble CD25Markedly elevated
Cerebrospinal fluid18 mononuclear cells per microliter, protein 70 mg/dL

Flow cytometry shows absent perforin expression in his NK cells. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
This infant meets criteria for familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (perforin deficiency) with CNS involvement. Induction with dexamethasone and etoposide (HLH-94 based) controls the hyperinflammation, with intrathecal methotrexate and hydrocortisone for CNS disease. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, the only cure for familial HLH, follows once the disease is in remission.

Takeaway: familial HLH: induce remission with dexamethasone and etoposide (plus intrathecal therapy for CNS disease), then transplant.

whyNot.B: Transplantation is curative but is performed after induction controls active disease; transplanting during uncontrolled HLH has poor outcomes.
whyNot.C: IVIG may help some secondary HLH but does not control familial HLH.
whyNot.D: Plasma exchange is not first-line induction for familial HLH.
whyNot.E: Untreated familial HLH is rapidly fatal.

items.objective: Begin HLH-94–based induction therapy for familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.

items.stemHtml: A 10-week-old boy is evaluated for a 3-cm necrotic ulcer in the perianal region that has enlarged over 2 weeks without forming pus. His umbilical cord separated at 6 weeks of age, and he had omphalitis. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F). Leukocyte count is 46,000/mm3 with 78% neutrophils; on repeat testing a week later, after antibiotics, it is 39,000/mm3. The peripheral smear shows mature neutrophils without blasts or abnormal granules. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Delayed cord separation, omphalitis, a necrotic ulcer without pus and persistent marked neutrophilia indicate leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1. Neutrophils lacking the β2 integrin CD18 cannot adhere firmly to endothelium and leave the circulation. The diagnosis is confirmed by flow cytometry showing absent or reduced CD18 (and CD11a/b/c) on leukocytes. Severe LAD-1 needs hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

Takeaway: neutrophilia without pus and delayed cord separation: test CD18 by flow cytometry.

whyNot.A: BCR-ABL1 testing is for chronic myeloid leukemia, which would show left-shifted myeloid precursors and basophilia, not mature neutrophilia in an infant with delayed cord separation.
whyNot.B: Marrow examination does not demonstrate the adhesion defect and is not needed.
whyNot.D: DHR testing detects CGD, in which pus forms and the cord separates normally.
whyNot.E: Immunoglobulin levels assess antibody deficiency, which does not cause neutrophilia or delayed cord separation.

items.objective: Confirm leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 with CD18 flow cytometry.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman is evaluated after treatment for disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex infection. She has had extensive warts on her hands and feet since adolescence and severe varicella as a child. HIV testing is negative. Absolute monocyte count is 20/mm3 (reference range, 200–800/mm3), and flow cytometry shows very low B cells and NK cells with near-normal T cells. Genetic testing shows a heterozygous GATA2 variant. Without definitive treatment, this patient is at greatest risk of developing which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
GATA2 deficiency causes monocytopenia, B- and NK-cell lymphopenia, disseminated nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, severe HPV and herpesvirus disease and pulmonary alveolar proteinosis. It carries a high lifetime risk of myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukemia, so marrow surveillance and early hematopoietic stem cell transplantation are recommended.

Takeaway: GATA2 deficiency: mycobacteria, warts, absent monocytes and NK cells, and a high risk of MDS/AML.

whyNot.B: Hepatocellular carcinoma follows cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B, not GATA2 deficiency.
whyNot.C: Medullary thyroid carcinoma is linked to RET mutations in MEN2.
whyNot.D: Pheochromocytoma is linked to MEN2, VHL, NF1 and succinate dehydrogenase variants.
whyNot.E: Renal cell carcinoma is linked to VHL and other renal cancer syndromes.

items.objective: Recognize myelodysplasia and leukemia risk in GATA2 deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man takes part in a long-term study of serodiscordant couples. His female partner has untreated HIV-1 infection; her virus has been shown to use only the CCR5 coreceptor. The couple have had condomless sex for 8 years, and the man has had more than 20 negative HIV antigen/antibody and RNA tests. Sequencing shows that he is homozygous for a 32-base-pair deletion in a chemokine receptor gene, so the receptor never reaches the cell surface. Which of the following steps of the HIV life cycle is most likely blocked in his cells?
items.explanationHtml:
After gp120 binds CD4, it changes shape and must bind a chemokine coreceptor (CCR5 for R5 virus) before gp41 can drive membrane fusion. Homozygous CCR5-Δ32 carriers make no surface CCR5, so R5 virus, the type usually transmitted, cannot enter their CD4 T cells or macrophages.

CD4 itself is normal in this man, and the later steps would only be reached if the virus could enter the cell. The same principle underlies maraviroc, a CCR5 antagonist that is used only after a tropism assay shows R5-only virus.

Takeaway: CCR5-Δ32 homozygosity blocks the coreceptor step of HIV entry and protects against R5-tropic virus.

whyNot.A: The deletion affects a chemokine receptor, not CD4; gp120 can still bind CD4 on his cells.
whyNot.C: Integration requires prior entry and reverse transcription, which R5 virus never achieves in his cells.
whyNot.D: Protease acts during maturation of new virions, a step that cannot occur without infection of the cell.
whyNot.E: Reverse transcription occurs in the cytoplasm after fusion; the block here is at the cell surface.

items.objective: Explain how CCR5-Δ32 homozygosity protects against R5-tropic HIV-1 entry.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman who moved to the United States from Guinea-Bissau 3 years ago has a reactive HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody immunoassay at a prenatal-planning visit. The HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay is nonreactive for HIV-1 and reactive for HIV-2. HIV-1 RNA is undetectable. CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 310/mm3. Antiretroviral therapy is planned. Including which of the following drugs in her regimen would add no antiviral activity against her infection?
items.explanationHtml:
HIV-2, which is concentrated in West Africa, has a reverse transcriptase whose NNRTI-binding pocket differs from that of HIV-1. NNRTIs such as efavirenz, nevirapine and rilpivirine therefore have no useful activity, and HIV-2 is also poorly susceptible to enfuvirtide.

NRTIs (tenofovir, emtricitabine) and INSTIs (dolutegravir) are active, as is boosted darunavir, so regimens for HIV-2 are built from these classes. Standard HIV-1 RNA assays do not quantify HIV-2, which is why her HIV-1 RNA is undetectable.

Takeaway: HIV-2 is intrinsically resistant to NNRTIs; build regimens from NRTIs plus an INSTI or a boosted protease inhibitor.

whyNot.A: Boosted darunavir retains activity against HIV-2 and is used in HIV-2 regimens.
whyNot.B: Integrase inhibitors such as dolutegravir are active against HIV-2 and are preferred anchors.
whyNot.D: Emtricitabine is a nucleoside analog that inhibits HIV-2 reverse transcriptase at its catalytic site.
whyNot.E: Tenofovir is an active nucleotide analog against HIV-2.

items.objective: Identify NNRTIs as inactive against HIV-2 and explain why.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man has taken bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide for 6 years, and every HIV RNA measurement during the last 5 years has been below the limit of detection. CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 780/mm3. He stops all medication on his own because he believes he is cured. Three weeks later, plasma HIV-1 RNA is 45,000 copies/mL, and genotype shows the same wild-type virus as at diagnosis. Which of the following is the most likely source of the rebound viremia?

options.label: A
options.html: Drug-resistant virus replicating at low levels

options.label: B
options.html: Free virions bound to follicular dendritic cells

options.label: C
options.html: Integrated provirus in resting memory CD4+ T cells

options.label: D
options.html: Unintegrated viral DNA in activated CD4+ T cells

options.label: E
options.html: Viral RNA retained within circulating neutrophils

items.explanationHtml:
HIV integrates into host DNA. In a small population of long-lived resting memory CD4+ T cells, the provirus is transcriptionally silent, so the cells make no virus and are invisible to the immune system and untouched by antiretroviral drugs, which act only on replicating virus. When ART stops, some of these cells are activated and reseed the plasma within weeks.

The rebound virus matches the archived wild-type virus, which fits reactivation of the latent reservoir rather than ongoing replication with resistance.

Takeaway: The latent reservoir of integrated provirus in resting memory CD4+ T cells is why ART controls but does not cure HIV.

whyNot.A: Ongoing replication with resistance would give detectable viremia on therapy and a resistant genotype; he had neither.
whyNot.B: Virions trapped on follicular dendritic cells decay over months on suppressive therapy and are not the stable reservoir after 6 years.
whyNot.D: Unintegrated viral DNA is labile and does not persist through years of suppression.
whyNot.E: Neutrophils lack CD4 and are not infected by HIV.

items.objective: Identify the latent proviral reservoir in resting memory CD4+ T cells as the source of viral rebound after stopping ART.

items.stemHtml:
A 52-year-old man with HIV has taken dolutegravir plus tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine for 7 years with an undetectable viral load. He reports bone pain and fatigue. He has no history of diabetes. Laboratory studies show:

Glucose, fasting92 mg/dL
Bicarbonate18 mEq/L
Phosphorus1.9 mg/dL (3.0–4.5)
Uric acid2.1 mg/dL (3.0–8.2)
Creatinine1.6 mg/dL (1.0 mg/dL one year ago)
Urine glucose2+
Urine protein1+, mostly low-molecular-weight

Which of the following parts of the nephron is most likely injured?
items.explanationHtml:
Glycosuria with a normal blood glucose, phosphate wasting, low uric acid, proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis and low-molecular-weight proteinuria together form Fanconi syndrome, a global failure of proximal tubular reabsorption. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate concentrates in proximal tubular cells through the basolateral organic anion transporters and damages their mitochondria. Phosphate wasting leads to osteomalacia, explaining the bone pain.

Switching to tenofovir alafenamide, which gives much lower plasma tenofovir levels, or to a tenofovir-free regimen usually halts the injury.

Takeaway: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate causes proximal tubulopathy (Fanconi syndrome) and bone loss.

whyNot.A: Collecting-duct injury causes concentrating defects or distal acidosis with hyperkalemia, not glycosuria and phosphaturia.
whyNot.B: Podocyte injury produces heavy albuminuria (nephrotic syndrome), not low-molecular-weight proteinuria with tubular wasting.
whyNot.C: Medullary interstitial disease (as in papillary necrosis) impairs concentration and does not explain glycosuria or phosphate wasting.
whyNot.E: Thick ascending limb dysfunction causes salt wasting with hypokalemic alkalosis, whereas this patient has acidosis and proximal solute losses.

items.objective: Recognize tenofovir disoproxil fumarate-induced Fanconi syndrome as proximal tubular injury.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old man with HIV infection who has not taken antiretroviral therapy has several painless purple nodules on both shins and a violaceous plaque on the hard palate. CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 90/mm3. A skin biopsy shows a dermal proliferation of spindle cells forming slit-like vascular channels that contain red cells, with scattered hemosiderin-laden macrophages and few neutrophils. A silver stain shows no organisms. Which of the following infectious agents is most likely responsible for this lesion?
items.explanationHtml:
Spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces with extravasated red cells and hemosiderin is Kaposi sarcoma, an endothelial-derived tumor caused by human herpesvirus 8 (Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus). Latent viral proteins such as LANA promote cell survival and proliferation, and immunostaining for LANA confirms the diagnosis.

Palate lesions are typical in HIV-associated disease. Starting ART often shrinks limited disease; extensive or visceral disease adds chemotherapy such as liposomal doxorubicin.

Takeaway: Kaposi sarcoma is an HHV-8-driven spindle-cell vascular tumor that appears at low CD4 counts.

whyNot.A: Bacillary angiomatosis from Bartonella shows lobular capillaries with neutrophils and silver-staining bacilli, both absent here.
whyNot.B: EBV drives HIV-associated lymphomas and oral hairy leukoplakia, not spindle-cell vascular tumors.
whyNot.D: HPV causes warts and anogenital and cervical squamous neoplasia, not violaceous vascular nodules.
whyNot.E: Molluscum produces umbilicated flesh-colored papules with intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies.

items.objective: Link the histology of Kaposi sarcoma to human herpesvirus 8.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old Black man is diagnosed with HIV infection after presenting with leg swelling. HIV-1 RNA is 480,000 copies/mL and CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 210/mm3. Blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. There is pitting edema to the knees. Serum creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL and albumin is 2.2 g/dL. A 24-hour urine collection contains 6.5 g of protein, and the urine sediment has no red cell casts. Ultrasonography shows enlarged, diffusely echogenic kidneys (13.5 cm each). Which of the following is the most likely finding on kidney biopsy?

options.label: A
options.html: Collapse of glomerular tufts with podocyte hypertrophy

items.explanationHtml:
Nephrotic-range proteinuria, rapidly worsening kidney function, little hypertension and large echogenic kidneys in a person of African ancestry with high-level viremia is HIV-associated nephropathy. Biopsy shows the collapsing variant of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, with hypertrophied, proliferating podocytes over collapsed capillary loops, plus microcystic tubular dilation and interstitial inflammation. HIV infects renal epithelial cells, and APOL1 risk variants greatly raise susceptibility.

Treatment is prompt ART plus an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker.

Takeaway: HIVAN is collapsing FSGS presenting with heavy proteinuria and large echogenic kidneys; treat with ART and RAAS blockade.

whyNot.B: Crescentic glomerulonephritis causes a nephritic picture with red cell casts and rapidly progressive failure, not bland nephrotic urine.
whyNot.C: IgA nephropathy presents with hematuria, often after mucosal infection, rather than massive bland proteinuria with enlarged kidneys.
whyNot.D: Wire-loop subendothelial deposits are typical of diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis, which has an active sediment.
whyNot.E: Membranous nephropathy causes nephrotic syndrome but is linked to hepatitis B, PLA2R antibodies or tumors, and does not give large echogenic kidneys with rapid failure.

items.objective: Recognize HIV-associated nephropathy and its collapsing FSGS histology.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old beekeeper is stung on the forearm. Within 10 minutes he has generalized hives, wheezing and lightheadedness, and his blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg. He had a large local reaction to a sting 6 months ago. Serum tryptase drawn 1 hour later is elevated. Which of the following events most directly triggered the release of mediators in this reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Activation of complement by venom-antibody complexes

options.label: B
options.html: Cross-linking of IgE bound to high-affinity Fc receptors

options.label: C
options.html: Direct toxic degranulation of mast cells by venom peptides

options.label: D
options.html: Recognition of venom peptides by sensitized CD4+ T cells

options.label: E
options.html: Release of cytokines by venom-activated macrophages

items.explanationHtml:
Prior exposure induced venom-specific IgE, which sits on FcεRI receptors of mast cells and basophils. On re-exposure, multivalent venom allergen cross-links adjacent IgE molecules, and the cell degranulates within minutes, releasing histamine and tryptase and then making leukotrienes and prostaglandins. This is a type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reaction, and the raised tryptase confirms mast cell activation.

Takeaway: Type I reactions start when allergen cross-links FcεRI-bound IgE on a previously sensitized mast cell.

whyNot.A: Complement activation by immune complexes is the type III mechanism; it takes hours to develop and does not explain the raised tryptase.
whyNot.C: Some venom components can activate mast cells directly, but the earlier sensitizing sting and the systemic reaction point to an IgE-mediated mechanism.
whyNot.D: Antigen recognition by sensitized T cells drives type IV reactions, which take 48–72 hours to develop.
whyNot.E: Macrophage cytokines do not produce urticaria, bronchospasm and hypotension within minutes.

items.objective: Identify cross-linking of FcεRI-bound IgE as the trigger of a type I hypersensitivity reaction.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman has had painful oral erosions for 2 months and, for 3 weeks, flaccid blisters on the trunk that break easily and leave raw areas. Gentle lateral pressure on normal-looking skin next to a blister causes the epidermis to separate. A biopsy shows a split just above the basal layer, with basal cells still attached to the basement membrane. Direct immunofluorescence shows IgG in a net-like pattern between keratinocytes. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of her disease?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibodies directed against a cell-surface adhesion protein

options.label: B
options.html: Circulating immune complexes deposited in dermal vessels

options.label: C
options.html: Cytotoxic T cells that kill keratinocytes after hapten binding

options.label: E
options.html: IgE-mediated degranulation of dermal mast cells

items.explanationHtml:
This is pemphigus vulgaris. IgG autoantibodies bind desmoglein 3 (and often desmoglein 1), the desmosomal cadherins that hold keratinocytes together. Loss of adhesion (acantholysis) gives intraepidermal, suprabasal blisters, a positive Nikolsky sign and mucosal erosions. Antibody binding to a fixed tissue antigen is a type II hypersensitivity mechanism.

Takeaway: Antibody against a fixed cell-surface or matrix antigen (here desmoglein) is type II hypersensitivity.

whyNot.B: Circulating immune complexes cause vasculitis and complement consumption (type III), not suprabasal acantholysis with intercellular IgG.
whyNot.C: T-cell killing of hapten-modified keratinocytes describes contact dermatitis or drug eruptions (type IV), and the immunofluorescence shows bound IgG.
whyNot.D: Histamine-driven leak produces wheals that resolve within hours, not chronic erosions with acantholysis.
whyNot.E: Mast cell degranulation causes urticaria, not intraepidermal blisters with intercellular IgG deposits.

items.objective: Recognize pemphigus vulgaris as a type II hypersensitivity against desmosomal proteins.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man receives a tetanus-diphtheria booster in the deltoid after a laceration. He received the same booster 2 years ago and several before that. Eight hours later the injection site is red, swollen, hard and painful over an area 7 cm across. He has no fever, rash or wheezing. A biopsy taken at this point would most likely show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Eosinophils and mast cells around dermal capillaries

options.label: C
options.html: Intraepidermal vesicles with lymphocytes in the epidermis

options.label: D
options.html: Neutrophils and immune complexes in small-vessel walls

options.label: E
options.html: Perivascular cuffs of CD4+ T cells and macrophages without neutrophils

items.explanationHtml:
Repeated toxoid boosters leave high titres of IgG antitoxin. Injected antigen meets this antibody in the tissue, and immune complexes form locally in small-vessel walls. They activate complement (C5a attracts neutrophils), which damage the vessel, giving the localized necrotizing vasculitis of an Arthus reaction. It peaks at 4–12 hours: later than type I reactions and earlier than type IV.

Takeaway: An Arthus reaction is a local type III reaction: immune complexes plus complement and neutrophils in vessel walls, peaking within hours.

whyNot.A: Eosinophils and mast cells fit an immediate (type I) or late-phase reaction, and he had no urticaria or wheeze.
whyNot.B: Caseating granulomas reflect a chronic T-cell and macrophage response to mycobacteria or fungi, not a reaction 8 hours after a toxoid.
whyNot.C: Intraepidermal spongiotic vesicles with lymphocytes are the picture of allergic contact dermatitis, which appears after 48–72 hours.
whyNot.E: T-cell and macrophage cuffs without neutrophils describe a delayed-type (type IV) reaction, which takes 2–3 days to develop.

items.objective: Explain the Arthus reaction as localized immune-complex (type III) vasculitis.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old hiker develops an itchy rash on both forearms 2 days after clearing brush along a trail. Examination shows linear streaks of erythematous papules and small vesicles where his arms were bare. He has had a similar rash once before after gardening, and none after other outdoor activities. Which of the following cells most directly causes the tissue damage in this rash?

options.label: E
options.html: T lymphocytes sensitized to hapten-modified skin proteins

items.explanationHtml:
This is allergic contact dermatitis to urushiol, the plant oleoresin. Urushiol is a hapten: it binds skin proteins, and Langerhans and dermal dendritic cells carry the modified proteins to lymph nodes to prime T cells. On re-exposure, memory CD8+ and CD4+ (Th1, Th17) cells home to the skin, kill hapten-bearing keratinocytes and release cytokines, producing spongiosis and vesicles after 24–72 hours. Linear streaks follow the lines where the plant brushed the skin.

Takeaway: Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed (type IV) T-cell reaction to a hapten, appearing 1–3 days after re-exposure.

whyNot.A: IgG is not needed for contact dermatitis, and antibody-mediated (type II or III) damage would not give linear vesicles 2 days after contact.
whyNot.B: Eosinophils dominate parasitic and late-phase allergic inflammation, not hapten-driven dermatitis.
whyNot.C: Mast cell histamine produces wheals within minutes, not vesicular streaks after 2 days.
whyNot.D: Neutrophils recruited by immune complexes cause an Arthus-type vasculitis within hours, not a vesicular dermatitis at 48 hours.

items.objective: Identify allergic contact dermatitis as a T-cell–mediated type IV reaction to a hapten.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman from rural Virginia has had three episodes of generalized hives, abdominal cramps and lightheadedness, each starting around midnight. Each time she had eaten a beef or pork dinner about 4 hours earlier. She tolerates chicken and fish. She had many tick bites last summer. Skin-prick testing with commercial beef extract is weakly positive. IgE against which of the following is most likely responsible?

options.label: A
options.html: A carbohydrate on mammalian meat proteins

options.label: B
options.html: A heat-labile protein in poultry and fish

options.label: D
options.html: Gelatin used as a food additive

options.label: E
options.html: Tick salivary proteins that cross-react with peanut

items.explanationHtml:
This is alpha-gal syndrome. Bites of the lone star tick sensitize some people to galactose-α-1,3-galactose, a sugar on the glycoproteins and glycolipids of non-primate mammals. Because the allergen is absorbed with dietary fat, symptoms start 3–6 hours after eating red meat, unlike most food anaphylaxis, which begins within minutes. Poultry and fish lack alpha-gal, so they are tolerated.

Takeaway: Delayed anaphylaxis hours after red meat, after tick bites, points to IgE against the carbohydrate alpha-gal.

whyNot.B: Poultry and fish do not carry alpha-gal, and she tolerates both, so an allergen shared with them cannot explain her reactions.
whyNot.C: Bovine serum albumin allergy causes reactions to beef and cow's milk within minutes, and it would not explain the reaction to pork or the tick-bite history.
whyNot.D: Gelatin can carry alpha-gal, but her reactions follow meat meals, and the causal IgE is directed against the sugar, not gelatin protein.
whyNot.E: Tick bites are not known to sensitize people to peanut, and peanut allergy would not explain reactions to red meat.

items.objective: Recognize alpha-gal syndrome as delayed IgE-mediated anaphylaxis to a mammalian carbohydrate after tick bites.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman with allergic asthma inhales cat dander during a laboratory challenge. Her FEV1 falls by 25% within 15 minutes and recovers within an hour after inhaled albuterol. Six hours later her FEV1 falls again, this time with a sputum sample full of eosinophils, and the second fall responds poorly to albuterol. Which of the following cytokines most directly drives the cellular infiltrate in the second phase?
items.explanationHtml:
The immediate response comes from mast cell degranulation (histamine, leukotrienes) and responds to bronchodilators. The late-phase response, 4–12 hours later, is an inflammatory infiltrate of eosinophils, Th2 cells and basophils. Th2 cells and type 2 innate lymphoid cells make IL-5, which drives eosinophil production, activation and survival; IL-4 and IL-13 add IgE class switching and mucus production. Anti-IL-5 antibodies such as mepolizumab reduce exacerbations in eosinophilic asthma.

Takeaway: The late-phase allergic response is an eosinophil-rich, Th2 (IL-5)-driven infiltrate that follows mast cell degranulation by hours.

whyNot.A: Interferon-γ is the Th1 cytokine that activates macrophages and opposes Th2 responses; it is not the driver of eosinophilia.
whyNot.B: Interleukin-2 expands activated T cells in general and does not specifically recruit or activate eosinophils.
whyNot.D: Interleukin-12 from dendritic cells pushes T cells toward Th1, the opposite of an allergic late phase.
whyNot.E: Interleukin-17 recruits neutrophils, which fits neutrophilic rather than eosinophilic airway inflammation.

items.objective: Explain the IL-5–driven eosinophilic late-phase response of type I hypersensitivity.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man received a deceased-donor kidney transplant 7 weeks ago. He missed several doses of his immunosuppressants while traveling. Serum creatinine has risen from 1.2 to 2.3 mg/dL. Donor-specific antibodies are not detected. Biopsy shows a dense interstitial infiltrate of lymphocytes that invade the tubular epithelium; C4d staining of peritubular capillaries is negative. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of the graft injury?

options.label: A
options.html: Deposition of preformed recipient antibodies on graft endothelium

options.label: B
options.html: Donor T cells in the graft attacking recipient tissues

options.label: C
options.html: Ischemic injury from prolonged cold storage of the kidney

options.label: D
options.html: Recipient T cells responding to donor MHC molecules

options.label: E
options.html: Toxic vasoconstriction of afferent arterioles by the drugs

items.explanationHtml:
Acute cellular (T cell–mediated) rejection typically appears weeks to months after transplantation, often after missed immunosuppression. Recipient CD8+ and CD4+ T cells recognize donor MHC directly on graft cells or as processed peptides on recipient antigen-presenting cells, then infiltrate the interstitium and tubules (tubulitis). Negative C4d and absent donor-specific antibodies argue against antibody-mediated rejection. It usually responds to pulse glucocorticoids.

Takeaway: Tubulitis without C4d weeks after a kidney transplant is acute T cell–mediated rejection against donor MHC.

whyNot.A: Preformed antibodies cause hyperacute rejection within minutes to hours of reperfusion, not weeks later, and C4d would be positive.
whyNot.B: Donor T cells attacking the host is graft-versus-host disease, which follows lymphocyte-rich grafts such as bone marrow, not kidneys.
whyNot.C: Cold ischemia causes delayed graft function in the first days, with tubular necrosis rather than lymphocytic tubulitis.
whyNot.E: Calcineurin-inhibitor vasoconstriction raises creatinine but does not produce a lymphocytic tubular infiltrate, and he had missed doses.

items.objective: Identify acute T cell–mediated rejection and its mechanism on a kidney-transplant biopsy.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman underwent kidney transplantation 5 months ago. Creatinine has risen gradually from 1.1 to 1.9 mg/dL. Tacrolimus trough concentrations are in range. Single-antigen bead testing shows new IgG antibodies against a donor HLA-DQ antigen. Biopsy shows neutrophils and mononuclear cells inside glomerular and peritubular capillaries. Which additional biopsy finding would best support the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: C
options.html: Intranuclear viral inclusions in tubular cells

items.explanationHtml:
Donor-specific antibodies binding graft endothelium activate the classical complement pathway. C4d, a stable split product of C4, stays covalently bound to the capillary wall and marks this antibody-mediated rejection (AMR); capillaritis (cells within glomerular and peritubular capillaries) is the matching histologic injury. Treatment targets the antibody: plasmapheresis, IVIG and other antibody-directed therapy, in addition to optimizing maintenance immunosuppression.

Takeaway: Donor-specific antibodies plus capillaritis and peritubular C4d indicate antibody-mediated rejection.

whyNot.B: Crescents signal rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis from recurrent or de novo glomerular disease, not antibody-mediated rejection.
whyNot.C: Intranuclear inclusions in tubular cells suggest BK polyomavirus nephropathy, which is driven by overimmunosuppression, not donor-specific antibodies.
whyNot.D: Isometric tubular vacuolization is a sign of calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity, and her tacrolimus levels are in range.
whyNot.E: Subepithelial deposits point to membranous nephropathy, a glomerular disease rather than rejection.

items.objective: Recognize peritubular C4d as the marker of antibody-mediated transplant rejection.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man had a bilateral lung transplant 3 years ago. Over the past 8 months he has had progressive exertional dyspnea without fever. FEV1 has fallen to 55% of his post-transplant best, with a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio. CT shows mosaic attenuation with air trapping on expiration. Transbronchial biopsy shows dense fibrous tissue narrowing and obliterating small bronchioles, with little active inflammation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Chronic rejection of the lung presents as bronchiolitis obliterans: months to years after transplantation, a progressive, largely irreversible obstructive defect with air trapping and fibrous obliteration of small airways. Repeated alloimmune and nonimmune injury to the airway epithelium leads to fibroproliferation. Chronic rejection in other organs shows the same theme of fibrosis and vascular narrowing (for example, graft arteriosclerosis in heart and kidney).

Takeaway: Progressive obstruction with fibrous obliteration of bronchioles years after lung transplant is chronic rejection.

whyNot.A: Acute cellular rejection shows perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates and usually occurs in the first year, often with fever, rather than dense fibrosis.
whyNot.C: CMV pneumonitis causes fever, hypoxemia and interstitial infiltrates with viral cytopathic change, not fixed small-airway fibrosis.
whyNot.D: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to hours of reperfusion from preformed antibodies.
whyNot.E: Lymphoproliferative disorder appears as masses or nodules with atypical lymphoid cells, not obliterated bronchioles.

items.objective: Recognize bronchiolitis obliterans as chronic rejection after lung transplantation.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old woman with acute myeloid leukemia received a myeloablative allogeneic stem cell transplant from a matched unrelated donor 4 weeks ago. Neutrophils engrafted 6 days ago. She now has a pruritic maculopapular rash on her palms, soles and ears, profuse watery diarrhea (2 L/day), and a total bilirubin of 3.4 mg/dL. Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Donor T cells reacting against recipient tissue antigens

options.label: C
options.html: Recipient B cells making antibodies against donor cells

options.label: D
options.html: Recipient T cells rejecting the donor stem cells

options.label: E
options.html: Reactivation of cytomegalovirus in the gut and liver

items.explanationHtml:
Acute graft-versus-host disease typically appears around engraftment. Donor T cells in the graft recognize recipient minor (and, with mismatch, major) histocompatibility antigens; conditioning-related tissue damage and cytokines amplify the response. The classic targets are skin (rash starting on palms, soles and ears), gut (secretory diarrhea) and liver (cholestasis). Prophylaxis uses calcineurin inhibitors with methotrexate or post-transplant cyclophosphamide; first-line treatment of significant disease is systemic glucocorticoids.

Takeaway: Rash, diarrhea and cholestasis around engraftment after allogeneic stem cell transplant are acute graft-versus-host disease.

whyNot.B: A drug eruption would not explain the combination of high-volume diarrhea and cholestatic liver injury.
whyNot.C: Recipient lymphocytes are largely eliminated by myeloablative conditioning, and antibody against donor cells would cause graft failure or cytopenias, not this triad.
whyNot.D: Host-versus-graft rejection causes graft failure with falling counts, but her neutrophils have engrafted.
whyNot.E: CMV can cause colitis and hepatitis but not an acral maculopapular rash; the skin, gut and liver triad at engraftment fits GVHD.

items.objective: Explain acute GVHD as donor T cells attacking recipient skin, gut and liver.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease from IgA nephropathy is being evaluated for a living-donor kidney transplant. He has three full siblings, all of whom share both of his parents. HLA typing of the siblings has not yet been done. For any one sibling, what is the probability of being HLA-identical to him (sharing both parental haplotypes)?
items.explanationHtml:
HLA genes on chromosome 6 are closely linked and are inherited as two haplotypes, one from each parent. Each sibling independently inherits one of two maternal and one of two paternal haplotypes, so the chance of sharing both with the patient is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. The chance of sharing exactly one haplotype is 1/2 and of sharing none is 1/4. Parents and children always share exactly one haplotype.

Takeaway: Each full sibling has a 25% chance of being HLA-identical, 50% haploidentical and 25% fully mismatched.

whyNot.A: Siblings can inherit the same two parental haplotypes, so the probability is not zero.
whyNot.B: 12.5% would apply only if three independent 50% events were needed; HLA is inherited as two linked haplotypes.
whyNot.D: 50% is the probability of sharing exactly one haplotype (haploidentical), not both.
whyNot.E: Only identical twins are certain to be HLA-identical; full siblings are not.

items.objective: Calculate the probability that a full sibling is HLA-identical from haplotype inheritance.

items.stemHtml: A 51-year-old woman received a liver transplant 9 months ago and takes tacrolimus and mycophenolate. Before transplantation she had no antibodies to Epstein-Barr virus; the donor was seropositive. She now has fevers, night sweats, weight loss and bulky cervical and abdominal lymphadenopathy. A node biopsy shows sheets of large atypical B cells, and in situ hybridization for EBV-encoded RNA is strongly positive. Which of the following best explains the development of this disorder?

options.label: A
options.html: Chromosomal damage to B cells from mycophenolate

options.label: B
options.html: Donor T cells transforming into lymphoma

options.label: C
options.html: Loss of T-cell control of EBV-driven B-cell proliferation

options.label: E
options.html: Viral integration that activates the MYC oncogene

items.explanationHtml:
This is post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder. EBV latency proteins drive B-cell proliferation, which cytotoxic T cells normally keep in check. Pharmacologic T-cell suppression removes that control. Risk is highest when a seronegative recipient receives an EBV-positive organ, in children, and with intense T-cell–depleting therapy. The first step in management is to reduce immunosuppression; rituximab (anti-CD20) is added for CD20+ disease.

Takeaway: PTLD is EBV-driven B-cell proliferation that escapes T-cell control under transplant immunosuppression; reduce immunosuppression first.

whyNot.A: Mycophenolate inhibits lymphocyte proliferation and does not cause B-cell transformation through chromosomal damage.
whyNot.B: The atypical cells are B cells, not T cells, and PTLD after solid-organ transplant usually arises from the recipient's own B cells.
whyNot.D: Reactive nodes from inflammation would not form sheets of atypical EBV-positive B cells.
whyNot.E: EBV stays largely episomal; MYC translocation is the lesion of Burkitt lymphoma, and EBV-driven PTLD depends on loss of immune surveillance.

items.objective: Explain post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder as EBV-driven B-cell growth released from T-cell surveillance.

items.stemHtml: A transplant program reviews cytomegalovirus risk in its kidney recipients before deciding on antiviral prophylaxis. Donor and recipient CMV IgG results are available for each patient. All receive the same induction and maintenance immunosuppression. Which of the following donor/recipient serostatus pairings carries the highest risk of CMV disease after transplantation?

options.label: E
options.html: Donor negative, recipient negative, with leukoreduced blood products

items.explanationHtml:
CMV establishes lifelong latency. A seronegative recipient of an organ from a seropositive donor (D+/R−) acquires the virus with the graft and has no pre-existing CMV-specific T cells, so primary infection under immunosuppression is most likely to become disease. Seropositive recipients have intermediate risk (reactivation or superinfection), and D−/R− pairs have the lowest. D+/R− recipients therefore receive the most intensive prevention, usually valganciclovir prophylaxis for months.

Takeaway: CMV risk after solid-organ transplant is highest in a seronegative recipient of a seropositive organ (D+/R−).

whyNot.A: D−/R− pairs have the lowest risk because neither the graft nor the recipient carries latent virus.
whyNot.B: A seropositive recipient has CMV-specific memory T cells, so reactivation risk is intermediate, not highest.
whyNot.D: D+/R+ recipients have pre-existing immunity and intermediate risk.
whyNot.E: A D−/R− pair is the lowest-risk group, and leukoreduced or CMV-seronegative blood products lower the residual risk further.

items.objective: Rank CMV risk by donor and recipient serostatus after solid-organ transplantation.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man with a kidney transplant takes azathioprine, tacrolimus and prednisone, with stable blood counts for 2 years. Three weeks ago he started a new drug for recurrent gout attacks. He now has fever and mouth ulcers. Leukocyte count is 900/mm3 (reference 4,500–11,000), hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL and platelets 41,000/mm3. Inhibition of which of the following enzymes by the new drug best explains these findings?
items.explanationHtml:
Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine, which is inactivated partly by xanthine oxidase (to 6-thiouric acid) and partly by thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT). Allopurinol and febuxostat inhibit xanthine oxidase, so 6-mercaptopurine and its active thioguanine nucleotides accumulate and suppress the marrow. If a xanthine oxidase inhibitor is needed, the azathioprine dose must be cut sharply with close count monitoring, or azathioprine is replaced.

Takeaway: Xanthine oxidase inhibitors (allopurinol, febuxostat) raise thiopurine levels and can cause pancytopenia with azathioprine.

whyNot.A: Cyclooxygenase inhibitors (NSAIDs) treat gout flares but do not alter thiopurine metabolism or cause pancytopenia this way.
whyNot.B: Dihydrofolate reductase is the target of methotrexate, which is not a gout drug.
whyNot.C: Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase is inhibited by mycophenolate, not by gout therapy.
whyNot.D: Low TPMT activity also causes thiopurine toxicity, but it is inherited, and his counts were stable for 2 years until the new drug.

items.objective: Explain the azathioprine–xanthine oxidase inhibitor interaction that causes marrow suppression.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman with Crohn disease starts a standard weight-based dose of azathioprine. Six weeks later she has fever, and her leukocyte count is 700/mm3 with 100 neutrophils/mm3 and platelets 38,000/mm3. She takes no other medications. Her brother had a similar reaction to mercaptopurine. Testing before treatment would most likely have shown which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) methylates 6-mercaptopurine to an inactive product. People with inherited low or absent TPMT activity (and, especially in East Asian and Hispanic populations, NUDT15 variants) build up toxic thioguanine nucleotides on standard doses and can develop life-threatening myelosuppression. TPMT (and NUDT15) genotype or enzyme activity is checked before starting azathioprine or mercaptopurine so the dose can be reduced or another drug chosen.

Takeaway: Check TPMT (and NUDT15) before thiopurines; deficiency causes severe myelosuppression at normal doses.

whyNot.A: G6PD deficiency causes oxidant hemolysis with drugs such as dapsone or primaquine, not pancytopenia with thiopurines.
whyNot.B: HLA-B*58:01 predicts severe cutaneous reactions to allopurinol, not marrow suppression from azathioprine.
whyNot.D: Acetylator status affects isoniazid, hydralazine and procainamide, not thiopurine metabolism.
whyNot.E: CYP2D6 metabolizes codeine and tamoxifen, among others; it does not inactivate thiopurines.

items.objective: Relate inherited TPMT deficiency to thiopurine-induced myelosuppression.

items.stemHtml: In a laboratory study, human CD4+ T cells are stimulated through the T-cell receptor and CD28 in the presence of tacrolimus. Compared with untreated cells, the treated cells show a normal rise in cytosolic calcium but almost no IL-2 mRNA. Failure of which of the following steps most directly explains the absent IL-2 transcription?

options.label: A
options.html: Binding of IL-2 to the IL-2 receptor α chain

options.label: B
options.html: Dephosphorylation and nuclear entry of NFAT

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibition of de novo guanine nucleotide synthesis

options.label: D
options.html: Phosphorylation of S6 kinase by mTOR

options.label: E
options.html: Release of IκB from NF-κB by IKK

items.explanationHtml:
Tacrolimus binds the immunophilin FKBP12 (cyclosporine binds cyclophilin), and the complex inhibits calcineurin, a calcium–calmodulin-dependent phosphatase. Calcineurin normally dephosphorylates NFAT so it can enter the nucleus and switch on IL-2 and other cytokine genes. The calcium signal is intact, but the step after it fails, so T cells do not make IL-2. Main adverse effects are nephrotoxicity, hypertension, neurotoxicity (tremor), hyperkalemia and new-onset diabetes (more with tacrolimus).

Takeaway: Calcineurin inhibitors block NFAT dephosphorylation and therefore IL-2 transcription, downstream of the calcium signal.

whyNot.A: IL-2 receptor binding happens after IL-2 is made and is blocked by basiliximab, not tacrolimus.
whyNot.C: Blocking de novo guanine synthesis through IMP dehydrogenase is the action of mycophenolate.
whyNot.D: mTOR signalling downstream of the IL-2 receptor is blocked by sirolimus and everolimus, which act after IL-2 is made.
whyNot.E: Glucocorticoids, not tacrolimus, interfere with NF-κB–driven transcription, mainly by inducing IκB and binding NF-κB.

items.objective: Explain how tacrolimus prevents IL-2 transcription through calcineurin–NFAT inhibition.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman with a kidney transplant has persistent tremor and rising creatinine on tacrolimus. Her physicians switch her to a drug that, like tacrolimus, binds FKBP12 but does not inhibit calcineurin. Six weeks later her creatinine is improving, but her LDL cholesterol has risen from 110 to 168 mg/dL, and a recent skin biopsy site is healing slowly. Which of the following is the most direct action of her new drug?

options.label: A
options.html: Blocks the IL-2 receptor α chain

options.label: E
options.html: Prevents CD28 binding to B7 molecules

items.explanationHtml:
Sirolimus (and everolimus) binds FKBP12, but the complex inhibits mTORC1 rather than calcineurin. Blocking mTOR prevents IL-2 receptor signalling from driving T cells from G1 into S phase. It is not itself nephrotoxic, which is why it is used to spare calcineurin inhibitors, but it causes hyperlipidemia, impaired wound healing, mouth ulcers, cytopenias, edema, proteinuria and pneumonitis.

Takeaway: Sirolimus inhibits mTORC1; it spares the kidney but causes hyperlipidemia and poor wound healing.

whyNot.A: Basiliximab blocks the IL-2 receptor α chain; it is an induction antibody, not an FKBP12-binding drug.
whyNot.B: Rituximab depletes CD20+ B cells and does not bind FKBP12 or cause hyperlipidemia.
whyNot.C: Mycophenolate inhibits IMP dehydrogenase and mainly causes GI upset and cytopenias.
whyNot.E: Belatacept blocks CD28 costimulation; it is a fusion protein, not an FKBP12-binding small molecule.

items.objective: Identify mTOR inhibition by sirolimus and its characteristic adverse effects.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old man with a heart transplant is maintained on prednisone, tacrolimus and a drug that inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase. Lymphocytes are hit harder by this drug than most other dividing cells. Which of the following best explains this selectivity?

options.label: A
options.html: Lymphocytes rely on de novo guanine synthesis

options.label: B
options.html: Lymphocytes express more FKBP12 than other cells

options.label: D
options.html: Lymphocytes rely on the salvage pathway for pyrimidines

options.label: E
options.html: Lymphocytes take the drug up through the IL-2 receptor

items.explanationHtml:
Mycophenolate (mycophenolic acid) inhibits IMP dehydrogenase, the rate-limiting enzyme of de novo guanine nucleotide synthesis. Most cells can recycle guanine through the HGPRT salvage pathway, but activated T and B lymphocytes rely heavily on the de novo pathway, so their proliferation is selectively suppressed. Adverse effects include diarrhea and other GI upset, cytopenias and teratogenicity; it is avoided in pregnancy.

Takeaway: Mycophenolate inhibits IMP dehydrogenase; lymphocytes depend on de novo guanine synthesis, so they are most affected.

whyNot.B: FKBP12 is bound by tacrolimus and sirolimus, not mycophenolate.
whyNot.C: Lymphocytes have thymidylate synthase; it is the target of fluorouracil, not mycophenolate.
whyNot.D: IMP dehydrogenase lies in purine synthesis; pyrimidine salvage is not what makes lymphocytes sensitive.
whyNot.E: Mycophenolic acid enters cells without the IL-2 receptor, which is a cytokine receptor and not a drug transporter.

items.objective: Explain why IMP dehydrogenase inhibition selectively suppresses lymphocytes.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis started infliximab 4 months ago. Before treatment, an interferon-γ release assay was positive, but she did not complete the recommended preventive therapy. She now has fever, weight loss and a right upper-lobe cavity, and sputum shows acid-fast bacilli. Loss of which of the following functions of the drug's target best explains this complication?

options.label: A
options.html: Activation of complement on mycobacterial surfaces

options.label: B
options.html: Class switching of B cells to IgA

options.label: C
options.html: Differentiation of Th17 cells in the lung

options.label: D
options.html: Maintenance of granulomas that contain bacilli

options.label: E
options.html: Production of neutralizing antibodies to mycobacteria

items.explanationHtml:
TNF-α from macrophages and T cells is needed to form and maintain granulomas, the structures that wall off latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis. TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept, certolizumab, golimumab) allow granulomas to break down and latent infection to reactivate, often with extrapulmonary or disseminated disease. Screening for latent TB (and hepatitis B) and treating latent TB before starting therapy prevents most cases.

Takeaway: TNF keeps granulomas intact; TNF inhibitors reactivate latent TB, so screen and treat latent infection first.

whyNot.A: Complement plays little part in containing intracellular mycobacteria, and TNF inhibitors do not block complement.
whyNot.B: IgA class switching is driven by TGF-β and other signals, not TNF, and antibodies do not control TB.
whyNot.C: Th17 differentiation depends mainly on IL-6, IL-23 and TGF-β, not TNF.
whyNot.E: Antibody responses are not the main defense against M. tuberculosis, which is controlled by cell-mediated immunity.

items.objective: Explain TB reactivation with TNF inhibitors through loss of granuloma maintenance.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man has received rituximab with chemotherapy for follicular lymphoma, followed by rituximab maintenance for the past year. Over 6 weeks he has developed progressive weakness of the left arm, word-finding difficulty and poor balance. He has no fever or headache. MRI shows several asymmetric T2-hyperintense lesions in the subcortical white matter without mass effect or contrast enhancement. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
items.explanationHtml:
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is caused by JC virus infecting oligodendrocytes and causing demyelination. It occurs with severe cellular immunodeficiency, including advanced HIV and therapies such as rituximab and natalizumab. Typical features are subacute focal deficits and non-enhancing white-matter lesions without mass effect; JC virus DNA in CSF supports the diagnosis. Treatment is restoration of immune function, which here means stopping rituximab.

Takeaway: Subacute focal deficits with non-enhancing white-matter lesions on rituximab suggest PML from JC virus.

whyNot.A: CMV encephalitis causes periventricular enhancement or ventriculitis with confusion, not discrete non-enhancing subcortical lesions.
whyNot.B: HSV encephalitis is acute, with fever and temporal-lobe involvement, not a 6-week course of white-matter lesions.
whyNot.D: Listeria causes meningitis or rhombencephalitis with fever, not afebrile multifocal demyelination.
whyNot.E: Toxoplasma produces ring-enhancing lesions with mass effect, usually in the basal ganglia, not non-enhancing white-matter lesions.

items.objective: Recognize PML from JC virus as a complication of rituximab and other immunosuppressive biologics.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old man has a painless genital ulcer and is given a single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin G for primary syphilis. Four hours later he has a temperature of 39.0°C, rigors, headache and myalgia, and the ulcer is more inflamed. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. He has no urticaria, wheezing or angioedema, and he tolerated amoxicillin last year. Which of the following best explains this reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Contaminating endotoxin in the penicillin preparation

options.label: B
options.html: Cytokine release triggered by lysis of the spirochetes

options.label: C
options.html: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation by penicillin

options.label: D
options.html: Immune complexes of penicillin and IgG in vessel walls

items.explanationHtml:
This is the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction. Rapid killing of spirochetes releases lipoproteins and other components that stimulate TNF, IL-6 and IL-8 release, causing fever, rigors and myalgia within hours of the first dose. It is self-limited (about a day) and treated with antipyretics; it is not an allergy, so penicillin is not stopped and future doses are not avoided. It also follows treatment of other spirochetal infections, such as Lyme disease and leptospirosis.

Takeaway: Fever and rigors hours after first treating syphilis are the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction from spirochete lysis, not penicillin allergy.

whyNot.A: Contamination would not explain a reaction that typically follows the first effective dose against spirochetes; the cytokines come from the dying organisms.
whyNot.C: An IgE reaction would cause urticaria, bronchospasm or hypotension, usually within an hour, and he has none.
whyNot.D: Immune-complex (serum sickness-like) reactions appear 1–2 weeks after exposure, not 4 hours.
whyNot.E: No streptococcal infection is present, and the syndrome follows effective treatment of the spirochete.

items.objective: Recognize the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after treatment of syphilis and distinguish it from drug allergy.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man comes to the clinic because of 5 days of fever, sore throat, a faint truncal rash and diffuse lymphadenopathy. He had condomless anal sex with a new partner 3 weeks ago. A fourth-generation HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody immunoassay is reactive. The HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay is negative for both. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Reassurance that the screen was falsely positive

items.explanationHtml:
In early (acute) infection, the p24 antigen arm of the screening assay turns positive before antibodies appear, so the differentiation assay can still be negative. The recommended algorithm resolves a reactive screen with a negative differentiation assay by testing for HIV-1 RNA. A positive RNA confirms acute HIV-1 infection; ART should then start as soon as possible, and he is highly infectious meanwhile.

Takeaway: Reactive Ag/Ab screen + negative differentiation assay → HIV-1 RNA to diagnose acute infection.

whyNot.A: The CD4 count stages known infection but does not confirm or exclude it.
whyNot.C: His symptoms and recent exposure make acute HIV likely; calling the screen falsely positive without RNA testing could miss the diagnosis.
whyNot.D: Waiting 3 months delays diagnosis and treatment during his most infectious phase.
whyNot.E: The Western blot is no longer part of the testing algorithm, and it would also be negative before antibodies form.

items.objective: Apply the HIV testing algorithm to diagnose acute HIV infection.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man asks about starting pre-exposure prophylaxis. He has sex with men, uses condoms inconsistently and had rectal gonorrhea 4 months ago. He feels well and has had no recent flu-like illness. His last HIV test was 1 year ago. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Hepatitis B surface antigen is negative and he is immune from vaccination. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step before prescribing prophylaxis?
items.explanationHtml:
PrEP is indicated given his ongoing risk and recent bacterial STI. HIV infection must be excluded first, because PrEP is a two-drug regimen that is inadequate treatment and could select for resistance in someone already infected. A laboratory antigen/antibody test (plus HIV RNA if he has had a recent exposure or symptoms of acute infection, and before long-acting injectable PrEP) is done at baseline and repeated during follow-up, along with renal function and STI testing.

Takeaway: Exclude HIV infection before starting PrEP, because a PrEP regimen under-treats established HIV and selects for resistance.

whyNot.A: A CD4 count has no role in deciding on or monitoring PrEP in an HIV-negative person.
whyNot.B: Bone density testing is not required before PrEP in a healthy young adult.
whyNot.D: Resistance testing is done after HIV is diagnosed, not as a PrEP screening test.
whyNot.E: A urine drug screen is not part of the PrEP evaluation and would not change the decision to prescribe.

items.objective: Order HIV testing before starting HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old nurse sustains a deep needlestick injury with a hollow-bore needle just used to draw blood from a patient with known HIV infection. The source patient's most recent viral load is unknown. The injury happened 90 minutes ago, and the site has been washed with soap and water. The nurse's baseline HIV test is pending. She is not pregnant and has normal kidney function. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Await the nurse's baseline HIV result before deciding on treatment

options.label: B
options.html: Obtain the source patient's viral load and treat only if detectable

options.label: C
options.html: Start a single nucleoside analog for 7 days

options.label: D
options.html: Start a three-drug regimen now for 28 days

options.label: E
options.html: Test the nurse for HIV in 6 weeks without starting treatment

items.explanationHtml:
Post-exposure prophylaxis works best when started as soon as possible, ideally within hours and no later than 72 hours. A deep injury with a hollow-bore needle from a source with HIV is a high-risk exposure. Current regimens use three drugs, typically an integrase inhibitor with two nucleoside/nucleotide analogs, for 28 days. Baseline and follow-up testing proceed in parallel, and PEP can be stopped if new information shows it is not needed.

Takeaway: Start three-drug PEP as soon as possible (within 72 hours) after a high-risk exposure and continue it for 28 days; don't wait for results.

whyNot.A: PEP is started before the baseline result returns; waiting loses the time window in which it works.
whyNot.B: An undetectable source viral load lowers risk, but it is unknown now, and PEP should not be delayed to obtain it.
whyNot.C: Single-drug, short regimens are no longer recommended because they are less effective.
whyNot.E: Testing alone without prophylaxis is inappropriate after a high-risk exposure to HIV-infected blood.

items.objective: Manage an occupational high-risk HIV exposure with prompt three-drug post-exposure prophylaxis.

items.stemHtml:
A 38-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with HIV after 2 months of weight loss and oral thrush. She has no cough, headache or visual symptoms, and chest radiography is normal. She has no drug allergies. Antiretroviral therapy is being started this week. Results:

TestResult
CD4+ T-lymphocyte count62/mm3
HIV-1 RNA240,000 copies/mL
Toxoplasma IgGPositive
Serum cryptococcal antigenNegative
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activityNormal

In addition to antiretroviral therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate prophylaxis?
items.explanationHtml:
With a CD4 count below 200/mm3 (and thrush), she needs Pneumocystis prophylaxis, and with a count below 100/mm3 and positive Toxoplasma IgG she also needs Toxoplasma prophylaxis. Daily double-strength trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole covers both. Prophylaxis can be stopped once ART has kept the CD4 count above 200/mm3 for at least 3 months.

Takeaway: CD4 <200 → PCP prophylaxis; CD4 <100 with Toxoplasma IgG → also toxo prophylaxis; daily TMP-SMX covers both.

whyNot.A: Routine Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis is no longer advised for people who start effective ART promptly.
whyNot.B: Dapsone alone covers Pneumocystis but not Toxoplasma; it is an alternative only for people who cannot take TMP-SMX, when pyrimethamine is added.
whyNot.C: Her cryptococcal antigen is negative, and primary antifungal prophylaxis is not recommended.
whyNot.D: Pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and leucovorin is treatment for active toxoplasmic encephalitis, which she does not have.

items.objective: Choose opportunistic-infection prophylaxis from CD4 count and Toxoplasma serology in advanced HIV.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man with HIV (CD4 count 45/mm3) was diagnosed with drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis 6 weeks ago and started four-drug therapy. Dolutegravir-based ART was started 2 weeks after TB treatment. He had been improving, but over the past 5 days he has had new fever and painful enlargement of a right cervical lymph node. He is alert, and his breathing is unlabored. Temperature is 38.4°C. HIV RNA has fallen by more than 2 log10. Sputum smears have converted to negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Stop antiretroviral therapy until TB treatment is completed

options.label: C
options.html: Stop antituberculous therapy and start second-line drugs

options.label: E
options.html: Treat a presumed new bacterial lymphadenitis with antibiotics alone

items.explanationHtml:
This is paradoxical TB-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome: worsening inflammation as T-cell function returns, with falling viral load and microbiologic response to TB drugs. Both treatments are continued. Anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs, or prednisone for moderate to severe reactions) treat the symptoms, and enlarging nodes can be aspirated. Other causes (drug resistance, a new infection, lymphoma) are considered if the course is atypical. ART is generally started within 2 weeks of TB treatment when the CD4 count is below 50/mm3, because early ART lowers mortality despite the higher IRIS risk.

Takeaway: Paradoxical IRIS: continue ART and the pathogen-directed therapy; treat the inflammation.

whyNot.B: Stopping ART would reverse immune recovery and raise the risk of further opportunistic infections and death.
whyNot.C: His TB is drug-susceptible and responding (smear conversion), so there is no reason to change regimens.
whyNot.D: Efavirenz is not more effective in IRIS, and switching does not address the inflammatory reaction.
whyNot.E: Worsening disease at sites of known TB soon after ART fits IRIS, and antibiotics alone would not treat it.

items.objective: Manage paradoxical TB-associated IRIS by continuing ART and TB therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman at 18 weeks' gestation has a reactive HIV antigen/antibody test at her first prenatal visit, confirmed by the differentiation assay. HIV-1 RNA is 38,000 copies/mL and the CD4 count is 520/mm3. Genotypic resistance testing has been sent. She feels well. Hepatitis B serologies are negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Defer antiretroviral therapy until after delivery

options.label: B
options.html: Give intravenous zidovudine during labor only

options.label: C
options.html: Start antiretroviral therapy at 28 weeks' gestation

options.label: D
options.html: Start antiretroviral therapy once the resistance results return

items.explanationHtml:
All pregnant people with HIV should start ART as soon as possible, whatever the CD4 count. Early suppression of the viral load is the strongest way to prevent perinatal transmission, which is very low when the viral load is undetectable at delivery. Treatment is started before resistance results return and adjusted if needed; dolutegravir-based regimens are among the preferred options in pregnancy. Viral load near delivery guides the mode of delivery and intrapartum zidovudine.

Takeaway: Pregnancy with HIV: start ART immediately, without waiting for resistance results or a later trimester.

whyNot.A: Deferring ART leaves the fetus exposed to a high maternal viral load and raises transmission risk.
whyNot.B: Intrapartum zidovudine alone is far less effective than sustained viral suppression during pregnancy.
whyNot.C: Waiting until 28 weeks wastes weeks in which the viral load could be suppressed.
whyNot.D: Resistance testing should not delay treatment; the regimen can be adjusted when results arrive.

items.objective: Start antiretroviral therapy immediately in pregnancy to prevent perinatal HIV transmission.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman has streptococcal pharyngitis confirmed by a rapid antigen test. Her chart lists a penicillin allergy. She says that at age 7 she had an itchy rash on the third day of a course of amoxicillin; there was no swelling, breathing difficulty, blistering, mucosal involvement or hospital stay, and she has not taken a penicillin since. She takes no other medications. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Direct oral amoxicillin challenge under observation

options.label: C
options.html: Prescribe azithromycin and keep the allergy label

options.label: D
options.html: Refer for penicillin skin testing in 3 months and treat with clindamycin now

items.explanationHtml:
Most people labelled penicillin-allergic tolerate penicillins. A remote, benign, delayed rash in childhood, without features of anaphylaxis or a severe cutaneous reaction, is a low-risk history. Current practice is a direct oral challenge with a single treatment dose of amoxicillin and about an hour of observation, without prior skin testing.
