If she tolerates it, she can be treated with amoxicillin and the allergy label removed, which avoids broader, less effective and more toxic alternatives.

Takeaway: Low-risk penicillin allergy history (remote benign rash): direct oral amoxicillin challenge, then delabel.

whyNot.B: Desensitization is for patients with likely IgE-mediated allergy who need a penicillin; her history is low risk, and it would not remove the label.
whyNot.C: Azithromycin is a less suitable first choice for streptococcal pharyngitis (macrolide resistance), and keeping an inaccurate label causes future harm.
whyNot.D: Delaying evaluation and using clindamycin exposes her to more adverse effects when she can be assessed today.
whyNot.E: Serum specific IgE tests have poor sensitivity and do not replace a challenge in a low-risk patient.

items.objective: Evaluate a low-risk penicillin allergy label with a direct oral amoxicillin challenge.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old woman with bipolar disorder started lamotrigine 3 weeks ago. For 2 days she has had fever, a burning rash that began on the face and trunk, and painful oral and genital erosions. Examination shows dusky purpuric macules with central blisters on the trunk; gentle pressure makes the epidermis slide off. Detached and detachable skin covers about 8% of her body surface area. Conjunctivae are injected. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Add a second mood stabilizer and continue lamotrigine at half the dose

options.label: B
options.html: Continue lamotrigine and start oral prednisone

options.label: C
options.html: Discharge home with topical glucocorticoids and follow up in 2 days

options.label: D
options.html: Start empiric intravenous antibiotics for staphylococcal scalded skin

options.label: E
options.html: Stop lamotrigine and admit to a burn unit

items.explanationHtml:
Fever, painful dusky macules, epidermal detachment under 10% of body surface area and two or more mucosal sites make this Stevens-Johnson syndrome; lamotrigine (especially early in treatment or with rapid dose escalation) is a classic culprit. The most important step is to stop the culprit drug immediately. Care is supportive (wound care, fluids, analgesia, eye and mucosal care) in a burn or intensive care setting, with ophthalmology review. The culprit drug must never be restarted.

Takeaway: SJS/TEN: stop the culprit immediately and give supportive care in a burn or intensive care unit.

whyNot.A: Any further exposure to the culprit drug, even at a lower dose, can worsen the reaction and is contraindicated.
whyNot.B: Continuing lamotrigine is dangerous whatever else is given, and the role of systemic glucocorticoids is uncertain.
whyNot.C: SJS can progress to TEN over days and needs inpatient supportive care, not outpatient topical treatment.
whyNot.D: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome spares mucous membranes and affects mainly young children; the drug history and mucosal erosions point to SJS.

items.objective: Manage Stevens-Johnson syndrome by withdrawing the culprit drug and giving supportive inpatient care.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man started allopurinol for recurrent gout 5 weeks ago. He now has fever, a widespread morbilliform rash, facial swelling and tender cervical and axillary lymph nodes. There are no blisters or mucosal erosions. Temperature is 38.9°C. Leukocyte count is 14,200/mm3 with 18% eosinophils and atypical lymphocytes. ALT is 410 U/L and creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 1.9 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms

items.explanationHtml:
DRESS begins 2–8 weeks after starting a drug, with fever, a widespread rash, facial edema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytes and internal organ involvement (most often liver, also kidney, lung and heart). Allopurinol, aromatic anticonvulsants, sulfonamides and some antibiotics are common causes; HLA-B*58:01 raises risk with allopurinol. Treatment is withdrawal of the drug and, for significant organ involvement, systemic glucocorticoids tapered slowly over weeks because relapse is common.

Takeaway: Weeks after a new drug: fever, rash, facial edema, eosinophilia and organ injury = DRESS.

whyNot.A: AGEP appears within days and consists of many small sterile pustules on erythema, usually without major organ injury.
whyNot.C: Serum sickness causes fever, urticarial rash and arthralgia 1–2 weeks after exposure, without marked eosinophilia or hepatitis.
whyNot.D: SJS has mucosal erosions and epidermal detachment, which he does not have.
whyNot.E: IgE-mediated urticaria appears within minutes to hours of a dose and does not cause hepatitis or kidney injury weeks later.

items.objective: Diagnose DRESS from timing, eosinophilia and internal organ involvement.

items.stemHtml: A 5-month-old girl is brought for a well-child visit. She has mild eczema controlled with emollients, has never had a reaction to food and is growing well. She has started iron-fortified cereal and puréed vegetables without problems. Her older brother has a peanut allergy. Her parents ask when she may eat peanut. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

options.label: A
options.html: Avoid peanut until a negative skin-prick test at 3 years of age

options.label: B
options.html: Avoid peanut until she is 12 months old

options.label: C
options.html: Give peanut only if serum peanut-specific IgE is undetectable

options.label: D
options.html: Introduce peanut-containing foods at home now

options.label: E
options.html: Start a hydrolyzed formula to prevent peanut sensitization

items.explanationHtml:
Early introduction of peanut lowers the risk of peanut allergy. An infant who is developmentally ready for solids, with mild eczema and no history of food reactions, can be given peanut at home around 4–6 months of age, as thinned peanut butter or peanut puffs (never whole peanuts), and kept in the diet regularly. A sibling's allergy is not a reason to delay. Infants with severe eczema or a prior food reaction may benefit from specialist evaluation first.

Takeaway: Introduce peanut early (around 4–6 months) in infants with mild or no eczema, even with an allergic sibling.

whyNot.A: Prolonged avoidance increases the chance of developing peanut allergy, and routine testing is not needed in a low-risk infant.
whyNot.B: Delaying peanut to 12 months forgoes the protective effect of early introduction.
whyNot.C: Screening IgE in a low-risk infant often gives clinically irrelevant positives and delays introduction.
whyNot.E: Hydrolyzed formulas do not prevent peanut allergy.

items.objective: Advise early peanut introduction to prevent peanut allergy in a low-risk infant.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old college student with known peanut allergy is brought to the emergency department 15 minutes after eating a cookie at a party. She has generalized hives, lip swelling, a hoarse voice and wheezing, and she vomited once. She did not use an epinephrine autoinjector. Pulse is 124/min, respirations are 26/min and blood pressure is 86/52 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 91% on room air. Which of the following is the most appropriate first medication?
items.explanationHtml:
This is anaphylaxis: skin and mucosal signs with airway, respiratory and circulatory involvement after a known allergen. Intramuscular epinephrine (0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/mL, up to 0.5 mg in adults) into the anterolateral thigh is the first treatment and can be repeated every 5–15 minutes. Its α1 effect counters vasodilation and mucosal edema, and its β2 effect relieves bronchospasm and stabilizes mast cells. Supine positioning, oxygen and intravenous fluids follow. Delay in giving epinephrine is linked to fatal outcomes.

Takeaway: Anaphylaxis: intramuscular epinephrine into the thigh first; everything else is adjunctive.

whyNot.A: Albuterol helps bronchospasm only and does nothing for airway edema or hypotension.
whyNot.B: H1 antihistamines relieve itching and hives but do not reverse airway obstruction or shock.
whyNot.D: H2 blockers are optional adjuncts with no effect on airway edema or blood pressure.
whyNot.E: Glucocorticoids act over hours and do not treat the acute reaction.

items.objective: Give intramuscular epinephrine first in anaphylaxis.

items.stemHtml: The student is given intramuscular epinephrine twice, plus oxygen and 2 L of normal saline. Her hives, hoarseness and wheezing resolve, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Four hours later she is asymptomatic and asks to go home. She has no history of asthma. Which of the following is the most appropriate step before she leaves?

options.label: A
options.html: Admit her to the intensive care unit for 48 hours

options.label: B
options.html: Prescribe a daily oral H1 antihistamine indefinitely

options.label: C
options.html: Prescribe a 2-week oral prednisone taper as the only measure

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat a serum tryptase level before discharge to decide on treatment

items.explanationHtml:
After anaphylaxis, patients are observed until stable (longer when epinephrine was needed more than once or the reaction was severe) and warned that symptoms can return hours later without new exposure (biphasic reaction). Before discharge she needs two epinephrine autoinjectors with training, an emergency action plan, advice on avoiding the allergen and allergist follow-up. Prednisone and antihistamines do not reliably prevent biphasic reactions and do not replace epinephrine.

Takeaway: Discharge after anaphylaxis: epinephrine autoinjectors (two), training, an action plan and allergist referral.

whyNot.A: ICU admission is not needed for a patient whose reaction has fully resolved and who has stayed stable for hours.
whyNot.B: Daily antihistamines do not prevent anaphylaxis and could mask early skin signs.
whyNot.C: Glucocorticoids have not been shown to prevent biphasic reactions, and they do not replace an autoinjector.
whyNot.E: Tryptase helps confirm mast cell activation but does not decide whether she needs an autoinjector.

items.objective: Plan discharge after anaphylaxis with epinephrine autoinjectors and allergy follow-up.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman at 16 weeks' gestation has a positive treponemal test and an RPR titer of 1:64. She has no symptoms, and her screening test 2 years ago was negative, so the duration of infection is unknown. At age 20 she had hives, throat tightness and hypotension within 30 minutes of a dose of intramuscular penicillin, and penicillin skin testing last year was positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Penicillin is the only treatment known to prevent congenital syphilis reliably. Syphilis of unknown duration is treated as late latent: benzathine penicillin G weekly for 3 weeks. A pregnant patient with a confirmed IgE-mediated penicillin allergy should be desensitized in a monitored setting and then treated with penicillin. Desensitization induces temporary tolerance, so it is maintained by continuing the doses without long gaps.

Takeaway: Syphilis in pregnancy with true penicillin allergy: desensitize and treat with penicillin.

whyNot.A: Ceftriaxone has not been shown to prevent congenital syphilis and is not an acceptable substitute in pregnancy.
whyNot.B: Doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy and is not adequate to prevent fetal infection.
whyNot.D: Azithromycin is unreliable because of resistance and does not prevent congenital syphilis.
whyNot.E: Deferring treatment allows fetal infection, stillbirth or congenital syphilis.

items.objective: Treat syphilis in pregnancy with penicillin after desensitization when the patient has a true penicillin allergy.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old man received a deceased-donor kidney transplant 4 months ago (donor CMV IgG positive, recipient negative) and completed 3 months of valganciclovir prophylaxis 3 weeks ago. He now has 6 days of fever, abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Leukocyte count is 2,800/mm3. Stool tests for bacterial pathogens and Clostridioides difficile are negative. Colonoscopy shows deep ulcers, and biopsies show enlarged cells with intranuclear inclusions; immunostaining is positive for CMV. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Late-onset CMV disease after prophylaxis ends is typical in D+/R− recipients. Tissue-invasive CMV colitis with severe symptoms is treated with intravenous ganciclovir (oral valganciclovir may be used for mild to moderate disease once the patient can absorb it), with dose adjustment for kidney function, plus a reduction in immunosuppression when possible. Viral load is followed until it clears. Foscarnet or cidofovir is reserved for resistant virus or intolerance.

Takeaway: Tissue-invasive CMV after transplant: intravenous ganciclovir (valganciclovir for milder disease); foscarnet only for resistance.

whyNot.A: Acyclovir has poor activity against CMV because CMV lacks the thymidine kinase that activates it.
whyNot.B: Cidofovir is nephrotoxic and kept for ganciclovir-resistant CMV, which is not suggested here.
whyNot.C: Foscarnet is a second-line drug for resistance or intolerance because of nephrotoxicity and electrolyte disturbances.
whyNot.E: Oseltamivir treats influenza and has no activity against CMV.

items.objective: Treat tissue-invasive CMV disease after solid-organ transplantation with ganciclovir.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old woman received a living-donor kidney transplant 8 months ago. Her creatinine has risen from a baseline of 1.1 to 1.7 mg/dL over 3 weeks. She has no fever, pain over the graft or change in urine output, and she has taken all her doses. Tacrolimus trough concentration is within her target range. Urinalysis shows 1+ protein and no casts. Ultrasound with Doppler shows no hydronephrosis, normal renal artery and vein flow and no fluid collection. BK virus DNA is not detected in plasma. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: CT angiography of the transplant artery

options.label: B
options.html: Empiric pulse methylprednisolone without further testing

options.label: D
options.html: Percutaneous biopsy of the transplant kidney

items.explanationHtml:
A sustained rise in creatinine without obstruction, vascular problems, drug toxicity or BK virus infection needs a tissue diagnosis. Biopsy distinguishes T cell–mediated rejection, antibody-mediated rejection (with C4d and donor-specific antibody testing), recurrent glomerular disease and other causes, each of which is treated differently. Donor-specific antibodies are checked at the same time.

Takeaway: Unexplained rising creatinine in a kidney transplant after ultrasound, drug levels and BK testing → allograft biopsy.

whyNot.A: Doppler flow is already normal, so CT angiography is unlikely to find a cause and adds contrast exposure.
whyNot.B: Empiric glucocorticoids may mistreat antibody-mediated rejection or another cause; a biopsy should guide therapy.
whyNot.C: Her tacrolimus level is already on target, and increasing the dose without a diagnosis risks toxicity.
whyNot.E: Waiting 3 months risks irreversible graft injury if this is rejection.

items.objective: Order an allograft biopsy for unexplained kidney transplant dysfunction after noninvasive evaluation.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man had a heart transplant 6 years ago and takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate and low-dose prednisone. He worked outdoors as a farmer for most of his life. At an annual visit he asks which cancer he is at greatest risk of developing as a transplant recipient, so that he knows what to watch for. Which of the following is the most likely answer?
items.explanationHtml:
Long-term immunosuppression raises the risk of virus-related and UV-related cancers. Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is the most common cancer after solid-organ transplantation, many times more frequent than in the general population, and it is more aggressive; his sun exposure adds to the risk. Recipients need strict sun protection and regular full skin examinations, and some benefit from switching to an mTOR inhibitor after multiple tumors. Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder and Kaposi sarcoma are also increased.

Takeaway: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is the most common cancer after solid-organ transplant; counsel sun protection and annual skin checks.

whyNot.A: Colorectal cancer screening follows general population guidance; its risk is not raised as much as skin cancer.
whyNot.C: Hepatocellular carcinoma risk relates mainly to viral hepatitis or cirrhosis, which he does not have.
whyNot.D: Pancreatic cancer is not one of the cancers most increased by transplant immunosuppression.
whyNot.E: Prostate cancer is not substantially increased by transplant immunosuppression.

items.objective: Counsel solid-organ transplant recipients about their high risk of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

items.stemHtml:
A 54-year-old man with a kidney transplant 2 years ago has had stable function on tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisone. Ten days ago he was prescribed a 14-day course of an antibiotic for community-acquired pneumonia while traveling. He now has tremor and headache. Blood pressure is 158/96 mm Hg (usual 128/80). Results:

TestTodayLast month
Tacrolimus trough (target 5–8 ng/mL)21 ng/mL6.4 ng/mL
Creatinine2.1 mg/dL1.2 mg/dL
Potassium5.6 mEq/L4.3 mEq/L
Magnesium1.3 mEq/L1.7 mEq/L

Which antibiotic most likely accounts for these findings?
items.explanationHtml:
Tacrolimus (like cyclosporine and sirolimus) is metabolized by CYP3A4 and transported by P-glycoprotein. Clarithromycin and erythromycin strongly inhibit CYP3A4, so tacrolimus levels rise and cause nephrotoxicity, hyperkalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypertension and neurotoxicity. Management is to stop the interacting drug, hold or reduce tacrolimus and recheck levels. Azithromycin interacts much less and is preferred when a macrolide is needed.

Takeaway: Clarithromycin (CYP3A4 inhibitor) raises tacrolimus levels; rifampin and other inducers lower them.

whyNot.A: Amoxicillin does not meaningfully affect CYP3A4 or tacrolimus levels.
whyNot.C: Doxycycline does not raise tacrolimus concentrations substantially.
whyNot.D: Levofloxacin is not a significant CYP3A4 inhibitor.
whyNot.E: Rifampin induces CYP3A4 and would lower tacrolimus levels, risking rejection rather than toxicity.

items.objective: Recognize CYP3A4-inhibitor interactions that cause calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman with end-stage liver disease from primary biliary cholangitis is on the transplant waiting list; a living-donor transplant is planned in 3 months. She has never had chickenpox or varicella vaccine, and varicella IgG is negative. She takes ursodiol only and is not immunosuppressed. MMR immunity is documented. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding varicella?

options.label: B
options.html: Live varicella vaccine 6 months after transplantation

options.label: C
options.html: No vaccine, with acyclovir after any exposure

items.explanationHtml:
Live vaccines are contraindicated after solid-organ transplantation because of lifelong immunosuppression, so seronegative candidates should receive live vaccines (varicella, MMR) before transplant, ideally at least 4 weeks beforehand, while they are not immunosuppressed. Inactivated vaccines can be given before or after transplant but work better before. Household contacts should also be vaccinated.

Takeaway: Give live vaccines to transplant candidates at least 4 weeks before transplant; they are contraindicated afterward.

whyNot.B: Live varicella vaccine is contraindicated after solid-organ transplant because she will remain immunosuppressed.
whyNot.C: Primary varicella after transplant can be severe or fatal, so prevention before transplant is preferred to relying on treatment.
whyNot.D: Vaccinating contacts helps but leaves her unprotected against exposures outside the household.
whyNot.E: Varicella-zoster immune globulin is post-exposure prophylaxis, not a way to build lasting immunity.

items.objective: Schedule live vaccines before solid-organ transplantation in seronegative candidates.

items.stemHtml: Based on the study summary, how many D+/R− kidney recipients would need to receive the study drug instead of standard-duration prophylaxis to prevent one case of CMV disease within 12 months?
items.explanationHtml:
The absolute risk reduction is 20% − 10% = 10% (0.10). The number needed to treat is 1/ARR = 1/0.10 = 10. The relative risk reduction (50%) sounds larger but does not tell clinicians how many patients must be treated for one to benefit.

Takeaway: NNT = 1 / absolute risk reduction; here 1 / (0.20 − 0.10) = 10.

whyNot.A: Five would need an absolute risk reduction of 20%, which would mean no CMV disease in the study group.
whyNot.B: Eight would need an absolute risk reduction of 12.5%, larger than the 10% observed.
whyNot.D: Twenty would correspond to a 5% absolute risk reduction; the observed reduction is 10%.
whyNot.E: Twenty-five would correspond to a 4% absolute risk reduction.

items.objective: Calculate the number needed to treat from event rates in a transplant prophylaxis trial.

items.stemHtml: Based on the study summary, which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: The study drug lowers mortality in D+/R− kidney recipients

options.label: B
options.html: The study drug lowers CMV disease at the cost of more neutropenia

options.label: C
options.html: The study drug should replace prophylaxis in CMV-seropositive recipients

options.label: D
options.html: The study drug works by preventing CMV latency in the graft

options.label: E
options.html: The study drug is equivalent to standard prophylaxis

items.explanationHtml:
The trial was powered for CMV disease, which fell from 20% to 10%, and leukopenia requiring dose interruption rose from 8% to 15%, so the best-supported conclusion is a benefit on the primary outcome with more neutropenia. Mortality was low and similar in both groups and the trial was not powered for it; only D+/R− kidney recipients were enrolled, so the results cannot be extended to seropositive recipients.

Takeaway: Conclude only what the primary outcome and reported harms support, within the enrolled population.

whyNot.A: Deaths were few and similar in both arms, and the trial was not powered for mortality.
whyNot.C: Only D+/R− recipients were enrolled, so the results do not apply to seropositive recipients.
whyNot.D: The study measured clinical outcomes, not the mechanism of CMV latency.
whyNot.E: CMV disease was halved and the difference was significant, so the drugs were not shown to be equivalent.

items.objective: Draw conclusions from a trial summary that respect its primary outcome, harms and population.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis that has not responded to methotrexate is to start adalimumab. She was born in the Philippines and moved to the United States 10 years ago. She has no cough, fever or weight loss. Which of the following should be done before the first dose?

options.label: A
options.html: Antinuclear antibody and anti–double-stranded DNA testing

items.explanationHtml:
TNF inhibitors can reactivate latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B. Before starting, patients are screened for latent TB (an interferon-γ release assay is preferred in BCG-vaccinated people; tuberculin skin testing is an alternative) and for hepatitis B (surface antigen, core antibody and surface antibody). Latent TB is treated before or soon after starting the biologic, and hepatitis B carriers get antiviral prophylaxis or monitoring. Live vaccines should be given before therapy starts, and inactivated vaccines brought up to date.

Takeaway: Before a TNF inhibitor: screen for latent TB (IGRA) and hepatitis B, and update vaccines.

whyNot.A: TNF inhibitors can induce autoantibodies, but routine ANA testing before treatment is not required and does not prevent harm.
whyNot.B: Echocardiography is reserved for patients with known heart failure or symptoms; it is not routine screening.
whyNot.D: Pulmonary function testing is not needed in a patient without lung symptoms.
whyNot.E: Serum protein electrophoresis screens for monoclonal gammopathy, which is not a contraindication assessed before TNF inhibitors.

items.objective: Screen for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B before starting a TNF inhibitor.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man with newly diagnosed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is to start chemotherapy that includes rituximab. Hepatitis B surface antigen is negative, total hepatitis B core antibody is positive, and surface antibody is positive. ALT is normal, and HBV DNA is undetectable. Which of the following is the most appropriate management regarding hepatitis B?

options.label: A
options.html: Defer rituximab until the core antibody becomes negative

options.label: B
options.html: Give a hepatitis B vaccine booster

options.label: C
options.html: No action, because the surface antibody is protective

options.label: E
options.html: Start entecavir before rituximab and continue it after treatment

items.explanationHtml:
A positive core antibody means past infection with persistent, controlled HBV in the liver, even when the surface antigen is negative and surface antibody is present. Anti-CD20 therapy causes profound B-cell depletion and has a high risk of HBV reactivation, which can cause fulminant hepatitis. Antiviral prophylaxis with a high-barrier drug (entecavir or tenofovir) is started before rituximab and continued for at least 12 months after the last dose, with monitoring after it is stopped.

Takeaway: Core antibody–positive patients starting rituximab need antiviral prophylaxis (entecavir or tenofovir), even if HBsAg is negative.

whyNot.A: Core antibody usually persists for life after infection, so waiting would delay lymphoma treatment indefinitely.
whyNot.B: A vaccine booster does not prevent reactivation of virus already latent in the liver.
whyNot.C: Surface antibody does not prevent reactivation when B cells are depleted; rituximab is a high-risk drug for HBV reactivation.
whyNot.D: Reactivation can occur during chemotherapy, and checking only afterward risks fulminant hepatitis.

items.objective: Give hepatitis B antiviral prophylaxis to core antibody–positive patients receiving rituximab.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old woman with metastatic melanoma is receiving pembrolizumab every 3 weeks; she has had 4 doses. For 5 days she has had 8–9 watery stools a day above her baseline, crampy abdominal pain and nocturnal stools. Temperature is 37.6°C, pulse 104/min and blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg. Stool PCR and Clostridioides difficile testing are negative. CT shows diffuse colonic wall thickening without perforation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Hold pembrolizumab and give systemic glucocorticoids

options.label: E
options.html: Stop pembrolizumab permanently and observe without treatment

items.explanationHtml:
Immune checkpoint inhibitors release T-cell brakes and can cause immune-related colitis. Seven or more stools a day over baseline with systemic features is severe (grade 3) colitis. Management is to hold the checkpoint inhibitor, give intravenous methylprednisolone (about 1–2 mg/kg/day), rehydrate and taper glucocorticoids over 4–6 weeks once improved. If there is no response within about 3 days, infliximab or vedolizumab is added. Infection is excluded first, as here.

Takeaway: Severe checkpoint-inhibitor colitis: hold the drug and give systemic glucocorticoids; add infliximab or vedolizumab if refractory.

whyNot.A: Antidiarrheals alone are for mild colitis; continuing the drug in severe colitis risks perforation.
whyNot.C: C. difficile testing is negative, so oral vancomycin is not indicated.
whyNot.D: Colectomy is reserved for perforation or failure of medical therapy.
whyNot.E: Stopping the drug without immunosuppressive treatment leaves severe colitis untreated.

items.objective: Manage severe immune checkpoint inhibitor colitis with drug interruption and glucocorticoids.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man with metastatic melanoma has received 3 doses of combined ipilimumab and nivolumab. For 10 days he has had severe headache, fatigue, nausea and lightheadedness on standing. Blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg supine and 82/54 mm Hg standing. Visual fields are normal. Sodium is 129 mEq/L and potassium 4.2 mEq/L. Morning cortisol is 1.8 μg/dL (reference 5–23) with a low ACTH. Free T4 is low with a low-normal TSH. MRI shows mild enlargement of the pituitary. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Checkpoint-inhibitor hypophysitis, most frequent with anti-CTLA-4 therapy, causes headache and loss of anterior pituitary hormones: secondary adrenal insufficiency (low cortisol with low ACTH), central hypothyroidism and hypogonadism. Glucocorticoid replacement comes first. Thyroid hormone is started only after glucocorticoid replacement, because levothyroxine speeds cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis. ACTH deficiency is often permanent, and mineralocorticoid production is preserved because aldosterone is controlled by angiotensin II.

Takeaway: Checkpoint-inhibitor hypophysitis: replace glucocorticoid first, then thyroid hormone; mineralocorticoid is not needed.

whyNot.A: Bromocriptine treats prolactinoma, not inflammatory hypophysitis with hormone deficiencies.
whyNot.B: Aldosterone secretion is intact in secondary adrenal insufficiency, and his potassium is normal.
whyNot.D: Starting thyroid hormone before glucocorticoid can precipitate adrenal crisis.
whyNot.E: The gland is only mildly enlarged with normal visual fields; surgery has no role.

items.objective: Treat checkpoint-inhibitor hypophysitis by replacing glucocorticoid before thyroid hormone.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis started oral methotrexate 15 mg once weekly 3 months ago. Her joint symptoms have improved. She now has recurrent painful mouth ulcers and nausea for a day after each dose. ALT is 56 U/L (reference 10–40), and blood counts and creatinine are normal. She drinks no alcohol and takes no other medications. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Add folic acid daily and continue methotrexate

options.label: B
options.html: Change methotrexate to a daily dosing schedule

items.explanationHtml:
Low-dose weekly methotrexate commonly causes mucositis, nausea and mild aminotransferase rises through folate antagonism. Folic acid supplementation (or folinic acid) reduces these effects without losing efficacy and should be given to everyone on methotrexate. Blood counts, liver enzymes and creatinine are monitored regularly; persistent ALT elevations above about three times the upper limit, cytopenias or kidney impairment call for dose reduction or stopping.

Takeaway: Methotrexate mucositis, nausea and mild ALT rise: add folic acid and continue the drug with monitoring.

whyNot.B: Daily dosing is a dangerous prescribing error that causes severe toxicity; methotrexate for arthritis is weekly.
whyNot.C: Intravenous leucovorin rescue is for high-dose methotrexate or overdose, not mild toxicity at weekly doses.
whyNot.D: A mildly raised ALT does not need a biopsy; monitoring and folate supplementation come first.
whyNot.E: Her arthritis is responding, and her side effects can be managed without stopping the drug.

items.objective: Reduce low-dose methotrexate adverse effects with folic acid supplementation.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman is diagnosed with giant cell arteritis and starts prednisone 50 mg daily, which is expected to be tapered over at least 6 months. She is postmenopausal, has had no fractures and has normal kidney function. DXA scan shows a femoral neck T-score of −2.1. Serum calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D are normal. She already takes adequate calcium and vitamin D. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional step to protect her bones?

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat DXA in 2 years before deciding

items.explanationHtml:
Glucocorticoids reduce bone formation and increase resorption, with fracture risk rising within the first months. An older adult starting long-term high-dose glucocorticoids with osteopenia is at high fracture risk, so pharmacologic prophylaxis is started at the same time as the glucocorticoid. An oral bisphosphonate such as alendronate is first-line; intravenous zoledronic acid, denosumab or teriparatide are alternatives in selected patients.

Takeaway: Long-term glucocorticoids plus high fracture risk: start a bisphosphonate along with calcium and vitamin D.

whyNot.A: Calcitonin has weak anti-fracture effect and is not recommended for glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis.
whyNot.C: Raloxifene has not been shown to prevent glucocorticoid-induced fractures and increases thrombosis risk.
whyNot.D: Most bone loss occurs in the first months of treatment, so waiting 2 years would miss the window to prevent it.
whyNot.E: Testosterone is not used for bone protection in women.

items.objective: Start bisphosphonate prophylaxis in a patient at high fracture risk who begins long-term glucocorticoids.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man with Crohn disease has been in remission on infliximab every 8 weeks for 2 years. He has had chickenpox in childhood. He asks about vaccination against shingles because his brother recently had it. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: Give live attenuated zoster vaccine after stopping infliximab for 3 months

options.label: B
options.html: Give live attenuated zoster vaccine now

options.label: C
options.html: Give recombinant adjuvanted zoster vaccine now

options.label: E
options.html: Shingles vaccination is not recommended for him

items.explanationHtml:
Live vaccines are contraindicated during biologic therapy, but the recombinant adjuvanted zoster vaccine is not live and can be given safely. It is recommended for adults 50 and older and for adults 19 and older who are or will be immunocompromised by disease or therapy, including TNF inhibitors, as two doses 2–6 months apart (the interval can be shortened to 1–2 months in immunocompromised patients). Stopping effective therapy for a live vaccine is not necessary.

Takeaway: Immunosuppressed adults (including on TNF inhibitors) can and should get the non-live recombinant zoster vaccine.

whyNot.A: Interrupting effective therapy risks a Crohn flare, and a non-live vaccine is available.
whyNot.B: Live vaccines are contraindicated while he takes infliximab.
whyNot.D: Varicella-zoster immune globulin is post-exposure prophylaxis for nonimmune people, and he is immune.
whyNot.E: Adults 19 and older who are immunocompromised by therapy are recommended to receive recombinant zoster vaccine.

items.objective: Recommend recombinant zoster vaccine for adults immunosuppressed by biologic therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of confusion and fever for 2 days. He returned 10 days ago from a 3-week business trip to Ghana and did not take chemoprophylaxis. Temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F), pulse is 118/min, and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. He is oriented to person but not to place or time and has neck suppleness without focal deficits. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, a platelet count of 48,000/mm3, glucose 54 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.1 mg/dL. A thin blood smear shows many erythrocytes containing two or more delicate ring forms, and about 9% of red cells are parasitized. Which of the following best explains his neurologic findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Adhesion of infected erythrocytes to cerebral venules

options.label: B
options.html: Direct invasion of neurons by merozoites

options.label: C
options.html: Immune complex vasculitis of cerebral arteries

items.explanationHtml:
High parasitemia with multiple rings per cell in a traveller from sub-Saharan Africa indicates Plasmodium falciparum. Mature-stage infected red cells express the parasite protein PfEMP1 on surface knobs. PfEMP1 binds endothelial receptors such as ICAM-1 and EPCR, so trophozoites and schizonts sequester in post-capillary venules of the brain, kidney, gut and placenta. Sequestration obstructs microvascular flow, causes local hypoxia and endothelial activation, and lets the parasite avoid splenic clearance; this is why only ring forms circulate.

Takeaway: cerebral malaria results from PfEMP1-mediated cytoadherence and sequestration of P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes in cerebral microvessels.

whyNot.B: Plasmodium merozoites invade only erythrocytes; they do not infect neurons or glia.
whyNot.C: Malaria can cause immune complex glomerulopathy (P. malariae), but cerebral malaria is not an arteritis.
whyNot.D: Hypnozoites belong to P. vivax and P. ovale and cause late relapse, not acute coma with high parasitemia.
whyNot.E: He has not received heparin; the thrombocytopenia of malaria reflects splenic sequestration and consumption.

items.objective: Explain how cytoadherence of P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes produces cerebral malaria.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of recurrent fevers every 48 hours for 1 week. Eight months ago she worked for 4 months on a forestry project in rural Papua New Guinea and took doxycycline prophylaxis throughout her stay and for 4 weeks after return. Temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F). The spleen tip is palpable. A thin blood smear shows enlarged erythrocytes containing amoeboid trophozoites and fine red stippling of the red cell membrane. Infection of erythrocytes by this species depends mainly on binding to which of the following red cell surface molecules?
items.explanationHtml:
A relapse months after leaving an endemic area despite doxycycline (which kills blood-stage, not liver hypnozoite, parasites), enlarged red cells, amoeboid trophozoites and Schüffner stippling point to Plasmodium vivax. P. vivax merozoites bind the Duffy antigen receptor for chemokines (DARC) through the Duffy-binding protein, and the species prefers young red cells (reticulocytes). People whose red cells lack Duffy antigen are largely resistant to P. vivax.

Takeaway: P. vivax invades reticulocytes through the Duffy antigen; its hypnozoites explain relapse after blood-stage prophylaxis.

whyNot.A: Band 3 is a binding partner in some P. falciparum invasion pathways, not the essential receptor for this species.
whyNot.C: Globoside is the receptor for parvovirus B19, which infects erythroid progenitors.
whyNot.D: Glycophorin A is used by P. falciparum, whose invasion is redundant across several receptors.
whyNot.E: Rh D has no known role as a malaria invasion receptor.

items.objective: Identify the Duffy antigen as the erythrocyte receptor used by Plasmodium vivax.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man comes to a travel clinic 3 days after returning from Haiti with fever, headache and myalgias. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 104/min, and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. He is alert, and there is no jaundice. A thin blood smear shows occasional ring forms in about 0.5% of erythrocytes, with no schizonts. He is treated with an oral drug that accumulates in the acidic food vacuole of the intraerythrocytic parasite. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism by which this drug kills the parasite?

options.label: A
options.html: Blockade of heme polymerization to hemozoin

options.label: B
options.html: Generation of free radicals by endoperoxide cleavage

items.explanationHtml:
Uncomplicated malaria acquired in Haiti, where P. falciparum remains chloroquine sensitive, can be treated with chloroquine. Chloroquine is a weak base that is trapped in the acidic digestive vacuole. There, the parasite digests hemoglobin and must detoxify the released heme by polymerizing it into inert hemozoin. Chloroquine binds heme and caps the growing polymer, so free heme accumulates and damages parasite membranes. Resistance (PfCRT transporter mutations) pumps the drug out of the vacuole.

Takeaway: chloroquine kills blood-stage parasites by preventing detoxification of heme into hemozoin.

whyNot.B: Endoperoxide activation is the mechanism of artemisinins such as artesunate, which do not act by concentrating in the vacuole as a weak base.
whyNot.C: Pyrimethamine and proguanil inhibit parasite dihydrofolate reductase; chloroquine does not.
whyNot.D: Atovaquone inhibits the parasite cytochrome bc1 complex and electron transport.
whyNot.E: Doxycycline binds the 30S subunit (of the apicoplast) and is too slow to use alone for acute malaria.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism of action of chloroquine against blood-stage Plasmodium.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man comes to the emergency department in August because of fever, fatigue and dark urine for 5 days. He underwent splenectomy after a car crash 20 years ago. He lives on an island off the coast of Massachusetts and gardens daily. He has not travelled outside the United States. Temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), pulse is 102/min, and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. Mild scleral icterus is present. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, a platelet count of 82,000/mm3, and total bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL. The peripheral blood smear is shown. Which of the following is the most likely vector of this infection?
items.explanationHtml:
Intraerythrocytic ring forms, some arranged as a tetrad (a cross of four merozoites), with no pigment or gametocytes, in an asplenic older adult from coastal New England in summer indicate babesiosis caused by Babesia microti. The parasite is transmitted by the blacklegged tick Ixodes scapularis, the same vector that carries Borrelia burgdorferi and Anaplasma phagocytophilum, so co-infection occurs. Transfusion of red cells is a second route. Asplenia, older age and immunosuppression predispose to high parasitemia and hemolysis.

Takeaway: intraerythrocytic rings and tetrads without pigment in a tick-exposed, asplenic patient mean Babesia, transmitted by Ixodes ticks.

whyNot.A: Aedes mosquitoes transmit dengue, Zika and chikungunya, none of which produce intraerythrocytic parasites.
whyNot.B: Anopheles transmits malaria, which is not acquired in Massachusetts; Plasmodium also produces pigment and gametocytes.
whyNot.C: The body louse transmits Bartonella quintana and epidemic typhus, which do not parasitize red cells as tetrads.
whyNot.E: Sandflies transmit Leishmania and Bartonella bacilliformis; neither fits a New England summer infection.

items.objective: Identify the vector of Babesia microti from its smear appearance and epidemiology.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of pallor and fatigue for 4 days. Ten days ago he had a low-grade fever and runny nose. He has hereditary spherocytosis, and his usual hemoglobin is 10.5 g/dL with reticulocytes 8%. Temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), and pulse is 128/min. He is pale, and the spleen is palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 5.6 g/dL, MCV 84 fL, and reticulocytes 0.1% of red cells (0.5-1.5%); leukocyte and platelet counts are normal. Which of the following cells is most likely infected by the causative agent?
items.explanationHtml:
A transient aplastic crisis in a child with chronic hemolysis after a viral prodrome is classically caused by parvovirus B19. The virus uses globoside (P antigen) as its receptor and replicates in dividing erythroid progenitors (BFU-E/CFU-E and pronormoblasts), causing cytolysis and a 1-2 week pause in erythropoiesis. In healthy people this pause is not noticed, but when red cell survival is only days to weeks, hemoglobin falls sharply. The marrow shows giant pronormoblasts with nuclear inclusions.

Takeaway: parvovirus B19 infects erythroid progenitors; with chronic hemolysis this causes aplastic crisis with reticulocytopenia.

whyNot.B: Hepatocyte infection (as in hepatitis viruses) does not suppress red cell production selectively.
whyNot.C: Mature red cells lack the replication machinery the virus needs; the defect is in production, as the reticulocytopenia shows.
whyNot.D: Platelet counts are normal, which argues against a megakaryocyte-targeted process.
whyNot.E: Increased splenic sequestration would raise, not suppress, the reticulocyte count.

items.objective: Identify erythroid progenitors as the target of parvovirus B19 in aplastic crisis.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 21 weeks' gestation comes for a scheduled ultrasound. Three weeks ago she had a symmetric arthralgia of the hands and wrists that resolved; her 4-year-old son had bright red cheeks and a lacy rash on his arms at about the same time. Vital signs are normal. Ultrasonography shows fetal ascites, pleural effusions and scalp edema. Doppler study shows an increased peak systolic velocity in the fetal middle cerebral artery. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of the fetal findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Alloimmune destruction of fetal red cells

options.label: C
options.html: High-output cardiac failure from fetal anemia

options.label: D
options.html: Lymphatic obstruction from a cystic hygroma

items.explanationHtml:
Erythema infectiosum in her son and maternal arthropathy indicate parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy. The virus crosses the placenta and infects fetal erythroid progenitors at a time when fetal red cell mass is expanding and red cell life span is short. Severe fetal anemia (detected by a raised middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity) leads to high-output cardiac failure, and myocarditis can add to it, producing nonimmune hydrops fetalis. Risk is greatest when infection occurs before about 20 weeks.

Takeaway: parvovirus B19 causes nonimmune hydrops fetalis through severe fetal anemia and high-output heart failure.

whyNot.A: Rh or other alloimmunization causes fetal anemia, but the maternal and sibling viral illness points to infection, not maternal antibodies.
whyNot.B: Hepatic involvement is not the main driver; the raised MCA velocity indicates anemia.
whyNot.D: Cystic hygroma with hydrops suggests aneuploidy such as Turner syndrome and does not raise MCA velocity.
whyNot.E: Placental insufficiency causes growth restriction and reduced flow, not anemia-related hydrops.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of hydrops fetalis caused by maternal parvovirus B19 infection.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of fever, headache and myalgias for 4 days. He lives in rural Arkansas and removed a tick from his thigh 10 days ago. Temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 120/74 mm Hg. There is no rash. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 2,300/mm3, a platelet count of 64,000/mm3, sodium 131 mEq/L, AST 142 U/L, and ALT 128 U/L. A blood smear shows mulberry-like cytoplasmic inclusions in monocytes. The most appropriate drug for this infection acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Binding to the 30S subunit, blocking aminoacyl-tRNA entry

options.label: B
options.html: Binding to the 50S subunit, blocking peptide translocation

items.explanationHtml:
Fever after a tick bite in the south-central United States with leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia, raised transaminases and morulae in monocytes indicates human monocytic ehrlichiosis due to Ehrlichia chaffeensis, transmitted by the lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum). Doxycycline is the drug of choice for all ages. It binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and prevents aminoacyl-tRNA from binding the acceptor (A) site, stopping protein synthesis. Treatment starts on clinical suspicion, without waiting for confirmation.

Takeaway: ehrlichiosis is treated with doxycycline, a 30S inhibitor that blocks aminoacyl-tRNA binding.

whyNot.B: This is the mechanism of macrolides, which are not effective treatment for ehrlichiosis.
whyNot.C: Beta-lactams act on cell wall synthesis; Ehrlichia lives inside host cell vacuoles, and beta-lactams do not treat it.
whyNot.D: Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase but are not recommended for ehrlichiosis.
whyNot.E: Rifampin inhibits RNA polymerase; it is an alternative mainly in pregnancy for anaplasmosis, not the drug of choice here.

items.objective: Relate the drug of choice for ehrlichiosis to its ribosomal mechanism.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician in June because of fever, chills, headache and muscle aches for 3 days. She lives in Wisconsin and hikes in wooded areas. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 126/80 mm Hg. Examination shows no rash, lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 2,900/mm3, a platelet count of 71,000/mm3, AST 96 U/L, and ALT 104 U/L. A buffy-coat smear shows clusters of small basophilic inclusions within the cytoplasm of neutrophils. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
items.explanationHtml:
Morulae within neutrophils in a febrile patient from the upper Midwest with leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases point to human granulocytic anaplasmosis. Anaplasma phagocytophilum is an obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacterium transmitted by Ixodes ticks. It lives in a host-derived vacuole in granulocytes. Doxycycline is the treatment.

Takeaway: morulae in neutrophils mean Anaplasma (Ixodes tick); morulae in monocytes mean Ehrlichia (lone star tick).

whyNot.B: Babesia parasitizes red cells, producing ring forms and tetrads, not inclusions in neutrophils.
whyNot.C: Lyme disease does not cause leukopenia, thrombocytopenia or intraleukocytic inclusions.
whyNot.D: E. chaffeensis forms morulae in monocytes and is transmitted mainly in the south-central and south-eastern United States.
whyNot.E: Rocky Mountain spotted fever infects endothelial cells and causes a petechial rash; it does not form morulae in neutrophils.

items.objective: Distinguish anaplasmosis from ehrlichiosis by the infected leukocyte and geography.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man who has been experiencing homelessness for 3 years is admitted with fever, fatigue and weight loss for 6 weeks. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 98/min, and blood pressure is 128/62 mm Hg. Examination shows excoriations over the trunk, body lice in the seams of his clothing, and a new diastolic murmur at the left sternal border. Echocardiography shows a vegetation on the aortic valve. Three sets of routine blood cultures show no growth after 5 days. Serology later shows high-titer antibodies against a fastidious Gram-negative bacillus. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
items.explanationHtml:
Subacute culture-negative endocarditis in a person with body lice indicates Bartonella quintana, a fastidious Gram-negative bacillus transmitted by louse feces scratched into the skin. It also causes trench fever (relapsing fever with shin pain) and bacillary angiomatosis in advanced HIV. Diagnosis rests on serology, PCR of valve tissue, or prolonged culture. Bartonella species are among the most frequent causes of culture-negative endocarditis.

Takeaway: body lice plus culture-negative endocarditis points to Bartonella quintana.

whyNot.B: Q fever causes culture-negative endocarditis after exposure to livestock birth products, not lice.
whyNot.C: Enterococci grow readily in routine blood cultures.
whyNot.D: Epidemic typhus is also louse-borne, but it causes acute fever with rash, not subacute endocarditis.
whyNot.E: S. gallolyticus grows in routine cultures and is linked to colorectal neoplasia, not lice.

items.objective: Identify Bartonella quintana as a louse-borne cause of culture-negative endocarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old college student is brought to the emergency department because of fever, confusion and a spreading rash for 8 hours. Temperature is 39.9°C (103.8°F), pulse is 138/min, and blood pressure is 78/40 mm Hg. Examination shows purpuric, non-blanching lesions over the trunk and legs, and oozing from venipuncture sites. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 31,000/mm3, prothrombin time 24 s, aPTT 58 s, fibrinogen 74 mg/dL (200-400 mg/dL), and markedly increased D-dimer. A blood smear shows schistocytes. Gram stain of blood shows Gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following most directly initiates this patient's coagulopathy?

options.label: C
options.html: Hepatic failure with decreased factor synthesis

options.label: D
options.html: Tissue factor expression by monocytes and endothelium

options.label: E
options.html: Vitamin K deficiency from poor intake

items.explanationHtml:
Meningococcemia with shock, purpura and bleeding, low platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged PT and aPTT, high D-dimer and schistocytes is disseminated intravascular coagulation. Endotoxin (lipooligosaccharide) and cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF-α induce tissue factor on monocytes and endothelial cells. Tissue factor with factor VIIa starts the extrinsic pathway throughout the microcirculation, while natural anticoagulants (antithrombin, protein C) are consumed and fibrinolysis is suppressed by PAI-1. Microthrombi consume platelets and factors, and secondary fibrinolysis raises D-dimer.

Takeaway: in sepsis-associated DIC, cytokine- and endotoxin-induced tissue factor triggers widespread thrombin generation and consumption.

whyNot.A: PF4 antibodies cause heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which does not prolong PT and aPTT or deplete fibrinogen.
whyNot.B: ADAMTS13 deficiency (TTP) causes microangiopathy with normal PT, aPTT and fibrinogen.
whyNot.C: Liver failure lowers factors but does not cause schistocytes, raised D-dimer and an acute fall in platelets with septic shock.
whyNot.E: Vitamin K deficiency prolongs PT first and does not cause thrombocytopenia, hypofibrinogenemia or schistocytes.

items.objective: Explain the initiating mechanism of disseminated intravascular coagulation in Gram-negative sepsis.

items.stemHtml: An 18-year-old woman comes to the student health clinic because of sore throat, fever and fatigue for 6 days. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F). Examination shows tonsillar enlargement with grey exudate, palatal petechiae, tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and a spleen tip palpable on deep inspiration. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 14,200/mm3 with 62% lymphocytes, many of which are large cells with abundant pale-blue cytoplasm that indents around neighbouring red cells. A heterophile antibody test is positive. The large atypical cells in her blood are most likely which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: B lymphocytes transformed by the virus

items.explanationHtml:
Infectious mononucleosis from Epstein-Barr virus begins with infection of oropharyngeal epithelium and B cells (via CD21). The atypical (reactive) lymphocytes in blood are mostly activated CD8+ cytotoxic T cells that proliferate to kill EBV-infected B cells. Their abundant cytoplasm scallops around adjacent red cells on the smear. This T-cell response, rather than the virus itself, drives the fever, lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly.

Takeaway: the atypical lymphocytes of mononucleosis are reactive CD8+ T cells, not infected B cells.

whyNot.A: Infected B cells are few in the blood; the reactive cells are the T cells responding to them.
whyNot.C: Monocytes have folded nuclei and grey cytoplasm and are not the atypical lymphocytes of mononucleosis.
whyNot.D: NK cells expand modestly but are not the dominant atypical population.
whyNot.E: Plasma cells are rare in blood and have eccentric nuclei with a perinuclear clearing.

items.objective: Identify the reactive CD8+ T cell as the atypical lymphocyte of EBV mononucleosis.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of fever, sore throat and fatigue for 1 week. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F). There is exudative pharyngitis, bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and mild splenomegaly. A rapid latex agglutination test of his serum is positive. The test detects antibodies that agglutinate horse erythrocytes but do not react with antigens of the causative virus. Which of the following best describes the antibodies detected by this test?

options.label: A
options.html: IgA directed against viral capsid antigen

options.label: B
options.html: IgE released after mast cell sensitization

options.label: C
options.html: IgG directed against Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen

options.label: D
options.html: IgG produced by long-lived plasma cells

options.label: E
options.html: IgM produced by polyclonally activated B cells

items.explanationHtml:
The monospot detects heterophile antibodies: IgM antibodies that agglutinate sheep or horse red cells but are not directed at EBV antigens. They arise because EBV polyclonally activates infected B cells, which secrete a range of antibodies, including these cross-reacting ones. The test can be negative in the first week of illness and in children younger than about 4 years; EBV-specific serology (VCA IgM, VCA IgG, EBNA) is used then.

Takeaway: heterophile antibodies are non-EBV-specific IgM from polyclonal B-cell activation.

whyNot.A: Antibodies to viral capsid antigen are EBV-specific and are measured by separate serology.
whyNot.B: IgE is not involved in the heterophile response.
whyNot.C: Anti-EBNA IgG is EBV-specific and appears weeks to months later, marking past infection.
whyNot.D: The heterophile antibodies are transient and wane over months, unlike long-lived IgG.

items.objective: Describe the nature and origin of heterophile antibodies in EBV infection.

items.stemHtml: A 20-year-old college football player is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after being tackled during practice. He was diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis 2 weeks ago. He reports severe left upper quadrant abdominal pain and pain at the tip of the left shoulder. Pulse is 124/min, and blood pressure is 92/58 mm Hg. The abdomen is tender in the left upper quadrant with guarding. Movement of the left shoulder is full and painless. Focused ultrasonography shows free intraperitoneal fluid. Which of the following nerves carries the afferent fibres responsible for his shoulder pain?
items.explanationHtml:
Splenic rupture is a feared complication of mononucleosis, most likely in the first 3-4 weeks while the spleen is enlarged and its capsule is stretched; it can follow minor trauma. Blood beneath the left hemidiaphragm irritates the diaphragmatic peritoneum, whose sensory supply is the phrenic nerve (C3-C5). Pain is referred to the C4 dermatome at the shoulder tip (Kehr sign).

Takeaway: shoulder-tip pain from splenic rupture is referred through the phrenic nerve (C3-C5).

whyNot.A: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and the skin over it; it carries no diaphragmatic sensation.
whyNot.B: Splanchnic visceral afferents give poorly localized abdominal pain, not shoulder-tip pain.
whyNot.D: The suprascapular nerve supplies the shoulder joint and rotator cuff, which are normal on examination.
whyNot.E: Vagal afferents carry visceral sensation that is not referred to the shoulder.

items.objective: Explain referred shoulder-tip pain after splenic rupture in mononucleosis.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old man comes to the physician because of fever, fatigue and malaise for 2 weeks. He has mild sore throat but no exudate. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F). There is minimal cervical lymphadenopathy and no splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 9,800/mm3 with 55% lymphocytes, 18% of which are atypical; AST is 88 U/L and ALT is 102 U/L. A heterophile antibody test is negative on two occasions. HIV-1/2 antigen-antibody and HIV RNA tests are negative. IgM antibodies against a double-stranded DNA herpesvirus are present. After recovery, this virus will most likely persist in a latent state in which of the following cells?
items.explanationHtml:
Heterophile-negative mononucleosis with atypical lymphocytes and mild hepatitis, after acute HIV is excluded, is most often caused by cytomegalovirus. Compared with EBV, CMV mononucleosis tends to occur in somewhat older adults and has less pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy. CMV establishes latency in CD34+ myeloid progenitors and monocytes; reactivation occurs as monocytes differentiate into macrophages and during immunosuppression. Latency in leukocytes is why CMV is transmitted by non-leukoreduced blood products and transplanted organs.

Takeaway: CMV, a cause of heterophile-negative mononucleosis, stays latent in monocytes and myeloid progenitors.

whyNot.A: Sensory ganglion neurons are the latency site of HSV-1, HSV-2 and varicella-zoster virus.
whyNot.B: Hepatocytes are infected during the acute illness but are not the latent reservoir.
whyNot.C: Memory B cells are the latency site of EBV, which is unlikely given repeatedly negative heterophile tests.
whyNot.E: Epithelial cells support lytic replication rather than long-term latency.

items.objective: Identify the latency site of cytomegalovirus after heterophile-negative mononucleosis.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a painless lump in the back of her neck for 5 weeks. She feels mildly tired. She recently adopted two kittens and enjoys rare steak. She is not pregnant. Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F). There are three mobile, non-tender, 1.5-cm lymph nodes in the left posterior cervical chain; there is no hepatosplenomegaly. Excisional biopsy of one node shows reactive follicular hyperplasia, small clusters of epithelioid histiocytes within and around germinal centres, and sinuses distended by monocytoid B cells. No granulomatous necrosis is present. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
items.explanationHtml:
Toxoplasmic lymphadenitis is the commonest clinical form of acute toxoplasmosis in immunocompetent adults: non-tender posterior cervical nodes with mild fatigue after contact with cat feces or ingestion of undercooked meat. The node shows a characteristic triad: florid follicular hyperplasia, small epithelioid histiocyte clusters that encroach on germinal centres, and monocytoid B-cell expansion of sinuses. Diagnosis is by serology (IgM and IgG, with IgG avidity to time infection). Immunocompetent, non-pregnant adults usually need no treatment.

Takeaway: follicular hyperplasia, epithelioid histiocyte clusters and monocytoid B cells in a posterior cervical node suggest toxoplasmosis.

whyNot.A: Cat-scratch disease produces necrotizing granulomas with central neutrophilic microabscesses, which are absent.
whyNot.B: EBV mononucleosis expands the paracortex with immunoblasts and causes pharyngitis and atypical lymphocytes.
whyNot.C: Tularemia causes a painful ulcer and suppurative, necrotizing lymphadenitis after rabbit or tick exposure.
whyNot.D: Tuberculous lymphadenitis shows caseating granulomas.

items.objective: Recognize the lymph node pattern and exposures of acute toxoplasmic lymphadenitis.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a tender swelling in his right armpit for 2 weeks. Three weeks ago, a small red papule appeared on the back of his right hand where the family's new kitten had scratched him. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). There is a healing 4-mm crusted papule on the dorsum of the right hand and a 3-cm tender, mobile right axillary lymph node with overlying erythema. Biopsy of the node shows necrotizing granulomas with stellate microabscesses containing neutrophils; a silver stain shows clumps of small pleomorphic bacilli. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
items.explanationHtml:
Cat-scratch disease is caused by Bartonella henselae, carried by young cats and their fleas. An inoculation papule appears 3-10 days after a scratch, followed 1-3 weeks later by tender regional lymphadenopathy draining that site. Histology shows necrotizing granulomas with stellate microabscesses; organisms are seen with Warthin-Starry silver stain. Serology or PCR confirms. Most cases resolve over weeks to months; azithromycin can shorten extensive lymphadenopathy.

Takeaway: regional adenitis weeks after a kitten scratch, with stellate necrotizing granulomas, means Bartonella henselae.

whyNot.B: Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis affects the head and neck of young children and shows acid-fast bacilli, not a cat scratch with silver-staining bacilli.
whyNot.C: Pasteurella causes rapid cellulitis within a day of a cat bite, not regional adenitis weeks later.
whyNot.D: Sporotrichosis follows plant or soil inoculation and spreads as nodules along lymphatics; it is a fungus.
whyNot.E: Toxoplasmosis causes non-tender nodes without necrotizing granulomas or bacilli.

items.objective: Identify Bartonella henselae from the history and node histology of cat-scratch disease.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a painless lump under her right jaw for 5 weeks. She has had no fever, weight loss or night sweats. Her immunizations are up to date, and she has had no contact with anyone with a chronic cough. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F). There is a 2.5-cm firm, non-tender submandibular node with thin, violaceous overlying skin; the rest of the examination is normal. An interferon-gamma release assay is negative. Excision of the node shows caseating granulomas, and culture grows a slow-growing acid-fast organism that does not belong to the tuberculosis complex. Which of the following is the most likely route by which she acquired this infection?

options.label: A
options.html: Hematogenous spread from a pulmonary focus

options.label: C
options.html: Inhalation of droplets from an adult with cavitary disease

options.label: D
options.html: Invasion through the oropharyngeal mucosa from the environment

items.explanationHtml:
Chronic, painless, unilateral cervicofacial adenitis in a well toddler with violaceous thinning skin and a negative interferon-gamma release assay is typical of nontuberculous mycobacterial lymphadenitis, usually Mycobacterium avium complex. Young children acquire these environmental organisms from soil, dust and water, which enter through the oropharyngeal mucosa or tonsils and drain to regional nodes. Complete surgical excision is both diagnostic and the most effective treatment; incision and drainage risks a chronic draining sinus.

Takeaway: nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis in toddlers comes from the environment through oropharyngeal mucosa, and excision is curative.

whyNot.A: A pulmonary primary focus with hematogenous spread would give systemic illness and lung findings, which she lacks.
whyNot.B: Milk-borne Mycobacterium bovis classically causes cervical adenitis but is rare where milk is pasteurized and would not grow as an environmental species.
whyNot.C: Droplet transmission applies to M. tuberculosis; she has no contact and a negative interferon-gamma release assay.
whyNot.E: Congenital mycobacterial infection presents in the neonatal period with disseminated disease.

items.objective: Contrast the acquisition of nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis with tuberculous lymphadenitis.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old gardener comes to the physician because of a red streak on his forearm for 1 day. Two days ago he scratched the back of his right hand on a rose thorn. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F). There is a tender erythematous linear streak running up the medial forearm from a small crusted wound on the hand, and tender swelling in the right axilla. Which of the following best explains the linear erythematous streak?

options.label: A
options.html: Bacterial spread within superficial lymphatic channels

options.label: B
options.html: Deep venous thrombosis of the forearm

options.label: D
options.html: Granulomatous nodules along a lymphatic pathway

items.explanationHtml:
Acute lymphangitis follows inoculation of bacteria (usually Streptococcus pyogenes, sometimes Staphylococcus aureus) into a skin break. The organisms travel in superficial lymphatic vessels toward the regional nodes, producing a tender erythematous streak from the wound proximally plus regional lymphadenitis. Upper limb lymphatics follow the superficial veins and drain mostly to axillary nodes. Treatment is an antistreptococcal antibiotic; failure to improve suggests abscess or a resistant organism.

Takeaway: a tender red streak from a wound to the regional nodes is lymphangitis, usually streptococcal, spreading in superficial lymphatics.

whyNot.B: Deep venous thrombosis produces diffuse limb swelling rather than a tender linear streak from a wound.
whyNot.C: Neoplastic lymphatic infiltration produces firm, non-tender indurated plaques over weeks, not an acute febrile streak.
whyNot.D: Chains of granulomatous nodules suggest sporotrichosis, which develops over weeks as discrete subcutaneous nodules.
whyNot.E: Superficial thrombophlebitis follows a palpable cord in a vein, commonly after cannulation, and is not preceded by a distal wound with fever.

items.objective: Explain the anatomic basis of acute lymphangitis and its regional nodal drainage.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man has enlarged, mildly tender cervical lymph nodes 10 days after an acute febrile illness with pharyngitis and fatigue. One node is biopsied because a mass lesion was suspected clinically. Histologic examination shows preserved nodal architecture with marked expansion of the interfollicular region by a mixture of small lymphocytes and large cells with vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli, scattered mitoses, and prominent high endothelial venules; germinal centres are present but not enlarged. Expansion of which of the following nodal compartments best accounts for these findings?
items.explanationHtml:
The paracortex is the T-cell zone of the lymph node, containing high endothelial venules through which lymphocytes enter. Viral infections, especially EBV, drive T-cell activation and produce paracortical (interfollicular) hyperplasia with immunoblasts, sometimes alarming enough to mimic lymphoma. Preserved overall architecture, a polymorphous mixture and prominent high endothelial venules favour a reactive process. Follicular hyperplasia instead indicates B-cell responses, and sinus histiocytosis indicates drainage of particulate material or adjacent tumour.

Takeaway: viral lymphadenitis causes paracortical (T-zone) hyperplasia with immunoblasts and preserved architecture.

whyNot.A: Capsular expansion occurs with fibrosis or metastatic infiltration, not with reactive immunoblasts.
whyNot.B: Medullary cord expansion reflects plasma cell proliferation, as in chronic antigenic stimulation.
whyNot.D: Follicular (germinal centre) hyperplasia is the B-cell pattern and is described here as not enlarged.
whyNot.E: Sinus histiocytosis widens the sinuses with macrophages, typically near a tumour or in drainage of inflammation.

items.objective: Match reactive lymph node patterns to the compartment and immune cell involved.

items.stemHtml: A 2-year-old boy is admitted because of fever for 10 days, irritability and abdominal distention. Temperature is 39.5°C (103.1°F), pulse is 150/min, and blood pressure is 80/45 mm Hg. The liver edge is 4 cm and the spleen 5 cm below the costal margins. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 1,800/mm3, a platelet count of 42,000/mm3, triglycerides 410 mg/dL, fibrinogen 95 mg/dL (200-400 mg/dL), and ferritin 12,400 ng/mL (30-300 ng/mL). Bone marrow aspiration shows macrophages that contain intact erythrocytes and lymphocytes. Genetic testing shows a homozygous loss-of-function variant in PRF1. Which of the following best explains the sustained inflammation in this patient?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibody-mediated clearance of blood cells by splenic macrophages

options.label: B
options.html: Clonal proliferation of macrophages carrying an activating kinase mutation

options.label: C
options.html: Failure of cytotoxic killing leading to persistent T-cell and macrophage activation

options.label: D
options.html: Impaired neutrophil oxidative burst with granuloma formation

options.label: E
options.html: Loss of regulatory T cells with multiorgan autoantibody production

items.explanationHtml:
Familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis follows biallelic defects in the granule-dependent cytotoxic pathway; PRF1 encodes perforin. Cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells engage targets but cannot kill them, so the immune synapse persists and antigen is never cleared. The activated T cells pour out interferon-gamma, which drives macrophage activation with IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α and ferritin release; activated macrophages ingest blood cells. Consumptive coagulopathy, high triglycerides (TNF-mediated lipoprotein lipase inhibition), cytopenias and a raised soluble CD25 follow. Untreated, it is fatal; treatment suppresses the T-cell/macrophage loop and is followed by hematopoietic cell transplantation in familial disease.

Takeaway: HLH arises when defective cytotoxic killing leaves T cells and macrophages chronically activated, with interferon-gamma as the central cytokine.

whyNot.A: Autoimmune cytopenias give a positive direct antiglobulin test and do not produce hyperferritinemia with hypofibrinogenemia and hemophagocytosis.
whyNot.B: A clonal histiocytic neoplasm (such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis) produces lytic bone lesions and skin disease rather than this hyperinflammatory picture.
whyNot.D: Defective oxidative burst causes recurrent catalase-positive infections and granulomas, not hemophagocytosis with high ferritin.
whyNot.E: Regulatory T-cell failure causes early autoimmune enteropathy and endocrinopathy, not cytopenias with hemophagocytosis.

items.objective: Explain how impaired cytotoxic granule function produces the hyperinflammation of HLH.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy with no significant medical history is admitted with 2 weeks of fever, sore throat and progressive fatigue. Temperature is 39.1°C (102.4°F). There is cervical lymphadenopathy and a spleen palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 2,100/mm3, a platelet count of 38,000/mm3, AST 310 U/L, ALT 275 U/L, ferritin 9,800 ng/mL (30-300 ng/mL), fibrinogen 110 mg/dL (200-400 mg/dL), and soluble CD25 markedly increased. Epstein-Barr virus DNA is detected in plasma at a high level. Which of the following cell populations is most likely driving his illness?

options.label: C
options.html: Mast cells releasing histamine and tryptase

options.label: E
options.html: Virus-transformed B lymphocytes forming sheets of blasts

items.explanationHtml:
This is secondary (acquired) hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis triggered by Epstein-Barr virus, the commonest infectious trigger. Whatever the trigger, the final common pathway is unrestrained activation of T lymphocytes that secrete interferon-gamma, which activates macrophages to produce ferritin and inflammatory cytokines. A high soluble CD25 (soluble IL-2 receptor) reflects T-cell activation, and ferritin above several thousand ng/mL with cytopenias, hypofibrinogenemia and splenomegaly supports the diagnosis. Other triggers include other herpesviruses, lymphoma (especially T-cell and NK-cell), and rheumatic disease (macrophage activation syndrome). Treatment addresses both the trigger and the immune activation.

Takeaway: secondary HLH is driven by interferon-gamma-secreting T cells; EBV is the classic trigger and soluble CD25 and ferritin are markers.

whyNot.A: Plasma cell neoplasia causes a monoclonal protein and bone disease, not hyperferritinemic cytopenias in an adolescent.
whyNot.C: Mast cell activation causes flushing, hypotension and raised tryptase, not cytopenias with hemophagocytosis.
whyNot.D: Neutrophil activation does not explain the extreme hyperferritinemia and low fibrinogen, and he is neutropenic.
whyNot.E: A monomorphic B-cell proliferation would be a lymphoma; the laboratory picture here is that of hemophagocytic syndrome.

items.objective: Identify activated interferon-gamma-producing T cells as the driver of EBV-triggered secondary HLH.

items.stemHtml: An 8-year-old girl with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis maintained on an interleukin-1 inhibitor is admitted because of unremitting fever for 5 days and new confusion. Temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F). She had been having daily spiking fevers with an evanescent rash before treatment. Laboratory studies now show hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 3,000/mm3, a platelet count of 65,000/mm3 (previously 520,000/mm3), ferritin 28,000 ng/mL (30-300 ng/mL), fibrinogen 90 mg/dL (200-400 mg/dL), triglycerides 380 mg/dL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate that has fallen from 85 to 12 mm/h. Which of the following best explains the fall in her erythrocyte sedimentation rate?

options.label: A
options.html: Consumption of fibrinogen by intravascular coagulation

options.label: D
options.html: Reduced red cell mass from hemolysis

options.label: E
options.html: Suppression of acute-phase protein gene transcription

items.explanationHtml:
A patient with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis who develops unremitting fever, falling platelet and leukocyte counts, extreme hyperferritinemia and encephalopathy has macrophage activation syndrome, the rheumatic form of secondary HLH. Consumptive coagulopathy depletes fibrinogen, and because the erythrocyte sedimentation rate depends on fibrinogen-driven rouleaux, it falls even as C-reactive protein and ferritin rise. A paradoxically falling sedimentation rate with a falling platelet count in an otherwise highly inflammatory illness is an important clue.

Takeaway: in macrophage activation syndrome, fibrinogen consumption lowers the ESR while ferritin and CRP rise.

whyNot.B: Leukocyte numbers have little effect on the erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
whyNot.C: Hypertriglyceridemia does not reduce rouleaux formation enough to normalize the sedimentation rate.
whyNot.D: Anemia if anything raises the measured sedimentation rate.
whyNot.E: Acute-phase signalling is maximal here; ferritin, itself an acute-phase protein, is extremely high.

items.objective: Explain the dissociation between ESR and other inflammatory markers in macrophage activation syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man with HIV infection who has not taken antiretroviral therapy for 2 years is admitted because of fever, night sweats and fatigue for 6 weeks. Temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F). There is generalized lymphadenopathy and a spleen palpable 6 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL, a platelet count of 88,000/mm3, albumin 2.4 g/dL, C-reactive protein 180 mg/L, and a polyclonal increase in serum immunoglobulins; CD4+ count is 70/mm3. Lymph node biopsy shows atrophic germinal centres penetrated by hyalinized vessels, expanded mantle zones, and sheets of plasmablasts in the interfollicular region that stain for human herpesvirus 8 latency-associated nuclear antigen. Which of the following cytokines most directly accounts for his fever, anemia, hypoalbuminemia and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia?
items.explanationHtml:
HHV-8-associated multicentric Castleman disease occurs mainly in people with uncontrolled HIV infection.
