HHV-8-infected plasmablasts produce a viral homolog of interleukin-6 and drive host IL-6 production. IL-6 causes fever, hepcidin-mediated anemia of inflammation, a high C-reactive protein, hypoalbuminemia, and B-cell stimulation with polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia; nodes show hyaline-vascular and plasmacytic features. Treatment includes antiretroviral therapy and rituximab for the HHV-8-driven form; the IL-6-directed antibody siltuximab is used in idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease.

Takeaway: Castleman disease is an IL-6-driven lymphoproliferation; the multicentric form in HIV is caused by HHV-8.

whyNot.A: IL-10 is raised in this disease but is immunosuppressive and does not drive the acute-phase response.
whyNot.B: IL-5 drives eosinophil production and is not responsible for this systemic inflammatory syndrome.
whyNot.D: TGF-β is immunosuppressive and profibrotic and does not cause this acute-phase picture.
whyNot.E: TNF-α contributes to inflammation but is not the dominant cytokine of this disease.

items.objective: Attribute the systemic features of multicentric Castleman disease to interleukin-6.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy has had large, non-tender cervical and axillary lymph nodes and a spleen palpable 5 cm below the costal margin since age 3 years. He has had two episodes of immune thrombocytopenia and one of autoimmune hemolytic anemia with a positive direct antiglobulin test. He has had no unusual infections. Laboratory studies show a raised serum vitamin B12 level, increased soluble FAS ligand, and an expanded population of circulating CD3+ T cells that express neither CD4 nor CD8 and carry the alpha-beta T-cell receptor. Repeated lymph node biopsies show reactive follicular and paracortical hyperplasia without clonal rearrangement. Which of the following cellular processes is most likely defective?

options.label: A
options.html: Antigen presentation on MHC class II molecules

options.label: B
options.html: Class switch recombination in germinal centre B cells

options.label: C
options.html: Extrinsic pathway apoptosis of activated lymphocytes

items.explanationHtml:
Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome is most often caused by heterozygous germline mutations in FAS (TNFRSF6). FAS-FASL signalling normally deletes activated lymphocytes after an immune response. When this extrinsic (death receptor) apoptosis pathway fails, lymphocytes accumulate, producing chronic non-malignant lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly from early childhood, autoimmune cytopenias, a raised vitamin B12 and soluble FAS ligand, and a characteristic expansion of alpha-beta double-negative (CD4−CD8−) T cells. Lymphoma risk is increased. Management is directed at the cytopenias; splenectomy is avoided where possible because of sepsis risk.

Takeaway: ALPS is a FAS-pathway apoptosis defect marked by double-negative alpha-beta T cells, lymphoproliferation and autoimmune cytopenias.

whyNot.A: Class II deficiency causes a severe combined immunodeficiency picture with infections, not autoimmune cytopenias with lymphoproliferation.
whyNot.B: Class switch defects cause hyper-IgM syndromes with infections and low IgG.
whyNot.D: Impaired phagocyte killing causes abscesses and granulomas, not a double-negative T-cell expansion.
whyNot.E: Failure of V(D)J recombination removes lymphocytes, causing severe combined immunodeficiency.

items.objective: Link defective FAS-mediated apoptosis to the findings of autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a scaly, greasy rash on the scalp and behind the ears for 3 months and a tender swelling of the skull for 2 weeks. He has also had increased thirst and urination. Temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F). There is seborrheic-appearing dermatitis of the scalp, several petechiae, and a 3-cm soft tender swelling over the right parietal bone. Skull radiographs show lytic lesions with sharply defined, non-sclerotic margins. Biopsy of the lesion shows sheets of mononuclear cells with grooved, reniform nuclei admixed with eosinophils; the cells stain for CD1a and langerin, and electron microscopy shows tennis-racket-shaped cytoplasmic granules. The neoplastic cells in this disorder are derived from which of the following lineages?

options.label: A
options.html: Follicular dendritic cells of germinal centres

items.explanationHtml:
Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a clonal neoplasm of myeloid dendritic cells; most cases carry activating MAP kinase pathway mutations, commonly BRAF V600E. The cells express CD1a, langerin (CD207) and S100, and contain Birbeck granules (tennis-racket-shaped) on electron microscopy. Multisystem disease in young children causes lytic bone lesions with punched-out margins, seborrheic-like skin disease, cytopenias from marrow involvement, and diabetes insipidus when the pituitary stalk is infiltrated. Treatment depends on whether risk organs (marrow, liver, spleen) are involved.

Takeaway: Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a CD1a/langerin-positive myeloid dendritic cell neoplasm with Birbeck granules and frequent BRAF V600E.

whyNot.A: Follicular dendritic cells are of mesenchymal origin and are CD21/CD35 positive, not CD1a positive.
whyNot.B: A B-cell neoplasm would express CD19/CD20 and would not contain Birbeck granules.
whyNot.C: Mesenchymal tumours of bone do not express CD1a or langerin.
whyNot.E: Thymic epithelium gives rise to thymoma, which does not present with lytic skull lesions and skin disease.

items.objective: Identify the cell of origin and markers of Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman comes to the physician because of tender swelling in the left side of her neck and low-grade fever for 3 weeks. She has lost 1 kg. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). There are two tender, 2-cm posterior cervical nodes; there is no rash, arthritis or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 3,400/mm3 and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 42 mm/h. Tests for Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, HIV and tuberculosis are negative, and antinuclear antibodies are not detected. Excisional biopsy shows paracortical patchy necrosis with abundant karyorrhectic debris, surrounded by crescentic histiocytes and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, with no neutrophils and no granulomas. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease (histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis) typically affects young adults with tender cervical lymphadenopathy, fever and sometimes leukopenia and a raised sedimentation rate. The node shows patchy paracortical necrosis full of karyorrhectic debris with crescentic histiocytes and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and a striking absence of neutrophils. It is self-limited over 1-4 months; supportive care or short courses of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs suffice, and corticosteroids are reserved for severe disease. Because lupus lymphadenitis is histologically similar, serologic follow-up is reasonable.

Takeaway: neutrophil-poor necrotizing lymphadenitis with karyorrhectic debris in a young adult is Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease, which resolves spontaneously.

whyNot.A: Cat-scratch disease shows stellate suppurative granulomas with neutrophils, which are absent.
whyNot.B: Hodgkin lymphoma shows Reed-Sternberg cells in a mixed inflammatory background, not karyorrhectic necrosis with crescentic histiocytes.
whyNot.D: Lupus lymphadenitis can look similar but features hematoxylin bodies and plentiful neutrophils, and antinuclear antibodies are absent here.
whyNot.E: Tuberculous adenitis shows caseating granulomas with giant cells and the tuberculosis tests are negative.

items.objective: Recognize the histology and natural history of Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a dry cough and fatigue for 2 months. Vital signs are normal, and lung auscultation is unremarkable. Chest radiography shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Mediastinal lymph node sampling shows tightly packed collections of epithelioid macrophages and multinucleated giant cells without central necrosis, rimmed by lymphocytes; stains and cultures for mycobacteria and fungi are negative. Which of the following best describes the immune mechanism forming these lesions?

options.label: A
options.html: CD4+ T-helper 1 cytokine signalling that activates macrophages

options.label: B
options.html: Immediate hypersensitivity with mast cell degranulation

options.label: C
options.html: Immune complex deposition with complement activation

options.label: E
options.html: Polyclonal B-cell activation with antibody-dependent cytotoxicity

items.explanationHtml:
Granuloma formation is a type IV (delayed, cell-mediated) hypersensitivity response. Antigen-presenting cells activate CD4+ T-helper 1 cells, which secrete interferon-gamma; interferon-gamma and TNF-α convert macrophages into epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells that aggregate into granulomas. In sarcoidosis the inciting antigen is unknown and the granulomas are non-necrotizing, which distinguishes them from the caseating granulomas of tuberculosis. Hilar adenopathy and lung involvement are the commonest manifestations, and the spleen and liver may be involved; infection must be excluded before immunosuppression.

Takeaway: sarcoid granulomas are a Th1/interferon-gamma-driven type IV response producing non-necrotizing epithelioid granulomas.

whyNot.B: Mast cell-mediated hypersensitivity causes bronchospasm and urticaria, not granulomas.
whyNot.C: Immune complex disease causes vasculitis and glomerulonephritis rather than compact epithelioid granulomas.
whyNot.D: Suppuration characterizes pyogenic infection and some zoonoses, not sarcoidosis.
whyNot.E: Antibody-mediated cytotoxicity destroys target cells and does not organize macrophages into granulomas.

items.objective: Explain the T-helper 1-dependent mechanism of non-necrotizing granuloma formation.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man has had enlarged, non-tender axillary and inguinal lymph nodes for 4 months. He has rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and reports no fever or weight loss. Examination shows symmetric small-joint synovitis and several 1.5-cm mobile nodes. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a polyclonal increase in gamma globulins. Lymph node biopsy shows numerous enlarged germinal centres of varying size and shape with well-defined mantle zones, frequent mitoses and tingible-body macrophages, and plasma cells in the medullary cords; flow cytometry shows no light chain restriction. Which of the following best accounts for this nodal pattern?

options.label: A
options.html: Clonal expansion of germinal centre B cells with BCL2 overexpression

options.label: B
options.html: Drainage of particulate antigen into nodal sinuses

options.label: D
options.html: Sustained B-cell responses driving germinal centre hyperplasia

options.label: E
options.html: T-cell activation expanding the interfollicular zone

items.explanationHtml:
Chronic immune stimulation, as in rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune diseases, produces reactive follicular hyperplasia: numerous germinal centres of different sizes and shapes, preserved mantle zones, brisk mitoses with tingible-body macrophages (apoptotic debris), and medullary plasmacytosis with polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. Features favouring follicular lymphoma instead are back-to-back monotonous follicles, loss of mantle zones, absence of tingible-body macrophages, and a clonal B-cell population with light chain restriction and BCL2 expression in germinal centre cells.

Takeaway: reactive follicular hyperplasia is polymorphous and polyclonal with tingible-body macrophages; follicular lymphoma is monotonous, clonal and BCL2-positive.

whyNot.A: Follicular lymphoma shows monotonous, crowded follicles with attenuated mantle zones, few mitoses and light chain restriction.
whyNot.B: Sinus histiocytosis widens the sinuses with macrophages and is not described here.
whyNot.C: Langerhans cell histiocytosis destroys nodal architecture with grooved nuclei and eosinophils.
whyNot.E: Paracortical hyperplasia follows viral infection and expands the T zone, not the follicles.

items.objective: Differentiate reactive follicular hyperplasia from follicular lymphoma on nodal findings.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of pallor, bruising and intermittent bone pain for 3 weeks. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F). There are scattered ecchymoses, non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy, and a spleen palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 7.0 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 24,000/mm3, and a platelet count of 28,000/mm3. The smear shows many medium-sized cells with scanty agranular cytoplasm and fine nuclear chromatin. Flow cytometry of marrow shows cells expressing CD19, CD10 and CD34 but not surface immunoglobulin. Demonstration of which of the following enzymes in these cells would best support the diagnosis?

options.label: E
options.html: Tyrosine kinase activity of a BCR::ABL1 fusion protein

items.explanationHtml:
A preschool child with cytopenias, bone pain, lymphadenopathy and circulating blasts expressing CD19, CD10 and CD34 without surface immunoglobulin has B-lymphoblastic leukemia, the commonest childhood malignancy. Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is expressed by immature lymphoid precursors and adds untemplated nucleotides at antigen receptor junctions; its presence confirms a lymphoblastic rather than myeloid or mature lymphoid process. Favourable features include age 1-9 years, a leukocyte count below 50,000/mm3, hyperdiploidy and ETV6::RUNX1; unfavourable features include infancy, KMT2A rearrangement, hypodiploidy and BCR::ABL1.

Takeaway: TdT positivity identifies lymphoblasts; CD10/CD19 without surface immunoglobulin indicates precursor B-cell disease.

whyNot.A: Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase is a feature of mature neutrophils and is used historically to separate reactive neutrophilia from chronic myeloid leukemia.
whyNot.B: Myeloperoxidase marks myeloid blasts; its presence would indicate acute myeloid leukemia instead.
whyNot.C: Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase is associated with hairy cell leukemia, a disease of older adults.
whyNot.E: A BCR::ABL1 fusion can occur in B-lymphoblastic leukemia but is a poor-prognosis feature, not the marker that establishes lymphoblastic lineage.

items.objective: Use TdT to establish lymphoblastic lineage in childhood acute leukemia.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue, gum bleeding and recurrent fevers for 1 month. He received chemotherapy including an alkylating agent for Hodgkin lymphoma 6 years ago. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F). Examination shows pallor, gingival hypertrophy and scattered petechiae; there is no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 32,000/mm3, and a platelet count of 36,000/mm3. The smear shows large cells with prominent nucleoli and occasional slender eosinophilic cytoplasmic rods. Coagulation studies are normal. Cytogenetics show monosomy 7. Which of the following best describes the material forming the cytoplasmic rods?

options.label: A
options.html: Aggregated azurophilic granule contents rich in myeloperoxidase

options.label: B
options.html: Condensed intermediate filaments of the cytoskeleton

options.label: D
options.html: Iron-laden mitochondria arranged around the nucleus

options.label: E
options.html: Partially degraded nuclear material within an autophagic vacuole

items.explanationHtml:
Auer rods are fused primary (azurophilic) granules containing myeloperoxidase and other lysosomal enzymes; they confirm myeloid lineage. This patient has therapy-related acute myeloid leukemia after alkylating agent exposure, which classically appears 5-7 years later with loss of chromosome 5 or 7 and a poor prognosis. Gingival infiltration suggests monocytic differentiation. Normal coagulation studies argue against acute promyelocytic leukemia, in which disseminated intravascular coagulation is characteristic.

Takeaway: Auer rods are coalesced myeloperoxidase-rich primary granules and mark myeloid blasts; alkylating agents cause therapy-related AML with chromosome 5/7 loss.

whyNot.B: Cytoskeletal aggregates are not visible as eosinophilic rods on routine stains.
whyNot.C: Hemoglobin crystals occur in red cells, such as in hemoglobin C disease.
whyNot.D: Perinuclear iron-laden mitochondria form ring sideroblasts in erythroid precursors.
whyNot.E: Nuclear debris within macrophages produces tingible bodies, not intracytoplasmic rods in blasts.

items.objective: Identify Auer rods as fused myeloperoxidase-containing granules in myeloid blasts.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman is found to have a leukocyte count of 42,000/mm3 on routine testing. She feels well. Examination shows small, mobile cervical and axillary lymph nodes and no splenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 13.2 g/dL and the platelet count is 210,000/mm3. The smear shows numerous small mature-appearing lymphocytes with scanty cytoplasm and several cells that are disrupted into smudges. Flow cytometry shows a monoclonal B-cell population with dim surface immunoglobulin that expresses CD19, CD23 and an antigen normally found on T lymphocytes. Which of the following antigens is most likely coexpressed by these B cells?
items.explanationHtml:
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a neoplasm of small mature B cells that aberrantly coexpress the T-cell-associated antigen CD5 along with CD19, CD20 (dim), CD23 and dim surface immunoglobulin with light chain restriction. Smudge (parachute) cells on the smear reflect the fragility of these lymphocytes. Mantle cell lymphoma is the other CD5-positive B-cell neoplasm, but it is CD23 negative and expresses cyclin D1. Complications include hypogammaglobulinemia with infections, autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenia, and transformation to aggressive large B-cell lymphoma.

Takeaway: CLL is a CD5+ CD23+ monoclonal B-cell neoplasm; smudge cells and absolute lymphocytosis are the clues on the smear.

whyNot.A: CD16 is a natural killer cell and granulocyte Fc receptor.
whyNot.B: CD3 is part of the T-cell receptor complex and is not aberrantly expressed by this B-cell neoplasm.
whyNot.D: CD56 is expressed by natural killer cells and plasma cell neoplasms.
whyNot.E: CD8 marks cytotoxic T cells and is not coexpressed in chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

items.objective: Recognize the immunophenotype of chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man comes to the physician because of worsening fatigue over 6 months. He has no bleeding or infections. Examination shows pallor and no organomegaly. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, MCV 104 fL, a leukocyte count of 3,100/mm3, a platelet count of 118,000/mm3, and reticulocytes 0.4% of red cells (0.5-1.5%). Serum vitamin B12, folate and thyrotropin are normal. The smear shows oval macrocytes and neutrophils with two nuclear lobes and reduced granules. Bone marrow examination shows increased cellularity with dysplastic erythroid precursors, 4% blasts, and ring sideroblasts; cytogenetics show an isolated deletion of the long arm of chromosome 5. Which of the following best explains the combination of a hypercellular marrow and peripheral cytopenias?

options.label: A
options.html: Apoptosis of dysplastic progenitors before they mature

options.label: D
options.html: Sequestration of blood cells in an enlarged spleen

options.label: E
options.html: Suppression of stem cells by an expanded T-cell clone

items.explanationHtml:
Myelodysplastic syndromes are clonal stem cell disorders of older adults. The clone proliferates in the marrow but its progeny are dysplastic and die by apoptosis before reaching the blood, so the marrow is hypercellular while the blood shows cytopenias with a low reticulocyte count: ineffective hematopoiesis. Dysplastic features include oval macrocytes, hypolobated hypogranular neutrophils and ring sideroblasts. Blasts remain below 20%, distinguishing it from acute leukemia. Isolated deletion of 5q carries a relatively favourable prognosis and responds to lenalidomide.

Takeaway: myelodysplastic syndrome causes cytopenias despite a hypercellular marrow because dysplastic progenitors undergo apoptosis.

whyNot.B: Immune destruction would raise the reticulocyte count and give a positive direct antiglobulin test.
whyNot.C: Fibrosis produces a hypocellular, fibrotic marrow with teardrop cells and a leukoerythroblastic smear.
whyNot.D: He has no splenomegaly, and sequestration does not cause dysplasia or ring sideroblasts.
whyNot.E: T-cell-mediated suppression, as in aplastic anemia, gives a hypocellular marrow without dysplasia.

items.objective: Explain ineffective hematopoiesis as the cause of cytopenias in myelodysplastic syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man comes to the physician because of painless enlargement of lymph nodes in the neck and groin for 3 months, with night sweats. Examination shows multiple 3-cm firm nodes and a spleen palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. Colonoscopy performed for anemia showed multiple small mucosal polyps, and biopsies showed lymphoid infiltration. Lymph node biopsy shows a monotonous population of small to medium lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear contours effacing the architecture; the cells are CD20 and CD5 positive and CD23 negative, and a nuclear protein that drives the G1 to S transition is strongly overexpressed. Which of the following genetic events most likely underlies this overexpression?

options.label: A
options.html: t(11;14) juxtaposing CCND1 to the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus

options.label: B
options.html: t(14;18) juxtaposing BCL2 to the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus

options.label: D
options.html: t(8;14) juxtaposing MYC to the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus

items.explanationHtml:
Mantle cell lymphoma carries t(11;14), which places CCND1 under the immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer and leads to constitutive cyclin D1 expression. Cyclin D1 with CDK4/6 phosphorylates retinoblastoma protein and releases E2F, driving cells from G1 into S phase. The tumour is CD5 positive but CD23 negative (unlike chronic lymphocytic leukemia) and often involves the gut as lymphomatous polyposis, the marrow and the blood at presentation. It behaves aggressively yet responds incompletely to therapy, so outcomes are intermediate.

Takeaway: mantle cell lymphoma is CD5+/CD23− with t(11;14) and cyclin D1 overexpression driving G1-S progression.

whyNot.B: This translocation causes follicular lymphoma, whose cells are CD10 positive and CD5 negative and which blocks apoptosis rather than driving the cell cycle.
whyNot.C: This fusion defines acute promyelocytic leukemia.
whyNot.D: This translocation defines Burkitt lymphoma, which shows a starry-sky pattern and a very high proliferation index.
whyNot.E: BCR::ABL1 drives chronic myeloid leukemia and some lymphoblastic leukemias, not a CD5+ mature B-cell lymphoma.

items.objective: Connect t(11;14) and cyclin D1 overexpression to mantle cell lymphoma.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man who emigrated from southwestern Japan 10 years ago comes to the physician because of an itchy rash, enlarged lymph nodes and fatigue for 2 months. Examination shows infiltrated erythematous plaques on the trunk and generalized lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 28,000/mm3 with many lymphocytes that have deeply indented multilobed nuclei, a platelet count of 180,000/mm3, calcium 13.4 mg/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase of 820 U/L. Flow cytometry shows a clonal CD4+ CD25+ T-cell population. Which of the following viral gene products most directly promotes proliferation of the infected cells?

options.label: B
options.html: A viral protein that degrades p53 through ubiquitin ligase recruitment

options.label: C
options.html: A viral reverse transcriptase that integrates randomly into oncogenes

options.label: D
options.html: A viral transactivator that activates NF-kappa B and the IL-2 receptor

options.label: E
options.html: Latent membrane protein 1 mimicking a CD40 signal

items.explanationHtml:
Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma follows infection with human T-lymphotropic virus 1, endemic in southwestern Japan, the Caribbean, parts of South America and west Africa. The viral Tax protein activates NF-kappa B and transcription of host genes including IL-2 and the IL-2 receptor alpha chain (CD25), producing autocrine growth stimulation, and it also disturbs cell cycle checkpoints and DNA repair. The tumour cells are clonal CD4+ CD25+ T cells with lobulated nuclei. Lytic bone lesions and parathyroid hormone-related protein cause hypercalcemia, and skin infiltration is common; strongyloidiasis is an associated co-infection.

Takeaway: HTLV-1 Tax activates NF-kappa B and IL-2 signalling, producing CD4+ CD25+ adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma with hypercalcemia.

whyNot.A: Viral IL-6 is an HHV-8 product that drives Castleman disease, not a clonal CD4+ T-cell leukemia.
whyNot.B: E6 of high-risk human papillomavirus degrades p53 and causes epithelial cancers.
whyNot.C: Reverse transcription is necessary for infection, but random integration does not explain the characteristic T-cell proliferation.
whyNot.E: LMP1 is an Epstein-Barr virus protein that transforms B cells.

items.objective: Describe how HTLV-1 Tax drives adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of fever, vomiting and drowsiness for 1 day. She returned 2 weeks ago from visiting family in Nigeria and took no chemoprophylaxis. Temperature is 39.7°C (103.5°F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. She is lethargic but rousable. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL, a platelet count of 44,000/mm3, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, glucose 52 mg/dL, and venous lactate 42 mg/dL (4.5-20 mg/dL). A rapid diagnostic test is positive for Plasmodium falciparum histidine-rich protein 2, and a thin smear shows 7% parasitemia. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Impaired consciousness, acidosis, hypoglycemia, acute kidney injury and parasitemia above 5% define severe falciparum malaria. Intravenous artesunate is the treatment of choice at all ages and in pregnancy: it clears parasites faster than quinine and lowers mortality. Give supportive care (glucose, careful fluids), monitor parasitemia, and once the patient can take oral medication complete a full course of an oral artemisinin-based combination. Patients should be monitored for delayed post-artesunate hemolysis for several weeks.

Takeaway: severe falciparum malaria is treated with intravenous artesunate, followed by a complete oral combination course.

whyNot.B: Oral therapy is inappropriate in severe malaria with vomiting and impaired consciousness; absorption is unreliable and parasite killing too slow.
whyNot.C: Atovaquone-proguanil is an option for uncomplicated malaria only, and this patient has severe disease with organ dysfunction.
whyNot.D: P. falciparum from west Africa is chloroquine resistant, and oral therapy cannot be used in severe malaria.
whyNot.E: Primaquine clears hypnozoites of P. vivax and P. ovale; it has no role as treatment of falciparum blood-stage infection.

items.objective: Select intravenous artesunate as treatment for severe falciparum malaria.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of fever and chills for 3 days. He returned 8 days ago from a 2-week trip to rural Uganda and stopped taking atovaquone-proguanil after the flight home. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 98/min, and blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg. He is alert, and examination shows no rash, jaundice or focal findings. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 5,200/mm3, a platelet count of 108,000/mm3, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and normal aminotransferases. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: Blood smears with a rapid antigen test

items.explanationHtml:
Fever in a traveller returning from sub-Saharan Africa requires immediate testing for malaria, whatever the chemoprophylaxis history, because partial prophylaxis delays but does not prevent disease. Thick smears detect low parasitemia, thin smears allow species identification and quantification of parasitemia, and a rapid antigen test gives a fast answer. A single negative set does not exclude malaria: repeat smears every 12-24 hours for a total of three sets before abandoning the diagnosis. Thrombocytopenia with fever in this setting is a strong clue.

Takeaway: in a febrile returning traveller, order thick and thin smears plus a rapid antigen test at once, and repeat if negative.

whyNot.A: Bacterial causes are possible, but malaria must be excluded first in any febrile traveller from an endemic area, and cultures do not detect it.
whyNot.C: Marrow examination is unnecessary when a peripheral smear and rapid test can establish the diagnosis.
whyNot.D: Dengue serology may be considered later, but untreated falciparum malaria is immediately life-threatening and must be excluded first.
whyNot.E: Legionella antigen testing is irrelevant without pneumonia and does not address the leading diagnosis.

items.objective: Order appropriate first-line testing for suspected malaria in a returning traveller.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fever, drenching sweats and fatigue for 1 week in July. She lives in coastal Rhode Island and works in her garden several times a week. She has a spleen and takes no immunosuppressive medication. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 130/78 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, a platelet count of 96,000/mm3, total bilirubin 2.0 mg/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase 420 U/L. A thin smear shows intraerythrocytic ring forms in 1.5% of erythrocytes, and Babesia microti DNA is detected by polymerase chain reaction. She is hemodynamically stable with normal renal function. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: Clindamycin and quinine with red cell exchange transfusion

items.explanationHtml:
Mild to moderate babesiosis in an immunocompetent patient is treated with atovaquone plus azithromycin for about 7-10 days; this combination is as effective as and better tolerated than clindamycin plus quinine, which is reserved for severe disease. Severe disease (parasitemia above about 10%, significant hemolysis, or organ dysfunction) is treated with intravenous clindamycin and quinine, often with red cell exchange transfusion. Asplenic, older and immunocompromised patients are at risk of relapse and may need longer therapy with monitoring of smears, and co-infection with Borrelia burgdorferi and Anaplasma should be considered.

Takeaway: treat uncomplicated babesiosis with atovaquone plus azithromycin; reserve clindamycin-quinine and exchange transfusion for severe disease.

whyNot.B: This combination with exchange transfusion is reserved for severe babesiosis with high parasitemia or organ dysfunction, which she does not have.
whyNot.C: Doxycycline treats the other Ixodes-borne infections but is not effective against Babesia.
whyNot.D: Artesunate is used for severe malaria; it is not the treatment for babesiosis.
whyNot.E: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole has no activity against Babesia species.

items.objective: Choose first-line therapy for uncomplicated babesiosis.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy with sickle cell anemia is brought to the emergency department because of fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion for 3 days. He had fever and a mild rash the week before. His baseline hemoglobin is 8.5 g/dL with a reticulocyte count of 10%. Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 132/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 96/56 mm Hg. He is pale with a systolic flow murmur; the spleen is not palpable and there is no pain crisis. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 4.2 g/dL, MCV 88 fL, reticulocytes 0.2% of red cells (0.5-1.5%), a leukocyte count of 7,400/mm3, a platelet count of 240,000/mm3, and total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
A sudden fall in hemoglobin with reticulocytopenia after a viral illness in a child with chronic hemolysis indicates transient aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19. Marrow erythropoiesis recovers in 1-2 weeks as antibody develops, so management is supportive: simple transfusion to relieve symptomatic anemia, with monitoring until the reticulocyte count rises. Droplet and contact precautions are needed because the patient is viremic and transmission to pregnant contacts and other patients with hemolytic anemia is a risk. Recurrence is rare because immunity is lasting.

Takeaway: treat aplastic crisis with simple transfusion and isolation; erythropoiesis recovers as antibody appears.

whyNot.A: Exchange transfusion is used for stroke, acute chest syndrome and other severe vaso-occlusive complications, not for aplastic crisis.
whyNot.B: Immune globulin is used in chronic parvovirus infection with persistent anemia in immunocompromised patients, not in self-limited aplastic crisis.
whyNot.D: Hydroxyurea reduces vaso-occlusive events over months and does not correct an acute severe anemia.
whyNot.E: Erythropoietin cannot work when erythroid progenitors are infected and depleted, and the endogenous level is already high.

items.objective: Manage transient aplastic crisis in a child with sickle cell anemia.

items.stemHtml:
A 57-year-old man comes to the emergency department in June because of fever, severe headache and myalgias for 3 days. He removed a tick from his calf 10 days ago after hiking in Minnesota. Temperature is 39.1°C (102.4°F), pulse is 102/min, and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. Examination shows no rash, meningismus or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies are shown.

TestResultReference range
Hemoglobin13.8 g/dL13.5-17.5 g/dL
Leukocyte count2,400/mm34,500-11,000/mm3
Platelet count68,000/mm3150,000-400,000/mm3
Sodium130 mEq/L136-145 mEq/L
Creatinine1.1 mg/dL0.6-1.2 mg/dL
AST128 U/L12-38 U/L
ALT140 U/L10-40 U/L

Blood smear review and polymerase chain reaction testing are pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Await polymerase chain reaction results before treating

items.explanationHtml:
Fever, headache and myalgias after Ixodes exposure in the upper Midwest with leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, mild hyponatremia and raised aminotransferases suggest human granulocytic anaplasmosis (or ehrlichiosis in regions with Amblyomma). Doxycycline is started empirically on suspicion, because confirmatory polymerase chain reaction and serology take time and delay worsens outcome; fever usually settles within 24-48 hours. Doxycycline is given to children as well, since short courses do not stain teeth appreciably. Lack of response within 48 hours should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.

Takeaway: treat suspected anaplasmosis or ehrlichiosis empirically with doxycycline without waiting for confirmation.

whyNot.A: Delaying treatment increases the risk of severe complications; therapy is started on clinical suspicion.
whyNot.B: Ceftriaxone treats Lyme neuroborreliosis and bacterial meningitis but has no activity against Anaplasma.
whyNot.C: Amoxicillin does not treat intracellular tick-borne bacteria.
whyNot.E: Hydroxychloroquine has no role in tick-borne bacterial infections.

items.objective: Initiate empiric doxycycline for suspected anaplasmosis.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman in the intensive care unit is being treated for Escherichia coli bacteremia from pyelonephritis. On the second day she develops oozing from intravenous sites and ecchymoses over the arms. Temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 112/min, and blood pressure is 104/62 mm Hg on norepinephrine. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 42,000/mm3 (previously 180,000/mm3), prothrombin time 22 s, aPTT 52 s, fibrinogen 88 mg/dL (200-400 mg/dL), and a markedly raised D-dimer. There is no intracranial or gastrointestinal bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibiotics and source control, with transfusion for bleeding

options.label: B
options.html: Plasma exchange with fresh frozen plasma replacement

options.label: C
options.html: Prophylactic platelet transfusion to keep the count above 100,000/mm3

items.explanationHtml:
Sepsis-associated disseminated intravascular coagulation improves only when the trigger is controlled, so prompt antimicrobial therapy and source control are the mainstay, with organ support. Blood products are given for bleeding or before procedures rather than to correct numbers: platelets for bleeding (or at very low counts), fresh frozen plasma for prolonged clotting times with bleeding, and cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate when fibrinogen is very low. Prophylactic-dose heparin for venous thromboembolism prevention is usually continued unless bleeding is significant; therapeutic anticoagulation is reserved for predominantly thrombotic presentations.

Takeaway: treat the underlying cause of DIC; give blood products for bleeding, not to normalize laboratory values.

whyNot.B: Plasma exchange treats thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, in which coagulation studies and fibrinogen are normal.
whyNot.C: Transfusion thresholds in disseminated intravascular coagulation are far lower, and prophylactic transfusion to that level is not supported.
whyNot.D: Recombinant factor VIIa is not indicated here and carries a substantial thrombotic risk.
whyNot.E: Antifibrinolytics are generally avoided in disseminated intravascular coagulation because they can worsen microvascular thrombosis.

items.objective: Manage sepsis-associated disseminated intravascular coagulation.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old college wrestler comes to the student health clinic for advice. He was diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis 10 days ago after a positive heterophile antibody test and is improving, with resolving sore throat and less fatigue. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F). The pharynx shows mild erythema without exudate, there is small posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and the spleen is palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin. He asks when he may return to competition. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: Avoid contact sports for at least 3 weeks from symptom onset and until the spleen is no longer enlarged

options.label: B
options.html: Avoid contact sports until the heterophile antibody test becomes negative

options.label: C
options.html: Begin a 5-day course of prednisone and resume training immediately

options.label: D
options.html: Obtain abdominal ultrasonography weekly and resume when splenic length is normal for height

options.label: E
options.html: Resume competition now, with a protective abdominal pad

items.explanationHtml:
Splenic rupture complicates a small proportion of cases of infectious mononucleosis, almost always within the first 3-4 weeks, and may follow minor or no trauma. Athletes are advised to avoid contact and collision sports and heavy lifting for at least 3 weeks from symptom onset, and longer while the spleen remains palpable or symptoms persist; light non-contact activity may resume earlier as tolerated. Other counselling points are that amoxicillin or ampicillin often produces a morbilliform rash, that fatigue can last weeks, and that corticosteroids are reserved for airway compromise.

Takeaway: after mononucleosis, hold contact sports for at least 3 weeks and until splenomegaly has resolved.

whyNot.B: Heterophile antibodies persist for months after recovery and do not reflect splenic size or rupture risk.
whyNot.C: Corticosteroids are reserved for impending airway obstruction and do not make the spleen safe.
whyNot.D: Routine serial imaging is not standard; splenic size varies with body habitus and imaging has not been shown to improve decisions.
whyNot.E: Padding does not prevent splenic rupture, and he still has a palpable spleen.

items.objective: Counsel an athlete on return to play after infectious mononucleosis.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of sore throat, fever and fatigue for 5 days. Temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F). There is tonsillar enlargement with exudate, palatal petechiae, and tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy; the spleen is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. A rapid streptococcal antigen test is negative, and a heterophile antibody test is negative. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 13,600/mm3 with 58% lymphocytes and 12% atypical lymphocytes, AST 72 U/L, and ALT 88 U/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: Excisional biopsy of a cervical lymph node

options.label: C
options.html: Peripheral blood flow cytometry for clonality

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat rapid streptococcal antigen testing in 48 hours

items.explanationHtml:
Heterophile antibody tests are insensitive early in illness (the first week) and in young children, so a negative test in a classic syndrome should be followed by Epstein-Barr virus-specific serology. Viral capsid antigen IgM with VCA IgG and absent Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen antibodies indicate acute primary infection; VCA IgG with EBNA antibodies indicates past infection. If EBV serology is negative, consider acute cytomegalovirus, acute HIV (which must be tested for, since it is treatable and transmissible), toxoplasmosis and drug reactions.

Takeaway: a heterophile-negative mononucleosis syndrome calls for EBV-specific serology, then CMV, HIV and toxoplasmosis testing.

whyNot.B: Biopsy is premature in an acute self-limited syndrome with atypical lymphocytes and transaminitis.
whyNot.C: Flow cytometry is unnecessary when the clinical picture indicates a reactive viral process.
whyNot.D: Repeating the streptococcal test does not explain the splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytosis and hepatitis.
whyNot.E: Diphtheria causes a grey adherent pseudomembrane with systemic toxicity in unimmunized patients and is not suggested here.

items.objective: Interpret a negative heterophile test and choose confirmatory EBV serology.

items.stemHtml: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a tender lump in the left armpit for 2 weeks. A kitten scratched her left forearm 4 weeks ago. Temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), and she is well-appearing and eating normally. Examination shows a healing papule on the left forearm and a 3-cm tender, mobile left axillary lymph node with mild overlying erythema and no fluctuance. Serum Bartonella henselae IgG titer is high. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Incision and drainage of the node

items.explanationHtml:
Typical cat-scratch disease resolves spontaneously over 2-4 months. A short course of azithromycin speeds the reduction in node size and is reasonable for bulky or uncomfortable lymphadenopathy, and antibiotic treatment is recommended for immunocompromised patients and systemic disease (hepatosplenic abscesses, neuroretinitis, endocarditis). Suppurative nodes are managed by needle aspiration rather than incision and drainage. Prevention centres on avoiding rough play with kittens, prompt washing of scratches and flea control.

Takeaway: azithromycin shortens bulky cat-scratch adenitis; aspirate rather than incise suppurative nodes.

whyNot.B: Biopsy is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or suspected malignancy; the diagnosis here is established.
whyNot.C: Incision and drainage of cat-scratch nodes risks a chronic draining sinus; needle aspiration is preferred if a node is fluctuant and painful.
whyNot.D: Parenteral aminoglycosides are used in severe systemic Bartonella infection such as endocarditis, not uncomplicated adenitis.
whyNot.E: A prolonged course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is not standard therapy for typical cat-scratch disease.

items.objective: Select management for regional cat-scratch lymphadenitis.

items.stemHtml: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a painless lump below the left jaw that has slowly enlarged over 6 weeks. He is active, feeding well and has had no fever, weight loss or night sweats. There is no contact with anyone with tuberculosis, and he has not travelled. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). There is a 2.5-cm firm, non-tender submandibular mass with a violaceous hue and thinning of the overlying skin. A tuberculin skin test shows 4 mm of induration, and an interferon-gamma release assay is negative. Chest radiography is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Complete surgical excision of the node

items.explanationHtml:
Chronic unilateral cervicofacial lymphadenitis in an otherwise well toddler, with violaceous thinning skin and negative tests for tuberculosis infection, is usually caused by nontuberculous mycobacteria such as Mycobacterium avium complex. Complete surgical excision gives the highest cure rate, confirms the diagnosis and avoids sinus formation. When excision would endanger the facial nerve or the disease is extensive, a macrolide-based regimen (for example azithromycin or clarithromycin with rifampin or ethambutol) is an alternative. Incision and drainage should be avoided.

Takeaway: excise nontuberculous mycobacterial cervical adenitis in children; use macrolide-based therapy when surgery is risky.

whyNot.B: Multidrug antituberculous therapy is for tuberculous disease; both tests of tuberculosis infection are negative and there is no exposure.
whyNot.C: Incision and drainage risks a chronically draining sinus tract and poor cosmetic outcome.
whyNot.D: Untreated nodes commonly break down through the skin and leave scarring, so observation alone is a poor choice for a node with thinning skin.
whyNot.E: Beta-lactams do not treat nontuberculous mycobacteria and would be expected to fail.

items.objective: Manage nontuberculous mycobacterial cervical lymphadenitis in a young child.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man comes to the physician because of a lump in his neck that he first noticed 6 weeks ago and that has slowly grown. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years and drinks alcohol daily. He reports no fever, night sweats or weight loss and has had no recent infection. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F). There is a 3-cm firm, non-tender node fixed to deeper tissues in the left supraclavicular area; the oral cavity and pharynx appear normal and there is no other lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. A complete blood count and a chest radiograph are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest

items.explanationHtml:
A persistent, hard, fixed, painless supraclavicular node in an older smoker is a high-risk presentation: supraclavicular location alone carries a high likelihood of malignancy. Features that raise concern are size above about 2 cm, hard or fixed texture, supraclavicular site, age above 40 years, duration beyond 4-6 weeks, and systemic (B) symptoms. Cross-sectional imaging of the neck and chest localizes a possible mucosal primary tumour or mediastinal disease and plans tissue sampling; it is obtained before biopsy so that the biopsy targets the most informative site.

Takeaway: a fixed supraclavicular node in an older smoker needs cross-sectional imaging and tissue diagnosis, not observation or antibiotics.

whyNot.B: Aspiration cytology alone often cannot classify lymphoma and may miss the primary tumour; imaging first guides where and how to biopsy.
whyNot.C: Observation is unsafe for a hard, fixed supraclavicular node in a smoker, which carries a high risk of malignancy.
whyNot.D: There is no sign of infection; empiric antibiotics would only delay diagnosis.
whyNot.E: Tuberculosis is unlikely with a fixed painless node, no systemic symptoms and a normal chest radiograph, and the test would not exclude cancer.

items.objective: Triage persistent supraclavicular lymphadenopathy in an older adult.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with a 3-cm hard, fixed left supraclavicular lymph node has undergone contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest. The scan shows the enlarged supraclavicular node, two 2-cm mediastinal nodes and no mucosal, pulmonary or abdominal mass; nasopharyngoscopy performed by an otolaryngologist shows normal mucosa. He remains without fever or weight loss. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: Excisional biopsy of the enlarged node

options.label: E
options.html: Serum lactate dehydrogenase and beta-2 microglobulin measurement

items.explanationHtml:
When imaging and endoscopy show no mucosal primary tumour, the enlarged node itself must be sampled. Excisional biopsy preserves architecture and is preferred when lymphoma is suspected, since classification depends on the pattern of growth as well as immunophenotype; a core needle biopsy with adequate tissue for immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry is an acceptable alternative in many centres. Fine-needle aspiration is best suited to confirming metastatic carcinoma, and a negative aspirate never ends the evaluation of a high-risk node.

Takeaway: sample a high-risk node with excisional or adequate core biopsy; aspiration cytology is not sufficient to classify lymphoma.

whyNot.A: Marrow examination is used for staging once a diagnosis is made; it is a poor first choice when an accessible node is available.
whyNot.C: Functional imaging shows metabolic activity but cannot give a tissue diagnosis.
whyNot.D: Watchful waiting delays diagnosis of a high-risk node that already has mediastinal disease.
whyNot.E: These markers help in prognosis but do not establish a diagnosis.

items.objective: Choose the biopsy approach for a high-risk lymph node when no primary tumour is found.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman is admitted because of fever for 3 weeks, drenching sweats and progressive weakness. She has received broad-spectrum antibiotics for 6 days without improvement, and blood, urine and respiratory cultures are negative. Temperature is 39.4°C (103°F), pulse is 118/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. The spleen is palpable 5 cm below the costal margin, and there is no rash or arthritis. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 1,900/mm3, a platelet count of 48,000/mm3, triglycerides 420 mg/dL, fibrinogen 105 mg/dL (200-400 mg/dL), AST 180 U/L, and ferritin 14,000 ng/mL (30-300 ng/mL). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Add empiric antifungal therapy and continue observation

options.label: C
options.html: Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy with testing for triggers

options.label: E
options.html: Transfuse platelets and discharge with outpatient follow-up

items.explanationHtml:
Prolonged fever unresponsive to antibiotics with splenomegaly, two- or three-lineage cytopenias, extreme hyperferritinemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hypofibrinogenemia and raised aminotransferases should prompt evaluation for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Marrow examination looks for hemophagocytosis and for an occult trigger, especially lymphoma, while soluble CD25, natural killer cell function, and testing for Epstein-Barr virus and other infections are sent in parallel. Because delay is dangerous, immunosuppressive treatment (commonly corticosteroids, with etoposide in severe or EBV-driven disease) is started once the diagnosis is probable, together with treatment of the trigger.

Takeaway: ferritin in the thousands with fever, cytopenias and splenomegaly calls for urgent marrow evaluation and a search for an HLH trigger.

whyNot.A: Adding antifungals does not address a hyperinflammatory syndrome that is already strongly suggested and would delay definitive diagnosis.
whyNot.B: Growth factor support does not treat the underlying immune activation and may aggravate inflammation.
whyNot.D: Splenectomy is not a diagnostic procedure for this syndrome and carries high operative risk in a critically ill patient.
whyNot.E: Discharge would be dangerous; untreated hemophagocytic syndrome has high mortality.

items.objective: Evaluate suspected hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis in an adult.

items.stemHtml:
A 7-year-old girl with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis is admitted because of 4 days of continuous fever and new lethargy. She had been improving on an interleukin-1 inhibitor. Temperature is 39.6°C (103.3°F), pulse is 142/min, and blood pressure is 88/50 mm Hg. The liver is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, and there is no new rash or joint swelling. Laboratory studies today and 2 weeks ago are shown.

TestResultReference range
Hemoglobin8.6 g/dL (was 10.8 g/dL)12.0-16.0 g/dL
Leukocyte count3,100/mm3 (was 14,000/mm3)4,500-11,000/mm3
Platelet count72,000/mm3 (was 480,000/mm3)150,000-400,000/mm3
Ferritin22,000 ng/mL (was 600 ng/mL)30-300 ng/mL
Fibrinogen95 mg/dL (was 520 mg/dL)200-400 mg/dL
AST320 U/L (was 40 U/L)12-38 U/L
Triglycerides390 mg/dLbelow 150 mg/dL

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: C
options.html: Flare of systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis

items.explanationHtml:
Macrophage activation syndrome is secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis arising in rheumatic disease, most often systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis. The diagnostic clue is a reversal of the usual inflammatory pattern: platelet count, leukocyte count and fibrinogen fall while ferritin, aminotransferases, triglycerides and D-dimer rise, with unremitting fever, hepatosplenomegaly and encephalopathy. Treatment is urgent high-dose corticosteroids, with anakinra or cyclosporine, and etoposide reserved for refractory cases; cultures are sent because infection can trigger the syndrome.

Takeaway: in systemic JIA, falling platelets and fibrinogen with soaring ferritin mean macrophage activation syndrome, not a flare.

whyNot.A: Sepsis is a consideration and cultures are sent, but the falling fibrinogen with extreme hyperferritinemia and falling platelets in a child with systemic arthritis fits macrophage activation syndrome.
whyNot.B: Hepatotoxicity alone does not cause pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia and hypofibrinogenemia.
whyNot.C: A flare raises platelet count, fibrinogen and leukocyte count; here all three have fallen.
whyNot.E: Thrombotic microangiopathy produces schistocytes with normal fibrinogen and would not cause hyperferritinemia of this magnitude.

items.objective: Diagnose macrophage activation syndrome from serial laboratory trends.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man with HIV infection is admitted because of fever, night sweats and fatigue for 2 months. He stopped antiretroviral therapy 18 months ago. Temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F). There is diffuse lymphadenopathy and a spleen palpable 6 cm below the costal margin; there are no violaceous skin lesions. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, a platelet count of 82,000/mm3, albumin 2.3 g/dL, C-reactive protein 165 mg/L, CD4+ count 90/mm3, and a high plasma human herpesvirus 8 viral load. Lymph node biopsy shows regressed germinal centres with hyalinized vessels, expanded mantle zones and interfollicular HHV-8-positive plasmablasts; there is no evidence of lymphoma. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: Chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone

items.explanationHtml:
HHV-8-associated multicentric Castleman disease in HIV infection is treated with rituximab, which depletes the CD20-positive HHV-8-infected plasmablasts, together with antiretroviral therapy; this approach has greatly improved survival. Concurrent Kaposi sarcoma can flare after rituximab, so it is looked for and may require added chemotherapy. The IL-6-directed antibody siltuximab is approved for idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease (HIV-negative, HHV-8-negative), and unicentric disease is cured by surgical excision.

Takeaway: HHV-8-associated multicentric Castleman disease is treated with rituximab plus antiretroviral therapy; siltuximab is for the idiopathic form.

whyNot.B: Combination chemotherapy is added only for aggressive or organ-threatening disease or concurrent lymphoma, which was excluded.
whyNot.C: Corticosteroids alone give only transient benefit and do not control the HHV-8-infected plasmablasts.
whyNot.D: Splenectomy does not treat a multicentric systemic lymphoproliferative disorder.
whyNot.E: Antiviral monotherapy does not reliably control established HHV-8-associated multicentric Castleman disease.

items.objective: Select treatment for HHV-8-associated multicentric Castleman disease.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a tender lump on his skull for 3 weeks and increased thirst and urination for 2 months. He drinks about 4 L of fluid daily and wets the bed nightly. Temperature is 37.2°C (99°F). There is a 3-cm soft, tender swelling over the left parietal bone and a greasy scalp rash; the liver and spleen are not enlarged. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 8,200/mm3, a platelet count of 290,000/mm3, sodium 148 mEq/L, and urine osmolality 110 mOsm/kg with serum osmolality 302 mOsm/kg. Skull radiographs show a lytic lesion with sharply defined margins, and biopsy shows CD1a-positive histiocytes with eosinophils. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: E
options.html: Topical corticosteroids to the scalp with observation

items.explanationHtml:
This child has multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis with bone, skin and pituitary involvement. Central diabetes insipidus from posterior pituitary infiltration is the commonest endocrine complication and is usually permanent; it requires desmopressin. Multisystem disease is treated with systemic chemotherapy, conventionally vinblastine with prednisone, and MAPK pathway inhibitors are used in refractory disease with BRAF V600E. Single-bone disease may be managed with curettage or observation. Long-term follow-up looks for further endocrine deficits, neurodegeneration and skeletal sequelae.

Takeaway: multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis needs systemic chemotherapy, and its diabetes insipidus needs desmopressin.

whyNot.A: Treating the diabetes insipidus alone leaves the multisystem histiocytic disease untreated and progressive.
whyNot.C: Fluid restriction is dangerous in central diabetes insipidus and does not treat the underlying disease.
whyNot.D: Radiotherapy is rarely used in children because of late effects and does not treat multisystem disease.
whyNot.E: Topical therapy addresses only the skin component of multisystem disease.

items.objective: Manage multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis with pituitary involvement.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of tender swelling in the right side of her neck and low-grade fever for 4 weeks. Excisional lymph node biopsy performed 3 days ago showed patchy paracortical necrosis with karyorrhectic debris, crescentic histiocytes and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, without neutrophils, granulomas or atypical lymphoid cells; immunohistochemistry showed no clonal population. Testing for Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, HIV, toxoplasmosis and tuberculosis is negative, and antinuclear antibodies are not detected. She has no rash, arthritis or oral ulcers. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: D
options.html: Supportive care with analgesics and follow-up

options.label: E
options.html: Whole-body positron emission tomography and empiric chemotherapy

items.explanationHtml:
Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is self-limited, resolving over about 1-4 months. Management is supportive, with analgesics or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain and fever; short courses of corticosteroids are reserved for severe or extranodal disease. Because the histology overlaps with lupus lymphadenitis and some patients later develop systemic lupus erythematosus, follow-up with repeat serologic testing and attention to new features such as rash, arthritis, cytopenias or nephritis is appropriate. Recurrence occurs in a minority.

Takeaway: Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease needs supportive care and follow-up for later lupus, not antibiotics or chemotherapy.

whyNot.A: Antituberculous therapy is unwarranted with negative testing and non-granulomatous histology.
whyNot.B: Cytotoxic immunosuppression is not used for a benign self-limited lymphadenitis.
whyNot.C: There is no clonal B-cell population to target.
whyNot.E: Empiric chemotherapy without a malignant diagnosis would be harmful, and imaging would not change management of established benign histology.

items.objective: Manage biopsy-proven Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman comes to the physician for evaluation of lymphadenopathy found incidentally. Chest radiography performed for a cough 3 weeks ago showed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. She now has no cough, dyspnea or chest pain, and she has lost no weight. Vital signs are normal, and physical examination including the skin, eyes and joints is unremarkable. Laboratory studies show calcium 9.6 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, and normal liver tests. Pulmonary function testing is normal, and mediastinal node sampling shows non-necrotizing granulomas with negative stains and cultures for mycobacteria and fungi. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
items.explanationHtml:
Asymptomatic stage I sarcoidosis (bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields) remits spontaneously in most patients and does not need treatment. Monitoring includes symptoms, spirometry with diffusing capacity, chest imaging as indicated, serum calcium and creatinine, liver tests, an electrocardiogram to screen for cardiac involvement, and ophthalmologic examination because uveitis can be asymptomatic. Systemic corticosteroids are started for progressive or symptomatic pulmonary disease, hypercalcemia, and cardiac, neurologic, ocular or renal involvement. The spleen and peripheral nodes may also be involved.

Takeaway: asymptomatic stage I sarcoidosis is observed with structured monitoring; steroids are for symptomatic or organ-threatening disease.

whyNot.A: Systemic corticosteroids are reserved for symptomatic or organ-threatening disease; asymptomatic hilar adenopathy often remits spontaneously.
whyNot.B: Tumor necrosis factor inhibitors are third-line therapy for refractory sarcoidosis.
whyNot.C: Steroid-sparing agents are used when corticosteroids are needed but poorly tolerated or ineffective.
whyNot.E: Surgical dissection has no therapeutic role in sarcoidosis.

items.objective: Decide whether to treat asymptomatic sarcoidosis with hilar adenopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old woman is referred after a routine blood count showed a leukocyte count of 48,000/mm3 with 85% small mature lymphocytes. She feels well, exercises daily and has had no infections, fevers or weight loss. Examination shows two 1.5-cm mobile cervical nodes; the spleen is not palpable. Hemoglobin is 13.4 g/dL and the platelet count is 215,000/mm3. Flow cytometry shows a monoclonal CD5+ CD19+ CD23+ B-cell population with kappa light chain restriction. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Begin a Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor

items.explanationHtml:
Early-stage chronic lymphocytic leukemia without anemia, thrombocytopenia, bulky or symptomatic adenopathy, splenomegaly, or constitutional symptoms is managed by observation, since earlier treatment has not improved survival. Indications to treat include progressive marrow failure with anemia or thrombocytopenia, massive or symptomatic lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly, rapid lymphocyte doubling, significant constitutional symptoms, and autoimmune cytopenias refractory to corticosteroids. When treatment is indicated, first-line therapy is targeted: a covalent Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor or time-limited venetoclax with an anti-CD20 antibody. Preventive care includes annual influenza and other recommended vaccinations and attention to infection risk from hypogammaglobulinemia; live vaccines are avoided.

Takeaway: asymptomatic early-stage CLL is observed; treat only for cytopenias, bulky or symptomatic disease, or constitutional symptoms.

whyNot.A: Targeted therapy is highly effective but is reserved for patients with indications for treatment; starting it earlier does not prolong survival.
whyNot.B: Alkylator monotherapy is outdated and, like any therapy, is not indicated in asymptomatic early-stage disease.
whyNot.C: This regimen is a standard first-line option, but only once treatment is indicated.
whyNot.E: Splenectomy has no role here; the spleen is not enlarged and cytopenias are absent.

items.objective: Decide when to start therapy in chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man is evaluated after a total protein of 9.0 g/dL was found on routine testing. He feels well, with no bone pain, fatigue or infections. Examination is unremarkable. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, calcium 9.4 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and a serum IgG kappa monoclonal protein of 1.4 g/dL; the serum free light chain ratio is 2.6 (reference 0.26-1.65). Bone marrow biopsy shows 7% clonal plasma cells, and whole-body low-dose CT shows no lytic lesions. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: E
options.html: Periodic monitoring of the monoclonal protein and blood counts

items.explanationHtml:
A monoclonal protein below 3 g/dL with fewer than 10% clonal marrow plasma cells and no myeloma-defining event is monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance; 10% or more plasma cells or a protein of 3 g/dL or more without myeloma-defining events is smoldering myeloma. Myeloma requires 10% or more clonal plasma cells (or a plasmacytoma) plus a myeloma-defining event: hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency attributable to the clone, anemia, lytic bone lesions, 60% or more plasma cells, a free light chain ratio of 100 or more with an involved chain of at least 100 mg/L, or more than one focal marrow lesion on MRI. This patient has none, so he is monitored; progression risk is stratified by protein size, isotype and light chain ratio.

Takeaway: without a myeloma-defining event, a monoclonal gammopathy is monitored rather than treated.

whyNot.A: Bisphosphonates are used in myeloma with bone disease, not in smoldering disease without lytic lesions or osteoporosis.
whyNot.B: Treatment is indicated for myeloma; this patient has monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, with no myeloma-defining event.
whyNot.C: Plasma exchange treats symptomatic hyperviscosity, which a modest IgG paraprotein does not cause.
whyNot.D: Transplantation is part of treatment for symptomatic myeloma, not smoldering disease.

items.objective: Apply diagnostic criteria to distinguish MGUS, smoldering myeloma and myeloma.

items.stemHtml: A 73-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of blurred vision, headache and confusion for 2 days. He has had 3 months of fatigue and recurrent nosebleeds. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 92/min, and blood pressure is 142/84 mm Hg. Funduscopy shows dilated, tortuous, sausage-shaped retinal veins with scattered hemorrhages. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, a platelet count of 130,000/mm3, calcium 9.3 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, and total protein 11.2 g/dL with an IgM monoclonal protein of 6.2 g/dL. Bone marrow biopsy shows a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with an MYD88 L265P mutation. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma secreting monoclonal IgM, nearly always with an MYD88 L265P mutation. Because pentameric IgM is large and largely intravascular, high levels raise serum viscosity, producing headache, visual blurring, mucosal bleeding, confusion and the classic dilated segmented retinal veins. Plasmapheresis removes IgM quickly and is the immediate treatment for symptomatic hyperviscosity; definitive therapy follows, with regimens such as a Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor or bendamustine with rituximab. Rituximab is withheld or delayed until viscosity is controlled because of the IgM flare, and red cell transfusion is avoided until then.

Takeaway: symptomatic hyperviscosity in Waldenström macroglobulinemia is treated first with plasmapheresis, before systemic therapy.

whyNot.A: Transplantation is not an initial treatment and does not relieve acute hyperviscosity.
whyNot.B: Corticosteroids do not rapidly remove the circulating IgM responsible for hyperviscosity.
whyNot.C: Transfusion raises whole blood viscosity further and can worsen symptoms; it is deferred until the paraprotein is reduced.
whyNot.E: Rituximab works too slowly and can transiently raise IgM (a flare), worsening hyperviscosity if given before plasmapheresis.

items.objective: Treat symptomatic hyperviscosity in Waldenström macroglobulinemia.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue, early satiety and drenching night sweats for 5 months, with a 6-kg weight loss. Examination shows pallor and a firm spleen palpable 10 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 13,400/mm3, and a platelet count of 110,000/mm3. The smear shows teardrop-shaped erythrocytes, nucleated red cells and occasional myelocytes. Attempted bone marrow aspiration yields no material, and the biopsy shows dense reticulin and collagen fibrosis with clustered, atypical megakaryocytes. Testing shows a JAK2 V617F mutation, and BCR::ABL1 is not detected. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms?
items.explanationHtml:
Primary myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by JAK2, CALR or MPL mutations, with marrow fibrosis, a dry tap, teardrop cells and a leukoerythroblastic smear from extramedullary hematopoiesis and massive splenomegaly. JAK inhibitors such as ruxolitinib reduce spleen size and constitutional symptoms and improve quality of life, with anemia and thrombocytopenia as the main adverse effects. Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation is the only curative option and is considered in younger, higher-risk patients; prognostic scores guide that decision. Transformation to acute leukemia can occur.

Takeaway: ruxolitinib relieves splenomegaly and symptoms in primary myelofibrosis; transplantation is the only cure.

whyNot.A: Phlebotomy is used in polycythemia vera; this patient is anemic.
whyNot.B: Imatinib treats BCR::ABL1-positive chronic myeloid leukemia, which has been excluded.
whyNot.C: Corticosteroids may transiently help anemia but do not reduce spleen size or symptom burden substantially.
whyNot.E: Splenic irradiation gives only temporary benefit and risks prolonged cytopenias; it is reserved for patients unsuitable for other options.

items.objective: Select JAK inhibitor therapy for symptomatic primary myelofibrosis.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman comes to the physician because of epigastric discomfort and early satiety for 4 months. She takes no medications. Vital signs are normal, and the abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness. Hemoglobin is 11.4 g/dL. Upper endoscopy shows thickened gastric folds with superficial erosions in the antrum. Biopsies show a dense lymphoid infiltrate of small B cells invading gastric glands, and immunohistochemistry confirms a monoclonal B-cell population; Helicobacter pylori organisms are seen. Staging CT and endoscopic ultrasonography show disease confined to the mucosa and submucosa with no lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: E
options.html: Rituximab with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone

items.explanationHtml:
Gastric extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma arises from chronic antigenic stimulation by Helicobacter pylori. For localized disease with demonstrable infection, eradication therapy alone produces lymphoma regression in most patients, so it is first-line; response is confirmed by endoscopic follow-up over months, since regression can be slow. Disease that persists, or that carries t(11;18) with API2::MALT1 (antibiotic unresponsive), is treated with involved-site radiotherapy or systemic therapy. Eradication is also given when infection is present in more advanced stages.

Takeaway: localized gastric MALT lymphoma with H. pylori is treated first by eradicating the infection, with endoscopic follow-up.

whyNot.A: Surgery is not needed for localized mucosal disease that frequently regresses with antibiotics.
whyNot.C: Radiotherapy is used when disease persists after eradication or when the infection is absent.
whyNot.D: Immunotherapy is reserved for disease that does not regress after eradication or that is advanced.
whyNot.E: Combination chemoimmunotherapy is for aggressive or advanced disease, not localized marginal zone lymphoma with active infection.

items.objective: Choose Helicobacter pylori eradication as first-line therapy for localized gastric MALT lymphoma.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man with newly diagnosed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is admitted for the first cycle of chemoimmunotherapy. He has bulky retroperitoneal disease, and serum lactate dehydrogenase is 1,150 U/L. Laboratory studies before treatment show creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, potassium 4.4 mEq/L, calcium 9.0 mg/dL, phosphorus 4.0 mg/dL, and uric acid 9.6 mg/dL (3.0-8.2 mg/dL). Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity is normal. In addition to intravenous fluids and close laboratory monitoring, which of the following is the most appropriate prophylaxis?
items.explanationHtml:
Bulky, rapidly proliferating lymphoma with a high lactate dehydrogenase, kidney impairment and a uric acid already above the reference range is high risk for tumor lysis syndrome. High-risk patients receive vigorous intravenous hydration plus rasburicase, a recombinant urate oxidase that converts existing uric acid to allantoin within hours; allopurinol only prevents further production and suits lower-risk patients. Rasburicase is contraindicated in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency because of hemolysis, so screening is performed when the risk is appreciable. Electrolytes, including potassium, phosphate, calcium and creatinine, are monitored frequently during the first days of treatment.

Takeaway: high-risk tumor lysis prophylaxis is hydration plus rasburicase; allopurinol suits intermediate risk and cannot lower existing urate.

whyNot.A: Allopurinol blocks new urate formation but does not lower the already markedly raised uric acid, which this high-risk patient needs.
whyNot.B: Calcium is given for symptomatic hypocalcemia or hyperkalemia with electrocardiographic changes, not as prophylaxis.
whyNot.D: Urinary alkalinization is no longer recommended; it raises the risk of calcium phosphate precipitation.
whyNot.E: Potassium binders treat hyperkalemia after it develops and have no prophylactic role here.

items.objective: Choose tumor lysis syndrome prophylaxis according to risk.

items.stemHtml: A 5-year-old girl is diagnosed with B-lymphoblastic leukemia after presenting with pallor, bruising and a leukocyte count of 22,000/mm3 with 60% blasts. Flow cytometry shows CD19+ CD10+ blasts expressing terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase. Diagnostic lumbar puncture shows no blasts in the cerebrospinal fluid, and neurologic examination is normal. Her parents ask why treatment includes repeated lumbar punctures with medication even though her spinal fluid is clear. Which of the following best explains this part of her treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Intrathecal therapy allows the total dose of systemic chemotherapy to be reduced

options.label: B
options.html: Intrathecal therapy prevents relapse from leukemic cells sheltered in the central nervous system

options.label: C
options.html: Intrathecal therapy reduces the risk of secondary brain tumours

options.label: D
options.html: Repeated sampling is needed to monitor response to systemic therapy

options.label: E
options.html: Repeated sampling screens for infectious meningitis during neutropenia

items.explanationHtml:
Lymphoblasts seed the leptomeninges early, where most systemically administered drugs penetrate poorly. Without central nervous system-directed treatment, isolated meningeal relapse is common, so every child receives prophylaxis: intrathecal methotrexate (with or without cytarabine and corticosteroid) throughout therapy, supported by systemic agents that reach the central nervous system such as high-dose methotrexate and dexamethasone. Cranial irradiation is now reserved for selected high-risk or overtly involved cases because of neurocognitive and second-tumour risks. Overall cure rates in childhood B-lymphoblastic leukemia now exceed 85-90% with risk-adapted therapy.

Takeaway: central nervous system prophylaxis with intrathecal chemotherapy is given to every child with ALL because the meninges are a sanctuary site.

whyNot.A: Intrathecal therapy supplements rather than replaces systemic chemotherapy; systemic doses are not reduced because of it.
whyNot.C: Intrathecal chemotherapy does not prevent second cancers; cranial irradiation, now largely avoided, increases that risk.
whyNot.D: Response is monitored by marrow minimal residual disease testing, not by serial spinal fluid sampling.
whyNot.E: Lumbar punctures are not used as routine infection screening in asymptomatic patients.

items.objective: Explain the rationale for central nervous system prophylaxis in childhood ALL.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man comes to the physician because of itchy, scaly patches on his trunk and buttocks that have waxed and waned for 6 years and have been treated as eczema and then as psoriasis without lasting benefit. In the past 4 months several patches have thickened into raised plaques. Examination shows well-demarcated erythematous scaly patches and two indurated plaques on the buttocks, involving about 12% of the body surface; there is no lymphadenopathy, erythroderma or palmoplantar involvement. Skin biopsy shows a band-like infiltrate of atypical lymphocytes with cerebriform nuclei in the upper dermis, with clusters of these cells within the epidermis; the cells are CD3+ CD4+ with loss of CD7. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: E
options.html: Systemic chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone

items.explanationHtml:
Mycosis fungoides is an indolent cutaneous T-cell lymphoma of mature CD4+ T cells that typically presents as patches and plaques in non-sun-exposed areas and is often misdiagnosed as eczema or psoriasis for years.
