Biopsy shows epidermotropism with intraepidermal clusters of atypical cerebriform lymphocytes. Early-stage disease (patches and plaques without nodal, visceral or blood involvement) is treated with skin-directed therapy: topical corticosteroids, topical chemotherapy or retinoids, and phototherapy, with excellent long-term survival. Sézary syndrome is the leukemic variant with erythroderma, lymphadenopathy and circulating clonal cells, and is treated systemically.

Takeaway: early-stage mycosis fungoides is treated with skin-directed therapy; Sézary syndrome is the erythrodermic leukemic variant.

whyNot.A: Transplantation is reserved for advanced, refractory disease, not early patch and plaque disease.
whyNot.B: Photopheresis is used mainly for erythrodermic disease with blood involvement, which he does not have.
whyNot.C: Systemic agents are reserved for advanced or refractory disease because skin-directed therapy controls early stages with fewer adverse effects.
whyNot.E: Multiagent chemotherapy gives short remissions with significant toxicity and is not used for early-stage disease.

items.objective: Select stage-appropriate therapy for mycosis fungoides.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of fatigue and shortness of breath on climbing stairs for 4 months. She underwent Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 3 years ago and has lost 45 kg (99 lb). She stopped menstruating at age 39 after endometrial ablation. She takes a daily multivitamin. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL, MCV 71 fL, RDW 17.8% (normal 11.5-14.5%), and serum ferritin 5 ng/mL (normal 15-200). Stool tests for occult blood are negative on three samples. Which of the following best explains this patient's anemia?

options.label: A
options.html: Bypass of the duodenum, the main site of iron absorption

options.label: B
options.html: Deficiency of intrinsic factor from the gastric remnant

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of jejunal folate transport after the anastomosis

options.label: E
options.html: Occult bleeding from a marginal ulcer

items.explanationHtml:
Non-heme iron is absorbed mostly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, after gastric acid helps reduce ferric to ferrous iron. Roux-en-Y gastric bypass routes food past the duodenum and creates a small, low-acid pouch, so iron deficiency is one of the most common long-term complications, and it often needs intravenous replacement.

Takeaway: after gastric bypass, microcytic anemia with a very low ferritin is usually malabsorptive iron deficiency.

whyNot.B: Loss of intrinsic factor causes vitamin B<sub>12</sub> deficiency with macrocytosis, not a microcytic anemia with a ferritin of 5 ng/mL.
whyNot.C: Inflammatory hepcidin excess traps iron in stores, so ferritin would be normal or high, not depleted.
whyNot.D: Folate deficiency produces macrocytosis and does not lower ferritin.
whyNot.E: A marginal ulcer can bleed, but repeated negative occult blood tests with a clear malabsorptive cause make this less likely than impaired absorption.

items.objective: Explain why Roux-en-Y gastric bypass causes iron deficiency anemia.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man comes to the clinic because of intermittent cramping abdominal pain, constipation and fatigue for 2 months. He has worked for 6 years at a plant that recycles automotive batteries. Blood pressure is 152/94 mm Hg. Examination shows weakness of wrist extension on the right. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL and MCV 78 fL. A peripheral smear shows coarse blue granules distributed throughout many red cells. The red cell inclusions in this patient result from inhibition of which of the following enzymes?
items.explanationHtml:
Basophilic stippling is aggregated ribosomal RNA. Pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase normally degrades RNA nucleotides as reticulocytes mature. Lead inhibits this enzyme (inherited deficiency of the same enzyme produces the same smear), so RNA remnants persist and stain as coarse blue dots. Lead separately inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, which explains the anemia, the raised zinc protoporphyrin and the neurologic and abdominal symptoms.

Takeaway: coarse basophilic stippling in lead poisoning reflects inhibited pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase.

whyNot.A: Lead does inhibit this enzyme, but that block raises aminolevulinic acid and causes neurovisceral toxicity; it does not cause RNA to aggregate in red cells.
whyNot.B: Ferrochelatase inhibition raises zinc protoporphyrin and contributes to microcytosis, but it does not produce cytoplasmic RNA granules.
whyNot.C: G6PD deficiency leads to Heinz bodies from oxidised hemoglobin, seen with supravital stains, not coarse basophilic granules from lead.
whyNot.E: This enzyme is deficient in porphyria cutanea tarda, which causes blistering skin disease rather than red cell inclusions.

items.objective: Identify the enzyme whose inhibition by lead produces basophilic stippling.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of numbness of both feet and unsteady walking for 3 weeks. For several months he has inhaled the contents of many small gas cartridges each weekend at parties. Examination shows reduced vibration and joint position sense in the toes, a positive Romberg sign and brisk knee reflexes. Hemoglobin is 12.1 g/dL and MCV 104 fL. Serum vitamin B12 is 310 pg/mL (normal 200-800). MRI of the spine shows increased T2 signal in the dorsal columns of the cervical cord. The inhaled substance most likely caused these findings by inactivating which of the following enzymes?
items.explanationHtml:
Nitrous oxide oxidises the cobalt atom of cobalamin, inactivating the vitamin's function as the cofactor of methionine synthase. Homocysteine cannot be remethylated, S-adenosylmethionine falls and myelin methylation fails, producing subacute combined degeneration. Serum B12 can be normal because the vitamin is present but inactive; methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are raised.

Takeaway: recreational nitrous oxide causes functional B12 deficiency by inactivating cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase.

whyNot.A: This enzyme is inhibited by methotrexate and trimethoprim, which cause folate-type megaloblastic changes without dorsal column disease.
whyNot.C: Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and causes macrocytosis, but it is not inhaled and does not cause myelopathy.
whyNot.D: 5-Fluorouracil inhibits thymidylate synthase; this would not explain a neurologic syndrome from inhaled gas.
whyNot.E: Transcobalamin II is a transport protein, not an enzyme, and nitrous oxide does not act on it.

items.objective: Explain how nitrous oxide produces a B12-deficiency myelopathy despite a normal serum B12.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old woman with vitiligo and hypothyroidism comes to the clinic because of fatigue and a sore tongue for 3 months. She takes levothyroxine. Her tongue is smooth and red. Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL, MCV 114 fL, leukocyte count 3,600/mm3 and platelet count 128,000/mm3. A peripheral smear shows oval macrocytes and neutrophils with six nuclear lobes. Serum methylmalonic acid is increased. Antibodies to intrinsic factor are present. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?

options.label: B
options.html: Increased gastric acid output after pentagastrin

options.label: D
options.html: Inflammation limited to the gastric antrum

items.explanationHtml:
Pernicious anemia is autoimmune atrophic gastritis of the body and fundus. Loss of parietal cells removes intrinsic factor and acid. Without acid, the antral G cells are released from somatostatin-mediated feedback and serum gastrin rises, sometimes markedly; chronic hypergastrinemia drives enterochromaffin-like cell hyperplasia and type 1 gastric neuroendocrine tumours. It clusters with other autoimmune diseases such as thyroiditis and vitiligo.

Takeaway: autoimmune gastritis gives achlorhydria with a high serum gastrin.

whyNot.A: Achlorhydria removes the acid brake on antral G cells, so gastrin rises rather than falls.
whyNot.B: Parietal cells are destroyed, so acid output is absent even after stimulation.
whyNot.D: Antral-predominant gastritis is typical of H. pylori; autoimmune gastritis targets the body and fundus, where parietal cells live.
whyNot.E: Villous atrophy suggests celiac disease, which more often causes iron or folate deficiency; intrinsic factor antibodies point to the stomach.

items.objective: Predict the gastric physiology of pernicious anemia.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man comes to the clinic because of progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnea for 2 months. Six weeks ago, a chest radiograph for cough showed a 6-cm anterior mediastinal mass, and he is awaiting surgery. He looks pale. Hemoglobin is 6.4 g/dL, MCV 92 fL, leukocyte count 6,800/mm3 with a normal differential, platelet count 245,000/mm3 and reticulocytes 0.1% of red cells. LDH, bilirubin and haptoglobin are within the reference ranges. A bone marrow biopsy shows normal cellularity with normal myeloid cells and megakaryocytes and almost no erythroid precursors. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Severe normocytic anemia with reticulocytes near zero, normal leukocytes and platelets and a marrow lacking only erythroid precursors defines pure red cell aplasia. An anterior mediastinal mass in an older adult suggests thymoma, which is associated with immune destruction of erythroid progenitors. Thymectomy alone often does not correct the anemia, and immunosuppression may be needed.

Takeaway: isolated anemia with absent reticulocytes and erythroid precursors plus an anterior mediastinal mass suggests thymoma-associated pure red cell aplasia.

whyNot.A: Anemia of inflammation is usually mild and keeps erythroid precursors in the marrow; it does not abolish reticulocytes.
whyNot.B: Aplastic anemia affects all three lines and gives a hypocellular marrow; this patient's leukocytes, platelets and cellularity are normal.
whyNot.C: Myelodysplasia shows dysplastic precursors, often in more than one line, rather than isolated absence of erythroid cells.
whyNot.D: Marrow infiltration produces a leukoerythroblastic smear and abnormal cells on biopsy, which are absent here.

items.objective: Diagnose pure red cell aplasia associated with thymoma.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease comes for follow-up. His estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 38 to 22 mL/min/1.73 m2 over 3 years. He reports more fatigue. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL, MCV 88 fL and reticulocytes 0.6% of red cells. Serum ferritin is 240 ng/mL (normal 15-200), transferrin saturation 31%, and serum vitamin B12 and folate are normal. Serum erythropoietin is within the laboratory reference range despite the anemia. Loss of which of the following cell types is the main cause of this patient's anemia?

options.label: B
options.html: Juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole

options.label: C
options.html: Macula densa cells of the distal tubule

options.label: D
options.html: Peritubular interstitial fibroblasts of the cortex

items.explanationHtml:
Erythropoietin is produced by specialised peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells in the renal cortex and outer medulla, which sense oxygen through hypoxia-inducible factor. As CKD scars the interstitium, erythropoietin output becomes inappropriately low for the degree of anemia. A "normal" erythropoietin level in a patient this anemic is therefore relatively deficient. Iron stores here are adequate, so the hormone deficit dominates.

Takeaway: anemia of CKD reflects loss of erythropoietin-producing peritubular interstitial cells.

whyNot.A: Mesangial cells support the glomerular tuft and produce matrix; they are not the source of erythropoietin.
whyNot.B: Juxtaglomerular cells secrete renin, not erythropoietin.
whyNot.C: The macula densa senses tubular sodium chloride for tubuloglomerular feedback; it does not make erythropoietin.
whyNot.E: Proximal tubule cells make 1α-hydroxylase for calcitriol, but erythropoietin comes from interstitial cells beside them.

items.objective: Identify the renal cell type that produces erythropoietin.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of abdominal distention and right upper quadrant pain for 1 week. For several months she has noticed dark urine on waking. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, leukocyte count 3,400/mm3, platelet count 96,000/mm3 and reticulocytes 4.2% of red cells. LDH is 1,450 U/L (normal 45-200) and haptoglobin is undetectable. A direct antiglobulin test is negative. Doppler ultrasonography shows occlusion of the hepatic veins. Flow cytometry shows that a population of her red cells and granulocytes lacks CD55 and CD59. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?

options.label: B
options.html: Germline mutation in the gene for complement factor H

options.label: C
options.html: Germline mutation in the gene for spectrin

options.label: D
options.html: Somatic mutation in a gene for GPI-anchor synthesis

options.label: E
options.html: Somatic mutation in the gene for JAK2

items.explanationHtml:
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria arises from an acquired (somatic) mutation of PIGA in a hematopoietic stem cell. Without the glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor, its progeny lack CD55 (decay-accelerating factor) and CD59 (which blocks the membrane attack complex), so complement lyses red cells in the vessels. The disease combines intravascular hemolysis, cytopenias from marrow failure and thrombosis at unusual sites such as the hepatic veins.

Takeaway: PNH is a somatic stem cell defect in GPI-anchor synthesis that removes complement regulators.

whyNot.A: An autoantibody would usually give a positive direct antiglobulin test, and it would not explain absent CD55 and CD59 on granulocytes.
whyNot.B: Factor H defects cause atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome with schistocytes and kidney injury, not loss of GPI-anchored proteins from blood cells.
whyNot.C: Spectrin defects cause inherited membrane disorders with spherocytes or elliptocytes, not complement-mediated lysis with thrombosis and cytopenias.
whyNot.E: JAK2 mutations cause myeloproliferative neoplasms, which can cause Budd-Chiari syndrome but with high, not low, counts.

items.objective: Relate the clinical triad of PNH to its molecular defect.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy is evaluated for lifelong anemia. He had neonatal jaundice treated with exchange transfusion. He plays soccer and has few symptoms. His parents are healthy. Examination shows scleral icterus and a spleen palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL, MCV 98 fL and reticulocytes 14% of red cells. The direct antiglobulin test is negative, G6PD activity is normal and eosin-5′-maleimide binding is normal. A smear shows scattered red cells with short, evenly spaced projections. Red cell 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate concentration is increased. A deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Pyruvate kinase catalyses the last ATP-generating step of glycolysis. When it is deficient, ATP falls, cation pumps fail, and potassium and water leak out, producing rigid, spiculated cells that are removed in the spleen. Intermediates above the block accumulate, including 2,3-BPG, which lowers hemoglobin's oxygen affinity and helps tissues extract oxygen, so children tolerate low hemoglobin well. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, so carrier parents are healthy.

Takeaway: Coombs-negative lifelong hemolysis with raised 2,3-BPG and normal G6PD suggests pyruvate kinase deficiency.

whyNot.A: Loss of this enzyme lowers 2,3-BPG and leads to erythrocytosis, the opposite of this picture.
whyNot.B: G6PD activity is normal, and G6PD deficiency causes episodic oxidant hemolysis rather than lifelong hemolysis with raised 2,3-BPG.
whyNot.C: Hexokinase acts at the first step of glycolysis, so its deficiency lowers downstream 2,3-BPG.
whyNot.D: This deficiency is suggested by prominent basophilic stippling, not raised 2,3-BPG with spiculated cells.

items.objective: Identify pyruvate kinase deficiency from its metabolic signature.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus comes to the clinic because of fatigue and yellow eyes for 10 days. Hemoglobin is 7.9 g/dL, reticulocytes 9% of red cells, LDH 420 U/L (normal 45-200), indirect bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL and haptoglobin 8 mg/dL (normal 30-200). Urinalysis shows no blood. A peripheral smear shows many small, round red cells lacking central pallor. The direct antiglobulin test is positive with anti-IgG and negative with anti-C3. Which of the following is the main mechanism of red cell destruction in this patient?

options.label: A
options.html: Complement membrane attack complex lysis in the circulation

options.label: B
options.html: Fc receptor-mediated phagocytosis by splenic macrophages

options.label: C
options.html: Fragmentation of red cells by fibrin strands in small vessels

options.label: D
options.html: Hepatic clearance of IgM-coated cells by complement receptors

options.label: E
options.html: Oxidative precipitation of hemoglobin within red cells

items.explanationHtml:
Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia is caused by IgG autoantibodies that bind red cells at body temperature. Splenic macrophages recognise the Fc portion of the bound IgG and either engulf the cell or remove part of its membrane; the remaining cell reseals as a spherocyte, which is later trapped and destroyed. Hemolysis is therefore mainly extravascular. SLE is a classic secondary cause.

Takeaway: warm AIHA destroys IgG-coated cells by Fc receptor-mediated splenic phagocytosis, producing spherocytes.

whyNot.A: Lysis in the circulation would cause hemoglobinuria; this IgG-only, C3-negative picture without hemoglobinuria points to extravascular removal.
whyNot.C: Microangiopathic hemolysis produces schistocytes and a negative direct antiglobulin test.
whyNot.D: This describes cold agglutinin disease, in which the DAT is positive for C3 and IgM is the antibody.
whyNot.E: Oxidant injury (for example in G6PD deficiency) produces Heinz bodies and bite cells with a negative DAT.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of extravascular hemolysis in warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man is receiving high-dose intravenous penicillin G for streptococcal endocarditis. On day 12 of therapy, his hemoglobin has fallen from 12.8 to 9.4 g/dL. Reticulocytes are 7% of red cells, indirect bilirubin is 2.6 mg/dL and haptoglobin is low. Urinalysis is negative for blood. The direct antiglobulin test is strongly positive with anti-IgG. His serum does not react with untreated donor red cells but reacts strongly with donor cells pre-incubated with penicillin. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this patient's hemolysis?

options.label: A
options.html: Drug binding to the red cell membrane, acting as a hapten

options.label: D
options.html: Drug-induced oxidation of hemoglobin to methemoglobin

options.label: E
options.html: Immune complexes that fix complement in the circulation

items.explanationHtml:
High-dose penicillin binds covalently to red cell membrane proteins. In some patients IgG forms against the drug-membrane complex (a hapten mechanism, a type II hypersensitivity). The coated cells are removed by splenic macrophages, giving a gradual extravascular hemolysis after a week or more of therapy. The test that shows reactivity only with drug-treated cells is the signature. Stopping penicillin ends the hemolysis.

Takeaway: high-dose penicillin causes extravascular hemolysis by a hapten mechanism with an IgG-positive DAT.

whyNot.B: Methyldopa-type autoantibodies react with untreated red cells, unlike this serum, which needs penicillin-coated cells.
whyNot.C: Drugs do not cause G6PD deficiency; oxidant drugs unmask an inherited one, with a negative DAT.
whyNot.D: Methemoglobinemia causes cyanosis and a low oxygen saturation, not a positive DAT for IgG.
whyNot.E: Immune complex-type reactions cause abrupt intravascular hemolysis with complement on cells and hemoglobinuria, which is absent here.

items.objective: Distinguish the hapten mechanism of drug-induced immune hemolysis from other mechanisms.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man with a mechanical aortic valve placed 9 years ago has had fatigue for several months. Hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL, reticulocytes 6% of red cells, LDH 880 U/L (normal 45-200) and haptoglobin is undetectable. A smear shows fragmented red cells. A urine sample has no red cells on microscopy, but its sediment contains cells with granules that stain blue with Prussian blue. The iron-containing material in these urine cells most likely came from which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Bilirubin conjugated in hepatocytes and excreted in urine

options.label: B
options.html: Free hemoglobin reabsorbed by proximal tubular cells

options.label: D
options.html: Hemosiderin-laden macrophages shed from the bladder wall

options.label: E
options.html: Red cells lysed in the bladder after glomerular bleeding

items.explanationHtml:
Once haptoglobin is saturated during intravascular hemolysis, free hemoglobin dimers pass the glomerulus. Proximal tubular cells reabsorb hemoglobin, degrade it and store the iron as hemosiderin. When these cells are shed, the urine contains hemosiderin-laden epithelial cells that stain with Prussian blue. Hemosiderinuria appears a few days after hemolysis begins and persists, so it marks chronic intravascular hemolysis, here from mechanical valve shearing.

Takeaway: urine hemosiderin comes from shed proximal tubular cells that reabsorbed filtered free hemoglobin.

whyNot.A: Conjugated bilirubin contains no iron and would not stain with Prussian blue.
whyNot.C: The haptoglobin-hemoglobin complex is too large to be filtered; it is cleared by macrophages through CD163.
whyNot.D: Urothelial and bladder macrophages are not the source; the iron-laden cells are desquamated tubular epithelium.
whyNot.E: Microscopy shows no red cells, and intact red cells lysing in urine would not leave stainable hemosiderin inside cells.

items.objective: Trace the renal handling of free hemoglobin in intravascular hemolysis.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy with newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma is admitted to start chemotherapy. Serum uric acid is 11.2 mg/dL, and he is given a single dose of intravenous rasburicase. Eighteen hours later he has dark urine and his oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry is 88% on room air despite a normal arterial PaO2. Hemoglobin has fallen from 11.6 to 7.9 g/dL. A smear shows red cells with eccentric clear areas and irregular bites. The direct antiglobulin test is negative. Which of the following best explains this reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibody formation against the recombinant enzyme

options.label: B
options.html: Hydrogen peroxide generated by urate oxidation

options.label: C
options.html: Microangiopathy from uric acid crystal deposition

options.label: D
options.html: Rapid lysis of tumour cells releasing potassium

items.explanationHtml:
Rasburicase is recombinant urate oxidase, which converts uric acid to allantoin and releases hydrogen peroxide. Normal red cells detoxify peroxide with reduced glutathione, regenerated by NADPH from G6PD. In G6PD deficiency the peroxide oxidises hemoglobin, causing Heinz bodies, bite and blister cells, hemolysis and methemoglobinemia (the pulse oximetry gap). Screening for G6PD deficiency before rasburicase is recommended where feasible, and methylene blue should be avoided for the methemoglobinemia.

Takeaway: rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide and can trigger hemolysis and methemoglobinemia in G6PD deficiency.

whyNot.A: Antibodies to rasburicase cause allergy or loss of efficacy, and an immune mechanism would usually give a positive DAT.
whyNot.C: Uric acid crystals injure the kidney tubules but do not fragment red cells or cause methemoglobinemia.
whyNot.D: Tumour lysis releases potassium, phosphate and urate, but this does not oxidise hemoglobin.
whyNot.E: Complement coating would give a positive DAT and would not explain methemoglobinemia.

items.objective: Explain why rasburicase causes oxidant hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl with sickle cell disease (HbSS) is brought for a routine visit. She has had two painful crises in the past year. Her spleen is not palpable. A peripheral smear shows sickled cells, target cells and small, round, dark purple inclusions in some red cells. Infection with which of the following organisms poses the greatest risk of rapidly fatal sepsis in this patient?
items.explanationHtml:
Repeated splenic infarction makes children with HbSS functionally asplenic early in life, shown here by a nonpalpable spleen and Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants normally removed by the spleen). The spleen is essential for clearing opsonised encapsulated bacteria and making antibodies to polysaccharide antigens, so S. pneumoniae causes fulminant sepsis and meningitis. Penicillin prophylaxis and pneumococcal vaccination prevent most of these deaths.

Takeaway: functional asplenia in sickle cell disease brings the greatest risk from Streptococcus pneumoniae.

whyNot.A: E. coli causes urinary and neonatal infection; it is not the leading cause of fulminant sepsis in functional asplenia.
whyNot.B: Listeria threatens neonates, pregnant people and those with impaired cell-mediated immunity, not specifically children with asplenia.
whyNot.C: Pseudomonas affects patients with neutropenia, burns, cystic fibrosis or hospital exposure.
whyNot.D: S. aureus is a common cause of osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease, but it is not the organism that causes fulminant sepsis after loss of splenic function.

items.objective: Link functional asplenia in sickle cell disease to pneumococcal sepsis.

items.stemHtml: A 21-year-old man comes to the clinic because of painless red urine for 2 days. He is a competitive runner and feels well. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Hemoglobin is 14.6 g/dL and MCV 86 fL. Urinalysis shows many red cells without casts or protein. A sickle solubility test is positive, and hemoglobin analysis shows 58% HbA and 38% HbS. He reports getting up to urinate two or three times each night. The site in the kidney where his red cells are most likely to sickle is best described as which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
Red cells in sickle trait contain less than half HbS and do not sickle under ordinary conditions. The renal medulla is the exception: the vasa recta carry blood slowly through tissue with low oxygen tension, high osmolality (which dehydrates red cells and concentrates HbS) and low pH. Sickling there infarcts papillae, causing painless hematuria, and damages the countercurrent system, causing hyposthenuria and nocturia. Sickle trait is also associated with renal medullary carcinoma.

Takeaway: sickle trait cells sickle in the hypoxic, hypertonic, acidic renal medulla.

whyNot.A: Glomerular blood is well oxygenated and isotonic, so trait cells do not sickle there; glomerular bleeding would also bring casts or protein.
whyNot.B: The proximal tubule lies in the cortex, where tissue oxygen is relatively high and osmolality normal.
whyNot.C: Cortical blood flow is high and oxygen is plentiful, so it does not provide the conditions for sickling.
whyNot.E: Bleeding from the urothelium suggests stones or tumour, not the sickling environment of sickle trait.

items.objective: Explain why sickle trait causes hematuria and hyposthenuria.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman of West African ancestry is evaluated for mild anemia found on a routine blood count. She feels well. Examination shows a spleen tip palpable on inspiration. Hemoglobin is 11.1 g/dL, MCV 79 fL and reticulocytes 3% of red cells. A peripheral smear shows many target cells and a few red cells containing dense, rod-shaped crystals. Sickle solubility testing is negative. Hemoglobin analysis shows a single abnormal hemoglobin that migrates with HbA2 at alkaline pH, and no HbA. Which of the following amino acid substitutions in the β-globin chain is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Glutamate replaced by glutamine at position 121

options.label: B
options.html: Glutamate replaced by lysine at position 26

options.label: C
options.html: Glutamate replaced by lysine at position 6

options.label: D
options.html: Glutamate replaced by valine at position 6

options.label: E
options.html: Histidine replaced by tyrosine at position 63

items.explanationHtml:
Hemoglobin C results from lysine replacing glutamate at β6. Swapping a negative for a positive residue makes HbC migrate slowly at alkaline pH, together with HbA2. HbC does not polymerise like HbS, but it is less soluble and crystallises in dehydrated cells, producing rod-shaped crystals, target cells and mild hemolysis with splenomegaly in homozygotes (HbCC).

Takeaway: HbC (Glu6Lys) causes target cells, intracellular crystals and mild hemolysis.

whyNot.A: Hemoglobin D-Punjab is caused by a substitution at position 121 and runs with HbS at alkaline pH, not with HbA<sub>2</sub>.
whyNot.B: Lysine at position 26 is hemoglobin E, common in Southeast Asian ancestry and associated with microcytosis without crystals.
whyNot.D: Valine at position 6 is HbS, which would give a positive solubility test and polymerise rather than crystallise.
whyNot.E: Tyrosine at the distal histidine forms an M hemoglobin that causes methemoglobinemia and cyanosis, not target cells and crystals.

items.objective: Identify hemoglobin C disease from its smear and electrophoresis.

items.stemHtml: A couple is referred for counselling after their first pregnancy ended at 26 weeks' gestation with fetal hydrops. Fetal blood contained almost entirely a hemoglobin made of four γ chains. Both partners are healthy and of Southeast Asian ancestry. Their hemoglobin concentrations are 11.6 g/dL and 12.4 g/dL, their MCVs are 66 fL and 68 fL, and both have normal serum ferritin and a normal adult hemoglobin electrophoresis pattern. Which of the following is the most likely α-globin genotype of each partner?
items.explanationHtml:
Hb Bart's (γ4) hydrops fetalis requires the fetus to inherit no functional α gene from either parent (−−/−−). Each parent must therefore carry a chromosome with both α genes deleted. The parents' mild microcytosis with normal iron and normal adult electrophoresis fits α-thalassemia trait from two deleted genes; to transmit a doubly deleted chromosome, the deletions must be in cis (−−/αα), an arrangement common in Southeast Asian ancestry. Each subsequent pregnancy has a 1 in 4 risk.

Takeaway: Hb Bart's hydrops arises when both parents carry the cis α-thalassemia deletion (−−/αα).

whyNot.A: A normal genotype would not produce microcytosis or allow a fetus to inherit no α genes.
whyNot.B: Silent carriers have one deleted gene and a normal blood count, and they cannot pass on a chromosome with no α genes.
whyNot.C: This trans arrangement gives trait-range microcytosis, but each chromosome still carries one α gene, so a fetus cannot inherit zero.
whyNot.E: Three deleted genes cause HbH disease with moderate hemolytic anemia, which these healthy partners do not have.

items.objective: Infer parental α-globin genotypes from a pregnancy affected by Hb Bart's hydrops.

items.stemHtml: A 10-year-old boy is evaluated for intermittent jaundice since infancy. His father had his spleen removed as a young man. Examination shows mild scleral icterus and splenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL, MCV 82 fL, MCHC 37.5 g/dL (normal 31-36) and reticulocytes 8% of red cells. The direct antiglobulin test is negative. The smear shows many small, dense red cells without central pallor. In which of the following locations are this patient's abnormal red cells mainly destroyed?

options.label: D
options.html: Splenic cords of the red pulp

items.explanationHtml:
In hereditary spherocytosis, defective vertical links between the membrane and the spectrin skeleton (ankyrin, band 3, spectrin, protein 4.2) lead to loss of membrane, so cells become spheres with a raised MCHC. To return to the circulation, red cells in the splenic cords must squeeze through narrow slits in the sinus walls. Spherocytes cannot deform enough, become trapped and are consumed by red pulp macrophages. Splenectomy therefore corrects the anemia even though the cells stay spherical. Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant.

Takeaway: spherocytes are trapped and destroyed in the splenic cords of the red pulp.

whyNot.A: Destruction before release (ineffective erythropoiesis) is typical of thalassemia and megaloblastic anemia, not a membrane defect with a high reticulocyte count.
whyNot.B: The liver clears heavily complement-coated cells, but spherocytes are trapped mainly because they cannot deform through the splenic cords.
whyNot.C: Intravascular complement lysis causes hemoglobinuria and is not the mechanism of hereditary spherocytosis.
whyNot.E: The white pulp holds lymphocytes for immune responses; red cell filtering happens in the red pulp.

items.objective: Locate the site of red cell destruction in hereditary spherocytosis.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman is admitted because of severe diffuse abdominal pain, vomiting and constipation for 2 days. Three weeks ago she began a very low-calorie diet. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Pulse is 118/min and blood pressure is 158/98 mm Hg. Serum sodium is 126 mEq/L. Her urine darkens on standing, and a spot urine porphobilinogen is markedly increased. Intravenous hemin is started. Which of the following is the primary mechanism by which this drug improves her condition?

options.label: B
options.html: Binding and urinary excretion of porphobilinogen

options.label: E
options.html: Supply of heme for hemoglobin synthesis

items.explanationHtml:
Acute intermittent porphyria is a partial deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase. When demand for hepatic heme rises (fasting, P450-inducing drugs, alcohol, luteal progesterone), ALA synthase 1 is induced and the precursors ALA and porphobilinogen pile up before the block, causing neurovisceral attacks. Infused hemin replenishes the regulatory heme pool in hepatocytes, which represses ALAS1 synthesis and rapidly lowers precursor production. Carbohydrate loading has a weaker effect in the same direction.

Takeaway: hemin treats acute porphyric attacks by negative feedback repression of hepatic ALA synthase.

whyNot.A: Hemin does not activate the deficient enzyme; patients keep about half its activity regardless.
whyNot.B: Hemin is not a binding agent for precursors; reduced production, not increased excretion, lowers porphobilinogen.
whyNot.C: Hemin does not act by blocking P450 enzymes, although P450-inducing drugs trigger attacks.
whyNot.E: The marrow is not heme-deficient in this disorder; the problem is hepatic overproduction of precursors.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of hemin in acute intermittent porphyria.

items.stemHtml:
A 31-year-old man with Crohn disease of the terminal ileum and colon comes to the clinic because of fatigue and exertional dyspnea for 6 weeks. He has had 4-6 loose stools daily with crampy pain for 2 months despite adalimumab, and his gastroenterologist is changing his biologic therapy. He took oral ferrous sulfate for 3 weeks but stopped because his diarrhea and cramps worsened. Laboratory studies:

TestResultReference range
Hemoglobin8.9 g/dL13.5-17.5 g/dL
MCV76 fL80-100 fL
Platelets468,000/mm3150,000-400,000/mm3
Ferritin48 ng/mL15-200 ng/mL
Transferrin saturation7%20-50%
C-reactive protein38 mg/Lbelow 5 mg/L
Vitamin B12410 pg/mL200-800 pg/mL

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his anemia?
items.explanationHtml:
He has iron deficiency on a background of inflammation: ferritin is raised by active Crohn disease, but a transferrin saturation of 7% with microcytosis and thrombocytosis shows depleted available iron. In active inflammatory bowel disease, inflammation-driven hepcidin blunts oral absorption, oral iron can worsen GI symptoms, and he has already been intolerant. Intravenous iron is preferred in active IBD, after oral intolerance, and when hemoglobin is below 10 g/dL. Treating the Crohn disease will also improve the inflammatory component.

Takeaway: give intravenous iron for iron deficiency in active IBD, especially with oral intolerance or hemoglobin below 10 g/dL.

whyNot.A: An ESA does not correct iron deficiency and works poorly without iron; it has no first-line role here.
whyNot.B: Lower-dose oral iron is reasonable in quiescent disease, but in active IBD with intolerance and hemoglobin below 10 g/dL, intravenous iron is preferred.
whyNot.D: He is stable without ischemic symptoms, so transfusion is not indicated at a hemoglobin of 8.9 g/dL.
whyNot.E: His B<sub>12</sub> is normal and the anemia is microcytic; ileal disease warrants B<sub>12</sub> monitoring, not empiric injections.

items.objective: Choose intravenous iron for iron deficiency anemia in active inflammatory bowel disease.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of burning and numbness of both feet for 6 months and mild forgetfulness. She has had type 2 diabetes for 14 years treated with metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, and gastroesophageal reflux treated with omeprazole for 8 years. Examination shows reduced vibration sense at the toes and absent ankle reflexes. Hemoglobin A1c is 6.8%. Hemoglobin is 11.4 g/dL and MCV 103 fL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Long-term metformin and proton pump inhibitor use both reduce vitamin B12 absorption, and this patient has macrocytosis, neuropathy and cognitive change. Neuropathy in a diabetic patient should not be assumed to be diabetic. Measure serum B12 (adding methylmalonic acid if the result is borderline). Periodic B12 testing is advised for people taking metformin long term, especially with neuropathy or anemia.

Takeaway: check B12 in patients on long-term metformin or acid suppression who develop macrocytosis or neuropathy.

whyNot.A: Marrow examination is premature before simple measurements of B<sub>12</sub> and folate.
whyNot.B: Imaging does not address the macrocytosis and the drug-related risk of a treatable vitamin deficiency.
whyNot.C: These would characterise the neuropathy but not identify its likely treatable cause.
whyNot.E: Empiric folate could correct the anemia while B<sub>12</sub>-related neurologic damage progresses.

items.objective: Test for vitamin B12 deficiency in a patient taking metformin and a proton pump inhibitor.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man comes to the clinic because of tingling of the hands and feet and difficulty walking in the dark for 2 months. Examination shows loss of vibration and position sense in the feet, a positive Romberg sign and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Hemoglobin is 8.8 g/dL, MCV 118 fL and the smear shows hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum vitamin B12 is 82 pg/mL (normal 200-800) and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies are positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: E
options.html: Vitamin B<sub>12</sub> 25 µg by mouth daily

items.explanationHtml:
He has pernicious anemia with subacute combined degeneration. With neurologic deficits, parenteral cobalamin is preferred: frequent intramuscular injections at first, then monthly for life. Reticulocytes rise within a week, and potassium should be monitored early in treatment of severe anemia. High-dose oral B12 (1,000-2,000 µg daily) is an alternative for maintenance in adherent patients, but low-dose oral supplements are inadequate without intrinsic factor.

Takeaway: treat pernicious anemia with neurologic signs with parenteral B12, lifelong.

whyNot.A: Folate alone may improve the blood count but does not treat, and can unmask, progressive B<sub>12</sub>-deficiency neurologic damage.
whyNot.C: He is stable; transfusion does not treat the deficiency and can precipitate heart failure in severe megaloblastic anemia.
whyNot.D: Plasma exchange has no role in pernicious anemia.
whyNot.E: A standard multivitamin dose relies on intrinsic factor, which is absent; only high oral doses work by passive diffusion.

items.objective: Treat pernicious anemia with neurologic involvement.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of gum bleeding, fatigue and bruising for 3 weeks. He takes no medications and has no toxic exposures. Leukocyte count is 1,100/mm3 with an absolute neutrophil count of 300/mm3, hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, MCV 99 fL, platelet count 9,000/mm3, and absolute reticulocyte count 18,000/mm3. Bone marrow biopsy shows 10% cellularity, mostly fat, with no abnormal cells or fibrosis. Cytogenetics are normal, chromosome breakage testing is negative and PNH flow cytometry shows no clone. He is HLA-typed with his family; his 22-year-old brother is a full HLA match. After transfusion support, which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
He has severe aplastic anemia: marrow cellularity below 25% with neutrophils below 500/mm3, platelets below 20,000/mm3 and reticulocytes below 60,000/mm3. Inherited marrow failure (negative breakage testing) and a PNH clone have been looked for. For younger patients with an HLA-matched sibling, allogeneic stem cell transplantation is first-line and offers cure. Older patients or those without a matched sibling receive horse antithymocyte globulin and cyclosporine with eltrombopag. Before transplant, use leukoreduced, irradiated products and avoid transfusions from relatives.

Takeaway: young patients with severe aplastic anemia and a matched sibling should proceed to allogeneic stem cell transplantation.

whyNot.A: Immunosuppression is the standard for patients without a matched sibling or who are older, but in a young patient with a matched sibling, transplant is preferred because it is curative and avoids relapse and clonal evolution.
whyNot.B: Growth factors cannot restore a marrow depleted of stem cells and do not treat the immune attack.
whyNot.C: Glucocorticoids alone are ineffective in aplastic anemia and add infection risk.
whyNot.D: Severe aplastic anemia is fatal without definitive therapy; supportive care alone is inadequate.

items.objective: Select definitive therapy for severe aplastic anemia in a young patient with a matched sibling donor.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman who received a kidney transplant 7 months ago comes to the clinic because of increasing fatigue for 6 weeks. She takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and prednisone. Graft function is stable. Hemoglobin is 6.1 g/dL (8 weeks ago 11.8 g/dL), MCV 90 fL, leukocyte count 5,200/mm3, platelet count 210,000/mm3 and reticulocytes 0.1% of red cells. Iron studies, vitamin B12 and folate are normal. Bone marrow shows absent erythroid maturation with a few giant pronormoblasts containing nuclear inclusions. Quantitative PCR for parvovirus B19 DNA in blood is strongly positive. In addition to red cell transfusion, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid progenitors through the P antigen and halts erythropoiesis. Healthy people clear it with neutralising antibody in days. Transplant recipients on intensive immunosuppression cannot, and develop persistent pure red cell aplasia with giant pronormoblasts. Serology is unreliable in this setting, so PCR confirms the diagnosis. Intravenous immune globulin supplies neutralising antibody, and immunosuppression is reduced where the graft allows.

Takeaway: chronic parvovirus B19 red cell aplasia in an immunocompromised host is treated with IVIG and reduced immunosuppression.

whyNot.A: Erythroid progenitors are being destroyed by the virus, so erythropoietin cannot stimulate them.
whyNot.B: Ganciclovir treats cytomegalovirus, not parvovirus B19, which has no specific antiviral therapy.
whyNot.D: Rituximab would further impair antibody production, the very defense she lacks.
whyNot.E: The anemia is from absent production, not splenic destruction, so splenectomy would not help.

items.objective: Treat persistent parvovirus B19 red cell aplasia in an immunocompromised patient.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman with CKD stage G4 from diabetic and hypertensive kidney disease comes for follow-up. She is not on dialysis. She has mild fatigue but no chest pain or dyspnea at rest. Estimated GFR is 21 mL/min/1.73 m2. Hemoglobin is 9.3 g/dL, MCV 85 fL and reticulocytes 0.7% of red cells. Ferritin is 64 ng/mL (normal 15-200), transferrin saturation 14% (normal 20-50%), and vitamin B12 and folate are normal. Stool occult blood testing is negative and her colonoscopy 2 years ago was normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Epoetin alfa targeting a hemoglobin of 13 g/dL

items.explanationHtml:
Before attributing anemia to erythropoietin deficiency or starting an ESA, correct iron deficiency. In CKD, iron is recommended when transferrin saturation is 30% or lower and ferritin is 500 ng/mL or lower; she has both. Oral iron is acceptable for patients not on dialysis, with intravenous iron if oral fails or is not tolerated. If hemoglobin stays below 10 g/dL after iron repletion, an ESA can be started, avoiding targets above about 11.5 g/dL.

Takeaway: in anemia of CKD, replete iron first and use ESAs only to modest hemoglobin targets.

whyNot.A: Targeting a normal hemoglobin with ESAs increased stroke, thrombosis and hypertension in trials, and iron should be repleted first.
whyNot.C: HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors are approved in the United States only for patients on dialysis, and iron repletion comes first regardless.
whyNot.D: She is stable with mild symptoms; transfusion also risks sensitisation in a likely future transplant candidate.
whyNot.E: Untreated iron deficiency is evident now, so waiting is not appropriate.

items.objective: Sequence iron repletion before ESA therapy in anemia of chronic kidney disease.

items.stemHtml: A 12-month-old boy is brought for a well-child visit. He is enrolled in Medicaid and lives in an apartment built in 1948. He is developing normally and eats a varied diet. Examination is normal. Hemoglobin is 11.4 g/dL. A screening fingerstick (capillary) blood lead level is 9 µg/dL (CDC blood lead reference value 3.5 µg/dL). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Capillary samples can be falsely raised by lead on the skin, so any capillary result at or above the reference value is confirmed with a venous sample, with timing based on the level. Management then follows the confirmed venous level: environmental investigation and removal of the source, nutritional counselling (iron and calcium), developmental monitoring and repeat testing for all elevated levels, oral succimer at 45 µg/dL or more, and hospital-based parenteral chelation at 70 µg/dL or more or with encephalopathy.

Takeaway: confirm a raised capillary blood lead level with a venous sample before acting on it.

whyNot.A: Radiography looks for ingested lead fragments in symptomatic children with high confirmed levels; it does not replace confirmation.
whyNot.B: Parenteral chelation is reserved for confirmed levels of 70 µg/dL or more or encephalopathy.
whyNot.C: Oral chelation is used for confirmed levels of 45 µg/dL or more, far above this result.
whyNot.D: An elevated capillary level needs prompt confirmation, not routine rescreening.

items.objective: Confirm a raised capillary blood lead level with venous testing.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of fatigue and dark yellow eyes for 2 weeks. She takes no medications. Pulse is 102/min and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. Examination shows scleral icterus and a spleen tip palpable below the costal margin. Hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL, reticulocytes 11% of red cells, LDH 510 U/L (normal 45-200), indirect bilirubin 3.4 mg/dL and haptoglobin undetectable. The smear shows numerous spherocytes. The direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG and weakly positive for C3. Leukocyte and platelet counts are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Spherocytes, signs of hemolysis and an IgG-positive DAT establish warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. First-line therapy is a glucocorticoid such as prednisone about 1 mg/kg daily, tapered over months after response, with folic acid and thromboprophylaxis if hospitalised. Look for secondary causes such as lymphoma, CLL, SLE and drugs. Rituximab follows for relapse or steroid dependence.

Takeaway: glucocorticoids are first-line therapy for warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

whyNot.A: Terminal complement inhibition treats PNH; warm AIHA is driven by IgG and splenic phagocytosis.
whyNot.B: Plasma exchange is the treatment for TTP and has no established first-line role in warm AIHA.
whyNot.D: Rituximab is the preferred second-line agent or an add-on in severe disease, not usually the sole first treatment.
whyNot.E: Splenectomy is reserved for disease that fails or relapses after medical therapy.

items.objective: Start glucocorticoids for newly diagnosed warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man with chronic lymphocytic leukemia that has not required treatment was diagnosed with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia 4 months ago. Hemoglobin rose from 6.9 to 11.8 g/dL with prednisone 1 mg/kg daily, but each time the dose has been tapered below 20 mg daily his hemoglobin has fallen below 9 g/dL with rising LDH. He now has new hyperglycemia and a vertebral compression fracture. Lymphocyte count is 18,000/mm3 and has been stable, and he has no lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly or B symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
He has steroid-dependent warm AIHA with significant glucocorticoid toxicity. The preferred second-line therapy is rituximab, which depletes CD20-positive B cells that produce the autoantibody and also treats the CLL clone behind it. AIHA alone in CLL can be treated with immunosuppression without starting full CLL therapy; CLL-directed therapy is considered when AIHA is refractory or the CLL itself needs treatment.

Takeaway: rituximab is the preferred second-line therapy for steroid-dependent or refractory warm AIHA.

whyNot.A: A thrombopoietin receptor agonist treats ITP and aplastic anemia, not autoimmune hemolysis.
whyNot.B: He is steroid dependent with serious adverse effects; escalating the dose adds toxicity without addressing the antibody source.
whyNot.C: IVIG has inconsistent benefit in warm AIHA and only a short-lived effect.
whyNot.E: Splenectomy is an option, but rituximab is preferred first, especially in older adults and when CLL is the driver.

items.objective: Choose rituximab for steroid-dependent warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman has had fatigue and purple discoloration of her fingertips, nose and ears in cold weather for 2 winters. She needed two red cell transfusions in the past 3 months despite staying indoors and dressing warmly. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL, reticulocytes 7% of red cells, LDH 390 U/L (normal 45-200) and haptoglobin is undetectable. The smear shows red cell clumping. The direct antiglobulin test is positive for C3 and negative for IgG. Serum immunofixation shows a small IgM kappa monoclonal protein. Testing for Mycoplasma and EBV is negative, and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
This is primary cold agglutinin disease: IgM autoantibody from a low-grade clonal B-cell disorder fixes complement on red cells in cooler body parts, producing acrocyanosis and C3-positive, IgG-negative DAT. Warming measures come first. Transfusion-dependent or symptomatic disease is treated with B-cell-directed therapy, rituximab alone or with bendamustine. Complement inhibition with sutimlimab (anti-C1s) is another option. Steroids and splenectomy do not work well.

Takeaway: symptomatic primary cold agglutinin disease is treated with warming plus rituximab-based therapy, not steroids or splenectomy.

whyNot.A: Azathioprine has little effect on the clonal B cells or complement activation that drive cold agglutinin disease.
whyNot.B: IVIG has no established benefit in cold agglutinin disease.
whyNot.C: Glucocorticoids are generally ineffective in cold agglutinin disease except at doses too toxic for long-term use.
whyNot.E: C3b-coated cells are cleared mainly in the liver, so splenectomy does not help.

items.objective: Choose B-cell-directed therapy for symptomatic cold agglutinin disease.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man comes to the clinic because of fatigue, intermittent difficulty swallowing and episodes of cola-colored urine, most noticeable in the morning, for 5 months. He has had no fever or medications. Hemoglobin is 8.7 g/dL, MCV 103 fL, leukocyte count 3,900/mm3, platelet count 118,000/mm3 and reticulocytes 5% of red cells. LDH is 1,320 U/L (normal 45-200), haptoglobin is undetectable and indirect bilirubin is 2.2 mg/dL. Urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows no red cells. The direct antiglobulin test is negative and the smear shows no schistocytes or spherocytes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis (very high LDH, absent haptoglobin, hemoglobinuria without red cells) with mild cytopenias and smooth muscle symptoms such as dysphagia points to paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. The diagnostic test is flow cytometry of peripheral blood, showing red cells lacking CD55 and CD59 and granulocytes lacking GPI-anchored proteins (FLAER). It also measures clone size.

Takeaway: test Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis with cytopenias by flow cytometry for PNH.

whyNot.A: A marrow examination may later assess marrow failure, but it does not diagnose the hemolytic process.
whyNot.B: EMA binding evaluates hereditary spherocytosis, which causes extravascular hemolysis with spherocytes rather than hemoglobinuria.
whyNot.C: Hemoglobinopathies do not explain acquired intravascular hemolysis with cytopenias in a previously well adult.
whyNot.D: Osmotic fragility also tests for spherocytosis, which is absent on the smear.

items.objective: Order flow cytometry to diagnose paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.

items.stemHtml: The 29-year-old man with fatigue, dysphagia and cola-colored morning urine has flow cytometry showing a large population of granulocytes and red cells lacking GPI-anchored proteins, confirming paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. He continues to need red cell transfusions. Treatment with ravulizumab, a long-acting C5 inhibitor, is planned. His routine adult vaccinations are up to date. Which of the following is the most appropriate step before starting this drug?
items.explanationHtml:
The membrane attack complex is the key defense against Neisseria meningitidis, so C5 inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab) raise the risk of invasive meningococcal disease many hundreds of times above that of the general population. Patients receive both MenACWY and MenB vaccines at least 2 weeks before the first dose, with antibiotic prophylaxis if treatment must start sooner, and they carry a card describing the risk. Vaccination lowers but does not eliminate the risk, so fever needs urgent evaluation.

Takeaway: vaccinate against meningococci (ACWY and B) at least 2 weeks before starting a C5 inhibitor.

whyNot.A: Hepatitis B testing is needed before B-cell-depleting therapy such as rituximab, not specifically before C5 inhibition.
whyNot.B: Latent tuberculosis screening is required before TNF inhibitors and similar drugs; C5 inhibition mainly raises the risk of Neisseria infection.
whyNot.D: Pneumococcal vaccination is routine, but terminal complement blockade specifically predisposes to meningococcal disease.
whyNot.E: Anticoagulation is for thrombosis; complement inhibition itself reduces thrombotic risk and does not require it beforehand.

items.objective: Vaccinate against meningococcus before starting complement C5 inhibition.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man returns from 6 months of work in Papua New Guinea with fever and chills every 48 hours for a week. A blood smear shows enlarged infected red cells with Schüffner dots, and rapid testing identifies Plasmodium vivax. He is treated with artemether-lumefantrine and his fever resolves. Hemoglobin is 12.6 g/dL. Before he is prescribed a drug to prevent relapse, which of the following is the most appropriate test?

options.label: E
options.html: Thick and thin smears every 6 hours

items.explanationHtml:
P. vivax and P. ovale form dormant liver hypnozoites that cause relapses weeks to months later. Radical cure needs primaquine or tafenoquine, both oxidant drugs that can cause severe hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. G6PD activity must be measured first; tafenoquine requires a quantitative result with normal activity, and patients with deficiency need an alternative regimen or specialist advice. Testing is also important in pregnancy, where both drugs are avoided.

Takeaway: test G6PD activity before primaquine or tafenoquine radical cure.

whyNot.A: Immune hemolysis is not the risk of the relapse-prevention drugs; oxidant hemolysis is.
whyNot.B: Hemoglobin variants do not change eligibility for primaquine or tafenoquine.
whyNot.D: Haptoglobin may be low after malaria but does not predict drug-induced hemolysis.
whyNot.E: His blood-stage infection has already been treated; serial smears do not address the dormant liver stages.

items.objective: Test G6PD activity before prescribing primaquine or tafenoquine.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old man was started on dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis 5 days ago. He now has dark urine, fatigue and yellow eyes. Hemoglobin is 9.0 g/dL (14.9 g/dL two weeks ago), reticulocytes 9% of red cells, LDH 640 U/L (normal 45-200) and haptoglobin undetectable. The smear shows blister cells and bite cells, and a supravital stain shows Heinz bodies. The direct antiglobulin test is negative. Dapsone is stopped. A quantitative G6PD activity measured today is within the reference range. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the cause of his hemolysis?

options.label: B
options.html: Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59

options.label: C
options.html: Rechallenge with dapsone at a lower dose

items.explanationHtml:
Dapsone-triggered hemolysis with Heinz bodies and bite cells strongly suggests G6PD deficiency. During and just after an episode, the oldest, most enzyme-deficient cells have been destroyed and the circulation is full of young cells with higher G6PD activity, so the assay can be falsely normal, especially in milder variants and in heterozygous women. Repeat the quantitative assay after recovery, roughly 3 months later (or test family members, or use genotyping). Dapsone can also cause dose-related oxidant hemolysis in people with normal G6PD, which a repeat normal result would support.

Takeaway: a normal G6PD level during acute hemolysis does not exclude deficiency; retest after recovery.

whyNot.A: The marrow is responding appropriately; marrow examination would not identify an enzyme defect.
whyNot.B: PNH causes Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis but not drug-triggered Heinz bodies and bite cells.
whyNot.C: Re-exposure could cause another dangerous hemolytic episode and is not a diagnostic test.
whyNot.D: Osmotic fragility tests for spherocytosis, which does not explain oxidant inclusions after a drug.

items.objective: Interpret a normal G6PD level during acute hemolysis.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman is in the hospital receiving intravenous ceftriaxone for pyelonephritis. Ten minutes into her sixth daily dose she develops back pain, dyspnea and dark red urine. Blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg and pulse is 118/min. Hemoglobin has fallen from 11.9 g/dL this morning to 8.1 g/dL. LDH is 1,150 U/L (normal 45-200), haptoglobin is undetectable and plasma is pink. The direct antiglobulin test is positive for C3. She received no blood products during this admission. In addition to supportive care, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Sudden intravascular hemolysis (hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, complement on cells, hypotension) during a dose of ceftriaxone after several days of therapy is typical of drug-dependent antibody hemolysis, which can be fatal. The key step is to stop the drug immediately and permanently, treat the infection with an agent from an unrelated class, support circulation and kidney function, and transfuse if needed. Document the reaction to prevent re-exposure.

Takeaway: stop the drug at once in suspected drug-induced immune hemolysis.

whyNot.A: Another third-generation cephalosporin may cross-react with the same drug-dependent antibody; switch to an unrelated class.
whyNot.B: The drug-dependent antibody keeps lysing cells while the drug is present; steroids do not make continuing it safe.
whyNot.D: Plasma exchange is not a standard treatment; removing the drug ends the reaction.
whyNot.E: Rituximab treats autoimmune hemolysis over weeks and has no role in drug-dependent hemolysis.

items.objective: Manage drug-induced immune hemolysis by stopping the offending drug.

items.stemHtml: A 13-year-old girl with sickle cell disease (HbSS) is admitted with a vaso-occlusive crisis in her back and legs and treated with intravenous morphine and fluids. On hospital day 2 she develops a temperature of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), cough and right-sided chest pain. Respiratory rate is 28/min and oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. Crackles are heard at the right base. Chest radiograph shows a new right lower lobe infiltrate. Hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL (baseline 8.1 g/dL). Oxygen by nasal cannula and incentive spirometry are started. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
A new infiltrate with fever, chest pain and hypoxemia in a patient with sickle cell disease is acute chest syndrome, a leading cause of death. Treatment includes an empiric parenteral cephalosporin plus a macrolide (covering pneumococcus, Mycoplasma and Chlamydia pneumoniae), oxygen, incentive spirometry, careful fluids and analgesia, and bronchodilators if there is wheeze. Simple transfusion is considered if hemoglobin falls more than 1 g/dL below baseline; exchange transfusion is used for severe or progressive disease.

Takeaway: treat acute chest syndrome with a cephalosporin plus a macrolide, oxygen and incentive spirometry.

whyNot.B: Diuresis is not indicated; the infiltrate is acute chest syndrome, not fluid overload, although fluids should be given judiciously.
whyNot.C: Inhaled nitric oxide has not shown benefit in acute chest syndrome.
whyNot.D: Oral amoxicillin lacks atypical coverage and is too weak for a hospitalised child with hypoxemia.
whyNot.E: Exchange is for severe or rapidly progressive disease; her hemoglobin is near baseline and she is maintaining saturation with oxygen.

items.objective: Start empiric antibiotics for acute chest syndrome.

items.stemHtml: The 13-year-old girl with HbSS has been receiving ceftriaxone, azithromycin, oxygen and incentive spirometry for acute chest syndrome. Twelve hours later she is more dyspneic. Respiratory rate is 40/min and oxygen saturation is 86% on 6 L/min of oxygen by face mask. Chest radiograph now shows infiltrates in both lower lobes and the right middle lobe. Hemoglobin is 8.0 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.html: Simple transfusion to a hemoglobin of 13 g/dL

items.explanationHtml:
Her acute chest syndrome is progressing: multilobar infiltrates and hypoxemia below 90% despite supplemental oxygen. Red cell exchange transfusion rapidly lowers the HbS fraction (target usually below about 30%) without raising hemoglobin and viscosity, and it is the treatment of choice for severe or worsening disease. Simple transfusion suits milder cases with a falling hemoglobin. Transfer to intensive care and continued antibiotics are also needed.

Takeaway: use exchange transfusion for severe or rapidly progressive acute chest syndrome.

whyNot.A: Imaging for embolism would delay treatment of a recognised, rapidly progressing acute chest syndrome.
whyNot.B: Glucocorticoids are not standard for acute chest syndrome and are associated with rebound pain crises.
whyNot.D: Raising hemoglobin well above 10 g/dL increases viscosity and can worsen vaso-occlusion.
whyNot.E: Broadening antibiotics does not address the sickling driving her respiratory failure.

items.objective: Choose exchange transfusion for severe acute chest syndrome.

items.stemHtml: The 13-year-old girl with HbSS recovers from severe acute chest syndrome after exchange transfusion and is ready for discharge. In the past year she has also had three hospital admissions for pain crises. She takes folic acid and has received all recommended vaccines. Her family has previously declined disease-modifying therapy, but now wishes to reduce future episodes. Her renal and liver function are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term therapy?

options.label: D
options.html: Monthly simple transfusions to hemoglobin 12 g/dL

items.explanationHtml:
Hydroxyurea is recommended for all children with HbSS from 9 months of age, and especially for those with recurrent pain or acute chest syndrome. By raising HbF and lowering neutrophil count and adhesion, it reduces pain crises, acute chest syndrome, hospitalisation and transfusion, and improves survival. It needs regular blood count monitoring for myelosuppression and counselling about contraception because it is teratogenic.

Takeaway: hydroxyurea is the core disease-modifying therapy after recurrent pain crises or acute chest syndrome.

whyNot.A: Aspirin does not reduce pain crises or acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease.
whyNot.C: Penicillin prophylaxis prevents pneumococcal sepsis in young children but does not reduce vaso-occlusive events.
whyNot.D: Chronic transfusion is for stroke prevention or selected refractory cases, and targets above 10 g/dL raise viscosity.
whyNot.E: Splenectomy is for recurrent splenic sequestration, not for pain crises and acute chest syndrome.

items.objective: Start hydroxyurea for recurrent vaso-occlusive complications of sickle cell disease.

items.stemHtml: A 5-year-old boy with HbSS is seen for routine follow-up. He has had no neurologic symptoms, and his neurologic examination is normal. He takes penicillin prophylaxis and folic acid. Screening transcranial Doppler ultrasonography shows a time-averaged mean maximum velocity of 224 cm/s in the left middle cerebral artery, and a repeat study 2 weeks later shows 218 cm/s. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Annual transcranial Doppler from age 2 to 16 detects children at high risk of a first stroke. A confirmed time-averaged mean maximum velocity of 200 cm/s or more is abnormal. Regular transfusions to keep HbS below about 30% reduce first stroke dramatically. After at least a year of transfusion, children without severe vasculopathy on imaging may transition to hydroxyurea under specialist care. Stopping transfusions without a substitute allows risk to return.

Takeaway: a confirmed abnormal transcranial Doppler in sickle cell disease calls for chronic transfusion.

whyNot.A: Antiplatelet therapy does not prevent the large-vessel vasculopathy of sickle cell disease.
whyNot.C: A confirmed velocity of 200 cm/s or more carries a high stroke risk, so waiting a year is unsafe.
whyNot.D: Anticoagulation has no role in primary stroke prevention in sickle cell disease.
whyNot.E: Whether to stop penicillin at age 5 is a separate decision and does nothing about his stroke risk.

items.objective: Start chronic transfusion after an abnormal transcranial Doppler screen.

items.stemHtml: A 2-year-old girl with HbSS is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after her parents noted a temperature of 39.3 °C (102.7 °F). She has had a runny nose for 2 days. She takes penicillin twice daily. She is alert and playful. Pulse is 140/min and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. Examination shows clear rhinorrhea, clear lungs and a spleen tip palpable 1 cm below the costal margin, unchanged from her last visit. A blood count, reticulocyte count and blood culture are drawn. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Fever of 38.5 °C (101.3 °F) or more in a child with sickle cell disease is an emergency because functional asplenia allows overwhelming pneumococcal sepsis, even in children taking penicillin. After rapid assessment and cultures, a parenteral third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone is given promptly, without waiting for laboratory results. Well-appearing children with reliable follow-up may be discharged after the dose; ill-appearing children are admitted.

Takeaway: give prompt parenteral ceftriaxone for fever in a child with sickle cell disease.

whyNot.A: Oral therapy is inadequate for possible pneumococcal bacteremia in a child with functional asplenia.
whyNot.C: She has no meningeal signs or altered mental status; routine lumbar puncture is not required before antibiotics.
whyNot.D: Waiting for culture results risks death from fulminant sepsis, which can progress within hours.
whyNot.E: Her hemoglobin has not been shown to fall and there is no sequestration; transfusion is not indicated.

items.objective: Treat fever in a child with sickle cell disease with prompt parenteral antibiotics.

items.stemHtml:
A 27-year-old woman of Vietnamese ancestry comes for preconception counselling. She feels well. She was given iron tablets twice in the past for "anemia" without any change in her blood count. Her partner, also of Vietnamese ancestry, has microcytosis on a recent blood count. Her laboratory studies:

TestResultReference range
Hemoglobin11.2 g/dL12.0-16.0 g/dL
MCV67 fL80-100 fL
Red cell count5.6 million/mm34.0-5.2 million/mm3
RDW13.6%11.5-14.5%
Ferritin86 ng/mL15-200 ng/mL
HbA22.4%2.0-3.5%
HbF0.6%below 2%
Abnormal hemoglobin bandsNoneNone

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Microcytosis with a high red cell count, normal RDW and normal ferritin suggests thalassemia trait. A normal HbA2 and HbF with normal iron makes β-thalassemia trait unlikely and points to α-thalassemia trait, which is invisible on adult electrophoresis. DNA analysis for α-globin deletions defines the genotype. Because both partners are of Southeast Asian ancestry, where the cis (−−/αα) deletion is common, the partner should also be tested, with genetic counselling and prenatal diagnosis options if both carry cis deletions.

Takeaway: microcytosis with normal iron and normal HbA2 calls for α-globin gene testing, especially before pregnancy.

whyNot.A: Marrow examination is invasive and does not identify the inherited globin defect.
whyNot.B: Ferritin is normal and iron has already failed twice; more iron risks overload.
whyNot.D: Both partners may carry an α-thalassemia deletion, and the cis arrangement risks a pregnancy with Hb Bart's hydrops, so testing changes counselling.
whyNot.E: HbH inclusions mark three-gene deletion disease; she has trait-range findings, and staining cannot define the genotype.

items.objective: Order α-globin gene analysis for suspected α-thalassemia trait before pregnancy.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy with transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia receives red cell transfusions every 3 weeks. Serum ferritin is 3,400 ng/mL. Cardiac MRI shows a myocardial T2* of 9 ms (normal above 20 ms) with a normal ejection fraction. He has been taking deferasirox, which is being changed because of rising creatinine, and his hematologist starts oral deferiprone. Which of the following is the most important monitoring for this drug?
items.explanationHtml:
Deferiprone is particularly effective at removing cardiac iron, which matters here because a low T2* indicates myocardial iron loading. Its major serious adverse effect is agranulocytosis, so the absolute neutrophil count is checked weekly, and patients stop the drug and seek care for fever. Arthropathy and GI upset are other effects. Deferoxamine and deferiprone may also be combined for severe cardiac iron.

Takeaway: deferiprone requires weekly neutrophil monitoring because of agranulocytosis.

whyNot.A: Audiology and eye monitoring are needed with deferoxamine, the parenteral chelator.
whyNot.B: Renal monitoring is required for deferasirox, the drug he is leaving.
whyNot.C: Zinc may fall with chelation, but this is not the major safety monitoring for deferiprone.
whyNot.D: Routine frequent slit-lamp examination is not the key safety step for this drug.

items.objective: Monitor the absolute neutrophil count during deferiprone therapy.

items.stemHtml: An 8-year-old girl with hereditary spherocytosis has needed five red cell transfusions in the past 2 years and has poor exercise tolerance. Her hemoglobin has been 7-8 g/dL at recent visits. Ultrasonography shows splenomegaly and no gallstones. Laparoscopic splenectomy is planned in 6 weeks. She has received all routine childhood vaccines on schedule and takes folic acid. Which of the following is the most appropriate preparation before surgery?

options.label: A
options.html: Elective cholecystectomy at the same operation

items.explanationHtml:
Splenectomy corrects anemia in severe hereditary spherocytosis but leaves the patient at lifelong risk of overwhelming infection from encapsulated organisms. Vaccines against pneumococcus, meningococcus (ACWY and B) and H. influenzae type b are given, or completed, at least 2 weeks before elective splenectomy. Delaying surgery until after about age 6 reduces infection risk. Afterwards, families learn to seek urgent care for fever, and many children receive penicillin prophylaxis.

Takeaway: vaccinate against encapsulated organisms at least 2 weeks before elective splenectomy.

whyNot.A: Cholecystectomy is combined with splenectomy only when gallstones are present; she has none.
whyNot.B: Her diagnosis is established; electrophoresis will not change surgical preparation.
whyNot.C: Hydroxyurea raises HbF in sickle cell disease and has no role in spherocytosis.
whyNot.D: Routine preoperative anticoagulation is not indicated in a child.

items.objective: Vaccinate before elective splenectomy for hereditary spherocytosis.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of severe abdominal pain, nausea and constipation for 3 days. She was started on carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia 2 weeks ago. She has had two similar but milder episodes over the past 2 years, both just before menses; CT scans of the abdomen were normal. Pulse is 124/min and blood pressure is 162/100 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft without peritoneal signs. Proximal arm strength is 4/5. Serum sodium is 124 mEq/L. A spot urine porphobilinogen is 30 times the upper limit of normal. Carbamazepine is stopped. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
This is an acute attack of acute intermittent porphyria triggered by carbamazepine, a P450 inducer, with recurrent premenstrual attacks, hyponatremia, autonomic signs and early motor neuropathy. The best treatment is intravenous hemin started as early as possible, plus removal of triggers, opioid analgesia, antiemetics, treatment of hyponatremia and close monitoring of strength and breathing. Carbohydrate loading is only a stopgap for mild attacks. Givosiran can reduce recurrences later.

Takeaway: treat an acute porphyric attack with neurologic signs or hyponatremia with intravenous hemin.

whyNot.A: Her abdomen is benign and imaging has been normal; surgery is not indicated and anesthesia carries extra risk.
whyNot.B: Low-dose hydroxychloroquine treats porphyria cutanea tarda, not acute attacks.
whyNot.D: Phenytoin is a P450 inducer that can worsen an acute attack.
whyNot.E: Phlebotomy lowers hepatic iron in porphyria cutanea tarda and does not treat neurovisceral attacks.

items.objective: Treat an acute attack of acute intermittent porphyria.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man comes to the clinic because of blisters and erosions on the backs of his hands for 4 months that heal with scarring and small white cysts. His skin tears with minor trauma. He drinks 4 beers daily. Examination shows hypertrichosis over the cheeks. Urine is reddish-brown. Plasma porphyrins are increased, and urine shows a large increase in uroporphyrin. Serum ferritin is 820 ng/mL (normal 15-200) and transferrin saturation 52%. Tests for hepatitis C and HIV are negative. He is advised to stop alcohol and to protect his skin from sunlight. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Blistering photosensitivity on the dorsal hands with skin fragility, milia, hypertrichosis and raised uroporphyrin indicates porphyria cutanea tarda. Hepatic iron drives the inhibition of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, and his high ferritin and alcohol use are susceptibility factors. Serial phlebotomy to lower ferritin into the low-normal range induces remission; low-dose hydroxychloroquine is the alternative, particularly when ferritin is not raised. HFE genotyping is reasonable given the iron studies.

Takeaway: treat porphyria cutanea tarda with phlebotomy (or low-dose hydroxychloroquine) plus removal of triggers.

whyNot.A: β-Carotene is used for erythropoietic protoporphyria, which causes painful photosensitivity without blisters.
whyNot.B: Hemin treats acute neurovisceral porphyric attacks, which do not occur in porphyria cutanea tarda.
whyNot.C: Carbohydrate loading represses ALA synthase in acute porphyrias and has no role here.
whyNot.D: Glucocorticoids do not correct the hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase inhibition.

items.objective: Treat porphyria cutanea tarda with iron reduction.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after a motorcycle crash. He has a deformed, swollen right thigh. Pulse is 128/min and blood pressure is 92/64 mm Hg. He has received no intravenous fluid. Hemoglobin is 14.6 g/dL and hematocrit is 44%. A CT scan shows a femoral shaft fracture with a large thigh hematoma. Which of the following best explains why his hemoglobin concentration is near normal?

options.label: A
options.html: Hemoconcentration from loss of plasma into the injured tissue

options.label: B
options.html: Rapid release of reticulocytes from the marrow

options.label: C
options.html: Red cells and plasma have been lost in the same proportion

options.label: D
options.html: Splenic contraction releasing stored red cells

options.label: E
options.html: Transcapillary refill of interstitial fluid into the vessels

items.explanationHtml:
Hemoglobin and hematocrit are concentrations. When whole blood is lost, red cells and plasma leave in the same proportion, so the ratio is unchanged even though total red cell mass and blood volume have fallen.
