The hemoglobin falls only as interstitial fluid shifts into the vessels and the kidneys retain salt and water, or as crystalloid is infused, over the next 24 to 72 hours. His tachycardia and borderline blood pressure are the reliable early signs of hemorrhage.

Takeaway: an early normal hemoglobin does not exclude major hemorrhage; judge early loss by hemodynamics.

whyNot.A: Plasma leaks into injured tissue, but the bleeding here is of whole blood; the main reason the ratio is preserved is that cells and plasma leave together.
whyNot.B: Reticulocyte release takes days, not 40 minutes, and could not offset a large loss of red cell mass.
whyNot.D: Splenic contraction adds a meaningful red cell reserve in some animals, but in humans it contributes little and does not explain a preserved ratio.
whyNot.E: Refill of interstitial fluid dilutes the remaining red cells and lowers the hemoglobin; it is the process that will make his hemoglobin fall over the next day.

items.objective: Explain why hemoglobin concentration is preserved immediately after acute whole-blood loss.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman is evaluated 8 days after an episode of melena from a duodenal ulcer, which was treated endoscopically. She received no transfusion and has had no further bleeding. On admission her hemoglobin was 12.9 g/dL; it reached its lowest value of 9.1 g/dL on day 3. Today she feels better. She takes omeprazole. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely today?

options.label: E
options.html: Undetectable haptoglobin with an increased LDH

items.explanationHtml:
After an acute bleed, falling oxygen delivery stabilises hypoxia-inducible factor in renal peritubular interstitial cells and erythropoietin rises within hours. The marrow responds over several days: reticulocytes start to rise after about 3 days and peak at about a week. On the smear, these large young cells stain blue-grey (polychromasia), and the MCV may rise slightly. A single acute bleed gives a normocytic anemia; chronic loss produces iron deficiency.

Takeaway: the reticulocyte response to acute blood loss appears after a few days and peaks at about a week.

whyNot.A: Erythropoietin rises within hours of reduced oxygen delivery and stays raised while she is anemic.
whyNot.B: Hypersegmentation reflects B12 or folate deficiency, not recovery from a single bleed.
whyNot.D: A single bleed of this size does not usually exhaust iron stores; microcytosis takes weeks to develop because existing red cells keep their size.
whyNot.E: Low haptoglobin and high LDH indicate hemolysis; luminal gastrointestinal blood is lost, not destroyed in the circulation.

items.objective: Predict the time course of the marrow response after acute blood loss.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis has had increasing jaundice and fatigue over 3 weeks. He has ascites and splenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL (2 months ago 10.9 g/dL), MCV 103 fL, reticulocytes 8%, total bilirubin 6.2 mg/dL with direct bilirubin 2.0 mg/dL, LDH 480 U/L (N 45-200) and haptoglobin undetectable. A direct antiglobulin test is negative. The peripheral smear shows many dense red cells with a few irregular, thorn-like surface projections of varying length. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his anemia?

options.label: C
options.html: Excess free cholesterol in the red cell membrane

options.label: D
options.html: Fragmentation on fibrin strands in small vessels

items.explanationHtml:
This is spur cell anemia, a hemolytic anemia of advanced cirrhosis. Abnormal lipoproteins transfer free cholesterol into the red cell membrane out of proportion to phospholipid. The membrane becomes rigid and develops a few irregular projections (acanthocytes). The spleen then remodels and destroys these cells, so the patient has brisk, DAT-negative hemolysis. It signals end-stage liver disease and a poor prognosis; liver transplantation is the definitive treatment.

Takeaway: acanthocytes with DAT-negative hemolysis in advanced cirrhosis mean spur cell anemia from membrane cholesterol excess.

whyNot.A: The negative direct antiglobulin test argues against autoimmune hemolysis.
whyNot.B: A cytoskeletal defect causes hereditary spherocytosis, which is inherited and produces round spherocytes, not spiculated cells.
whyNot.D: Microangiopathic hemolysis produces schistocytes (helmet cells and fragments), not dense cells with irregular spikes.
whyNot.E: Oxidant hemolysis, as in G6PD deficiency, produces bite cells and Heinz bodies, usually after an exposure.

items.objective: Identify the membrane mechanism of spur cell anemia in advanced liver disease.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old woman has 2 months of pruritus and fatigue. Alkaline phosphatase is 690 U/L, GGT 520 U/L and total bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL. Antimitochondrial antibodies are positive. Hemoglobin is 12.8 g/dL and MCV 99 fL. The peripheral smear shows many red cells with a central dense spot of hemoglobin surrounded by a pale ring and a dense outer rim. Which of the following best explains the appearance of these red cells?

options.label: A
options.html: Decreased membrane surface area relative to cell volume

options.label: B
options.html: Excess alpha-globin chains precipitating within the cell

options.label: C
options.html: Increased membrane surface area relative to cell volume

items.explanationHtml:
Cholestasis raises plasma cholesterol and lecithin, which equilibrate into the red cell membrane. The cell gains membrane without gaining volume, so on a dried smear the excess membrane bulges in the centre, producing a target cell. These cells survive normally and the change reverses if the cholestasis resolves. Her antimitochondrial antibodies and cholestatic enzymes indicate primary biliary cholangitis.

Takeaway: target cells form when membrane surface area rises relative to volume, as with membrane lipid loading in cholestatic liver disease.

whyNot.A: Loss of membrane relative to volume makes spherocytes, which are small, dense and lack central pallor.
whyNot.B: Excess alpha chains precipitate in beta-thalassemia, which also produces target cells but with marked microcytosis, not in a cholestatic adult with a high-normal MCV.
whyNot.D: Shearing produces fragmented schistocytes, not intact target cells.
whyNot.E: Hemoglobin S polymerisation produces sickle cells; she has no hemoglobinopathy.

items.objective: Explain the formation of target cells in cholestatic liver disease.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 26 weeks' gestation comes for a routine prenatal visit. She feels well and takes a prenatal vitamin. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL (12.9 g/dL before pregnancy), MCV 89 fL and platelets 210,000/mm3. Ferritin is 48 ng/mL (N 15-150). Which of the following best explains the change in her hemoglobin concentration?

options.label: A
options.html: Decreased erythropoietin production by the kidney

options.label: D
options.html: Plasma volume rising more than red cell mass

options.label: E
options.html: Suppression of the marrow by estrogen

items.explanationHtml:
In pregnancy, plasma volume increases by about 40 to 50%, whereas red cell mass increases by only about 20 to 30%. The hemoglobin concentration therefore falls, most markedly in the second trimester. This physiologic dilution lowers viscosity and improves placental perfusion. For the second trimester, anemia is defined as a hemoglobin below 10.5 g/dL, so her value is expected.

Takeaway: the physiologic anemia of pregnancy is dilutional: plasma expands more than red cell mass.

whyNot.A: Erythropoietin rises in pregnancy; red cell mass increases, not decreases.
whyNot.B: Normal pregnancy does not cause hemolysis, and she has no evidence of it.
whyNot.C: Her normal MCV and ferritin argue against iron deficiency.
whyNot.E: Estrogen does not suppress erythropoiesis in pregnancy; red cell mass rises by about a quarter.

items.objective: Explain the dilutional fall in hemoglobin in normal pregnancy.

items.stemHtml: A 10-week-old girl, born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, is brought for a well-child visit. She is breastfeeding well and gaining weight along the 50th percentile. Examination is normal apart from mild pallor. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL (18.0 g/dL at birth), MCV 88 fL, reticulocytes 0.8% and leukocyte and platelet counts are normal. The smear is unremarkable. Which of the following is the primary cause of the change in her hemoglobin since birth?

options.label: A
options.html: Destruction of fetal red cells by maternal antibodies

options.label: B
options.html: Fall in erythropoietin as oxygenation rises

options.label: E
options.html: Switch from gamma-globin to beta-globin synthesis

items.explanationHtml:
The fetus lives in a low-oxygen environment and makes red cells at a high rate. When the newborn starts breathing, arterial oxygen saturation and tissue oxygenation rise, renal erythropoietin production falls, and red cell production nearly stops for several weeks. Shorter fetal red cell survival and rapid expansion of blood volume add to the fall. The result is the physiologic nadir at about 2 to 3 months; erythropoietin then rises and production resumes.

Takeaway: the physiologic nadir of infancy results from suppressed erythropoietin after the rise in oxygenation at birth.

whyNot.A: Alloimmune hemolysis presents in the first days with jaundice and a positive direct antiglobulin test, not as a quiet fall over weeks.
whyNot.C: Term infants have enough iron stores for the first 4 to 6 months; her MCV is normal.
whyNot.D: Folate deficiency causes macrocytosis and is unusual in a thriving breastfed infant.
whyNot.E: The globin switch changes the hemoglobin type but does not reduce red cell production or concentration.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of the physiologic anemia of infancy.

items.stemHtml: A 20-month-old boy is brought for a routine visit. He drinks about 40 oz (1.2 L) of whole cow's milk daily, mostly from a bottle, and eats little meat or fortified cereal. He is pale and his weight is at the 85th percentile. Hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL, MCV 61 fL and RDW 18.9% (N 11.5-14.5%). Ferritin is 4 ng/mL (N 7-140). In addition to displacing iron-rich foods, which of the following properties of cow's milk most directly contributes to his anemia?

options.label: A
options.html: Calcium and casein that inhibit non-heme iron absorption

options.label: B
options.html: High lactose content that causes osmotic diarrhea

options.label: C
options.html: High vitamin C content that oxidises ferrous iron

options.label: D
options.html: Low folate content that impairs DNA synthesis

items.explanationHtml:
Cow's milk is low in iron and its iron is poorly absorbed. Its calcium and casein inhibit absorption of non-heme iron from the rest of the diet, and large volumes fill the child so that he eats fewer iron-rich foods. In infants given cow's milk before 12 months, milk-protein enterocolitis can also cause occult intestinal blood loss. The microcytosis, high RDW and very low ferritin confirm iron deficiency.

Takeaway: excess cow's milk causes toddler iron deficiency through low iron content, inhibition of absorption and displacement of iron-rich foods.

whyNot.B: Lactose intolerance is uncommon at this age and causes diarrhea, not iron deficiency.
whyNot.C: Cow's milk is low, not high, in vitamin C, and vitamin C enhances rather than impairs iron absorption.
whyNot.D: Folate deficiency causes macrocytosis; he is microcytic with a very low ferritin.
whyNot.E: Phytates come from grains and legumes, not milk, and they bind non-heme iron.

items.objective: Explain how high cow's milk intake causes iron deficiency in toddlers.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman has 6 months of fatigue, weight gain, constipation and cold intolerance. Her menstrual periods stopped 2 years ago. She has dry skin, delayed relaxation of the ankle reflexes and a pulse of 56/min. Hemoglobin is 10.9 g/dL, MCV 97 fL, reticulocytes 0.4% and the smear shows no hypersegmented neutrophils. Ferritin, vitamin B12 and folate are normal. TSH is 38 uU/mL and free T4 0.3 ng/dL. Which of the following most likely explains her anemia?

options.label: A
options.html: Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced erythropoietin drive from lower tissue oxygen demand

items.explanationHtml:
Thyroid hormone raises the basal metabolic rate and therefore tissue oxygen consumption. In hypothyroidism, oxygen demand falls, so the kidneys sense adequate oxygen delivery at a lower red cell mass and produce less erythropoietin. The result is a mild, normocytic or slightly macrocytic, hypoproliferative anemia that corrects over months of levothyroxine. Always look for coexisting iron or B12 deficiency.

Takeaway: hypothyroidism causes a mild hypoproliferative anemia through lower oxygen demand and less erythropoietin.

whyNot.A: Pernicious anemia often accompanies autoimmune thyroid disease, but her normal B12 and lack of hypersegmentation exclude it.
whyNot.B: Menorrhagia is a cause in premenopausal hypothyroid women, but she is postmenopausal and her ferritin is normal.
whyNot.C: Thyroid autoantibodies do not attack red cells, and her low reticulocyte count indicates underproduction.
whyNot.D: Glycosaminoglycan deposition affects skin and soft tissue; it does not replace the marrow.

items.objective: Identify the mechanism of anemia in hypothyroidism.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman has fatigue 3 years after a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. She stopped taking her supplements a year ago. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL, MCV 91 fL and RDW 21.4% (N 11.5-14.5%). The peripheral smear shows a mixture of small, pale red cells and large oval red cells, with several neutrophils that have six nuclear lobes. Which of the following best explains her normal MCV?

options.label: B
options.html: Combined iron and vitamin B12 deficiency

items.explanationHtml:
Roux-en-Y bypass excludes the duodenum, where iron is absorbed, and reduces gastric acid and intrinsic factor contact, so iron and B12 deficiencies often develop together. Microcytes from iron deficiency and macrocytes from B12 deficiency average out to a normal MCV. The clue is the very high RDW with a dimorphic smear and hypersegmented neutrophils.

Takeaway: a normal MCV with a high RDW and a dimorphic smear suggests mixed microcytic and macrocytic deficiencies.

whyNot.A: Inflammation causes a normocytic anemia with a normal RDW, and would not explain the hypersegmented neutrophils or the two red cell populations.
whyNot.C: Myelodysplasia can be dimorphic, but her bypass, stopped supplements and hypersegmented neutrophils point to two nutritional deficiencies.
whyNot.D: Hypothyroidism gives a uniform, mildly macrocytic or normocytic picture with a normal RDW.
whyNot.E: Acute bleeding gives normocytic cells and reticulocytosis, not hypersegmented neutrophils or microcytes.

items.objective: Recognise mixed nutritional anemia behind a normal MCV.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has a routine blood count before elective knee arthroscopy. Her hemostasis has been normal through two dental extractions and a cesarean delivery. She takes no medications. Examination shows no petechiae or splenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 13.4 g/dL, leukocytes 6,800/mm3 and platelets 38,000/mm3. The peripheral smear prepared from the same EDTA tube is shown. Which of the following best explains her platelet count?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibody-mediated platelet clumping in the collection tube

options.label: B
options.html: Immune destruction of platelets by the spleen

options.label: D
options.html: Platelet consumption in disseminated intravascular coagulation

options.label: E
options.html: Sequestration of platelets in the spleen

items.explanationHtml:
The smear shows platelet aggregates among normal red cells. In pseudothrombocytopenia, EDTA chelates calcium and alters the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa complex, exposing hidden epitopes. Naturally occurring antibodies in some healthy people then clump platelets in the tube, and the analyser undercounts them. Her lifelong normal hemostasis and the clumps on the smear fit. A count from a citrate tube will be normal, and no treatment is needed.

Takeaway: before working up isolated thrombocytopenia in a well patient, look for EDTA-induced clumping on the smear.

whyNot.B: Immune thrombocytopenia produces scattered, sometimes large platelets on the smear, not aggregates.
whyNot.C: Inherited macrothrombocytopenias show single giant platelets on the smear, not clusters of normal-sized ones.
whyNot.D: DIC occurs in very ill patients with bleeding or thrombosis and abnormal coagulation tests.
whyNot.E: She has no splenomegaly, and sequestration does not produce clumps on the smear.

items.objective: Recognise EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia from the smear and history.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man whose parents emigrated from Ghana comes for a pre-employment examination. He feels well, with no history of serious infection or mouth ulcers. Examination is normal. Leukocytes are 3,100/mm3 with 38% neutrophils; hemoglobin and platelets are normal. His blood counts 2 and 5 years ago were similar. Red cell phenotyping shows absence of a chemokine receptor normally present on erythrocytes. The red cells of this patient are most likely resistant to invasion by which of the following organisms?
items.explanationHtml:
His ANC is about 1,180/mm3, stable for years, with no infections. This is the Duffy-null associated neutrophil count. People homozygous for a promoter variant of ACKR1 do not express the Duffy antigen (a chemokine receptor) on red cells. Their circulating neutrophil count is lower because neutrophils are distributed differently between blood and tissues, but marrow reserves and infection risk are normal. The Duffy antigen is the receptor that P. vivax uses to invade reticulocytes, so its absence protects against vivax malaria, which explains the high frequency of the variant in West Africa.

Takeaway: Duffy-null individuals have a benign lower neutrophil count and resist P. vivax invasion.

whyNot.A: Babesia enters red cells by other receptors; Duffy negativity gives no protection.
whyNot.B: Bartonella adheres to and invades red cells independently of the Duffy antigen.
whyNot.C: P. falciparum uses glycophorins and other ligands, and Duffy-null red cells are fully susceptible.
whyNot.D: P. malariae does not depend on the Duffy antigen for invasion.

items.objective: Link the Duffy-null phenotype to benign neutropenia and resistance to vivax malaria.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl is brought for evaluation of recurrent fevers, painful mouth ulcers and swollen gums. Her parents keep a diary showing that episodes last about 5 days and recur roughly every 3 weeks. Between episodes she is well. Her father had similar episodes as a child that became milder in adulthood. Blood counts taken three times a week for 6 weeks show the ANC falling below 200/mm3 for 4 to 5 days in each 21-day period, with normal counts in between. A mutation in the gene encoding which of the following is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Periodic neutropenia every 3 weeks with fever, aphthous ulcers and gingivitis, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, is cyclic neutropenia. It is caused by heterozygous mutations in ELANE, the gene for neutrophil elastase; the misfolded protein triggers apoptosis of myeloid precursors in waves. Serial counts over 6 weeks are needed to show the cycle. G-CSF reduces the depth and length of the nadirs.

Takeaway: cyclic neutropenia, with nadirs about every 21 days, is caused by autosomal dominant ELANE mutations.

whyNot.A: CD18 deficiency causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency with persistent neutrophilia, not periodic neutropenia.
whyNot.B: Lysosomal trafficking regulator mutations cause Chediak-Higashi syndrome with giant granules and albinism.
whyNot.C: NADPH oxidase defects cause chronic granulomatous disease with normal neutrophil numbers.
whyNot.E: WAS mutations cause X-linked thrombocytopenia with small platelets and eczema.

items.objective: Identify the gene defect in cyclic neutropenia.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman has 2 days of fever and severe sore throat. Six weeks ago she was diagnosed with Graves disease and started on a drug to lower thyroid hormone synthesis, plus propranolol. Temperature is 39.1 °C (102.4 °F). The pharynx is inflamed with a shallow ulcer on the tonsil. Leukocytes are 1,100/mm3 with 4% neutrophils; hemoglobin and platelets are normal. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of the drug most likely responsible for her blood count?

options.label: B
options.html: Competitive inhibition of iodide uptake by the sodium-iodide symporter

options.label: C
options.html: Destruction of thyroid follicular cells by beta radiation

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of thyroid hormone release from the gland

items.explanationHtml:
Fever and pharyngitis with an ANC of about 44/mm3 weeks after starting an antithyroid drug is thionamide-induced agranulocytosis. Methimazole and propylthiouracil inhibit thyroid peroxidase, blocking iodide organification and coupling of iodotyrosines; propylthiouracil also inhibits peripheral deiodination of T4 to T3. Agranulocytosis is idiosyncratic and usually immune-mediated, appears in the first months, and requires stopping the drug and treating as febrile neutropenia. Cross-reactivity makes switching to the other thionamide unsafe.

Takeaway: thionamides (thyroid peroxidase inhibitors) can cause agranulocytosis early in therapy; fever or sore throat warrants an immediate count.

whyNot.A: Propranolol controls adrenergic symptoms but is not a recognised cause of agranulocytosis.
whyNot.B: This is the action of perchlorate, which is not used in this setting.
whyNot.C: Radioactive iodine is not given as a daily drug and does not cause agranulocytosis.
whyNot.D: High-dose iodide inhibits hormone release, but it is not the antithyroid drug started at diagnosis and does not cause agranulocytosis.

items.objective: Link agranulocytosis to the thionamide class and its mechanism of action.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because of a rash on his legs and easy bruising that began 2 days ago. Three weeks ago he had a cold with a runny nose and low-grade fever. He appears well. There are scattered petechiae on the legs and several bruises on the shins; there is no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 12.4 g/dL, leukocytes 7,600/mm3 with a normal differential, and platelets 11,000/mm3. The smear shows a few large platelets and normal red and white cells. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his thrombocytopenia?

options.label: A
options.html: Consumption of platelets in microvascular thrombi

options.label: B
options.html: IgG-coated platelets cleared by splenic macrophages

options.label: C
options.html: Infiltration of the marrow by lymphoblasts

items.explanationHtml:
Abrupt isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child a few weeks after a viral illness is childhood immune thrombocytopenia. Autoantibodies, usually IgG against glycoprotein IIb/IIIa, coat platelets, and splenic macrophages remove them through Fc-gamma receptors. The marrow responds with young, larger platelets. Most children recover within months.

Takeaway: childhood ITP is post-viral IgG-mediated splenic clearance of platelets in a well child with an otherwise normal blood count.

whyNot.A: Thrombotic microangiopathy produces schistocytes and anemia; his red cells are normal.
whyNot.C: Leukemia usually lowers more than one lineage and often causes adenopathy, organomegaly or blasts.
whyNot.D: Maternal antibodies affect newborns and are cleared within weeks of birth, not at age 4.
whyNot.E: The illness ended weeks ago, and the large platelets show active production with peripheral destruction.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of platelet destruction in childhood ITP.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman has had immune thrombocytopenia for 2 years. Each attempt to taper prednisone below 10 mg daily has led to a fall in platelets below 20,000/mm3 with gum bleeding. Her hematologist starts a once-daily oral drug and tells her to take it at least 2 hours before or 4 hours after dairy products, antacids and mineral supplements. Her platelet count rises to 95,000/mm3 over 3 weeks. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of this drug?
items.explanationHtml:
The oral drug with the instruction to separate doses from polyvalent cations (calcium, magnesium, aluminium, iron) is eltrombopag. It binds the transmembrane domain of the thrombopoietin receptor (MPL) on megakaryocytes and activates JAK2-STAT signalling, which raises platelet production. It chelates polyvalent cations, which reduces its absorption. Monitor liver enzymes because of hepatotoxicity.

Takeaway: eltrombopag is an oral thrombopoietin-receptor agonist that must be taken apart from calcium and other polyvalent cations.

whyNot.B: Fc-receptor blockade is how intravenous immunoglobulin acts; it is given intravenously, not as a daily tablet.
whyNot.C: Rituximab depletes B cells and is an intravenous infusion.
whyNot.D: Fostamatinib is an oral SYK inhibitor, but it does not chelate cations, so it carries no such dietary spacing advice.
whyNot.E: Calcineurin inhibitors suppress T cells and are not standard ITP therapy.

items.objective: Identify the mechanism of action of eltrombopag in chronic ITP.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man with chronic immune thrombocytopenia has a platelet count of 9,000/mm3 and needs an urgent laparoscopic cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis. He receives intravenous immunoglobulin, and his platelet count rises to 85,000/mm3 within 48 hours. Which of the following best explains this rapid rise?

options.label: D
options.html: Removal of circulating autoantibody from plasma

options.label: E
options.html: Saturation of Fc-gamma receptors on splenic macrophages

items.explanationHtml:
Intravenous immunoglobulin floods macrophage Fc-gamma receptors in the spleen and liver, so antibody-coated platelets are no longer cleared. It also saturates the neonatal Fc receptor, which speeds the breakdown of all IgG, including the autoantibody. The count rises within 1 to 3 days, which is why IVIG is chosen when a rapid rise is needed, such as before urgent surgery or with serious bleeding.

Takeaway: IVIG raises the platelet count in ITP within days by blocking macrophage Fc receptors.

whyNot.A: Raised production takes about a week to show in the blood; IVIG works faster by reducing clearance.
whyNot.B: COX inhibition (aspirin) impairs platelet function and does not raise the count.
whyNot.C: ITP is not caused by antibodies against thrombopoietin.
whyNot.D: Removing antibody from plasma describes plasma exchange, not immunoglobulin infusion.

items.objective: Explain the rapid action of intravenous immunoglobulin in ITP.

items.stemHtml: A boy born at 39 weeks' gestation to a 27-year-old primigravida is noted to have widespread petechiae and a cephalohematoma 2 hours after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. He is feeding well and appears otherwise healthy. His platelet count is 14,000/mm3; hemoglobin and leukocyte counts are normal. The mother is healthy, takes no medications except prenatal vitamins, and her platelet count is 245,000/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the newborn's thrombocytopenia?

options.label: C
options.html: Maternal IgG against a paternal platelet antigen

items.explanationHtml:
Severe thrombocytopenia in a well newborn whose mother has a normal platelet count suggests neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia. The mother lacks a platelet antigen inherited by the fetus from the father, most often HPA-1a, and makes IgG against it. The IgG crosses the placenta and destroys fetal platelets. Unlike Rh disease, the first pregnancy is often affected. The main danger is intracranial hemorrhage.

Takeaway: a thrombocytopenic well newborn with a normal maternal platelet count suggests alloimmune (NAIT) rather than maternal autoimmune thrombocytopenia.

whyNot.A: Congenital CMV usually causes growth restriction, hepatosplenomegaly, microcephaly or a blueberry-muffin rash, not isolated thrombocytopenia in a thriving infant.
whyNot.B: Maternal ITP antibodies would also lower the mother's own count, which is normal.
whyNot.D: Placental insufficiency causes growth restriction and mild thrombocytopenia, often with polycythemia.
whyNot.E: Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT but leaves the platelet count normal.

items.objective: Distinguish neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia from other causes of neonatal thrombocytopenia.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man with cirrhosis due to chronic hepatitis C has a platelet count of 62,000/mm3. He has no bleeding. He has had two episodes of ascites. Ultrasonography shows a nodular liver and a spleen 17 cm long (N up to 12). Hemoglobin is 12.1 g/dL and leukocytes 3,400/mm3. A marrow biopsy done before referral showed normal cellularity with abundant megakaryocytes. In addition to splenic sequestration, which of the following best explains his low platelet count?
items.explanationHtml:
Thrombopoietin is made mainly by hepatocytes at a constant rate. In cirrhosis, less is made, so megakaryocytes get a weaker signal, while portal hypertension causes splenomegaly that traps a large fraction of platelets. This is why oral thrombopoietin-receptor agonists can raise the count before procedures in chronic liver disease. Hepatitis C can also cause immune thrombocytopenia, but the two mechanisms described here are the usual cause.

Takeaway: thrombocytopenia in cirrhosis results from splenic sequestration plus reduced hepatic thrombopoietin.

whyNot.A: Antibodies to platelet factor 4-heparin complexes cause HIT, which requires heparin exposure.
whyNot.B: Chronic stable cirrhosis does not cause ongoing DIC with this picture.
whyNot.C: His marrow shows abundant megakaryocytes, which argues against a primary production failure in the marrow.
whyNot.D: Folate deficiency causes macrocytosis and megaloblastic changes, which are not described.

items.objective: Explain the mechanisms of thrombocytopenia in chronic liver disease.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man with polycythemia vera had a transient ischemic attack 3 months ago. Despite phlebotomy and low-dose aspirin, his hematocrit has risen each month and the platelet count is 780,000/mm3. A new oral drug is started. Six weeks later his MCV has risen from 84 fL to 104 fL, and he has a painful ulcer above the ankle. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of the new drug?

options.label: B
options.html: Inhibition of JAK1 and JAK2 kinases

items.explanationHtml:
A high-risk patient with PV (age over 60 and prior cerebral ischemia) needs cytoreduction. The first-line drug, hydroxyurea, inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, which reduces the deoxyribonucleotides needed for DNA synthesis. Impaired DNA synthesis in red cell precursors causes macrocytosis, and mucocutaneous toxicity includes mouth and leg ulcers. Other adverse effects are cytopenias and skin cancers.

Takeaway: hydroxyurea, the usual cytoreductive drug for high-risk PV, inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and causes macrocytosis and leg ulcers.

whyNot.A: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; it is not used for cytoreduction in PV.
whyNot.B: Ruxolitinib inhibits JAK1/2; it causes anemia and thrombocytopenia but not a rising MCV with leg ulcers, and it is usually second-line.
whyNot.C: Anagrelide inhibits phosphodiesterase 3 and lowers platelets only; it does not control the hematocrit.
whyNot.E: Interferon alfa causes flu-like symptoms, depression and thyroid problems, not macrocytosis with leg ulcers.

items.objective: Identify the mechanism and adverse effects of hydroxyurea in polycythemia vera.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old woman with JAK2 V617F-positive polycythemia vera has had phlebotomy every 2 to 4 weeks for 6 months and takes aspirin. Her hematocrit is now 43%, down from 56%. She feels well apart from mild fatigue. MCV has fallen from 88 fL to 72 fL, and ferritin is 6 ng/mL (N 15-150). Platelets are 520,000/mm3. Which of the following best explains how the treatment keeps her hematocrit controlled?

options.label: B
options.html: Iron deficiency limits further red cell production

options.label: C
options.html: Phlebotomy removes the JAK2-mutant stem cells

options.label: E
options.html: Repeated volume loss suppresses the marrow

items.explanationHtml:
Each phlebotomy removes red cells and with them about 200 to 250 mg of iron. Over months, the deliberate iron deficiency limits hemoglobin synthesis, so even unregulated JAK2-mutant precursors cannot make many new red cells. Her microcytosis and low ferritin are expected. Giving iron would remove this brake and the hematocrit would rise again.

Takeaway: phlebotomy controls PV partly by inducing iron deficiency; microcytosis is the expected result and is not treated with iron.

whyNot.A: Aspirin inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase-1; it has no effect on erythropoiesis.
whyNot.C: Phlebotomy removes mature red cells; the mutant clone in the marrow is unaffected.
whyNot.D: Her erythropoietin stays suppressed; the JAK2-mutant precursors grow independently of it.
whyNot.E: Volume loss does not suppress the marrow; the response to bleeding is increased production.

items.objective: Explain why iron deficiency develops and helps control the hematocrit in phlebotomy-treated PV.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man has a hematocrit of 55% on a routine examination. He has smoked 1.5 packs of cigarettes daily for 30 years and works as a delivery driver. He has no snoring, lung disease or cardiac history. Spleen is not palpable. Pulse oximetry on room air is 97%. Serum erythropoietin is mildly increased and JAK2 V617F is not detected. Carboxyhemoglobin is 9% (N under 3% in nonsmokers). Which of the following best explains his erythrocytosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Autonomous proliferation of an erythroid clone

options.label: B
options.html: Decreased plasma volume with normal red cell mass

options.label: C
options.html: Ectopic erythropoietin secretion by a tumour

items.explanationHtml:
Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with an affinity more than 200 times that of oxygen. Carboxyhemoglobin cannot carry oxygen and shifts the dissociation curve of the remaining hemoglobin to the left, so less oxygen is released to tissues. The renal oxygen sensor responds with more erythropoietin. Standard pulse oximetry reads carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin and gives a falsely reassuring saturation; co-oximetry measures it. Smoking cessation corrects the erythrocytosis.

Takeaway: smoker's erythrocytosis is driven by carboxyhemoglobin, which reduces oxygen delivery and raises erythropoietin despite a normal pulse oximetry reading.

whyNot.A: A clonal disorder would suppress erythropoietin and usually carry a JAK2 mutation; neither is present.
whyNot.B: Plasma volume contraction occurs in smokers but cannot explain a raised erythropoietin level.
whyNot.C: Possible in theory, but his high carboxyhemoglobin gives a clear hypoxic explanation.
whyNot.E: Carbon monoxide does not lower arterial oxygen tension; his oxygen tension and dissolved oxygen are normal.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of secondary erythrocytosis in smokers.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has 3 months of morning headaches, vomiting and unsteady gait. She had a retinal hemangioblastoma treated with laser at age 26, and her father died of renal cell carcinoma. Examination shows dysmetria of the left arm. Hematocrit is 54%, and serum erythropoietin is high. MRI shows a cystic left cerebellar mass with an enhancing mural nodule. Loss of function of a protein that normally has which of the following roles is most likely?

options.label: B
options.html: Blocking the cell cycle at the G1 checkpoint

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibiting mTOR through the tuberin complex

items.explanationHtml:
Retinal and cerebellar hemangioblastomas with a family history of renal cell carcinoma indicate von Hippel-Lindau disease. The VHL protein is part of a ubiquitin ligase that marks hypoxia-inducible factor alpha for proteasomal degradation when oxygen is present. Without it, HIF accumulates and drives VEGF, causing vascular tumours, and erythropoietin, which some hemangioblastomas secrete. Her erythrocytosis is therefore erythropoietin-driven.

Takeaway: cerebellar hemangioblastoma can secrete erythropoietin; VHL loss stabilises HIF and drives EPO and VEGF.

whyNot.A: Neurofibromin activates RAS GTPase; its loss causes neurofibromatosis type 1.
whyNot.B: Retinoblastoma protein controls G1 arrest; it is not linked to hemangioblastoma or erythrocytosis.
whyNot.C: TSC2 (tuberin) loss causes tuberous sclerosis with hamartomas, not hemangioblastomas.
whyNot.D: Mismatch repair defects cause Lynch syndrome, with colorectal and endometrial cancers.

items.objective: Link VHL-related hemangioblastoma to erythropoietin-driven erythrocytosis.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman has a platelet count of 940,000/mm3 on three counts over 6 months. She has occasional burning pain in her toes. She has no infection, inflammatory disease or blood loss, and ferritin and CRP are normal. Hemoglobin and leukocytes are normal, and the spleen tip is just palpable. BCR-ABL1 testing is negative and JAK2 V617F is not detected. A marrow biopsy shows clusters of large megakaryocytes with hyperlobulated nuclei. A mutation in which of the following genes is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Sustained thrombocytosis with no reactive cause, a normal BCR-ABL1 test and large hyperlobulated megakaryocytes indicates essential thrombocythemia. Driver mutations are JAK2 V617F in about half, CALR in about a quarter and MPL in a few percent. In JAK2-negative ET, a CALR mutation is therefore the most likely; the mutant calreticulin binds and activates the thrombopoietin receptor. CALR-mutant ET tends to have higher platelet counts and a lower thrombotic risk than JAK2-mutant disease.

Takeaway: in JAK2-negative essential thrombocythemia, a CALR mutation is the most likely driver.

whyNot.A: BRAF V600E is the driver of hairy cell leukemia and Langerhans cell histiocytosis, not essential thrombocythemia.
whyNot.C: FLT3 internal tandem duplications occur in acute myeloid leukemia with blasts.
whyNot.D: KIT D816V drives systemic mastocytosis.
whyNot.E: This fusion defines acute promyelocytic leukemia, which presents with cytopenias and DIC.

items.objective: Identify the driver mutations of essential thrombocythemia.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman is admitted with fever, abdominal pain and profuse watery diarrhea after a course of clindamycin. Stool testing is positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin. Leukocytes are 58,000/mm3 with 78% segmented neutrophils, 14% bands, 3% metamyelocytes, 1% myelocytes and no blasts or basophils. Neutrophils show coarse dark cytoplasmic granules and pale blue cytoplasmic inclusions. The spleen is not palpable. Which of the following additional findings is most likely?

options.label: E
options.html: Teardrop red cells with nucleated red cells

items.explanationHtml:
Extreme neutrophilia with a left shift, toxic granulation and Döhle bodies in a patient with severe C. difficile colitis is a leukemoid reaction. Activated, mature neutrophils contain abundant leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, so the LAP score is high. In CML the clonal neutrophils have a low LAP score. BCR-ABL1 testing is now the definitive way to separate the two when doubt remains. The count falls as the infection is treated.

Takeaway: a leukemoid reaction shows toxic, mature neutrophils with a high LAP score, no basophilia and an obvious reactive cause.

whyNot.A: Basophilia points toward CML; she has no basophils.
whyNot.C: Blasts at this level define acute leukemia, which does not fit her smear.
whyNot.D: BCR-ABL1 defines CML, which would show basophils, a myelocyte peak and usually splenomegaly.
whyNot.E: A leukoerythroblastic smear with teardrop cells suggests marrow fibrosis or infiltration.

items.objective: Distinguish a leukemoid reaction from chronic myeloid leukemia.

items.stemHtml: A 42-year-old man has 4 months of fatigue, cough, itchy rash and, over the past 2 weeks, dyspnea and leg edema. He has not travelled outside the United States and takes no medications. Leukocytes are 21,000/mm3 with 46% eosinophils on repeated counts. Stool examinations and Strongyloides serology are negative. Serum tryptase and vitamin B12 are raised. Echocardiography shows apical thickening of both ventricles with an apical thrombus and restrictive filling. Molecular testing of blood detects a fusion gene formed by a small interstitial deletion on chromosome 4. Which of the following drugs is most likely to induce remission?
items.explanationHtml:
Sustained hypereosinophilia with cardiac damage (endomyocardial fibrosis with mural thrombus), raised tryptase and B12 and a chromosome 4 deletion is a myeloid neoplasm with the FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion. The fusion makes a constitutively active PDGFR-alpha tyrosine kinase that is highly sensitive to imatinib, often at low doses. Early treatment can prevent progression of the restrictive cardiomyopathy.

Takeaway: FIP1L1-PDGFRA-positive hypereosinophilia is an imatinib-responsive tyrosine kinase-driven neoplasm.

whyNot.A: Parasitic causes have been excluded, and an antihelminthic does not treat a clonal myeloid disorder.
whyNot.B: ATRA treats acute promyelocytic leukemia with PML-RARA.
whyNot.D: Ivermectin treats strongyloidiasis, which has been excluded.
whyNot.E: Anti-IgE therapy treats allergic asthma and urticaria, not a clonal eosinophilic neoplasm.

items.objective: Select targeted therapy for FIP1L1-PDGFRA-positive hypereosinophilia.

items.stemHtml: A boy born at 38 weeks' gestation to a mother with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes weighs 4,450 g. At 3 hours of age he is ruddy and jittery and feeds poorly. Blood glucose is 32 mg/dL. Venous hematocrit is 69%. Which of the following best explains the high hematocrit?

options.label: A
options.html: Delayed clamping of the umbilical cord

options.label: D
options.html: Increased fetal erythropoietin from chronic fetal hypoxia

items.explanationHtml:
Maternal hyperglycemia causes fetal hyperglycemia and fetal hyperinsulinemia. Insulin raises fetal metabolic rate and oxygen consumption, and maternal vascular disease can reduce placental oxygen delivery. The resulting chronic fetal hypoxia raises erythropoietin and red cell mass. After birth, the hyperinsulinemia persists while the maternal glucose supply stops, causing hypoglycemia, and the larger red cell mass increases the risk of jaundice and hyperviscosity.

Takeaway: infants of diabetic mothers develop polycythemia from hyperinsulinemia-driven fetal hypoxia and erythropoietin release.

whyNot.A: Delayed cord clamping can raise the hematocrit, but the maternal diabetes explains this infant's case.
whyNot.B: Neonatal thyrotoxicosis follows maternal Graves disease, not diabetes.
whyNot.C: Dehydration at 3 hours of age is unlikely and would not explain the macrosomia and hypoglycemia.
whyNot.E: Clonal erythrocytosis is not a feature of neonates.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of polycythemia in infants of diabetic mothers.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with hypertension has a hematocrit of 52% (previously 44%) 6 weeks after hydrochlorothiazide was added to his regimen. He has no snoring or lung disease and does not smoke. Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. BUN is 28 mg/dL and creatinine 1.3 mg/dL (previously 15 mg/dL and 1.0 mg/dL). Serum erythropoietin is normal. Which of the following best explains his high hematocrit?

options.label: A
options.html: Autonomous erythropoietin production by the kidney

options.label: C
options.html: Hypoxia-driven increase in red cell mass

options.label: D
options.html: Left shift of the oxygen dissociation curve

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced plasma volume with a normal red cell mass

items.explanationHtml:
A rise in hematocrit after starting a thiazide, with a rising BUN to creatinine ratio, normal oxygenation and a normal erythropoietin, indicates relative polycythemia. The red cell mass is unchanged; plasma volume has fallen, so the same red cells are more concentrated. Correcting the volume status corrects the hematocrit.

Takeaway: relative polycythemia is a fall in plasma volume with a normal red cell mass, often from diuretics or dehydration.

whyNot.A: His erythropoietin is normal and the change followed a diuretic, which points to volume contraction.
whyNot.B: A clonal process would suppress erythropoietin and is unlikely to appear within weeks of a new diuretic.
whyNot.C: His oxygen saturation is normal and he has no sleep or lung disease.
whyNot.D: Nothing in his history causes high oxygen affinity, such as carbon monoxide or a hemoglobin variant.

items.objective: Distinguish relative polycythemia from absolute erythrocytosis.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man is admitted with melena. He takes naproxen for back pain. After 1 L of crystalloid, pulse is 88/min and blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg, with no orthostatic change. He has no chest pain or dyspnea and no history of heart disease. Hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL (baseline 13.8 g/dL). An intravenous proton pump inhibitor is started and endoscopy is scheduled within 24 hours. Which of the following is the most appropriate transfusion strategy at this time?

options.label: A
options.html: Monitor the hemoglobin and transfuse if it falls below 7 g/dL

options.label: B
options.html: Transfuse 1 unit of packed red cells now

options.label: C
options.html: Transfuse 2 units of packed red cells now

options.label: D
options.html: Transfuse fresh frozen plasma with red cells

options.label: E
options.html: Transfuse to keep the hemoglobin above 10 g/dL

items.explanationHtml:
In hemodynamically stable patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding, a restrictive threshold of 7 g/dL lowers rebleeding and mortality compared with a liberal one. A higher threshold (about 8 g/dL) applies to patients with cardiovascular disease, and unstable patients with brisk ongoing bleeding are transfused on clinical grounds. This patient is stable and above the threshold, so he needs monitoring, acid suppression and endoscopy.

Takeaway: transfuse stable upper GI bleeding patients without cardiovascular disease only below 7 g/dL.

whyNot.B: A stable patient without cardiovascular disease above 7 g/dL does not benefit from transfusion, which adds risk.
whyNot.C: Two units in a stable patient above the restrictive threshold expose him to risk without benefit.
whyNot.D: There is no coagulopathy or massive bleeding to justify plasma.
whyNot.E: A liberal target in upper gastrointestinal bleeding is linked to more rebleeding and higher mortality than a restrictive one.

items.objective: Apply the restrictive transfusion threshold in stable upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

items.stemHtml:
An 81-year-old woman is on postoperative day 2 after hemiarthroplasty for a femoral neck fracture. She has coronary artery disease with a stent placed 4 years ago and takes aspirin. She feels tired but has no chest pain or dyspnea. Pulse is 94/min and blood pressure 128/70 mm Hg. Her drain output has been minimal since surgery. Laboratory results:

TestPreoperativePostoperative day 2
Hemoglobin11.6 g/dL7.7 g/dL
MCV91 fL92 fL
Platelets238,000/mm3201,000/mm3
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL1.0 mg/dL
Troponin I-0.02 ng/mL

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Give intravenous iron and no transfusion

options.label: B
options.html: Observe and repeat the hemoglobin in 24 hours

options.label: D
options.html: Transfuse 1 unit of packed red cells

options.label: E
options.html: Transfuse 3 units of packed red cells

items.explanationHtml:
For patients with pre-existing cardiovascular disease or after orthopedic surgery, a threshold of about 8 g/dL is used; a hip fracture trial in older adults with cardiovascular risk found this as safe as a liberal strategy. She is below it, so one unit is given, followed by reassessment of symptoms and hemoglobin. One unit raises hemoglobin by about 1 g/dL. Giving units singly limits circulatory overload, a particular risk in older adults.

Takeaway: in stable patients with cardiovascular disease or after orthopedic surgery, transfuse one unit at a time when hemoglobin is below about 8 g/dL.

whyNot.A: Iron takes weeks to raise hemoglobin; with cardiovascular disease and a hemoglobin below 8 g/dL she meets the threshold for transfusion.
whyNot.B: Waiting would suit a patient without cardiovascular disease above 7 g/dL, but she has coronary disease and is below 8 g/dL.
whyNot.C: Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents act slowly and increase thrombotic risk after orthopedic surgery.
whyNot.E: Stable patients receive one unit at a time with reassessment; several units raise the risk of circulatory overload in an older adult.

items.objective: Apply the transfusion threshold for an older adult with cardiovascular disease after orthopedic surgery.

items.stemHtml: An 18-month-old girl is brought for a routine visit. She drinks about 36 oz (1 L) of whole milk daily, much of it from a bottle at night, and is a picky eater who refuses meat. She was born at term and has developed normally. She is pale; weight is at the 75th percentile. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL, MCV 63 fL, RDW 18.2% (N 11.5-14.5%) and platelets 498,000/mm3. Blood lead level is below 3.5 ug/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Milk restriction and oral iron, with a 4-week recheck

options.label: D
options.html: Switch from whole milk to goat's milk at the same volume

items.explanationHtml:
Excess cow's milk is the classic cause of iron deficiency in toddlers. The diagnosis is supported by microcytosis, a high RDW and reactive thrombocytosis. Management is to limit milk to about 16 to 24 oz (500 to 700 mL) daily, stop the bottle, add iron-rich foods and give oral elemental iron at about 3 mg/kg/day. A hemoglobin rise of at least 1 g/dL after about 4 weeks confirms the diagnosis; iron then continues for about 3 more months to replete stores.

Takeaway: treat toddler iron deficiency with milk limitation and oral iron, and confirm by a hemoglobin rise in 4 weeks.

whyNot.A: Electrophoresis is reserved for children who do not respond to iron; her history and high RDW point strongly to iron deficiency.
whyNot.C: Marrow examination is not needed for typical nutritional iron deficiency.
whyNot.D: Goat's milk is also poor in iron and the volume problem remains.
whyNot.E: She is well compensated; chronic iron deficiency corrects with oral iron, and transfusion is reserved for cardiovascular compromise.

items.objective: Manage cow's milk-associated iron deficiency in a toddler.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 30 weeks' gestation has fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Her hemoglobin was 10.2 g/dL at 24 weeks with an MCV of 77 fL and ferritin of 9 ng/mL (N 15-150). She stopped two different oral ferrous salt preparations because of severe nausea and constipation despite alternate-day dosing. Today hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL and MCV 74 fL. Vital signs are normal and the fetus is growing appropriately. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Folic acid at a higher dose

options.label: E
options.html: Reassurance that this is physiologic anemia

items.explanationHtml:
This is iron deficiency anemia in the third trimester with failure of oral iron. Intravenous iron is appropriate in the second and third trimesters when oral iron is not tolerated or does not work, and it raises hemoglobin faster, which matters before delivery. Modern formulations rarely cause serious hypersensitivity. Physiologic dilution never causes microcytosis.

Takeaway: use intravenous iron in the second or third trimester when oral iron fails or is not tolerated.

whyNot.A: An ESA will not work without iron and is not used for iron deficiency in pregnancy.
whyNot.B: Her microcytosis and low ferritin indicate iron, not folate, deficiency.
whyNot.D: She is stable; transfusion is reserved for severe symptoms, hemodynamic compromise or imminent delivery with severe anemia.
whyNot.E: Physiologic dilution does not cause microcytosis or a low ferritin.

items.objective: Choose intravenous iron for oral-iron-refractory iron deficiency in late pregnancy.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man who runs competitively and trains about 110 km (70 miles) per week comes for a preparticipation examination. He feels well and his race times are improving. He eats a varied diet that includes meat. Examination is normal; resting pulse is 46/min. Hemoglobin is 12.9 g/dL, MCV 90 fL, RDW 12.8% (N 11.5-14.5%), and leukocyte and platelet counts are normal. Ferritin is 92 ng/mL (N 20-250) and the reticulocyte count is 1.1%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Endurance training expands plasma volume more than red cell mass, giving a slightly low hemoglobin with normal indices, normal ferritin and normal reticulocytes. This athletes' pseudoanemia is dilutional and needs no treatment. Low ferritin, microcytosis or symptoms would instead suggest true iron deficiency.

Takeaway: a mildly low hemoglobin with normal indices and ferritin in an endurance athlete is dilutional pseudoanemia.

whyNot.A: He has no iron deficiency or bleeding, so there is no source to look for.
whyNot.B: His normal MCV and RDW give no reason to suspect a hemoglobinopathy.
whyNot.D: His ferritin is normal; iron would not raise his hemoglobin and can cause harm.
whyNot.E: His mild, asymptomatic dilutional anemia is not harmful and does not call for less training.

items.objective: Recognise athletes' pseudoanemia and limit testing.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis who has been abstinent for 8 months has 1 month of worsening jaundice and fatigue. He has ascites and a palpable spleen. Hemoglobin is 7.4 g/dL (2 months ago 10.6 g/dL), MCV 104 fL, reticulocytes 9%, total bilirubin 8.4 mg/dL with direct bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL, LDH 510 U/L (N 45-200) and haptoglobin undetectable. Folate and B12 are normal. A direct antiglobulin test is negative. The smear shows numerous red cells with a few irregular spiny projections. His MELD score is 26. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
DAT-negative hemolysis with acanthocytes in advanced cirrhosis is spur cell anemia. It reflects severe liver dysfunction and carries a poor prognosis. The red cell membrane abnormality comes from the abnormal plasma lipoproteins, so the only definitive treatment is liver transplantation, after which the abnormality resolves. His high MELD score already makes him a candidate for evaluation.

Takeaway: spur cell anemia marks end-stage cirrhosis; refer for liver transplant evaluation.

whyNot.B: The negative direct antiglobulin test excludes autoimmune hemolysis; steroids would add infection risk.
whyNot.C: Plasma exchange is used in TTP, which has schistocytes and severe thrombocytopenia, not spur cells.
whyNot.D: Transfused cells soon acquire the same membrane defect, so transfusion gives only brief benefit.
whyNot.E: Splenectomy in decompensated cirrhosis with portal hypertension carries prohibitive risk and does not address the cause.

items.objective: Manage spur cell anemia in advanced cirrhosis.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman has 1 week of easy bruising and pinpoint red spots on her legs. She has no fever, weight loss, joint pain or recent illness, and takes no medications or supplements. She has not been screened for sexually transmitted or bloodborne infection. Vital signs are normal. Examination shows scattered petechiae on both legs and a few bruises; there is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 13.1 g/dL, leukocytes 6,900/mm3 with a normal differential and platelets 18,000/mm3. The smear confirms thrombocytopenia with some large platelets and no clumps or schistocytes. PT and aPTT are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional test in the initial evaluation?
items.explanationHtml:
Isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal smear apart from large platelets, in a well adult with a normal examination, is most likely immune thrombocytopenia, a diagnosis of exclusion. Testing for HIV and hepatitis C is recommended in adults because both cause secondary ITP and treating them can raise the count. A marrow biopsy is reserved for atypical features.

Takeaway: test adults with suspected ITP for HIV and hepatitis C; a marrow biopsy is not routinely needed.

whyNot.A: With no schistocytes or anemia, a thrombotic microangiopathy is not suspected.
whyNot.B: Marrow examination is not needed for typical isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal smear and examination.
whyNot.C: There is no splenomegaly or other finding that imaging would clarify.
whyNot.E: Antiplatelet antibody tests are neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose ITP.

items.objective: Select the recommended initial tests for suspected ITP in an adult.

items.stemHtml: The same 33-year-old woman's HIV and hepatitis C tests are negative, and she is diagnosed with immune thrombocytopenia. Two days later she notices bleeding from her gums when brushing her teeth. There is no blood in her stool or urine and no headache. Vital signs are normal, and neurologic examination is normal. Platelet count is 15,000/mm3 and hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Newly diagnosed adult ITP with a platelet count below 30,000/mm3, or with bleeding, is treated first with glucocorticoids: prednisone for no more than about 6 weeks including taper, or a short course of high-dose dexamethasone. IVIG is added when a rapid rise is needed, such as with serious bleeding. Mucosal bleeding without hemodynamic or neurologic compromise is not life-threatening, so platelet transfusion is not needed.

Takeaway: first-line therapy for newly diagnosed adult ITP with platelets below 30,000/mm3 or bleeding is a short course of glucocorticoids.

whyNot.B: Transfused platelets are destroyed within hours in ITP; transfusion is reserved for life-threatening bleeding.
whyNot.C: Rituximab is a second-line option, not initial therapy.
whyNot.D: Thrombopoietin-receptor agonists are second-line for persistent or steroid-dependent ITP.
whyNot.E: Splenectomy is a later option, usually delayed for at least 12 months from diagnosis.

items.objective: Choose initial treatment for newly diagnosed adult ITP.

items.stemHtml: The same woman responded to prednisone, with a platelet count of 140,000/mm3 after 2 weeks. Over the next 7 months, each attempt to taper prednisone below 15 mg daily has been followed by a fall in platelets to below 20,000/mm3 with bruising. She has gained 9 kg and has new insomnia. Platelet count today is 22,000/mm3. She has no plans for pregnancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
She has steroid-dependent ITP 7 months after diagnosis. Second-line options are a thrombopoietin-receptor agonist (eltrombopag, romiplostim, avatrombopag), rituximab or splenectomy. Because remission can still occur in the first year, splenectomy is usually delayed until at least 12 months, and TPO-receptor agonists are generally preferred over rituximab for durable response. Prolonged steroids should be avoided.

Takeaway: for steroid-dependent adult ITP within the first year, add a TPO-receptor agonist rather than continuing steroids or performing splenectomy.

whyNot.A: Long-term glucocorticoids add toxicity without durable benefit and should be avoided.
whyNot.C: IVIG gives only a short rise and is for emergencies or bridging, not maintenance.
whyNot.D: She has bruising and counts near 20,000/mm<sup>3</sup> off steroids, so she needs treatment.
whyNot.E: Splenectomy is usually deferred until at least 12 months after diagnosis because ITP can still remit.

items.objective: Choose second-line therapy for steroid-dependent adult ITP.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 35 weeks' gestation comes for a routine prenatal visit. She has had no bleeding, bruising or headache, and no history of low platelets before pregnancy. Blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg, and examination shows no petechiae and no edema. Urinalysis shows no protein. A platelet count today is 108,000/mm3; at 12 weeks it was 214,000/mm3. Hemoglobin is 11.4 g/dL, and aminotransferases and the smear are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Cesarean delivery to protect the fetus

items.explanationHtml:
A mild fall in platelets (usually above 70,000/mm3) late in pregnancy, with a normal earlier count, no bleeding history, no hypertension and normal liver tests, is gestational thrombocytopenia. It reflects dilution and faster clearance, causes no maternal or fetal bleeding, and resolves after delivery. Monitoring is all that is needed; a fall below about 70,000/mm3 or new hypertension would prompt evaluation for ITP or preeclampsia.

Takeaway: mild third-trimester thrombocytopenia with normal earlier counts and no other findings is gestational and needs only monitoring.

whyNot.A: Gestational thrombocytopenia carries no fetal bleeding risk, and mode of delivery follows obstetric indications.
whyNot.B: IVIG is used for ITP with low counts or bleeding, not for mild gestational thrombocytopenia.
whyNot.C: Glucocorticoids treat ITP in pregnancy when counts are low; her mild late fall needs no treatment.
whyNot.D: Her count is safe for delivery and neuraxial anesthesia; transfusion has no role.

items.objective: Recognise and manage gestational thrombocytopenia.

items.stemHtml:
A 74-year-old man has 4 months of fatigue and two episodes of pneumonia. His sole medication is amlodipine, and he seldom drinks alcohol. Examination shows pallor and a few petechiae; there is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Laboratory results:

TestResult
Hemoglobin8.7 g/dL
MCV106 fL
Reticulocytes0.4%
Leukocytes2,300/mm3 (neutrophils 35%)
Platelets54,000/mm3
Vitamin B12620 pg/mL (N 200-800)
Folate, serum11 ng/mL (N above 4)
CopperNormal
TSH2.1 uU/mL
HIV antibody/antigenNegative

The smear shows macro-ovalocytes and neutrophils with bilobed nuclei and sparse granules; there are no blasts. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Macrocytic pancytopenia with a low reticulocyte count, normal B12, folate and copper, and dysplastic hypogranular, hypolobated neutrophils in an older adult strongly suggests myelodysplastic syndrome. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy with cytogenetics (and usually molecular testing) confirms the diagnosis, counts blasts and assigns a risk category that guides treatment.

Takeaway: after excluding nutritional and drug causes, unexplained pancytopenia, especially with dysplasia, needs a marrow biopsy with cytogenetics.

whyNot.A: His spleen is not enlarged on examination, and the smear already points to marrow dysplasia.
whyNot.C: His B12 level is clearly normal, so methylmalonic acid adds little.
whyNot.D: Progressive pancytopenia with infections needs a diagnosis now, not watchful waiting.
whyNot.E: His folate is normal, so empiric folic acid would only delay the diagnosis.

items.objective: Select the definitive test for unexplained macrocytic pancytopenia in an older adult.

items.stemHtml: A girl born at 38 weeks' gestation to a healthy 30-year-old primigravida has widespread petechiae at 1 hour of age. She is feeding well, and vital signs are normal. Her platelet count is 12,000/mm3; hemoglobin and leukocyte counts are normal, and PT and aPTT are normal. The mother's platelet count is 232,000/mm3, and she has no history of ITP or lupus. Cranial ultrasonography shows no hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.label: C
options.html: Observation with a repeat count in 1 week

items.explanationHtml:
Severe thrombocytopenia in a well newborn whose mother has a normal count suggests neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia. Because of the risk of intracranial hemorrhage, a count this low is treated at once with platelet transfusion. Antigen-negative platelets are preferred if available, but random-donor platelets should not be delayed. IVIG is often added. Confirm with maternal antibody and parental platelet antigen typing. Future pregnancies need specialist antenatal care.

Takeaway: treat severe neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia promptly with platelet transfusion, without waiting for antigen-matched units.

whyNot.A: Exchange transfusion treats severe hyperbilirubinemia or hemolysis, not isolated thrombocytopenia.
whyNot.B: Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT, which is normal here; the platelet count is the problem.
whyNot.C: A count this low carries a real risk of intracranial hemorrhage and needs prompt treatment.
whyNot.D: Glucocorticoids act too slowly and are not the treatment for neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia.

items.objective: Manage severe neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia.

items.stemHtml:
A 51-year-old man has 6 months of headaches and itching after hot showers. He does not smoke, has no snoring and has had no prior blood clot. Blood pressure is 134/84 mm Hg. He has facial plethora, and the spleen tip is palpable. Laboratory results:

TestResult
Hemoglobin18.9 g/dL
Hematocrit57%
Leukocytes12,800/mm3
Platelets530,000/mm3
Erythropoietin, serum2 mU/mL (N 4-26)
JAK2 V617FDetected
Oxygen saturation, room air97%

Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: Observation with a repeat count in 6 months

options.label: C
options.html: Phlebotomy to a hematocrit below 45% and aspirin

items.explanationHtml:
Erythrocytosis with a JAK2 V617F mutation and a low erythropoietin establishes polycythemia vera. He is under 60 with no prior thrombosis, so he is low risk. All patients receive phlebotomy to a hematocrit below 45% and low-dose aspirin. Cytoreduction with hydroxyurea or interferon is added for high-risk disease or for poor tolerance of phlebotomy, progressive splenomegaly or severe symptoms.

Takeaway: treat low-risk PV with phlebotomy to hematocrit below 45% and low-dose aspirin.

whyNot.A: Cytoreduction is for high-risk patients (age 60 or older or prior thrombosis); he is low risk, and phlebotomy is needed whatever drug is used.
whyNot.B: Untreated PV carries a high risk of thrombosis; he needs treatment now.
whyNot.D: A target below 45% lowers cardiovascular death and major thrombosis compared with a looser target.
whyNot.E: Without a thrombosis there is no indication for anticoagulation, and it does not control the hematocrit.

items.objective: Manage low-risk polycythemia vera.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman with polycythemia vera diagnosed 9 months ago has had phlebotomy every 4 to 6 weeks and takes low-dose aspirin. She now has mild fatigue but no dyspnea or chest pain, and no prior thrombosis. Hematocrit is 42%, MCV 73 fL (previously 89 fL), platelets 460,000/mm3 and ferritin 5 ng/mL (N 15-150). Her primary care physician has suggested oral iron. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Colonoscopy to find a source of bleeding

items.explanationHtml:
Phlebotomy induces iron deficiency by design; it limits red cell production by the JAK2-mutant clone. Microcytosis and a low ferritin are expected, and mild fatigue usually does not justify iron, which would push the hematocrit up and increase phlebotomy needs. Iron is considered only for severe symptomatic deficiency, with close hematocrit monitoring. Her hematocrit is at target, so she continues phlebotomy as needed and aspirin.

Takeaway: do not give iron for phlebotomy-induced iron deficiency in PV; it is part of the treatment.

whyNot.A: Her iron deficiency is explained by the phlebotomies; she has no other sign of blood loss.
whyNot.C: Iron replacement removes the intended brake on red cell production and drives the hematocrit back up.
whyNot.D: Oral iron will raise the hematocrit and increase the need for phlebotomy.
whyNot.E: Aspirin lowers thrombotic risk in PV and is not the cause of her low ferritin.

items.objective: Manage expected iron deficiency during phlebotomy for polycythemia vera.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old man has a hematocrit of 54% on routine testing. His wife reports loud snoring and pauses in his breathing at night, and he falls asleep while reading. He does not smoke and takes lisinopril. BMI is 38 kg/m2, and neck circumference is 47 cm. There is no splenomegaly. Oxygen saturation is 95% on room air while awake. Serum erythropoietin is at the upper limit of normal and JAK2 V617F is not detected. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Erythrocytosis with a normal or high erythropoietin and no JAK2 mutation is secondary. His snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness and obesity point to obstructive sleep apnea, which causes nocturnal hypoxemia even when daytime saturation is normal. Polysomnography confirms it, and treatment with CPAP usually lowers the hematocrit.

Takeaway: evaluate secondary erythrocytosis with normal daytime saturation for nocturnal hypoxemia from sleep apnea.

whyNot.A: His normal erythropoietin and negative JAK2 point away from a myeloproliferative neoplasm.
whyNot.B: There is no sign of lung disease that would need imaging first.
whyNot.C: Exon 12 testing is for patients with suspected PV and low erythropoietin who are V617F negative.
whyNot.E: Measured red cell mass is rarely needed and would not identify the cause he most likely has.

items.objective: Choose the next diagnostic step for suspected sleep apnea-related erythrocytosis.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man who moved to the United States from rural Cambodia 6 years ago is admitted with a severe exacerbation of asthma. He has intermittent epigastric discomfort and an itchy, migrating rash on his trunk. The admitting team plans high-dose systemic glucocorticoids. Leukocytes are 11,900/mm3 with 14% eosinophils (absolute count 1,670/mm3). Strongyloides serology has been sent, and results will take 5 days. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional treatment now?
items.explanationHtml:
Eosinophilia, abdominal symptoms and a migrating trunk rash (larva currens) in a person from an endemic region suggest chronic strongyloidiasis. Glucocorticoids can trigger hyperinfection and disseminated disease with gram-negative sepsis. When steroids cannot wait for test results, give empiric ivermectin, the drug of choice.

Takeaway: give empiric ivermectin before high-dose steroids when Strongyloides exposure is possible and results are pending.

whyNot.A: Imatinib treats clonal PDGFRA-rearranged eosinophilia, which is not suspected before parasites are excluded.
whyNot.C: Anti-IL-5 therapy lowers eosinophils but does not treat Strongyloides and is not the urgent need here.
whyNot.D: Metronidazole treats protozoa and anaerobes, not Strongyloides.
whyNot.E: Praziquantel treats schistosomes and tapeworms and is ineffective against Strongyloides.

items.objective: Prevent Strongyloides hyperinfection before glucocorticoid therapy in a patient with eosinophilia.

items.stemHtml: A boy born at 39 weeks' gestation after delayed cord clamping is noted by the nurse to look ruddy at 4 hours of age. He is feeding well, active and pink, with normal vital signs. A capillary heel-stick hematocrit is 68%. Blood glucose is 58 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Capillary samples overestimate the hematocrit by several percentage points, especially with poor peripheral perfusion. Neonatal polycythemia is defined by a venous hematocrit above 65%, so the first step is a venous sample. An asymptomatic infant with confirmed polycythemia is managed with feeding, glucose and bilirubin monitoring; partial exchange transfusion is reserved for symptoms of hyperviscosity.

Takeaway: confirm a high neonatal capillary hematocrit with a venous sample before acting.

whyNot.A: He is feeding well and has no signs of dehydration; the hematocrit is not yet confirmed.
whyNot.C: This is reserved for confirmed polycythemia with symptoms of hyperviscosity.
whyNot.D: Removing blood without replacement causes hypovolemia and is not used in neonates.
whyNot.E: There is no jaundice to treat.

items.objective: Confirm suspected neonatal polycythemia with a venous hematocrit.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old woman has a platelet count of 1,380,000/mm3, stable over 4 months. She has had two episodes of prolonged nosebleeds and heavy bleeding after a dental extraction. Ferritin and CRP are normal, and there is no history of surgery or infection. BCR-ABL1 is negative and a CALR mutation is detected. A marrow biopsy is consistent with essential thrombocythemia. Her hematologist is considering low-dose aspirin. Which of the following tests is most appropriate before starting it?
items.explanationHtml:
At platelet counts above about 1,000,000/mm3, large von Willebrand multimers bind the expanded platelet mass and are cleared, causing an acquired von Willebrand syndrome. Her mucosal and post-extraction bleeding fit. Aspirin would add to the bleeding risk, so von Willebrand factor activity (ristocetin cofactor) is checked first. If it is low, aspirin is withheld and cytoreduction lowers the platelet count, which corrects the defect.

Takeaway: check von Willebrand factor activity before aspirin in essential thrombocythemia with platelets above about 1 million/mm3.

whyNot.A: She has bleeding, not thrombosis, and no other features of antiphospholipid syndrome.
whyNot.B: Thrombophilia testing does not explain her bleeding and does not change aspirin decisions.
whyNot.C: Her driver mutation (CALR) is already known; exon 12 testing is for suspected PV.
whyNot.D: Aggregation studies are not the standard way to assess bleeding risk from extreme thrombocytosis.

items.objective: Recognise acquired von Willebrand syndrome in extreme thrombocytosis before antiplatelet therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man is evaluated for recurrent nosebleeds since childhood and prolonged bleeding after removal of his wisdom teeth. His parents are first cousins. He has had no joint swelling. Examination shows scattered petechiae on both shins. Platelet count is 85,000/mm3, and the peripheral smear shows many platelets nearly as large as red blood cells. PT and aPTT are normal. Von Willebrand factor antigen and activity are normal. On aggregometry, his platelets respond normally to ADP, collagen and epinephrine but do not agglutinate with ristocetin; adding normal plasma does not correct the ristocetin response. Which of the following platelet surface molecules is most likely deficient?
items.explanationHtml:
Lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding with mild thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, an absent ristocetin response that is not corrected by normal plasma (a source of von Willebrand factor) and normal responses to other agonists is Bernard-Soulier syndrome. It is an autosomal recessive (hence the consanguinity) deficiency of the GpIb-IX-V complex, the platelet receptor for von Willebrand factor, so platelets cannot adhere to injured subendothelium.

Takeaway: absent ristocetin response plus large platelets and no correction with normal plasma means a GpIb defect, not von Willebrand disease.

whyNot.B: GpIIb/IIIa deficiency (Glanzmann thrombasthenia) abolishes aggregation to ADP, collagen and epinephrine but leaves ristocetin agglutination and platelet size normal.
whyNot.C: GpVI is a collagen receptor; its loss would blunt the collagen response, which is normal here, and does not cause giant platelets.
whyNot.D: P-selectin mediates platelet-leukocyte adhesion after activation; it does not explain an isolated ristocetin defect.
whyNot.E: P2Y<sub>12</sub> defects impair ADP-induced aggregation, which is normal in this patient.

items.objective: Identify Bernard-Soulier syndrome as GpIb-IX-V deficiency from giant platelets and an uncorrected ristocetin defect.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of easy bruising, frequent gum bleeding with tooth brushing and bleeding that lasted several hours after a lip laceration last month. Her parents are healthy. Examination shows multiple bruises on the shins and forearms. Platelet count is 260,000/mm3, and platelets are normal in size on the smear. PT and aPTT are normal. Platelet aggregation studies show no aggregation in response to ADP, collagen, epinephrine or arachidonic acid; the response to ristocetin is normal. Clot retraction is absent. Which of the following steps in platelet plug formation is most likely impaired?

options.label: A
options.html: Adhesion of platelets to von Willebrand factor

options.label: B
options.html: Cross-linking of activated platelets by fibrinogen

options.label: C
options.html: Release of ADP from dense granules

options.label: D
options.html: Synthesis of thromboxane A<sub>2</sub> by cyclooxygenase-1

options.label: E
options.html: Translocation of phosphatidylserine to the outer membrane

items.explanationHtml:
Normal count and size, absent aggregation with every agonist except ristocetin and absent clot retraction indicate Glanzmann thrombasthenia: deficiency or dysfunction of GpIIb/IIIa (αIIbβ3). Activated GpIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen, which bridges adjacent platelets; without it, platelets adhere but cannot aggregate, and the fibrin network cannot be pulled together (clot retraction).

Takeaway: aggregation absent to all agonists but ristocetin = GpIIb/IIIa defect (Glanzmann).

whyNot.A: Adhesion via von Willebrand factor and GpIb is intact, as shown by the normal ristocetin response.
whyNot.C: Dense granule storage defects blunt the secondary wave of aggregation but do not abolish aggregation to all agonists or clot retraction.
whyNot.D: A cyclooxygenase defect (or aspirin) abolishes the arachidonic acid response but leaves ADP and collagen responses largely intact.
whyNot.E: Defective phosphatidylserine exposure (Scott syndrome) impairs procoagulant activity with normal aggregation studies.

items.objective: Localize Glanzmann thrombasthenia to failed fibrinogen-mediated platelet aggregation via GpIIb/IIIa.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man is scheduled for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Preoperative aPTT is 74 s; PT is 12 s, and the platelet count is normal. He had a tonsillectomy at age 7 years, four dental extractions and a knee arthroscopy, all without abnormal bleeding. He takes no medications, and there is no family history of bleeding. A 1:1 mixing study with normal plasma fully corrects the aPTT, and the correction persists after 2 hours of incubation at 37 °C. Deficiency of which of the following factors is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
A markedly prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing indicates a factor deficiency in the intrinsic pathway. The patient has passed several hemostatic challenges, including tonsillectomy and dental extractions, without bleeding.
