Factor XII (like prekallikrein and high-molecular-weight kininogen) is needed for contact activation in the test tube but not for hemostasis in vivo, so its deficiency prolongs the aPTT without causing bleeding. No plasma or factor replacement is needed before surgery.

Takeaway: long aPTT that corrects with mixing in a person who has never bled points to factor XII deficiency.

whyNot.A: Factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT, which is normal here.
whyNot.B: Even mild hemophilia A would be expected to cause bleeding after tonsillectomy or dental extraction.
whyNot.C: Hemophilia B causes bleeding with surgical challenges similar to hemophilia A.
whyNot.D: Factor XI deficiency typically causes bleeding after surgery at sites rich in fibrinolytic activity, such as tonsils and tooth sockets, which this man tolerated.

items.objective: Recognize factor XII deficiency as a cause of a prolonged aPTT without clinical bleeding.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man is in the intensive care unit 10 days after emergency colectomy for perforated diverticulitis. He has had no oral or enteral intake since surgery and has received intravenous dextrose-containing fluids and meropenem. Today the nurse notes oozing around his central venous catheter and from venipuncture sites. Laboratory studies show PT 28 s, INR 2.6, aPTT 44 s, platelet count 240,000/mm3, and fibrinogen 380 mg/dL (N = 200–400). Twenty-four hours after a dose of an intravenous vitamin, the PT is 13 s. The vitamin given is a cofactor for which of the following protein modifications?
items.explanationHtml:
No dietary intake plus a broad-spectrum antibiotic that eliminates menaquinone-producing gut flora causes vitamin K deficiency. The PT is prolonged more than the aPTT because factor VII has the shortest half-life; platelets and fibrinogen are normal, and the PT corrects within a day of vitamin K. Vitamin K is the cofactor for γ-glutamyl carboxylase, which converts glutamate residues on factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S to γ-carboxyglutamate. These residues bind calcium and anchor the factors to phospholipid membranes.

Takeaway: vitamin K enables γ-carboxylation of glutamate; antibiotics plus no intake can deplete it within days to weeks.

whyNot.B: Proteolytic cleavage activates zymogens such as prothrombin but does not require vitamin K.
whyNot.C: N-linked glycosylation occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum without a vitamin K cofactor.
whyNot.D: Lysine and proline hydroxylation in collagen requires vitamin C, whose deficiency causes vascular bleeding with a normal PT.
whyNot.E: Serine phosphorylation by kinases is not vitamin-dependent and does not explain a corrected PT.

items.objective: Explain the role of vitamin K in γ-carboxylation of clotting factors in a patient with acquired deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis is admitted with hepatic encephalopathy. He has ascites, spider angiomas and splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show PT 21 s, aPTT 42 s, platelet count 72,000/mm3, fibrinogen 140 mg/dL (N = 200–400) and albumin 2.4 g/dL. The PT does not change after 3 days of intravenous vitamin K. Individual coagulation factor assays are ordered. The activity of which of the following factors is most likely to be normal or increased?
items.explanationHtml:
Hepatocytes synthesize fibrinogen and factors II, V, VII, IX, X and XI, so their activities fall in cirrhosis and do not respond to vitamin K. Factor VIII is made mainly by liver sinusoidal and other endothelial cells, is carried by von Willebrand factor (which rises in cirrhosis) and is an acute phase reactant; its activity is normal or high. In DIC, by contrast, factor VIII is consumed and low.

Takeaway: factor VIII stays normal or high in liver disease and falls in DIC.

whyNot.A: Prothrombin is a hepatocyte-derived, vitamin K-dependent factor and is low in cirrhosis.
whyNot.B: Factor V is made by hepatocytes; it is low in liver disease (though normal in pure vitamin K deficiency).
whyNot.C: Factor VII falls early in liver failure because of its short half-life; that explains the long PT.
whyNot.E: Factor X is synthesized by hepatocytes and is reduced in cirrhosis.

items.objective: Recognize that factor VIII is preserved in liver disease because it is produced by endothelial cells.

items.stemHtml: A 9-day-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of oozing from his umbilical stump for 3 days. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and received intramuscular vitamin K at birth. His parents are first cousins. Hemoglobin is 12.5 g/dL, and platelet count is 290,000/mm3. PT is 13 s, aPTT is 34 s and fibrinogen is 260 mg/dL (N = 200–400). A clot formed from his plasma dissolves when placed in 5 mol/L urea, while a clot from control plasma does not. Deficiency of a protein with which of the following functions is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Activating factor X on the platelet surface

items.explanationHtml:
Umbilical stump bleeding in a neonate from a consanguineous family, with normal PT, aPTT, fibrinogen and platelets, suggests factor XIII deficiency. Factor XIIIa is a transglutaminase that forms covalent bonds between glutamine and lysine residues of adjacent fibrin monomers. Uncross-linked fibrin is held together only by noncovalent bonds, so the clot dissolves in 5 mol/L urea. The screening tests are normal because they end when the first fibrin strands form.

Takeaway: normal screening tests plus umbilical bleeding and urea-soluble clot = factor XIII deficiency.

whyNot.A: Tenase activity (IXa with VIIIa) is part of the intrinsic pathway; a defect would prolong the aPTT.
whyNot.B: Thrombin cleaves fibrinogen; a defect would prolong the PT, aPTT and thrombin time.
whyNot.D: Loss of α2-antiplasmin causes delayed bleeding with normal screening tests, but the clot is cross-linked and insoluble in urea.
whyNot.E: PAI-1 deficiency causes delayed bleeding from excess fibrinolysis, but clot solubility in urea is normal.

items.objective: Identify factor XIII deficiency from normal coagulation screening, umbilical bleeding and a urea-soluble clot.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis comes to the emergency department because of large spontaneous bruises on her arms and trunk for 1 week and a painful swelling of her right thigh since yesterday. She had a hip replacement 5 years ago without excessive bleeding. She takes methotrexate and folic acid. Examination shows extensive ecchymoses and a tense, tender right thigh. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL and platelet count is 230,000/mm3. PT is 13 s and aPTT is 78 s. After 1:1 mixing with normal plasma, the aPTT is 38 s immediately and 66 s after 2 hours of incubation at 37 °C. Which of the following best explains her coagulation abnormality?

options.label: C
options.html: Consumption of factors in microvascular thrombi

options.label: D
options.html: Impaired hepatic synthesis of clotting factors

items.explanationHtml:
New, severe soft-tissue and muscle bleeding in an older adult with an autoimmune disease, an isolated prolonged aPTT and a mixing study that corrects at first but prolongs again after incubation at 37 °C is acquired hemophilia A. An IgG autoantibody inactivates factor VIII slowly and in a time- and temperature-dependent way. Factor VIII activity will be low and the Bethesda assay positive.

Takeaway: a time-dependent inhibitor on mixing in a previously normal adult with new bleeding is an autoantibody to factor VIII.

whyNot.A: A lupus anticoagulant acts immediately on mixing and predisposes to thrombosis rather than bleeding.
whyNot.C: DIC would lower the platelet count and prolong the PT, and a factor deficiency would correct on mixing.
whyNot.D: Liver disease prolongs the PT first, and mixing would correct the abnormality.
whyNot.E: Low von Willebrand factor would cause mucosal bleeding and a long aPTT that corrects with mixing; it does not appear de novo at 74 years with a time-dependent inhibitor.

items.objective: Explain acquired hemophilia A as a time-dependent autoantibody against factor VIII.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit with septic shock from Escherichia coli pyelonephritis and bacteremia. On the second day he is oozing blood from venipuncture and catheter sites, and dusky purpura appears on his fingertips. Platelet count is 38,000/mm3, PT 24 s, aPTT 58 s, fibrinogen 90 mg/dL (N = 200–400) and D-dimer markedly elevated. The peripheral smear shows occasional schistocytes. Which of the following is the principal initiating event of this coagulopathy?

options.label: B
options.html: Contact activation of factor XII by bacteria

items.explanationHtml:
Thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer and schistocytes in septic shock indicate disseminated intravascular coagulation. Endotoxin and cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α) induce tissue factor on monocytes and endothelial cells, which drives systemic thrombin generation. At the same time thrombomodulin and protein C activation are suppressed and PAI-1 rises. Microthrombi cause ischemia (acral purpura), and consumption of platelets and factors causes bleeding.

Takeaway: sepsis-associated DIC is driven by tissue factor expression, not by the contact pathway.

whyNot.A: Antibodies to ADAMTS13 cause TTP, in which PT, aPTT and fibrinogen are normal.
whyNot.B: Contact activation can be triggered in sepsis but contributes little to thrombin generation; tissue factor is the main driver.
whyNot.C: Marrow suppression lowers platelets but does not prolong the PT and aPTT or lower fibrinogen.
whyNot.D: Hepatic dysfunction may contribute, but it does not explain microthrombi, schistocytes and the high D-dimer.

items.objective: Identify tissue factor expression as the trigger of sepsis-associated DIC.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman develops a left popliteal deep vein thrombosis 2 days after a 10-hour flight. She takes a combined oral contraceptive. Her mother had a pulmonary embolism at age 40 years. Genetic testing shows that she is heterozygous for a guanine-to-adenine substitution at position 20210 in the 3′ untranslated region of the prothrombin gene. Which of the following best explains how this variant increases her risk of thrombosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Decreased binding of thrombin to thrombomodulin

options.label: C
options.html: Production of factor Va resistant to activated protein C

options.label: D
options.html: Production of thrombin resistant to antithrombin

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced hepatic synthesis of protein S

items.explanationHtml:
The prothrombin G20210A variant lies outside the coding sequence, so the protein made is normal. The change increases the efficiency of mRNA 3′ end processing and stability, so more prothrombin is made; plasma levels are roughly 30% higher in heterozygotes, which favours thrombin generation. Her risk was compounded by estrogen and prolonged immobility.

Takeaway: prothrombin G20210A raises the amount of a normal protein; factor V Leiden changes the protein's resistance to inactivation.

whyNot.A: Thrombomodulin binding is unaffected because the thrombin molecule is structurally normal.
whyNot.C: Resistance of factor Va to activated protein C is the mechanism of factor V Leiden, a different gene.
whyNot.D: Thrombin produced from the variant gene has a normal sequence and normal sensitivity to antithrombin.
whyNot.E: Protein S levels are lowered by estrogen, but this variant affects the prothrombin gene, not protein S.

items.objective: Explain that the prothrombin G20210A variant increases plasma prothrombin concentration.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man with biopsy-proven membranous nephropathy has sudden left flank pain and gross hematuria. Urine protein excretion is 9 g/24 h, and serum albumin is 1.9 g/dL. CT shows thrombosis of the left renal vein. An intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion is started. Over the next 36 hours the dose is increased well above the usual range, but the aPTT stays between 34 and 38 s, and the anti-factor Xa activity remains below the target range. Urinary loss of which of the following proteins best explains the poor response to heparin?
items.explanationHtml:
Heparin has no anticoagulant action of its own: it binds antithrombin and accelerates its inactivation of thrombin and factor Xa. Antithrombin (about 58 kDa, similar in size to albumin) is lost in the urine in heavy proteinuria, which both promotes thrombosis (renal vein thrombosis is classic in membranous nephropathy) and causes heparin resistance. A low anti-Xa level confirms a true lack of heparin effect rather than an aPTT artefact.

Takeaway: heparin resistance with nephrotic syndrome points to urinary antithrombin loss.

whyNot.B: Urinary plasminogen loss can impair fibrinolysis but does not change heparin's anticoagulant effect.
whyNot.C: Protein C loss favours thrombosis, but heparin does not act through protein C.
whyNot.D: Free protein S may fall in nephrotic syndrome, but heparin's anti-Xa effect does not depend on it.
whyNot.E: Heparin releases tissue factor pathway inhibitor from endothelium, but its main anti-Xa effect requires antithrombin.

items.objective: Link heparin resistance in nephrotic syndrome to urinary loss of antithrombin.

items.stemHtml: A 2-day-old girl born at term develops rapidly spreading purple-black skin lesions with blistering on her buttocks, thighs and scalp. She received vitamin K at birth. Blood cultures are negative. Platelet count is 60,000/mm3, fibrinogen is low and D-dimer is markedly elevated. Protein C activity is undetectable. Both parents have protein C activity about half of normal, and her father had a deep vein thrombosis at age 30 years. The deficient protein normally limits coagulation by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Binding and neutralizing tissue factor-factor VIIa complexes

options.label: B
options.html: Blocking von Willebrand factor binding to platelets

options.label: C
options.html: Cleaving activated factors V and VIII

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibiting thrombin and factor Xa as a serpin

items.explanationHtml:
Neonatal purpura fulminans with undetectable protein C activity and heterozygous parents indicates homozygous (or compound heterozygous) protein C deficiency. Protein C is activated when thrombin binds thrombomodulin on endothelium; activated protein C, with protein S, proteolytically inactivates factors Va and VIIIa. Without it, dermal microvessels thrombose and the skin infarcts. Treatment is protein C concentrate (or plasma) followed by long-term anticoagulation.

Takeaway: activated protein C cleaves Va and VIIIa; complete deficiency causes neonatal purpura fulminans.

whyNot.A: Neutralizing TF-VIIa-Xa is the role of tissue factor pathway inhibitor.
whyNot.B: Inhibition of von Willebrand factor binding is not a function of protein C (ADAMTS13 regulates vWF multimer size).
whyNot.D: Plasminogen activation is carried out by tissue plasminogen activator and urokinase.
whyNot.E: Serpin inhibition of thrombin and Xa is the function of antithrombin.

items.objective: Describe the anticoagulant action of activated protein C and the presentation of its homozygous deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus comes to the physician because of swelling of her left leg for 3 days. She has had two pregnancy losses at 9 and 11 weeks' gestation. Ultrasonography shows a left femoral vein thrombus. Before any anticoagulant is given, platelet count is 118,000/mm3, PT is 12 s and aPTT is 56 s. The aPTT does not correct after 1:1 mixing with normal plasma, but it shortens when excess phospholipid is added to the test. She has no history of abnormal bleeding. Which of the following best explains the prolonged aPTT?

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced synthesis of vitamin K-dependent factors

items.explanationHtml:
Venous thrombosis, recurrent early pregnancy loss, mild thrombocytopenia and SLE suggest antiphospholipid syndrome. Its antibodies (directed mainly against β2-glycoprotein I and prothrombin bound to phospholipid) occupy the phospholipid surface in the aPTT reagent, so the clotting time is prolonged in vitro (lupus anticoagulant). Mixing does not dilute the inhibitor enough to correct, and adding excess phospholipid overcomes it. In vivo the same antibodies activate endothelium, platelets and complement and cause thrombosis, not bleeding.

Takeaway: the lupus anticoagulant prolongs the aPTT in the tube but causes clots in the patient.

whyNot.B: A factor VIII autoantibody causes bleeding and is not overcome by extra phospholipid.
whyNot.C: Factor XII deficiency would correct on mixing.
whyNot.D: The sample was drawn before any heparin, and heparin's effect would not be reversed by excess phospholipid.
whyNot.E: Vitamin K-dependent factor deficiency prolongs the PT first and corrects on mixing.

items.objective: Explain the in vitro prolongation of the aPTT by lupus anticoagulant despite a prothrombotic state.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old man is diagnosed with a first unprovoked deep vein thrombosis of the right femoral vein. Kidney and liver function are normal. He is started on oral apixaban at a fixed dose, without initial parenteral anticoagulation and without plans for routine coagulation monitoring. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of this drug?

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase

options.label: D
options.html: Irreversible blockade of the P2Y<sub>12</sub> receptor

items.explanationHtml:
Apixaban (like rivaroxaban and edoxaban) binds the active site of factor Xa directly, inhibiting both free Xa and Xa within the prothrombinase complex, without needing antithrombin. Predictable pharmacokinetics allow fixed dosing without routine monitoring. Apixaban and rivaroxaban can be started without a parenteral lead-in, using a higher initial dose for the first days.

Takeaway: the "-xaban" drugs are direct factor Xa inhibitors.

whyNot.B: Direct thrombin inhibition is the mechanism of dabigatran, argatroban and bivalirudin.
whyNot.C: VKORC1 inhibition is the mechanism of warfarin, which requires INR monitoring and a heparin overlap.
whyNot.D: Irreversible P2Y<sub>12</sub> blockade describes clopidogrel and prasugrel, antiplatelet drugs not used alone to treat DVT.
whyNot.E: Antithrombin potentiation is the mechanism of heparins and fondaparinux, which are given parenterally.

items.objective: State the mechanism of apixaban as a direct factor Xa inhibitor.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman develops a deep vein thrombosis of the right femoral vein 4 months after starting a combined oral contraceptive containing ethinyl estradiol and a progestin. She has had no recent travel, surgery or injury, and she does not smoke. There is no family history of thrombosis. Which of the following effects of ethinyl estradiol most directly contributes to her thrombosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Oral estrogen reaches the liver at high concentration through the portal circulation and increases hepatic synthesis of fibrinogen and factors II, VII, VIII and X. It also lowers free protein S and induces an acquired resistance to activated protein C. The net effect is a hypercoagulable state, which is why the risk is concentrated in the first months of use and is greater with oral than transdermal estrogen.

Takeaway: oral estrogen promotes VTE mainly by increasing hepatic procoagulant production and reducing natural anticoagulant activity.

whyNot.A: Estrogen raises, not lowers, fibrinogen synthesis.
whyNot.B: Prostacyclin inhibits platelet aggregation; more of it would oppose thrombosis.
whyNot.D: Estrogen tends to lower or not change antithrombin; more antithrombin would protect against thrombosis.
whyNot.E: Erythrocytosis is an effect of androgens, not estrogens.

items.objective: Explain how oral estrogen increases venous thrombosis risk.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of weight loss and dull epigastric pain that radiates to his back. During the past 6 weeks, painful, red, cord-like swellings have appeared in succession along superficial veins of his left forearm, right thigh and chest wall, each fading as a new one appears. He was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus 2 months ago. Which of the following mechanisms most likely underlies his thrombotic tendency?

options.label: B
options.html: Clonal JAK2-driven increase in red cell mass

options.label: C
options.html: Complement lysis of cells lacking GPI-anchored proteins

options.label: D
options.html: Inherited resistance of factor Va to activated protein C

options.label: E
options.html: Tumor-cell expression of tissue factor and mucins

items.explanationHtml:
Weight loss, back-radiating epigastric pain and new-onset diabetes in an older adult suggest pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) reflects cancer-associated hypercoagulability: tumor cells express tissue factor and release procoagulant microparticles and mucins, which activate platelets and the coagulation cascade. Unexplained migratory thrombophlebitis warrants a search for occult cancer.

Takeaway: migratory superficial thrombophlebitis is a clue to visceral adenocarcinoma, especially pancreatic.

whyNot.A: HIT requires recent heparin exposure and causes thrombocytopenia, neither of which is described.
whyNot.B: Polycythemia vera causes thrombosis but would not explain epigastric pain radiating to the back and new diabetes.
whyNot.C: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria causes hemolysis and thrombosis in unusual sites such as hepatic veins, not migratory thrombophlebitis with an abdominal mass picture.
whyNot.D: Factor V Leiden causes deep venous thrombosis, typically with a provoking factor, not this migratory superficial pattern with constitutional symptoms.

items.objective: Recognize Trousseau syndrome as cancer-associated hypercoagulability driven by tumor procoagulants.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman with blood group O, Rh-positive, is receiving a unit of packed red blood cells on the orthopedic ward after repair of a hip fracture. Ten minutes into the transfusion she reports chills, low back pain and burning at the intravenous site. Temperature is 38.9 °C (102 °F), pulse is 124/min and blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg. Urine in her catheter bag turns dark red. The unit is found to be group A and labelled for another patient. Which of the following most directly causes destruction of the transfused cells?

options.label: A
options.html: Cytokines released from donor leukocytes during storage

options.label: B
options.html: Neutrophil activation by donor anti-HLA antibodies

options.label: C
options.html: Phagocytosis of IgG-coated cells by splenic macrophages

options.label: D
options.html: Recipient IgE binding to donor plasma proteins

items.explanationHtml:
This is an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction from ABO incompatibility. Group O individuals have naturally occurring IgM (and some IgG) anti-A and anti-B. IgM binds the group A donor cells and activates the classical complement pathway to the membrane attack complex, lysing the cells within the circulation: hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, fever, back pain, hypotension and risk of DIC and acute kidney injury.

Takeaway: ABO-incompatible transfusion causes intravascular hemolysis through complement-fixing IgM isohemagglutinins.

whyNot.A: Stored leukocyte cytokines cause febrile non-hemolytic reactions without hemoglobinuria or shock.
whyNot.B: Donor anti-HLA antibodies cause TRALI, which presents with hypoxemia and pulmonary infiltrates.
whyNot.C: Splenic removal of IgG-coated cells is extravascular hemolysis, typical of delayed reactions days later.
whyNot.D: IgE against plasma proteins causes urticarial or anaphylactic reactions, which do not lyse red cells.

items.objective: Explain the immune mechanism of an acute ABO hemolytic transfusion reaction.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man with celiac disease and recurrent sinusitis is receiving a unit of packed red blood cells for symptomatic anemia from a bleeding duodenal ulcer. Within 3 minutes of starting the transfusion he becomes short of breath with audible wheezing, facial swelling and generalized hives. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 130/min and blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Bacterial endotoxin in the transfused unit

options.label: C
options.html: Hemolysis of donor red cells by anti-A antibodies

options.label: D
options.html: Hydrostatic pulmonary edema from volume overload

items.explanationHtml:
Bronchospasm, angioedema, urticaria and hypotension within minutes, without fever, is anaphylaxis. Selective IgA deficiency is associated with celiac disease and recurrent sinopulmonary infections. Some IgA-deficient people form anti-IgA antibodies that react with IgA in the small amount of plasma left in a red cell unit, triggering mast cell activation and complement. Future transfusions should use washed cellular products or products from IgA-deficient donors.

Takeaway: anaphylaxis at the start of a transfusion in a patient with IgA deficiency is caused by recipient anti-IgA antibodies.

whyNot.A: Septic reactions cause high fever, rigors and hypotension, not wheezing, angioedema and hives without fever.
whyNot.B: Donor anti-neutrophil antibodies cause TRALI, with hypoxemia and infiltrates, usually with fever and without urticaria.
whyNot.C: ABO hemolysis causes fever, back pain and hemoglobinuria rather than urticaria and bronchospasm.
whyNot.D: Volume overload develops over hours, with hypertension and raised jugular venous pressure, not within 3 minutes with hypotension.

items.objective: Identify anti-IgA antibodies in IgA deficiency as the cause of transfusion-associated anaphylaxis.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, received 2 units of packed red blood cells for postpartum hemorrhage. Her antibody screen before transfusion was negative. Nine days later she comes to the physician because of fatigue and yellow eyes. Hemoglobin is 7.4 g/dL (9.8 g/dL the day after transfusion), total bilirubin is 3.6 mg/dL, direct bilirubin is 0.4 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase is elevated and haptoglobin is low. Urine is negative for blood. The direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG and negative for C3. The antibody screen is now positive, and anti-Jka is identified. Which of the following best explains her anemia?
items.explanationHtml:
This is a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction. Earlier pregnancies sensitized her to the Kidd antigen Jka, but the antibody had fallen below detectable levels, so the pretransfusion screen was negative. The transfused Jka-positive cells triggered a secondary (memory) IgG response within days. IgG-coated cells are removed by splenic macrophages, giving extravascular hemolysis: falling hemoglobin, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, a positive IgG DAT and no hemoglobinuria. She should carry an antibody card and receive Jka-negative blood in the future.

Takeaway: hemolysis 3–14 days after transfusion with a new alloantibody (often Kidd) is an anamnestic IgG response.

whyNot.B: Septic reactions appear during or shortly after transfusion with fever and shock, not 9 days later with a new antibody.
whyNot.C: Microangiopathic hemolysis gives schistocytes and a negative DAT.
whyNot.D: Preformed IgM anti-A or anti-B causes immediate intravascular hemolysis, and the antibody here is an IgG alloantibody to Jk<sup>a</sup>.
whyNot.E: Warm autoimmune hemolysis involves an autoantibody against the patient's own cells, not a specific alloantibody that appeared after transfusion.

items.objective: Explain a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction as an anamnestic IgG alloantibody response.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man with chronic lymphocytic leukemia completed treatment with fludarabine-based chemotherapy 2 months ago. Twelve days ago he received 2 units of nonirradiated packed red blood cells. He now has fever, an erythematous maculopapular rash on his palms and trunk, and profuse watery diarrhea. Serum ALT is 210 U/L. Hemoglobin is 7.0 g/dL, leukocyte count is 600/mm3 and platelet count is 9,000/mm3. Bone marrow biopsy shows marked hypocellularity with lymphocytic infiltrates. Which of the following processing steps for the transfused units would most likely have prevented this condition?
items.explanationHtml:
Rash, diarrhea, hepatitis and pancytopenia from marrow aplasia 1–2 weeks after transfusion in a patient treated with a purine analogue is transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease. Viable donor T cells engraft because the recipient's cellular immunity cannot eliminate them, then attack host tissues, including hematopoietic cells (unlike GVHD after stem cell transplant, where the marrow is donor-derived). It is usually fatal. Irradiation of cellular products damages lymphocyte DNA and prevents their proliferation; fludarabine and other purine analogues are an indication for irradiated products.

Takeaway: irradiate cellular blood products for profoundly immunosuppressed recipients to prevent TA-GVHD.

whyNot.A: CMV-safe products prevent CMV infection, which does not cause this rash-diarrhea-aplasia syndrome after transfusion.
whyNot.C: Leukoreduction lowers but does not reliably remove enough lymphocytes to prevent TA-GVHD.
whyNot.D: Volume reduction lowers plasma volume to limit overload; it leaves lymphocytes in the product.
whyNot.E: Washing removes plasma proteins (useful for allergic or anti-IgA reactions) but not viable T cells.

items.objective: Identify irradiation as the product modification that prevents transfusion-associated GVHD.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman undergoing liver resection receives 2 units of fresh frozen plasma for intraoperative bleeding. Ninety minutes later in the recovery room she has dyspnea; oxygen saturation is 82% on 6 L/min of oxygen. Temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 118/min and blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg. Jugular venous pressure is not elevated, and crackles are heard throughout both lungs. Chest x-ray shows new bilateral diffuse infiltrates with a normal heart size. Echocardiography shows normal left ventricular function, and BNP is 60 pg/mL. The leukocyte count has fallen from 9,800/mm3 to 3,100/mm3. One plasma donor is a woman with four previous pregnancies. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Hydrostatic overload of the pulmonary circulation

options.label: E
options.html: Transmission of bacteria in the unit

items.explanationHtml:
Hypoxemia and bilateral infiltrates within 6 hours of a plasma-rich product, with fever, hypotension, transient leukopenia and no evidence of volume overload (normal JVP, BNP and heart function), is transfusion-related acute lung injury. Antibodies against HLA or human neutrophil antigens, common in donors sensitized by pregnancy, bind recipient neutrophils that have been primed in the lung by surgery or illness. Activated neutrophils damage the capillary endothelium, causing noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. Treatment is supportive; diuretics do not help.

Takeaway: TRALI = donor anti-leukocyte antibodies + primed recipient neutrophils = noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.

whyNot.A: Hydrostatic overload (TACO) causes hypertension, raised jugular venous pressure and a high BNP.
whyNot.B: IgE-mediated reactions cause urticaria, bronchospasm and angioedema without bilateral infiltrates and leukopenia.
whyNot.D: Anti-IgA anaphylaxis begins within minutes with urticaria and bronchospasm, not 90 minutes later with lung infiltrates.
whyNot.E: Bacterial contamination causes rigors and shock but not isolated noncardiogenic pulmonary edema with a donor history pointing to alloantibodies.

items.objective: Explain the immune mechanism of TRALI and distinguish it from circulatory overload.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old man with a gunshot wound to the abdomen undergoes emergency laparotomy. Over 3 hours he receives 14 units of packed red blood cells, 12 units of plasma and 2 units of apheresis platelets. Bleeding is now controlled, but his blood pressure remains low despite the transfusions, and the ECG shows a QTc of 520 ms. Serum ionized calcium is 0.70 mmol/L (N = 1.12–1.32), potassium is 4.8 mEq/L and magnesium is 1.6 mEq/L. Which of the following constituents of the transfused products most likely caused the calcium abnormality?
items.explanationHtml:
Blood products are anticoagulated with citrate, which chelates ionized calcium. The liver normally metabolizes citrate within minutes, but massive transfusion, shock, hypothermia and liver hypoperfusion overwhelm this. Low ionized calcium reduces myocardial contractility and vascular tone, prolongs the QT interval and impairs coagulation. Ionized calcium should be monitored and replaced during massive transfusion.

Takeaway: citrate in stored blood causes hypocalcemia during massive transfusion.

whyNot.A: Adenine supports red cell ATP during storage; it does not bind calcium.
whyNot.C: Dextrose is a red cell energy source in storage solutions and does not affect calcium.
whyNot.D: Mannitol stabilizes red cell membranes in storage; it has no calcium-binding effect.
whyNot.E: Sodium chloride in additive solution is osmotically neutral and does not lower ionized calcium.

items.objective: Explain citrate-induced hypocalcemia during massive transfusion.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman with acute myeloid leukemia receiving induction chemotherapy is given a unit of apheresis platelets that was collected 5 days earlier. Twenty minutes into the transfusion she has shaking chills. Temperature is 40.1 °C (104.2 °F) (37.2 °C before the transfusion), pulse is 132/min and blood pressure is 78/40 mm Hg. There is no rash or wheezing. A Gram stain of the residual product shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which of the following properties of this blood component most increases the risk of this complication compared with red cell units?
items.explanationHtml:
High fever, rigors and hypotension during a platelet transfusion, with organisms in the bag, is a septic transfusion reaction. Platelets must be stored at 20–24 °C with agitation to remain functional, and bacteria introduced at collection (usually skin flora such as staphylococci) multiply at that temperature. Red cells are refrigerated at 1–6 °C, which inhibits most bacteria except cold-tolerant organisms such as Yersinia enterocolitica. Bacterial testing and pathogen-reduction methods reduce this risk.

Takeaway: room-temperature storage makes platelets the blood component most often contaminated with bacteria.

whyNot.A: Apheresis collection from one donor lowers donor exposure and does not increase bacterial growth.
whyNot.B: Donor leukocytes cause febrile non-hemolytic reactions, not bacteremia with organisms seen in the product.
whyNot.C: Plasma content relates to allergic reactions and TRALI rather than bacterial proliferation.
whyNot.E: Citrate is used in all components and does not support bacterial growth.

items.objective: Explain why platelet products carry the highest risk of septic transfusion reactions.

items.stemHtml:
A 58-year-old woman with stage 5 chronic kidney disease not yet on dialysis had a tunneled hemodialysis catheter placed in the right internal jugular vein 2 hours ago. The insertion site continues to ooze blood despite 20 minutes of firm manual pressure. She takes no antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs. Pulse is 88/min and blood pressure is 142/84 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show:

TestResult
Hemoglobin8.6 g/dL
Platelet count210,000/mm3
PT / INR13 s / 1.0
aPTT32 s
Fibrinogen330 mg/dL (N = 200–400)
Urea nitrogen118 mg/dL
Creatinine8.9 mg/dL

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Persistent oozing with normal platelet count, PT, aPTT and fibrinogen in advanced uremia indicates uremic platelet dysfunction. Desmopressin releases von Willebrand factor and factor VIII from endothelial stores and improves platelet adhesion within about an hour; it is the first choice for active bleeding or before an urgent procedure. Longer-term measures include starting dialysis, correcting anemia and, for recurrent bleeding, conjugated estrogens.

Takeaway: for acute uremic bleeding, give desmopressin; dialysis and anemia correction improve platelet function over time.

whyNot.A: Cryoprecipitate is a second-line option for uremic bleeding when desmopressin fails; it is not the first step.
whyNot.C: Plasma corrects factor deficiencies, but her PT and aPTT are normal.
whyNot.D: Transfused platelets quickly acquire the uremic defect, and her count is normal.
whyNot.E: Vitamin K corrects a prolonged PT from deficiency; her PT is normal.

items.objective: Treat uremic platelet dysfunction bleeding with desmopressin.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy with severe hemophilia A (factor VIII activity below 1%) is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after falling off his bicycle. He receives factor VIII prophylaxis three times weekly; his last dose was 2 days ago. An inhibitor screen 3 months ago was negative. His right knee is painful, warm and swollen, and he holds it in flexion and refuses to bear weight. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F). There is no head injury. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
An acute hemarthrosis in severe hemophilia A is treated at once with factor VIII concentrate to a level that stops the bleeding, followed by rest, ice, compression, elevation and later physiotherapy. Treatment should not wait for imaging or other tests; rapid replacement limits pain, synovial damage and the long-term risk of hemophilic arthropathy.

Takeaway: in hemophilia, give the missing factor first and investigate later.

whyNot.A: Arthrocentesis is rarely needed and would increase bleeding before factor replacement.
whyNot.C: Plasma contains too little factor VIII per volume to reach hemostatic levels and carries volume and transfusion risks; concentrate is available.
whyNot.D: Desmopressin raises factor VIII only in mild hemophilia A; in severe disease there are no stores to release.
whyNot.E: Imaging is not needed to diagnose a typical hemarthrosis and would delay replacement.

items.objective: Treat an acute hemarthrosis in severe hemophilia A with immediate factor VIII replacement.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy with severe hemophilia A is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after falling from a playground slide. He is treated with recombinant factor VIII when bleeding occurs, and over the past 2 months his bleeds have needed more doses than before to stop. His left thigh is tense, swollen and tender. Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL (11.0 g/dL 1 month ago). One hour after a standard dose of factor VIII the swelling is still enlarging. The aPTT is 92 s and does not correct after 1:1 mixing with normal plasma. The inhibitor titer is 18 Bethesda units. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy at this time?
items.explanationHtml:
Declining response to factor VIII, an aPTT that fails to correct on mixing and a Bethesda titer of 18 indicate a high-titer inhibitor (alloantibody against factor VIII). Infused factor VIII is neutralized, so serious bleeding is treated with a bypassing agent: recombinant activated factor VII or activated prothrombin complex concentrate, which generate thrombin without factor VIII. Later management includes immune tolerance induction and prophylaxis that does not depend on factor VIII.

Takeaway: hemophilia with a high-titer inhibitor and active bleeding needs a bypassing agent, not more factor VIII.

whyNot.A: Cryoprecipitate contains factor VIII, which the inhibitor will neutralize.
whyNot.B: Desmopressin is ineffective in severe hemophilia A and would release factor VIII that the inhibitor inactivates.
whyNot.C: Plasma supplies little factor VIII and is neutralized by the inhibitor.
whyNot.E: Standard doses are overwhelmed by a high-titer inhibitor, as the enlarging hematoma shows.

items.objective: Treat bleeding in hemophilia A with a high-titer inhibitor using a bypassing agent.

items.stemHtml: A 6-week-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of vomiting and increasing sleepiness for 12 hours. He was born at home at term, and his parents declined all injections after birth. He is exclusively breastfed and has gained weight appropriately. He is lethargic, and the anterior fontanelle is bulging. There are no other bruises or injuries. CT of the head shows an acute subdural hemorrhage. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL and platelet count is 310,000/mm3. INR is 6.8 and aPTT is 88 s. Neurosurgery is consulted. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
An exclusively breastfed infant who did not receive vitamin K prophylaxis, presenting at 2–12 weeks with intracranial hemorrhage, a markedly prolonged INR and aPTT and a normal platelet count, has late vitamin K deficiency bleeding. Give vitamin K parenterally at once; for life-threatening bleeding, also give prothrombin complex concentrate or plasma for immediate correction. Look for underlying cholestasis or malabsorption. A coagulopathy does not end the evaluation for abusive head trauma when the history or examination is concerning.

Takeaway: late vitamin K deficiency bleeding presents as intracranial hemorrhage in unprophylaxed breastfed infants; treat with vitamin K plus rapid factor replacement.

whyNot.A: Desmopressin releases von Willebrand factor and factor VIII, which are not the deficient factors.
whyNot.B: Hemophilia A prolongs the aPTT but not the INR.
whyNot.C: IVIG treats immune thrombocytopenia; the platelet count is normal.
whyNot.D: Platelets are normal; the defect is a lack of functional vitamin K-dependent factors.

items.objective: Treat late vitamin K deficiency bleeding in an infant who missed prophylaxis.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old woman is in the intensive care unit with septic shock from acute cholangitis. Biliary drainage by ERCP was performed 6 hours ago, and she is receiving piperacillin-tazobactam and norepinephrine. She is now oozing blood from her arterial line and venipuncture sites, and there is fresh blood in her nasogastric aspirate. After 2 units of fresh frozen plasma, laboratory studies show platelet count 64,000/mm3, INR 1.8, aPTT 45 s, fibrinogen 80 mg/dL (N = 200–400) and markedly elevated D-dimer. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
She has bleeding with DIC from sepsis. The trigger is being treated (drainage, antibiotics). Blood products are given for bleeding guided by the abnormality: fibrinogen remains far below about 150 mg/dL despite plasma, so cryoprecipitate (or fibrinogen concentrate) is the next step. Her platelet count is above 50,000/mm3, so platelets are not the priority.

Takeaway: in bleeding DIC, replace fibrinogen with cryoprecipitate when it stays below about 150 mg/dL.

whyNot.B: Heparin is reserved for DIC with predominant thrombosis, not active bleeding.
whyNot.C: Platelet transfusion in bleeding DIC is aimed at counts below about 50,000/mm<sup>3</sup>.
whyNot.D: Recombinant VIIa is not recommended in DIC and may increase thrombosis.
whyNot.E: Antifibrinolytics are generally avoided in DIC because they can worsen microvascular thrombosis.

items.objective: Choose cryoprecipitate for bleeding DIC with persistent hypofibrinogenemia.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man with cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C comes to the clinic because of increasing abdominal distention over 3 weeks. He has no fever or abdominal pain and no history of bleeding. Examination shows tense ascites without tenderness. A diagnostic and large-volume paracentesis is planned. Hemoglobin is 11.2 g/dL, platelet count is 48,000/mm3 and INR is 2.0. Which of the following is the most appropriate management before the procedure?
items.explanationHtml:
Paracentesis is a low-bleeding-risk procedure. In cirrhosis, reduced procoagulants are balanced by reduced natural anticoagulants, so the INR and platelet count do not predict procedural bleeding. Prophylactic plasma or platelets are not recommended: they rarely normalize the tests, delay the procedure, add volume (which can raise portal pressure) and carry TACO, TRALI and allergic risks.

Takeaway: do not correct the INR or platelet count before paracentesis in cirrhosis.

whyNot.A: Cryoprecipitate replaces fibrinogen and is not indicated without bleeding or known hypofibrinogenemia.
whyNot.B: Desmopressin has no proven benefit for procedural bleeding in cirrhosis and can cause hyponatremia.
whyNot.C: Plasma does not reduce bleeding after paracentesis and adds volume and transfusion risk.
whyNot.E: Prophylactic platelets are not needed for a low-risk procedure such as paracentesis.

items.objective: Avoid prophylactic blood products before paracentesis in cirrhosis despite an elevated INR.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old widower is brought to the clinic by his daughter because of bleeding gums and a painful, swollen left knee. He lives alone, and for the past year he has eaten mainly toast, tea and canned soup. Examination shows swollen, purple gums that bleed easily, small hemorrhages around hair follicles on his thighs with coiled hairs, ecchymoses on the backs of both legs and a left knee effusion. Hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL, MCV 84 fL, platelet count 280,000/mm3, and PT and aPTT are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, gum disease, ecchymoses and hemarthrosis with normal platelets and coagulation tests in an older adult with a diet lacking fruit and vegetables indicate scurvy. Vitamin C is required for hydroxylation of collagen, and deficient collagen makes vessel walls fragile. Oral vitamin C stops bleeding within days; treatment should begin on clinical suspicion, with dietary counselling and a search for other deficiencies and for depression or social isolation.

Takeaway: bleeding with normal coagulation tests and perifollicular hemorrhages suggests vitamin C deficiency.

whyNot.B: B<sub>12</sub> deficiency causes macrocytic anemia and neuropathy, not perifollicular hemorrhage and hemarthrosis.
whyNot.C: Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anemia; the MCV here is normal and the bleeding pattern is vascular.
whyNot.D: Vitamin K deficiency would prolong the PT, which is normal.
whyNot.E: Thiamine deficiency causes neuropathy, Wernicke encephalopathy or heart failure, not bleeding.

items.objective: Diagnose and treat scurvy as a cause of bleeding with normal coagulation tests.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of progressive swelling and aching of his entire left leg for 4 days. He has had no recent surgery, travel, immobilization or injury, and he has no history of cancer; age-appropriate cancer screening is up to date. He takes no medications. Pulse is 84/min, respirations are 14/min, blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. The whole left leg is swollen, the left calf circumference is 4 cm greater than the right, there is pitting edema confined to the left leg, and there is tenderness along the medial thigh. No alternative diagnosis seems likely. Imaging is available in the department around the clock. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
His Wells score is 4 (whole leg swollen, calf asymmetry over 3 cm, unilateral pitting edema, tenderness along the deep veins), so DVT is likely. With high pretest probability, go directly to compression ultrasonography. A negative D-dimer would not safely exclude DVT at this probability, and a positive one would not confirm it.

Takeaway: DVT likely by Wells → ultrasound; DVT unlikely → D-dimer first.

whyNot.B: Contrast venography is invasive and has been replaced by ultrasound as the first imaging test.
whyNot.C: He has no chest symptoms, tachycardia or hypoxemia to justify CT pulmonary angiography.
whyNot.D: D-dimer is used to exclude DVT in low-probability patients; in high-probability patients it cannot exclude it.
whyNot.E: Thrombophilia testing does not diagnose an acute DVT and is unreliable during acute thrombosis.

items.objective: Choose compression ultrasonography when DVT is likely by pretest probability.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man has had swelling of his entire left leg for 4 days without any provoking factor. Compression ultrasonography shows occlusive thrombus in the left common femoral and popliteal veins. He has no chest pain or dyspnea, and vital signs are normal. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, liver function tests are normal and platelet count is 250,000/mm3. He has no history of bleeding and takes no medications. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
For proximal DVT in a patient without cancer, pregnancy, severe renal impairment, antiphospholipid syndrome or a mechanical valve, a direct oral anticoagulant is preferred over warfarin: it is at least as effective, causes less major bleeding and needs no INR monitoring. Apixaban and rivaroxaban can be started without parenteral heparin, using a higher dose for the first days.

Takeaway: a DOAC is first-line for most patients with acute DVT.

whyNot.B: Aspirin is much less effective than anticoagulation for treating acute DVT.
whyNot.C: Thrombolysis is reserved for limb-threatening thrombosis (phlegmasia), not uncomplicated femoropopliteal DVT.
whyNot.D: An IVC filter is indicated only when anticoagulation is contraindicated.
whyNot.E: Warfarin alone takes days to work and initially lowers protein C; it needs at least 5 days of heparin overlap.

items.objective: Select a direct oral anticoagulant as first-line treatment for uncomplicated proximal DVT.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man has taken apixaban for 3 months for a first unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis of the left leg. His leg swelling has resolved, and he has had no bleeding. No provoking factor has been identified, and age-appropriate cancer screening is normal. He has one or two alcoholic drinks a month, takes no other medications and has normal kidney function and hemoglobin. He asks how long he should continue the medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue for 3 more months, then stop

options.label: E
options.html: Stop now if thrombophilia tests are negative

items.explanationHtml:
After a first unprovoked proximal DVT or PE, the risk of recurrence after stopping anticoagulation is high (roughly 10% in the first year and about 30% at 5 years) and does not fall by treating longer before stopping. For patients without a high bleeding risk, guidelines favour extended anticoagulation with no planned stop date, reassessed at least yearly; reduced-dose apixaban or rivaroxaban is an option in this phase.

Takeaway: unprovoked proximal VTE with low bleeding risk → extended anticoagulation; provoked by a major transient factor → 3 months.

whyNot.A: A fixed 6-month course only delays recurrence; it does not lower the risk once treatment stops.
whyNot.C: Stopping at 3 months is appropriate for VTE provoked by a major transient risk factor, not for unprovoked VTE.
whyNot.D: Aspirin lowers recurrence far less than anticoagulation and is reserved for patients who decline or cannot take an anticoagulant.
whyNot.E: A negative inherited thrombophilia panel does not make an unprovoked event low-risk, so testing should not decide duration.

items.objective: Recommend extended-duration anticoagulation after a first unprovoked proximal DVT with low bleeding risk.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old man comes to the urgent care clinic because of mild aching and fullness in his right calf for 2 days. Four days ago he drove for 7 hours. He has no history of cancer, surgery, immobilization or thrombosis, and he takes no medications. Vital signs are normal. The right calf circumference is 1.5 cm greater than the left. There is no pitting edema, no tenderness along the deep veins and no superficial venous dilation. Pretest probability of deep vein thrombosis is assessed as low. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
items.explanationHtml:
His Wells score is 0, so DVT is unlikely. The next step is a high-sensitivity D-dimer: a negative result excludes DVT without imaging, and only a positive result leads to compression ultrasonography. This sequence avoids unnecessary imaging and false-positive findings.

Takeaway: low pretest probability of DVT → D-dimer first; negative D-dimer ends the workup.

whyNot.A: Ultrasound is the first test when DVT is likely; in low-probability patients it follows a positive D-dimer.
whyNot.B: Contrast venography is invasive and no longer a first-line test.
whyNot.C: CT venography is reserved for suspected pelvic or caval thrombosis and adds contrast and radiation.
whyNot.E: Anticoagulation without a diagnosis is not justified at low pretest probability.

items.objective: Use a D-dimer as the first test when pretest probability of DVT is low.

items.stemHtml:
A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 16 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of swelling and pain in her left leg for 3 days. Compression ultrasonography shows a thrombus in the left femoral vein. She has no history of thrombosis and no chest symptoms. Laboratory studies show:

TestResult
Hemoglobin11.4 g/dL
Platelet count228,000/mm3
PT12 s
aPTT30 s
Creatinine0.6 mg/dL
ALT18 U/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate anticoagulant?
items.explanationHtml:
Low-molecular-weight heparin is the anticoagulant of choice for VTE in pregnancy: it does not cross the placenta, has predictable dosing and a lower risk of HIT and osteoporosis than unfractionated heparin. It is continued through pregnancy and for at least 6 weeks postpartum (minimum total 3 months), with a plan to stop it before delivery or neuraxial anesthesia.

Takeaway: treat VTE in pregnancy with LMWH; avoid warfarin and DOACs.

whyNot.A: Direct oral anticoagulants cross the placenta and lack safety data in pregnancy.
whyNot.C: Fondaparinux is a second-line option, used mainly with heparin allergy or HIT.
whyNot.D: Rivaroxaban, like other DOACs, is avoided in pregnancy.
whyNot.E: Warfarin crosses the placenta and causes embryopathy and fetal bleeding.

items.objective: Choose low-molecular-weight heparin to treat VTE during pregnancy.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man underwent mitral valve replacement with a bileaflet mechanical prosthesis for rheumatic mitral stenosis 4 days ago. He is in sinus rhythm and is receiving an intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion. Creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL. Before discharge he asks to take "one of the newer blood thinners that doesn't need blood tests." Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term oral antithrombotic therapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Patients with mechanical heart valves require a vitamin K antagonist. Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated: in a randomized trial dabigatran caused more valve thrombosis, stroke and bleeding than warfarin, and a factor Xa inhibitor trial in mechanical aortic valves was stopped early for excess events. Mechanical mitral valves need a higher INR target than mechanical aortic valves. Explain to the patient why the newer drugs are unsafe for him.

Takeaway: mechanical valve → warfarin; DOACs are contraindicated.

whyNot.A: Apixaban has not been shown to be safe with mechanical valves and is not recommended.
whyNot.B: Aspirin alone does not prevent valve thrombosis and embolism.
whyNot.C: Dabigatran increased thrombotic and bleeding events with mechanical valves.
whyNot.D: Rivaroxaban, like other DOACs, is contraindicated with mechanical valves.

items.objective: Select warfarin over DOACs for anticoagulation with a mechanical heart valve.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman is diagnosed with a right popliteal deep vein thrombosis 2 weeks after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, which was followed by 3 weeks of limited mobility in a brace. She has no previous thrombosis, and no relatives have had thrombosis. She is started on rivaroxaban, and a 3-month course is planned. She has read about "clotting genes" and asks whether she should be tested. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step regarding thrombophilia testing?

options.label: B
options.html: Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene testing

options.label: C
options.html: Full thrombophilia panel after anticoagulation ends

options.label: E
options.html: Protein C, protein S and antithrombin levels now

items.explanationHtml:
Her DVT was provoked by a major transient risk factor (surgery with immobility), so 3 months of anticoagulation is appropriate whatever a thrombophilia test shows. Testing would not change her treatment, may cause anxiety or false reassurance, and has implications for insurance and family members. Explain this to her; reconsider only if circumstances change (for example, an unprovoked recurrence or plans that would be affected by a result).

Takeaway: do not test for thrombophilia after VTE provoked by surgery; results will not change management.

whyNot.A: Antiphospholipid testing matters after unprovoked or unusual thrombosis, arterial events or pregnancy morbidity, none of which apply; DOACs also interfere with lupus anticoagulant assays.
whyNot.B: Genetic testing would not change the duration or choice of anticoagulation after a surgically provoked DVT.
whyNot.C: Delaying testing avoids interference but does not make an unnecessary test useful.
whyNot.E: Functional levels fall during acute thrombosis and are affected by anticoagulants, and testing is not indicated anyway.

items.objective: Avoid thrombophilia testing after VTE provoked by a major transient risk factor.

items.stemHtml: Based on the study summary, approximately how many patients need to be treated with drug Q for 12 months to prevent one recurrent VTE?
items.explanationHtml:
Absolute risk reduction = 7.8% − 1.8% = 6.0% = 0.060. Number needed to treat = 1 / 0.060 ≈ 16.7, rounded up to 17. Rounding up is conventional so that at least one event is prevented.

Takeaway: NNT = 1 / absolute risk reduction, rounded up.

whyNot.A: 6 is the absolute risk reduction expressed in percentage points, not the NNT.
whyNot.B: 13 is the reciprocal of the placebo event rate alone (1 / 0.078), which ignores the treated group.
whyNot.D: 56 is the reciprocal of the drug Q event rate (1 / 0.018).
whyNot.E: 167 would correspond to an absolute risk reduction of 0.6 percentage points, a decimal error.

items.objective: Calculate the number needed to treat from event rates in a trial of extended anticoagulation.

items.stemHtml: A physician is deciding whether to apply the results of this study to patients in her practice. To which of the following patients do the results most directly apply?

options.label: A
options.html: A 38-year-old woman who had a PE while taking an estrogen-containing contraceptive

options.label: B
options.html: A 50-year-old man who completed 6 months of treatment for a first unprovoked PE

options.label: C
options.html: A 57-year-old woman with metastatic colon cancer and a femoral DVT

options.label: D
options.html: A 62-year-old man with DVT and persistent triple-positive antiphospholipid antibodies

options.label: E
options.html: A 70-year-old man with a first unprovoked DVT and creatinine clearance of 22 mL/min

items.explanationHtml:
Results apply most directly to patients who resemble the enrolled population (external validity). The trial enrolled adults with a first unprovoked proximal DVT or PE after 6–12 months of initial anticoagulation and excluded active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome and severe renal impairment. The 50-year-old man matches these criteria. For him, the trial suggests extended reduced-dose therapy substantially lowers recurrence without a clear rise in major bleeding, though the trial was not powered to exclude a small bleeding difference.

Takeaway: apply trial results to patients who meet the trial's inclusion and exclusion criteria.

whyNot.A: A VTE associated with estrogen is provoked by a minor transient risk factor, so she does not meet the unprovoked inclusion criterion.
whyNot.C: Active cancer was an exclusion criterion, and cancer-associated VTE has different recurrence and bleeding risks.
whyNot.D: Antiphospholipid syndrome was excluded; warfarin is preferred in triple-positive patients.
whyNot.E: Creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min was an exclusion criterion, and drug exposure and bleeding risk differ in severe renal impairment.

items.objective: Judge the external validity of a trial by comparing a patient with its enrollment criteria.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman with myelodysplastic syndrome is receiving her second unit of packed red blood cells in an outpatient infusion center. Forty minutes into the unit she develops itchy, raised wheals on her chest and arms. The transfusion is paused. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg (130/78 mm Hg before the transfusion) and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. There is no wheezing, stridor, lip or tongue swelling, or dyspnea. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Antihistamine and resume the unit once hives resolve

options.label: B
options.html: Discard the unit and transfuse washed cells

options.label: E
options.html: Return the unit for a hemolysis workup

items.explanationHtml:
Isolated urticaria with normal vital signs and no respiratory or mucosal involvement is a mild allergic (urticarial) reaction, caused by recipient IgE against donor plasma proteins. It is the one reaction in which the transfusion may be restarted: pause, give an antihistamine, and resume the same unit slowly once symptoms resolve, with close observation. Any fever, hypotension, dyspnea or angioedema changes this to a stop-and-investigate reaction.

Takeaway: hives alone → pause, antihistamine, resume; anything more → stop.

whyNot.B: Washed products are reserved for recurrent severe allergic or anaphylactic reactions, not a first mild urticarial episode.
whyNot.C: Epinephrine treats anaphylaxis, which requires hypotension, airway or mucosal involvement.
whyNot.D: Furosemide treats circulatory overload, which presents with dyspnea, hypertension and raised venous pressure.
whyNot.E: Hemolysis causes fever, pain, hypotension or dark urine; isolated hives do not require a hemolysis workup.

items.objective: Manage a mild urticarial transfusion reaction by pausing, giving an antihistamine and resuming.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old woman with heart failure (ejection fraction 30%) and chronic kidney disease is admitted with fatigue and exertional chest tightness. Hemoglobin is 6.4 g/dL due to slow gastrointestinal blood loss. She receives 2 units of packed red blood cells, each over 1 hour. One hour after the second unit she becomes acutely short of breath and cannot lie flat. Temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 28/min, blood pressure is 176/94 mm Hg (132/70 mm Hg before transfusion) and oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. Jugular venous pressure is 10 cm H2O, and there are crackles at both lung bases and an S3. Chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly, vascular redistribution and small bilateral effusions. BNP is 1,450 pg/mL (420 pg/mL on admission). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Dyspnea, hypertension, raised jugular venous pressure, an S3, radiographic congestion and a sharp rise in BNP within hours of transfusion in an older adult with heart failure and kidney disease is transfusion-associated circulatory overload. Treatment is to stop any ongoing transfusion, sit the patient upright, give oxygen and give an IV loop diuretic. Prevention: transfuse one unit at a time, slowly, with diuretic planning in high-risk patients.

Takeaway: TACO (hypertension, high BNP, congestion) responds to diuretics; TRALI (hypotension, normal filling pressures) does not.

whyNot.A: Epinephrine treats anaphylaxis, which causes hypotension and urticaria, not hypertension with congestion.
whyNot.B: Antihistamines treat urticarial reactions and do not relieve pulmonary edema from volume overload.
whyNot.D: Glucocorticoids have no role in hydrostatic pulmonary edema.
whyNot.E: More fluid would worsen circulatory overload.

items.objective: Recognize and treat transfusion-associated circulatory overload in an older adult with heart failure.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man is on the surgical ward 1 day after a colectomy for colon cancer. Fifteen minutes after a unit of packed red blood cells is started, he reports chills, nausea and pain in his lower back. Temperature is 38.8 °C (101.8 °F) (37.0 °C before the transfusion), pulse is 118/min and blood pressure is 92/58 mm Hg (124/80 mm Hg before). The urine in his catheter bag has become reddish. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Fever, chills, back pain, hypotension and hemoglobinuria within minutes of starting red cells suggest an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, most often from an ABO identification error. The severity depends on the volume of incompatible blood given, so the first step is to stop the transfusion immediately, keep the IV open with saline, recheck the patient's identity against the unit, notify the blood bank and send the unit and new samples (DAT, repeat type and crossmatch, hemolysis tests, cultures). Then give fluids to maintain urine output and treat shock and DIC.

Takeaway: for any serious transfusion reaction, stop the transfusion first.

whyNot.A: Slowing the infusion still delivers incompatible blood; fever with hypotension is not managed as a febrile non-hemolytic reaction.
whyNot.B: Antihistamines treat urticaria and do nothing for hemolysis.
whyNot.C: Cultures are part of the workup, but continuing the transfusion while drawing them adds incompatible blood.
whyNot.D: Furosemide treats overload, and continuing the unit would worsen hemolysis.

items.objective: Stop the transfusion immediately when an acute hemolytic reaction is suspected.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after being stabbed in the left upper abdomen. He received 1 L of crystalloid during transport. Pulse is 136/min and blood pressure is 78/44 mm Hg. Focused assessment with sonography for trauma shows free fluid in the left upper quadrant and pelvis. He has no head injury. The massive transfusion protocol is activated, and he is being taken to the operating room for laparotomy. Which of the following is the most appropriate resuscitation strategy until bleeding is controlled?

options.label: A
options.html: Crystalloid boluses to a systolic pressure of 120 mm Hg

options.label: B
options.html: Plasma, platelets and red cells in about a 1:1:1 ratio

options.label: C
options.html: Red cells alone until coagulation results return

options.label: D
options.html: Red cells and plasma in a 4:1 ratio

items.explanationHtml:
Hemorrhagic shock from penetrating trauma calls for damage control resuscitation: rapid surgical control, minimal crystalloid, permissive hypotension (systolic around 80–90 mm Hg until bleeding is controlled, in the absence of brain injury) and early balanced transfusion with plasma, platelets and red cells in roughly a 1:1:1 ratio (or whole blood). Tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury reduces bleeding deaths, and ionized calcium is monitored and replaced.

Takeaway: in massive hemorrhage, give products in a balanced ratio early and limit crystalloid.

whyNot.A: Large crystalloid volumes dilute clotting factors, worsen acidosis and hypothermia, and aiming for normal pressure before control increases bleeding.
whyNot.C: Red cells alone cause dilutional coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia; waiting for laboratory results delays correction.
whyNot.D: A high red cell to plasma ratio was associated with worse outcomes than balanced resuscitation.
whyNot.E: Vasopressors do not replace lost volume and are not first-line in hemorrhagic shock.

items.objective: Apply balanced 1:1:1 blood product resuscitation in traumatic hemorrhagic shock.

items.stemHtml:
A 36-year-old woman had a massive postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony after a vaginal delivery. Over 2 hours she received 10 units of packed red blood cells, 8 units of plasma, 1 unit of apheresis platelets and 10 units of cryoprecipitate, and bleeding has now been controlled with an intrauterine balloon. She remains hypotensive at 82/50 mm Hg despite a norepinephrine infusion; pulse is 112/min. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QTc of 530 ms. Laboratory studies show:

TestResult
Hemoglobin8.2 g/dL
Platelet count82,000/mm3
INR1.4
Fibrinogen210 mg/dL (N = 200–400)
Potassium4.9 mEq/L
Calcium, ionized0.68 mmol/L (N = 1.12–1.32)
Magnesium1.6 mEq/L
Arterial pH7.29
Lactate3.4 mmol/L
Temperature36.4 °C

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
After massive transfusion, citrate in the products has lowered her ionized calcium to a dangerous level, which explains hypotension resistant to vasopressors (reduced contractility and vascular tone) and a long QTc; it also impairs coagulation. Give IV calcium (calcium chloride through a central line, or calcium gluconate) and recheck frequently. Other targets are acceptable: fibrinogen above 200 mg/dL, platelets above 50,000/mm3 and an INR of 1.4 with bleeding controlled.

Takeaway: check and replace ionized calcium during and after massive transfusion, especially with refractory hypotension.

whyNot.A: The INR and fibrinogen are acceptable and bleeding is controlled; more plasma adds volume without fixing the cause of hypotension.
whyNot.C: Potassium is 4.9 mEq/L, so treatment for hyperkalemia is not indicated.
whyNot.D: Mild lactic acidosis improves with perfusion; bicarbonate also lowers ionized calcium further.
whyNot.E: Adding a vasopressor does not address the hypocalcemia that is impairing contractility and vascular tone.

items.objective: Treat citrate-induced hypocalcemia after massive transfusion with intravenous calcium.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man with acute myeloid leukemia is on day 12 of induction chemotherapy. He feels tired but has no headache, fever, or gum, nose, urinary or stool bleeding. Examination shows a few petechiae on his ankles. Hemoglobin is 8.3 g/dL, absolute neutrophil count is 0/mm3 and platelet count is 7,000/mm3. No procedures are planned. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
For hospitalized adults with hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia from chemotherapy or marrow failure, prophylactic platelet transfusion is recommended when the count falls below 10,000/mm3, because this reduces spontaneous bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage. Higher thresholds apply for procedures (about 20,000/mm3 for a central line, 50,000/mm3 for lumbar puncture or major surgery) or active bleeding.

Takeaway: chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia below 10,000/mm3 → prophylactic platelets.

whyNot.A: IVIG is used for immune platelet destruction, not marrow failure from chemotherapy.
whyNot.B: Withholding platelets until bleeding begins increases the risk of serious hemorrhage at counts below 10,000/mm<sup>3</sup> in this setting.
whyNot.C: Plasma replaces clotting factors and does not raise the platelet count.
whyNot.E: Thrombopoietin receptor agonists act over days to weeks and are not used to prevent bleeding during AML induction.

items.objective: Apply the prophylactic platelet transfusion threshold in chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman is in the intensive care unit on day 4 of treatment for pneumonia with septic shock. Vasopressors were stopped yesterday, and she is now alert and breathing comfortably on 2 L/min of oxygen. She has no chest pain and no history of coronary artery disease. There is no evidence of bleeding. Pulse is 92/min and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. Hemoglobin is 7.4 g/dL (8.1 g/dL yesterday), and MCV is 88 fL. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of her anemia?
items.explanationHtml:
A restrictive transfusion strategy (threshold hemoglobin 7 g/dL) is as safe as a liberal one for hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults, including ICU patients with sepsis, and avoids transfusion risks. With a hemoglobin of 7.4 g/dL, no bleeding, no symptoms of inadequate oxygen delivery and no coronary disease, she should be monitored. When transfusion is indicated, a single unit is given and the patient reassessed.

Takeaway: stable inpatients without cardiovascular disease are transfused at hemoglobin below 7 g/dL, one unit at a time.

whyNot.A: Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents do not reduce transfusion meaningfully in acute critical illness and increase thrombotic risk.
whyNot.B: There is no evidence of iron deficiency; anemia of critical illness does not respond quickly to IV iron.
whyNot.D: Her hemoglobin is above the restrictive threshold of 7 g/dL and she is stable.
whyNot.E: Two units exceed the need even when transfusion is indicated; single-unit transfusion with reassessment is preferred.

items.objective: Apply a restrictive red cell transfusion threshold in a stable critically ill patient.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man with severe aplastic anemia is receiving a unit of apheresis platelets in the day hospital. Fifteen minutes after the start he has violent shaking chills. Temperature is 39.8 °C (103.6 °F) (37.0 °C before the transfusion), pulse is 128/min and blood pressure is 84/46 mm Hg. There is no urticaria, wheezing or facial swelling. The transfusion is stopped, normal saline is started, and the patient's identity matches the unit label. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
High fever, rigors and hypotension during a platelet transfusion strongly suggest a septic transfusion reaction; platelets are stored at room temperature and carry the highest risk of bacterial contamination. After stopping the transfusion, obtain blood cultures from the patient and culture the product bag, start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and resuscitate. Notify the blood bank so co-components from the same donation are quarantined. A hemolysis workup (DAT, hemolysis tests) is sent at the same time.

Takeaway: fever with hypotension during platelet transfusion → stop, culture patient and bag, start antibiotics.

whyNot.A: Fever with hypotension is not a febrile non-hemolytic reaction; observation delays treatment of possible sepsis.
whyNot.C: There are no allergic features, and restarting a possibly contaminated unit is dangerous.
whyNot.D: Epinephrine treats anaphylaxis, which lacks high fever and presents with urticaria, wheezing or angioedema.
whyNot.E: Furosemide treats circulatory overload, which causes hypertension rather than fever with hypotension.

items.objective: Manage a suspected septic transfusion reaction with cultures and empiric antibiotics.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of 3 months of fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Two years ago he underwent mechanical mitral valve replacement for rheumatic disease. He takes warfarin, and his INR has been in the target range. He has no melena or hematochezia, and fecal occult blood testing is negative twice. A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL, MCV 74 fL, reticulocytes 6%, LDH 820 U/L (reference 45-200), haptoglobin below 10 mg/dL (reference 30-200) and ferritin 9 ng/mL (reference 15-200). The direct antiglobulin test is negative. The smear shows microcytic red cells with helmet cells and triangular fragments. Which of the following best explains the low ferritin?

options.label: A
options.html: Chronic bleeding from the gastrointestinal tract

options.label: B
options.html: Decreased duodenal iron absorption caused by hepcidin

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of iron in the urine as hemoglobin and hemosiderin

options.label: E
options.html: Utilization of iron stores by an expanded erythroid marrow

items.explanationHtml:
A new regurgitant murmur with fragmentation hemolysis after mechanical valve replacement suggests a paravalvular leak. The hemolysis is intravascular: free hemoglobin saturates haptoglobin, is filtered by the glomerulus and is either lost as hemoglobin or taken up by proximal tubular cells, which are later shed as hemosiderin. Months of this drain iron stores, producing a superimposed iron deficiency with microcytosis.

Takeaway: chronic intravascular hemolysis, as with a leaking prosthetic valve, causes iron deficiency through hemoglobinuria and hemosiderinuria.

whyNot.A: Repeated negative fecal occult blood tests and no melena make gastrointestinal loss unlikely, even on warfarin.
whyNot.B: Hepcidin rises with inflammation and lowers absorption, but anemia of inflammation gives a normal or high ferritin, not 9 ng/mL.
whyNot.C: Macrophage iron sequestration raises ferritin; extravascular destruction also recycles iron rather than losing it.
whyNot.E: Erythroid expansion uses iron but recycles it from destroyed cells; it does not empty stores unless iron leaves the body.

items.objective: Explain how chronic intravascular hemolysis from a prosthetic valve produces iron deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old military recruit comes to the clinic because his urine turned red-brown after a 30-km march in boots on paved roads. He feels well and has no muscle pain or weakness. Similar episodes occurred after two earlier marches and cleared within several hours. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), and blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg. Examination is normal. Urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, and microscopy shows 0 to 2 red cells per high-power field. Serum creatine kinase is 140 U/L (reference 25-200). Hemoglobin is 15.1 g/dL, and the peripheral smear is normal. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his urine findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Complement-mediated lysis of cells lacking GPI-anchored proteins

options.label: B
options.html: Glomerular basement membrane leakage of red cells

options.label: C
options.html: Myoglobin release from injured skeletal muscle

options.label: D
options.html: Oxidative denaturation of hemoglobin in red cells

options.label: E
options.html: Repetitive mechanical trauma to red cells in the feet

items.explanationHtml:
Heme-positive urine without red cells means hemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria. A normal creatine kinase excludes rhabdomyolysis. Episodes that follow prolonged impact on the soles and clear within hours are exertional (march) hemoglobinuria: red cells are crushed as they pass through superficial plantar vessels, releasing hemoglobin that is filtered once haptoglobin is saturated.

Takeaway: transient hemoglobinuria after prolonged marching or running with normal CK is mechanical hemolysis in the soles; cushioned footwear prevents it.

whyNot.A: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria causes hemolysis unrelated to marching, typically with cytopenias or thrombosis and abnormal blood counts.
