whyNot.B: Glomerular bleeding would show many red cells, often dysmorphic, on urine microscopy.
whyNot.C: Myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis would come with muscle pain and a markedly raised creatine kinase.
whyNot.D: Oxidant hemolysis needs a trigger such as a drug or infection in G6PD deficiency and would show bite cells or Heinz bodies.

items.objective: Identify exertional (march) hemoglobinuria as mechanical red-cell injury and distinguish it from rhabdomyolysis.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman is admitted with confusion and petechiae. Hemoglobin is 7.9 g/dL, platelet count 12,000/mm3, LDH 1,640 U/L (reference 45-200) and creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. PT and aPTT are normal, the direct antiglobulin test is negative, and the smear shows many schistocytes. ADAMTS13 activity is 3% with an inhibitor present. Daily plasma exchange and glucocorticoids are begun, together with a drug that is a humanized single-domain antibody fragment. This drug most likely prevents new microthrombi by blocking which of the following interactions?

options.label: B
options.html: ADP binding to the platelet P2Y12 receptor

options.label: C
options.html: Fibrinogen binding to platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa

options.label: E
options.html: von Willebrand factor binding to platelet glycoprotein Ib

items.explanationHtml:
The drug is caplacizumab, which binds the A1 domain of von Willebrand factor. In immune TTP, ADAMTS13 is inhibited, so ultra-large vWF multimers persist and capture platelets through GPIb under shear. Blocking this adhesion step stops new microthrombi while plasma exchange and immunosuppression remove the inhibitor and restore ADAMTS13.

Takeaway: caplacizumab blocks vWF A1-GPIb binding, the adhesion step that drives microthrombi in TTP.

whyNot.A: Removal of the inhibitor is achieved by plasma exchange and immunosuppression, not by this antibody fragment.
whyNot.B: P2Y12 blockade describes clopidogrel and related drugs, which are not used to treat TTP.
whyNot.C: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors such as eptifibatide block aggregation but are not TTP therapy.
whyNot.D: Direct thrombin inhibitors block fibrin formation; TTP thrombi are platelet- and vWF-rich with normal coagulation times.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism of caplacizumab in immune TTP.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of pallor, puffy eyelids and decreased urination for 2 days. One week ago he had bloody diarrhea after attending a petting zoo. Hemoglobin is 7.1 g/dL, platelet count 52,000/mm3 and creatinine 2.4 mg/dL. The smear shows schistocytes, and PT and aPTT are normal. Stool testing detects a toxin that binds globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) on glomerular endothelial cells. Which of the following is the intracellular action of this toxin?

options.label: B
options.html: ADP-ribosylation of the Gs alpha subunit

options.label: C
options.html: Cleavage of SNARE proteins at nerve terminals

options.label: D
options.html: Increase in intracellular cGMP in enterocytes

options.label: E
options.html: Removal of an adenine from 28S ribosomal RNA

items.explanationHtml:
Shiga toxin and Shiga-like toxins of enterohemorrhagic E coli bind Gb3, are internalized, and their A subunit acts as an N-glycosidase that removes a specific adenine from the 28S rRNA of the 60S ribosomal subunit. Protein synthesis stops, endothelial cells are injured and become prothrombotic, and platelet-fibrin thrombi form in glomerular capillaries, producing hemolytic uremic syndrome.

Takeaway: Shiga toxin inactivates the 60S ribosome by depurinating 28S rRNA, injuring glomerular endothelium and causing HUS.

whyNot.A: ADP-ribosylation of EF-2 is the action of diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A.
whyNot.B: ADP-ribosylation of Gs alpha is the action of cholera toxin and the heat-labile toxin of enterotoxigenic E coli, which cause watery diarrhea.
whyNot.C: SNARE cleavage is the action of botulinum and tetanus toxins.
whyNot.D: Raised cGMP is the action of the heat-stable enterotoxin of enterotoxigenic E coli, which causes watery diarrhea without HUS.

items.objective: Relate the mechanism of Shiga toxin to the pathogenesis of hemolytic uremic syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man is evaluated for fatigue and decreased urine output. Two weeks ago he had an upper respiratory infection. He has had no diarrhea. His older brother required dialysis after a similar illness. Blood pressure is 168/96 mm Hg. Hemoglobin is 8.0 g/dL, platelet count 64,000/mm3, LDH 980 U/L (reference 45-200), haptoglobin undetectable and creatinine 4.6 mg/dL. The smear shows schistocytes. PT and aPTT are normal. ADAMTS13 activity is 68% (reference above 60%). Serum C3 is low, and C4 is normal. Stool testing for Shiga toxin is negative. Loss of function of which of the following proteins most likely underlies his condition?
items.explanationHtml:
Thrombotic microangiopathy with severe kidney injury, normal ADAMTS13 activity, no Shiga toxin, a family history and low C3 with normal C4 indicates complement-mediated (atypical) HUS. The most frequently affected regulator is factor H, which normally protects host endothelium by inactivating C3b of the alternative pathway. Without it, complement attacks glomerular endothelium after a trigger such as infection. C5 inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab) are first-line.

Takeaway: complement-mediated HUS reflects alternative-pathway dysregulation, most often of factor H; ADAMTS13 is not severely reduced.

whyNot.A: ADAMTS13 deficiency causes TTP, but his ADAMTS13 activity is normal.
whyNot.B: C1 inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema with low C4, not thrombotic microangiopathy.
whyNot.C: CD59 loss (with CD55) in PNH causes complement lysis of red cells, but PNH does not produce schistocytes with this renal TMA picture and low C3.
whyNot.E: Absent GPIb causes Bernard-Soulier syndrome, with large platelets and bleeding, not hemolysis.

items.objective: Identify factor H dysregulation as a cause of complement-mediated HUS.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman in the intensive care unit has gram-negative bacteremia from pyelonephritis. On hospital day 2 she oozes blood from venipuncture sites. Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL and platelet count 41,000/mm3. The peripheral smear shows occasional schistocytes. A consultant must decide whether the findings reflect disseminated intravascular coagulation or a thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura-like process. Which of the following laboratory findings most strongly supports disseminated intravascular coagulation?
items.explanationHtml:
In DIC, tissue factor exposed during sepsis drives widespread thrombin generation, which consumes fibrinogen and other clotting factors along with platelets. A low fibrinogen with prolonged PT and aPTT is therefore characteristic. In TTP and HUS, platelet-vWF or platelet-fibrin microthrombi form without consumption of soluble coagulation factors, so PT, aPTT and fibrinogen stay normal.

Takeaway: consumption of fibrinogen and clotting factors (low fibrinogen, long PT/aPTT) separates DIC from TTP and HUS.

whyNot.A: Low haptoglobin indicates hemolysis and occurs in DIC, TTP and HUS alike.
whyNot.C: LDH rises with hemolysis and tissue ischemia in all thrombotic microangiopathies.
whyNot.D: Reticulocytosis reflects a marrow response to any hemolysis and does not identify the cause.
whyNot.E: Schistocytes occur in both DIC and TTP and so cannot separate them.

items.objective: Use coagulation tests to distinguish disseminated intravascular coagulation from TTP and HUS.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy has had a continuous-flow left ventricular assist device for 14 months. He comes to the device clinic because his urine has been dark for 2 days. The device controller shows intermittent power spikes. Serum LDH is 2,350 U/L (reference 45-200), up from 310 U/L a month ago, and plasma free hemoglobin is markedly elevated. The serum concentration of a plasma protein that binds free hemoglobin dimers and delivers them to macrophages through CD163 is undetectable. Which of the following proteins is this?
items.explanationHtml:
Rising LDH, hemoglobinuria and power spikes suggest LVAD pump thrombosis with severe shear hemolysis. Free hemoglobin dissociates into alpha-beta dimers, which are bound by haptoglobin; the complex is taken up by macrophages through the CD163 scavenger receptor, so haptoglobin is consumed and becomes undetectable in intravascular hemolysis.

Takeaway: haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin and is consumed in intravascular hemolysis; hemopexin binds free heme.

whyNot.A: Albumin binds some free heme (as methemalbumin) but not hemoglobin dimers, and it is not cleared through CD163.
whyNot.B: Ceruloplasmin carries copper and is not involved in hemoglobin scavenging.
whyNot.D: Hemopexin also falls in severe hemolysis, but it binds free heme, not hemoglobin dimers, and is cleared by CD91.
whyNot.E: Transferrin carries ferric iron in plasma, not hemoglobin.

items.objective: Explain haptoglobin depletion as the marker of intravascular hemolysis in device-related shear injury.

items.stemHtml: A 42-year-old man is admitted to a burn center after a house fire with full-thickness burns over 45% of his body surface area. Twelve hours after admission, his hemoglobin has fallen from 16.8 g/dL to 12.9 g/dL despite hemoconcentration, and his plasma is pink. The peripheral smear shows numerous small dense red cells without central pallor and small budding fragments. The direct antiglobulin test is negative. Which of the following best explains these red-cell changes?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibody-mediated removal of membrane by splenic macrophages

options.label: B
options.html: Deficiency of ankyrin in the red-cell membrane

options.label: C
options.html: Heat denaturation of the spectrin membrane skeleton

options.label: D
options.html: Oxidative precipitation of hemoglobin as Heinz bodies

options.label: E
options.html: Shearing of red cells by fibrin strands in arterioles

items.explanationHtml:
Red cells passing through heated tissue are damaged directly: spectrin denatures at roughly 49°C, the membrane skeleton loses its integrity, and cells bud off fragments and become microspherocytes. This produces acute intravascular hemolysis within the first day or two after severe burns, with a negative DAT.

Takeaway: severe burns cause thermal hemolysis with microspherocytes and fragments from heat-denatured spectrin.

whyNot.A: Antibody-mediated membrane loss (warm autoimmune hemolysis) would give a positive DAT.
whyNot.B: Ankyrin deficiency in hereditary spherocytosis is lifelong and inherited, not an acute change after a burn.
whyNot.D: Heinz bodies and bite cells come from oxidant stress, typically in G6PD deficiency, not from heat.
whyNot.E: Fibrin strand shearing in DIC can follow burns later, but it produces schistocytes with thrombocytopenia, not immediate microspherocytosis in pink plasma.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of thermal red-cell injury after extensive burns.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman with immune thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura reaches remission after daily plasma exchange and glucocorticoids. To reduce the risk of relapse, she is given an intravenous monoclonal antibody that depletes the cells that produce her anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibody. Which of the following is the target of this antibody?
items.explanationHtml:
Rituximab is a chimeric anti-CD20 antibody that depletes mature B cells through complement-dependent and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. Removing the B-cell precursors of plasma cells lowers anti-ADAMTS13 antibody production over weeks and reduces TTP relapse. Long-lived plasma cells lack CD20, which is why the effect is delayed.

Takeaway: rituximab targets CD20 on B cells and lowers relapse in immune TTP by reducing anti-ADAMTS13 antibody production.

whyNot.A: Anti-CD3 antibodies target T cells, which do not secrete the autoantibody.
whyNot.C: Anti-CD25 antibodies block the IL-2 receptor on activated T cells and are used in transplant induction.
whyNot.D: Alemtuzumab targets CD52 on lymphocytes broadly and is not used to prevent TTP relapse.
whyNot.E: C5 inhibitors treat complement-mediated HUS, not antibody-mediated ADAMTS13 deficiency.

items.objective: Identify the target of rituximab and its role in immune TTP.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman has had progressive exertional dyspnea and two episodes of melena over 6 months. Colonoscopy and upper endoscopy show several small angiodysplastic lesions in the cecum. She has a harsh late-peaking systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border, and echocardiography shows severe aortic stenosis. Platelet count, PT and aPTT are normal. Von Willebrand factor multimer analysis shows loss of the largest multimers. Which of the following best explains the multimer pattern?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibody-mediated clearance of von Willebrand factor

options.label: B
options.html: Decreased endothelial synthesis of von Willebrand factor

options.label: C
options.html: Increased ADAMTS13 cleavage of shear-unfolded von Willebrand factor

options.label: D
options.html: Inherited defect of von Willebrand factor multimerization

items.explanationHtml:
Very high shear across a stenotic aortic valve (or through an LVAD) stretches von Willebrand factor, exposing the cleavage site for ADAMTS13. The largest, most hemostatically active multimers are destroyed, causing an acquired von Willebrand syndrome. Angiodysplasia bleeds readily in this setting; the combination of aortic stenosis and GI angiodysplasia bleeding is known as Heyde syndrome, and valve replacement corrects the multimer defect.

Takeaway: high shear from aortic stenosis or an LVAD unfolds vWF so that ADAMTS13 removes the largest multimers, causing acquired von Willebrand syndrome.

whyNot.A: Autoantibodies can cause acquired von Willebrand syndrome in lymphoproliferative disease, but her severe aortic stenosis provides a shear mechanism.
whyNot.B: Reduced synthesis lowers all multimers proportionally rather than selectively removing the largest ones.
whyNot.D: An inherited multimerization defect (type 2A) would have caused lifelong bleeding and does not explain onset with valve disease.
whyNot.E: Microvascular platelet consumption would cause thrombocytopenia, but her platelet count is normal.

items.objective: Explain shear-induced loss of large von Willebrand multimers in aortic stenosis and assist devices.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man had a splenectomy 6 months ago after a motorcycle collision. He feels well. A routine CBC shows hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL, leukocyte count 9,800/mm3 and platelet count 470,000/mm3. The peripheral blood smear is shown. The small round inclusions seen in several red cells persist because of the loss of which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Kupffer cell phagocytosis of senescent cells

options.label: E
options.html: Pooling of platelets in the spleen

items.explanationHtml:
The smear shows Howell-Jolly bodies, small round DNA remnants left when the erythroblast nucleus is extruded, and a few target cells. Normally splenic red-pulp macrophages remove such inclusions as cells squeeze from the cords into the sinuses (pitting), and the cell returns to the circulation. After splenectomy this pitting function is lost, so the inclusions persist. The mild thrombocytosis reflects loss of splenic platelet pooling.

Takeaway: Howell-Jolly bodies persist after splenectomy because splenic pitting of red-cell inclusions is lost.

whyNot.A: Kupffer cells remove some damaged cells but do not take over pitting of inclusions from circulating cells.
whyNot.B: Loss of marginal-zone IgM responses explains infection risk, not the smear inclusions.
whyNot.C: Nuclear extrusion in the marrow is intact; the remnants form normally and are usually cleared later by the spleen.
whyNot.E: Loss of splenic platelet pooling explains his thrombocytosis, not red-cell inclusions.

items.objective: Relate Howell-Jolly bodies on a smear to loss of splenic pitting.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman who had a splenectomy 4 years ago for hereditary spherocytosis is brought to the emergency department 12 hours after the onset of fever and malaise. She is hypotensive and has purpura on her legs. Blood cultures grow gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci. She received no vaccines after her surgery. Loss of which of the following splenic functions most directly increased her susceptibility to this infection?

options.label: A
options.html: Antigen presentation to CD8+ T cells in the periarteriolar sheath

options.label: B
options.html: Clearance of opsonized encapsulated bacteria by marginal-zone macrophages

options.label: C
options.html: Neutrophil oxidative burst in the red pulp

options.label: D
options.html: Production of IgA by follicular plasma cells

options.label: E
options.html: Storage of complement components in the white pulp

items.explanationHtml:
Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection is classically caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. Its polysaccharide capsule resists phagocytosis unless the organism is coated with antibody and complement. The splenic marginal zone holds macrophages that clear opsonized and poorly opsonized bacteria from slowly flowing blood, and marginal-zone B cells make rapid T-cell-independent IgM against capsular polysaccharides. Both functions are lost after splenectomy.

Takeaway: the marginal zone of the spleen clears encapsulated bacteria and makes anti-polysaccharide IgM, which is why asplenia predisposes to pneumococcal sepsis.

whyNot.A: CD8+ T-cell responses defend against intracellular pathogens, not extracellular encapsulated bacteria.
whyNot.C: Neutrophil oxidative burst is a circulating and tissue function that persists after splenectomy; its failure (chronic granulomatous disease) predisposes to catalase-positive organisms.
whyNot.D: IgA protects mucosal surfaces and is made mainly in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, not in the spleen.
whyNot.E: Complement proteins are made mainly by the liver; the spleen is not a complement store.

items.objective: Explain why loss of the splenic marginal zone predisposes to encapsulated bacterial sepsis.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman undergoes laparoscopic splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenia refractory to medical therapy. The surgeon divides the ligament containing the splenic artery and vein close to the splenic hilum. On postoperative day 4, she has left upper quadrant pain and fever, and the fluid from her left subphrenic drain has an amylase concentration of 9,200 U/L. Injury to a structure that lies in the same ligament as the splenic vessels most likely caused these findings. Which of the following structures was injured?

options.label: E
options.html: Upper pole of the left kidney

items.explanationHtml:
The splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament carries the splenic artery and vein and the tail of the pancreas, which often reaches the splenic hilum. Dividing the hilar vessels can injure the pancreatic tail, producing a pancreatic leak with amylase-rich drain fluid and a peripancreatic collection.

Takeaway: the tail of the pancreas lies in the splenorenal ligament with the splenic vessels and is at risk during splenectomy.

whyNot.A: The stomach is joined to the spleen by the gastrosplenic ligament (short gastric vessels); gastric injury would not cause amylase-rich fluid.
whyNot.B: The left adrenal gland is retroperitoneal, superomedial to the kidney, and not within the splenorenal ligament.
whyNot.C: The splenic flexure attaches by the splenocolic and phrenicocolic ligaments; colonic injury would cause feculent drainage.
whyNot.E: The kidney lies behind the posterior layer of the ligament, and a renal injury would produce urine leak or hematuria rather than amylase-rich fluid.

items.objective: Identify the contents of the splenorenal ligament and the risk to the pancreatic tail during splenectomy.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old girl with sickle cell anemia (HbSS) is brought to the emergency department with fever to 40.1°C (104.2°F) and lethargy that began 8 hours ago. Her family stopped her daily oral antibiotic several months ago. Blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg. Blood cultures grow gram-positive diplococci that are alpha-hemolytic and optochin-sensitive. Which of the following bacterial structures is most responsible for this organism's ability to cause bloodstream infection in this child?

options.label: B
options.html: M protein on the cell surface

options.label: C
options.html: Pili that mediate attachment to the urinary tract

options.label: E
options.html: Protein A that binds the Fc portion of IgG

items.explanationHtml:
Children with HbSS develop functional asplenia early in life through repeated splenic infarction. Streptococcus pneumoniae evades complement deposition and phagocytosis with its polysaccharide capsule; clearance of such organisms depends on anticapsular antibody and splenic macrophages. Daily penicillin until at least age 5 and conjugate vaccination are the preventive measures her family stopped.

Takeaway: the pneumococcal polysaccharide capsule is the main virulence factor exploited in functional asplenia of sickle cell disease.

whyNot.A: Endotoxin (lipid A) is found in gram-negative bacteria; pneumococcus is gram-positive.
whyNot.B: M protein is the antiphagocytic protein of Streptococcus pyogenes, which is beta-hemolytic and bacitracin-sensitive.
whyNot.C: P pili are a uropathogenic E coli virulence factor and do not explain pneumococcal sepsis.
whyNot.E: Protein A is a Staphylococcus aureus virulence factor; S aureus is catalase-positive and grows in clusters.

items.objective: Link functional asplenia in sickle cell disease to capsule-mediated pneumococcal virulence.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old woman with long-standing celiac disease has fatigue. She admits that she has not followed a gluten-free diet for several years. Hemoglobin is 10.6 g/dL, MCV 82 fL and platelet count 452,000/mm3. The peripheral smear shows target cells, occasional acanthocytes and numerous red cells containing a single small, dense, round purple inclusion near the edge of the cell. Ultrasonography shows a small spleen. Which of the following most likely explains the red-cell inclusions?
items.explanationHtml:
The single small round purple inclusions are Howell-Jolly bodies, which the spleen normally removes. Celiac disease is an established cause of splenic atrophy and functional hyposplenism, particularly with poorly controlled disease, and together with target cells and thrombocytosis it explains the smear. Hyposplenism carries the same infection risk as surgical asplenia, so she should be offered the vaccines given to asplenic patients.

Takeaway: celiac disease can cause functional hyposplenism, recognized by Howell-Jolly bodies and a small spleen.

whyNot.A: Basophilic stippling is many fine dots spread through the cell, not a single round inclusion.
whyNot.C: Hemoglobin H precipitates appear as many small inclusions with supravital stains and accompany microcytosis, not a single body on Wright stain.
whyNot.D: Parasites such as Plasmodium or Babesia form rings or tetrads, and she has no exposure or fever.
whyNot.E: Folate deficiency can cause Howell-Jolly bodies but would raise the MCV and would not explain a small spleen.

items.objective: Recognize celiac disease as a cause of functional hyposplenism with Howell-Jolly bodies.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old man with cirrhosis from alcohol use has stopped drinking for 2 years. Examination shows spider angiomas, shifting dullness and a spleen palpable 6 cm below the left costal margin. Hemoglobin is 11.2 g/dL, MCV 94 fL, leukocyte count 2,900/mm3 and platelet count 58,000/mm3. Serum folate and vitamin B12 are normal. A bone marrow biopsy shows normal cellularity with all three lineages present and maturing normally. Which of the following best explains his pancytopenia?

options.label: B
options.html: Infiltration of the marrow by fibrosis

options.label: C
options.html: Pooling and destruction of blood cells in a congested spleen

items.explanationHtml:
Portal hypertension from cirrhosis congests the spleen, which enlarges and holds a larger fraction of circulating platelets and leukocytes while its expanded macrophage mass shortens red-cell survival. Splenomegaly, cytopenias and a normal marrow define hypersplenism. Reduced hepatic thrombopoietin production adds to the thrombocytopenia in cirrhosis.

Takeaway: hypersplenism from portal hypertension causes cytopenias with a normal marrow through splenic pooling and destruction.

whyNot.A: Immune destruction usually affects one lineage and would not explain the congestive splenomegaly; no autoimmune features are present.
whyNot.B: Marrow fibrosis would appear on biopsy and is typically accompanied by teardrop cells and leukoerythroblastosis.
whyNot.D: Direct alcohol toxicity to the marrow resolves within weeks of abstinence, and he has abstained for 2 years.
whyNot.E: Viral marrow suppression would reduce precursors on biopsy, whereas his marrow is normally cellular.

items.objective: Explain hypersplenism from portal hypertension as a cause of pancytopenia with a normal marrow.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man who recently came to the United States from South Sudan has had intermittent fever, weight loss of 9 kg and abdominal fullness for 3 months. His skin has darkened. The spleen extends to the right iliac fossa, and the liver is enlarged. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL, leukocyte count 2,100/mm3 and platelet count 72,000/mm3. Serum total protein is 9.4 g/dL with polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. A bone marrow aspirate shows macrophages packed with small oval organisms, each with a nucleus and a rod-shaped kinetoplast. Which of the following transmitted this infection?
items.explanationHtml:
Fever, weight loss, massive hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, darkened skin and hypergammaglobulinemia in someone from East Africa suggest visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar). Amastigotes with a nucleus and kinetoplast fill macrophages of the spleen, liver and marrow. Leishmania donovani complex is transmitted by phlebotomine sand flies. Pancytopenia results largely from hypersplenism and marrow involvement.

Takeaway: visceral leishmaniasis, spread by sand flies, causes massive splenomegaly with pancytopenia and amastigotes in macrophages.

whyNot.A: Anopheles transmits malaria, which also enlarges the spleen, but Plasmodium lives in red cells and has no kinetoplast.
whyNot.B: Ixodes ticks transmit Babesia and Borrelia, which do not produce amastigotes in macrophages.
whyNot.D: Triatomine bugs transmit Trypanosoma cruzi, causing cardiomyopathy and megaviscera in Latin America.
whyNot.E: Tsetse flies transmit African trypanosomiasis, which presents with extracellular trypomastigotes and sleeping sickness.

items.objective: Identify visceral leishmaniasis as a cause of massive splenomegaly and name its vector.

items.stemHtml: An 18-year-old college athlete with a 2-week history of sore throat, fatigue and fever is struck in the left flank during a rugby match. Within an hour he has left upper quadrant pain and pain at the tip of his left shoulder. Pulse is 118/min, and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. A heterophile antibody test is positive. The shoulder pain is most likely carried by afferent fibers of which of the following nerves?
items.explanationHtml:
Infectious mononucleosis enlarges the spleen and makes it prone to rupture after minor trauma. Blood beneath the left hemidiaphragm irritates the diaphragmatic peritoneum, whose sensory supply comes from the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5). Pain is referred to the skin of the shoulder, which shares the C4 dermatome (Kehr sign).

Takeaway: diaphragmatic irritation from splenic rupture refers pain to the left shoulder through the phrenic nerve.

whyNot.A: The greater splanchnic nerve carries visceral pain from foregut organs to the epigastrium, not the shoulder.
whyNot.B: Lower intercostal nerves supply the peripheral diaphragm and the abdominal wall, producing local rather than shoulder pain.
whyNot.D: The spinal accessory nerve is motor to the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid and carries no peritoneal sensation.
whyNot.E: Vagal afferents carry visceral sensation that is poorly localized and not referred to the shoulder.

items.objective: Explain referred left shoulder pain after splenic rupture.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with long-standing atrial fibrillation who stopped taking his anticoagulant 2 months ago has sudden severe left upper quadrant pain. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). Contrast-enhanced CT shows a peripheral, wedge-shaped, nonenhancing area in the spleen with its base at the capsule. He recovers with analgesia and anticoagulation. If the affected tissue had been examined microscopically 3 days after onset, which of the following would most likely have been seen?

options.label: B
options.html: Coagulative necrosis with preserved cell outlines

options.label: C
options.html: Fat necrosis with calcium soap deposition

items.explanationHtml:
Embolic occlusion of a splenic arterial branch from atrial fibrillation produces an infarct. The spleen has an end-arterial supply, so infarcts are wedge-shaped with the base at the capsule. Like the heart and kidney, solid organs infarct with coagulative necrosis: proteins denature, enzymatic digestion is limited, and ghost outlines of cells persist for days before inflammatory clearance and fibrosis.

Takeaway: splenic infarcts are wedge-shaped, pale and show coagulative necrosis, the pattern of ischemia in solid organs except the brain.

whyNot.A: Caseous necrosis is the pattern of tuberculosis and some fungal infections, not ischemia.
whyNot.C: Fat necrosis occurs in pancreatitis and breast trauma, where lipases release fatty acids.
whyNot.D: Fibrinoid necrosis affects vessel walls in malignant hypertension and vasculitis, not the downstream parenchyma.
whyNot.E: Liquefactive necrosis is the pattern of brain infarcts and abscesses.

items.objective: Describe the gross and microscopic pathology of a splenic infarct.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman underwent laparoscopic splenectomy for chronic immune thrombocytopenia 3 years ago, and her platelet count normalized. She now has recurrent petechiae, and her platelet count is 18,000/mm3. The peripheral smear shows no Howell-Jolly bodies. Scintigraphy with heat-damaged radiolabelled red cells shows a 2-cm focus of uptake near the former splenic hilum. From which embryonic structure did this tissue arise?
items.explanationHtml:
The absence of Howell-Jolly bodies after splenectomy and a focus that takes up damaged red cells indicate an accessory spleen that has grown and resumed destroying antibody-coated platelets. The spleen and accessory spleens develop from mesenchymal condensations in the dorsal mesogastrium; failure of these buds to fuse leaves separate nodules, most often near the hilum.

Takeaway: the spleen arises from mesoderm in the dorsal mesogastrium; unfused buds become accessory spleens that can cause ITP relapse after splenectomy.

whyNot.B: Foregut endoderm forms epithelial organs such as the liver and pancreas, but the spleen is mesodermal.
whyNot.C: The midgut mesentery gives rise to the mesentery of the small bowel, not splenic tissue.
whyNot.D: The septum transversum contributes to the diaphragm and liver stroma.
whyNot.E: The ventral mesogastrium forms the lesser omentum and falciform ligament, into which the liver grows.

items.objective: Identify the embryologic origin of the spleen and the significance of accessory splenic tissue.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man has a drug-eluting coronary stent placed for an acute coronary syndrome and is discharged on aspirin and clopidogrel. Five weeks later he has stent thrombosis despite documented full adherence. Pharmacogenetic testing shows that he is homozygous for a loss-of-function allele of the gene encoding a hepatic cytochrome P450 enzyme. Which of the following best explains the treatment failure?

options.label: A
options.html: Accelerated hepatic inactivation of active drug

options.label: B
options.html: Decreased conversion of a prodrug to its active metabolite

options.label: C
options.html: Increased renal clearance of the parent drug

options.label: D
options.html: Mutation in the P2Y12 receptor binding site

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced intestinal absorption due to P-glycoprotein

items.explanationHtml:
Clopidogrel is a prodrug that requires two oxidative steps, largely by CYP2C19, to form the thiol metabolite that irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 receptor. Patients homozygous for loss-of-function alleles (such as *2 or *3) generate little active metabolite and have higher rates of stent thrombosis. Ticagrelor or prasugrel, which do not depend on CYP2C19, are alternatives.

Takeaway: CYP2C19 poor metabolizers cannot activate the prodrug clopidogrel, increasing stent thrombosis risk.

whyNot.A: Loss of CYP2C19 function reduces activation; it does not speed up inactivation.
whyNot.C: Clopidogrel is not cleared unchanged by the kidney to an important degree, and the genetic finding concerns a hepatic enzyme.
whyNot.D: Receptor mutations are not the mechanism; the defect lies in drug metabolism.
whyNot.E: P-glycoprotein variants are not a P450 enzyme and are not the established cause of clopidogrel resistance.

items.objective: Explain how CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles reduce clopidogrel efficacy.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old woman taking dabigatran for atrial fibrillation falls at home and is brought to the emergency department with a headache and vomiting. CT of the head shows an acute subdural hematoma, and neurosurgery is planned. She took her last dose 5 hours ago. Creatinine is 1.5 mg/dL. Thrombin time is markedly prolonged. Which of the following describes the mechanism of the most appropriate agent to reverse her anticoagulation?

options.label: A
options.html: Cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors

options.label: B
options.html: Humanized antibody fragment that binds the drug

options.label: C
options.html: Polycationic protein that neutralizes an anionic polysaccharide

options.label: D
options.html: Recombinant inactive factor Xa that acts as a decoy

options.label: E
options.html: Replacement of factors II, VII, IX and X

items.explanationHtml:
Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor; the prolonged thrombin time confirms a meaningful drug effect. Idarucizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody fragment (Fab) that binds free and thrombin-bound dabigatran with far greater affinity than thrombin does, neutralizing it within minutes. It is the preferred reversal for life-threatening bleeding or urgent surgery.

Takeaway: idarucizumab, a Fab that binds dabigatran, is the specific reversal agent for dabigatran.

whyNot.A: Vitamin K is the cofactor for gamma-carboxylation and reverses warfarin, not a direct thrombin inhibitor.
whyNot.C: Protamine neutralizes heparin, a polyanion, and has no effect on dabigatran.
whyNot.D: Andexanet alfa is a decoy for factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban and rivaroxaban, not for dabigatran.
whyNot.E: Prothrombin complex concentrate replaces vitamin K-dependent factors and is preferred for warfarin; it is only a fallback for dabigatran when idarucizumab is unavailable.

items.objective: Match the dabigatran reversal agent to its mechanism.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman with a pulmonary embolism is treated with an oral anticoagulant that requires no laboratory monitoring. One month later she needs emergency surgery for a perforated viscus, and her surgeon asks how the drug works. The drug directly binds the active site of a coagulation factor that is free in plasma or assembled in the prothrombinase complex, without the need for a plasma cofactor. Which of the following agents is she most likely taking?
items.explanationHtml:
The prothrombinase complex is factor Xa with factor Va on a phospholipid surface. Apixaban (like rivaroxaban and edoxaban) is an oral direct factor Xa inhibitor that binds free and prothrombinase-bound Xa without antithrombin. Its reversal options are andexanet alfa or 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate.

Takeaway: oral direct factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) inhibit free and prothrombinase-bound Xa without antithrombin.

whyNot.B: Dabigatran is a direct oral inhibitor, but of thrombin, not of the prothrombinase enzyme factor Xa.
whyNot.C: Enoxaparin is injected and needs antithrombin as a cofactor to inhibit factor Xa.
whyNot.D: Fondaparinux is injected and acts through antithrombin rather than binding Xa directly.
whyNot.E: Warfarin needs INR monitoring and reduces synthesis of functional factors rather than binding an active enzyme.

items.objective: Distinguish direct factor Xa inhibitors from antithrombin-dependent and vitamin K antagonist anticoagulants.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man becomes dusky and short of breath 30 minutes after his pharynx was sprayed several times with a topical anesthetic for transesophageal echocardiography. Pulse oximetry reads 85% on 6 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula and does not change with 100% oxygen by face mask. An arterial blood sample is chocolate-brown; PaO2 is 210 mm Hg. Which of the following best explains his impaired tissue oxygen delivery?

options.label: A
options.html: Carbon monoxide bound to ferrous heme iron

options.label: B
options.html: Oxidation of heme iron to the ferric state

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondria

options.label: E
options.html: Right-to-left intracardiac shunting of venous blood

items.explanationHtml:
Benzocaine and related local anesthetics oxidize heme iron from ferrous (Fe2+) to ferric (Fe3+), forming methemoglobin, which cannot bind oxygen. The remaining ferrous hemes in partly oxidized tetramers hold oxygen more avidly, shifting the dissociation curve to the left and further impairing unloading. Dissolved oxygen (PaO2) is normal, pulse oximetry hovers near 85%, and co-oximetry confirms the diagnosis; methylene blue is the treatment unless G6PD deficiency is present.

Takeaway: methemoglobin (ferric heme) cannot carry oxygen and left-shifts the curve; suspect it with cyanosis, normal PaO2 and SpO2 near 85% after an oxidant drug.

whyNot.A: Carboxyhemoglobin gives cherry-red, not chocolate-brown, blood and needs a carbon monoxide exposure.
whyNot.C: Cytochrome oxidase inhibition (cyanide) impairs oxygen use, causing lactic acidosis without cyanosis or brown blood.
whyNot.D: Low 2,3-BPG shifts the curve left (as in stored blood) but does not discolor blood or depress pulse oximetry readings.
whyNot.E: A right-to-left shunt would lower PaO2, whereas his PaO2 is high on supplemental oxygen.

items.objective: Explain the pathophysiology of benzocaine-induced methemoglobinemia.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man with newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma has a serum uric acid of 12.4 mg/dL and creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL before chemotherapy. He is given an intravenous enzyme that converts uric acid to allantoin. Within 24 hours he has dark urine, scleral icterus and cyanosis. Hemoglobin falls from 13.8 to 8.9 g/dL, and the smear shows bite cells. Later testing shows G6PD deficiency. A byproduct of the enzymatic reaction most likely caused his hemolysis. Which of the following is this byproduct?
items.explanationHtml:
Rasburicase is recombinant urate oxidase. It oxidizes uric acid to allantoin, carbon dioxide and hydrogen peroxide. Red cells detoxify peroxide through glutathione, which must be kept reduced with NADPH from G6PD. In G6PD deficiency, peroxide oxidizes hemoglobin, producing Heinz bodies, bite cells, acute hemolysis and methemoglobinemia. G6PD status is checked in at-risk patients before rasburicase.

Takeaway: rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide and is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.

whyNot.A: Allantoin is the soluble, nontoxic product that rasburicase is meant to form.
whyNot.C: Hypoxanthine accumulates with allopurinol, which blocks xanthine oxidase, not with rasburicase.
whyNot.D: Xanthine oxidase acts upstream of uric acid and is not the enzyme given here.
whyNot.E: Uric acid crystals cause nephropathy, but rasburicase lowers uric acid, and crystals do not cause bite cells.

items.objective: Explain why rasburicase causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old man with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus osteomyelitis has received IV vancomycin for 8 days. He now has gum bleeding and petechiae on his legs. Platelet count is 7,000/mm3, down from 260,000/mm3 on admission. He has received no heparin, including line flushes. Hemoglobin, leukocyte count, PT and aPTT are normal, and the smear shows no schistocytes or platelet clumps. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his thrombocytopenia?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibodies against platelet factor 4-heparin complexes that activate platelets

options.label: C
options.html: Consumption of platelets by tissue factor-driven thrombin generation

options.label: E
options.html: Platelet aggregation on unfolded von Willebrand multimers

items.explanationHtml:
An abrupt, severe fall in platelets 5 to 10 days after starting a drug, with no other cytopenias and normal coagulation, is typical of drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia. Vancomycin is a recognized cause. Drug-dependent antibodies bind platelet GP IIb/IIIa or GP Ib/IX only when the drug is present, leading to rapid clearance of coated platelets. The count recovers after the drug is stopped.

Takeaway: drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia is caused by drug-dependent antibodies against platelet glycoproteins and causes bleeding, not thrombosis.

whyNot.A: PF4-heparin antibodies cause heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which needs heparin exposure and causes thrombosis.
whyNot.C: Tissue factor-driven consumption (DIC) would prolong PT and aPTT and produce schistocytes.
whyNot.D: Dose-related megakaryocyte toxicity develops gradually and usually affects other lineages too, as with chemotherapy.
whyNot.E: Platelet aggregation on ultra-large vWF multimers is the mechanism of TTP, which causes hemolysis with schistocytes.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old man with streptococcal endocarditis has received high-dose IV penicillin G for 12 days. He now has fatigue and mild jaundice. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, down from 12.8 g/dL, with reticulocytes 7% and many spherocytes on the smear. The direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG and negative for complement (C3). An eluate from his red cells reacts with penicillin-coated red cells but not with untreated red cells. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his anemia?

options.label: A
options.html: Drug acting as a hapten on the red-cell membrane

options.label: B
options.html: Drug-antibody immune complexes that fix complement on red cells

options.label: D
options.html: Oxidant injury to hemoglobin in G6PD-deficient cells

options.label: E
options.html: Shear injury to red cells on infected valve vegetations

items.explanationHtml:
At high doses, penicillin binds covalently to red-cell membrane proteins and acts as a hapten. IgG antibodies against penicillin coat these cells, which are removed by splenic macrophages (extravascular hemolysis with spherocytes). The DAT is IgG-positive and the eluate reacts only with drug-coated cells. Hemolysis stops once the drug is withdrawn.

Takeaway: high-dose penicillin causes hapten-type immune hemolysis: IgG-positive DAT, extravascular, drug-coated cells only.

whyNot.B: Immune-complex (drug-dependent antibody) hemolysis, as with ceftriaxone, activates complement, gives a C3-positive DAT and is usually intravascular.
whyNot.C: True drug-induced autoantibodies, as with methyldopa, react with untreated red cells, unlike this eluate.
whyNot.D: Oxidant hemolysis gives a negative DAT with bite cells and Heinz bodies.
whyNot.E: Shear injury would give schistocytes and a negative DAT.

items.objective: Distinguish hapten, immune-complex and autoantibody mechanisms of drug-induced hemolysis.

items.stemHtml:
A 28-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 24 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department because of a 20-minute episode of word-finding difficulty and new bruising on her arms. She has had no headache, visual change or abdominal pain. Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse 98/min and blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg. Petechiae are present on her legs. Fundal height is appropriate for dates, and fetal heart tones are normal. Neurologic examination is now normal. Laboratory results:

TestResultReference
Hemoglobin7.6 g/dL12.0-16.0 g/dL
Platelets9,000/mm3150,000-400,000/mm3
MCV89 fL80-100 fL
Reticulocytes5.8%0.5-1.5%
LDH1,280 U/L45-200 U/L
Haptoglobinbelow 10 mg/dL30-200 mg/dL
AST / ALT34 / 29 U/L12-38 / 10-40 U/L
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL0.6-1.2 mg/dL
INR1.00.8-1.1
Fibrinogen390 mg/dL200-400 mg/dL
Direct antiglobulin testnegativenegative
Urine proteinnegativenegative

The peripheral smear shows many schistocytes. ADAMTS13 activity has been sent. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Cesarean delivery after a course of glucocorticoids for fetal lung maturity

items.explanationHtml:
Microangiopathic hemolysis with profound thrombocytopenia, a neurologic event, normal coagulation, normal blood pressure, normal aminotransferases and near-normal creatinine indicate thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, which pregnancy can unmask. Treatment should not wait for ADAMTS13 activity: start therapeutic plasma exchange with glucocorticoids, and add caplacizumab and rituximab for immune TTP once confirmed, or plasma for congenital TTP. Delivery does not treat TTP.

Takeaway: suspected TTP in pregnancy is treated with urgent plasma exchange, not delivery; normal BP and liver tests argue against HELLP.

whyNot.A: Delivery treats HELLP and preeclampsia, but she is normotensive with normal liver tests, and delivery does not resolve TTP.
whyNot.B: IVIG treats immune thrombocytopenia, which does not cause hemolysis with schistocytes.
whyNot.C: Magnesium prevents eclamptic seizures in preeclampsia, which is unlikely with normal blood pressure and no proteinuria.
whyNot.D: Platelet transfusion may worsen microthrombosis in TTP and is reserved for life-threatening bleeding.

items.objective: Recognize TTP in pregnancy and begin plasma exchange rather than delivery.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man comes to the physician because of 2 months of fatigue and dark urine in the mornings. Eight months ago he had mechanical mitral valve replacement for severe mitral regurgitation. He takes warfarin, and his INR is 3.0. A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex, which was not present at his 3-month postoperative visit. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL, platelet count 236,000/mm3, LDH 1,050 U/L (reference 45-200) and haptoglobin undetectable. The direct antiglobulin test is negative. The smear shows schistocytes. Transthoracic echocardiography shows normal prosthetic leaflet motion, but the left atrium is obscured by acoustic shadowing from the prosthesis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: D
options.html: Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59

items.explanationHtml:
Fragmentation hemolysis with a normal platelet count and a new regurgitant murmur after mechanical mitral valve replacement points to a paravalvular leak, whose narrow high-velocity jet shears red cells. Transthoracic imaging cannot see behind a mitral prosthesis well because of shadowing; transesophageal echocardiography visualizes the left atrial side of the sewing ring and is the most accurate test. Severe hemolysis or heart failure from a leak is treated with surgical repair or percutaneous closure, with iron and folate in the meantime.

Takeaway: new hemolysis and a regurgitant murmur after mechanical valve replacement suggest a paravalvular leak; TEE is the test of choice.

whyNot.A: ADAMTS13 testing is for suspected TTP, which is very unlikely with a normal platelet count.
whyNot.B: Marrow biopsy is not needed; the high LDH, low haptoglobin and schistocytes already explain the anemia as peripheral destruction.
whyNot.C: Abdominal CT angiography would look for mesenteric disease, which does not explain hemolysis with a new murmur.
whyNot.D: Flow cytometry for PNH is not the next step when a valvular cause with schistocytes is evident.

items.objective: Choose transesophageal echocardiography to evaluate suspected paravalvular leak hemolysis.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman is evaluated 6 days after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery because of decreasing urine output and edema. Blood pressure is 152/94 mm Hg; her blood pressures during pregnancy were normal. Hemoglobin is 7.9 g/dL, platelet count 71,000/mm3, LDH 1,320 U/L (reference 45-200), haptoglobin undetectable and creatinine 3.8 mg/dL. AST and ALT are normal. The smear shows schistocytes. PT and aPTT are normal. ADAMTS13 activity is 58% (reference above 60%), and stool testing for Shiga toxin is negative. Treatment with eculizumab is planned. Which of the following is the most important measure before or at the start of this therapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Postpartum thrombotic microangiopathy with prominent kidney injury, ADAMTS13 activity that is not severely reduced and no STEC indicates complement-mediated HUS, and a C5 inhibitor is first-line. Blocking C5 prevents formation of the membrane attack complex, which is essential for killing Neisseria meningitidis, so patients receive MenACWY and MenB vaccines before treatment, and antibiotic prophylaxis if treatment must begin before vaccine protection develops.

Takeaway: vaccinate against meningococcus (ACWY and B) before C5 inhibitor therapy, adding antibiotic prophylaxis if treatment cannot wait.

whyNot.A: Hepatitis B screening is required before rituximab, not before C5 inhibition.
whyNot.B: Latent tuberculosis screening is needed before TNF inhibitors, not complement inhibitors.
whyNot.D: TPMT testing guides azathioprine and mercaptopurine dosing.
whyNot.E: Varicella serology matters before live vaccines or some immunosuppressants, but the key risk with C5 blockade is meningococcal infection.

items.objective: Vaccinate against meningococcus before starting C5 inhibitor therapy for complement-mediated HUS.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman training for a marathon comes to the clinic because she has noticed red-brown urine three times in the past month, each time within an hour after a run longer than 25 km on city streets. The color clears by evening, and urine on rest days is normal. She has no muscle pain, abdominal pain or fever, and takes no medications. Blood pressure is 114/70 mm Hg, and examination is normal. A urine sample collected after this morning's long run is dipstick-positive for blood with 1 red cell per high-power field. Hemoglobin is 13.4 g/dL, platelet count 248,000/mm3, creatine kinase 180 U/L (reference 25-200) and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL. The smear is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Brief heme-positive urine without red cells after long runs on hard surfaces, with normal CK, kidney function, blood counts and smear, is exertional (march) hemoglobinuria from mechanical trauma to red cells in the feet. It is benign; cushioned shoes and softer running surfaces reduce it. Persistent hemoglobinuria, cytopenias or thrombosis would instead prompt testing for PNH.

Takeaway: exertional hemoglobinuria with normal CK and blood counts needs reassurance and better cushioning, not invasive tests.

whyNot.A: Cystoscopy evaluates hematuria with red cells on microscopy, which she does not have.
whyNot.B: Flow cytometry for PNH is reserved for hemolysis that is persistent or accompanied by cytopenias or thrombosis.
whyNot.C: IV fluids treat rhabdomyolysis, which is excluded by a normal creatine kinase.
whyNot.D: Kidney biopsy is for glomerular disease with proteinuria, red-cell casts or declining function.

items.objective: Manage exertional hemoglobinuria with reassurance and preventive measures.

items.stemHtml:
A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of pallor, irritability and decreased urination for 1 day. Seven days ago she developed abdominal cramps and diarrhea that became bloody on the second day; the diarrhea has resolved. She attended a county fair with animal exhibits 2 days before the illness. She has had no fever or rash. Temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse 136/min and blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg. She is pale with periorbital edema and scattered petechiae. Abdominal examination shows mild diffuse tenderness without masses. Laboratory results:

TestResultReference
Hemoglobin6.9 g/dL11.5-13.5 g/dL (age 3)
Platelets41,000/mm3150,000-400,000/mm3
Leukocytes14,200/mm35,500-15,500/mm3 (age 3)
LDH2,040 U/Lbelow 300 U/L (age 3)
Urea nitrogen (BUN)68 mg/dL7-18 mg/dL
Creatinine2.2 mg/dL0.2-0.4 mg/dL (age 3)
PT / aPTT12 s / 30 s11-15 s / 25-40 s
Direct antiglobulin testnegativenegative
Urinalysis2+ protein, 2+ bloodnegative

The peripheral smear shows schistocytes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
The triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury arising about a week after bloody diarrhea, with animal contact, in a young child is Shiga toxin-associated HUS, most often from E coli O157:H7. Normal PT and aPTT and a negative DAT exclude DIC and autoimmune hemolysis. Stool testing for Shiga toxin or STEC confirms the cause, and the case is reported to public health.

Takeaway: MAHA, thrombocytopenia and AKI a week after bloody diarrhea in a young child is STEC-HUS.

whyNot.A: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis causes edema, hematuria and kidney injury, but not schistocytes or thrombocytopenia.
whyNot.B: DIC would prolong PT and aPTT and usually occurs in a critically ill, septic child.
whyNot.D: IgA vasculitis causes palpable purpura with a normal platelet count and does not produce hemolysis.
whyNot.E: Immune thrombocytopenia causes isolated thrombocytopenia without anemia, hemolysis or kidney injury.

items.objective: Diagnose Shiga toxin-associated HUS from its triad and prodrome.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old girl is hospitalized with Shiga toxin-associated hemolytic uremic syndrome after bloody diarrhea. She has received isotonic IV fluids and one red-cell transfusion. Over the next 36 hours she makes almost no urine. She now has crackles at both lung bases, increasing periorbital and pedal edema, and oxygen saturation of 91% on room air. Weight is up 8% from admission. Blood pressure is 128/84 mm Hg. Serum potassium is 6.9 mEq/L despite medical measures, bicarbonate 13 mEq/L and BUN 112 mg/dL. Hemoglobin is 7.4 g/dL and platelet count 38,000/mm3. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Management of STEC-HUS is supportive. Anuria with fluid overload, refractory hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis and rising BUN are indications for dialysis (peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis, depending on the center). Most children recover kidney function over days to weeks.

Takeaway: dialysis is indicated in STEC-HUS for refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, fluid overload or prolonged anuria.

whyNot.A: Antibiotics are avoided in STEC infection and do not treat established HUS or its complications.
whyNot.C: C5 inhibition is first-line for complement-mediated HUS, not for typical STEC-HUS with clear dialysis indications.
whyNot.D: Plasma exchange is the treatment for TTP and has no established role in typical pediatric STEC-HUS.
whyNot.E: Platelet transfusion is reserved for bleeding or procedures and does not address her life-threatening metabolic problems.

items.objective: Identify indications for dialysis in Shiga toxin-associated HUS.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old girl who required 9 days of dialysis for Shiga toxin-associated hemolytic uremic syndrome is ready for discharge. Her urine output has recovered, creatinine is 0.5 mg/dL and falling, hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL and platelet count is 212,000/mm3. Blood pressure is 104/62 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows trace protein. Her parents ask what follow-up she needs once she has recovered. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?

options.label: B
options.html: Daily oral antibiotic prophylaxis for 1 year

options.label: C
options.html: Discharge without further follow-up once creatinine normalizes

options.label: D
options.html: Long-term blood pressure and kidney monitoring

options.label: E
options.html: Monthly complete blood counts for 1 year

items.explanationHtml:
Most children recover from STEC-HUS, but a meaningful minority develop hypertension, proteinuria or chronic kidney disease, sometimes years later. The risk is greater after prolonged anuria or dialysis. She needs long-term follow-up with blood pressure, urinalysis for protein and serum creatinine. Recurrence of typical STEC-HUS is rare.

Takeaway: after STEC-HUS, especially when dialysis was needed, follow blood pressure, proteinuria and kidney function long term.

whyNot.A: ADAMTS13 monitoring is for TTP, which this is not.
whyNot.B: Antibiotic prophylaxis has no role, and antibiotics do not prevent kidney sequelae.
whyNot.C: Normal creatinine at discharge does not exclude later hypertension, proteinuria or CKD.
whyNot.E: Hematologic recovery after typical HUS is durable and recurrence is rare; blood counts would not detect her main long-term risk, which is kidney damage.

items.objective: Plan long-term kidney follow-up after Shiga toxin-associated HUS.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman with chronic immune thrombocytopenia has had persistent platelet counts below 20,000/mm3 with mucosal bleeding despite glucocorticoids, a thrombopoietin receptor agonist and rituximab. After discussion she chooses laparoscopic splenectomy. She has received all routine childhood vaccines but no pneumococcal or meningococcal vaccines as an adult. Surgery can be scheduled at any time in the next 2 months. Which of the following is the most appropriate timing of vaccination against encapsulated bacteria?

options.label: B
options.html: On the day of surgery, before induction

items.explanationHtml:
For elective splenectomy, pneumococcal, meningococcal (ACWY and B) and Hib vaccines are given at least 2 weeks before surgery so that antibody responses develop while the spleen is present. Because she received rituximab, responses may be blunted; when possible vaccines are given before B-cell-depleting therapy or once B cells recover, but surgery should be timed to allow at least 2 weeks after vaccination.

Takeaway: vaccinate at least 2 weeks before an elective splenectomy.

whyNot.B: Vaccination on the day of surgery leaves no time for an antibody response before the spleen is removed.
whyNot.C: Vaccinating at discharge is the fallback after emergency splenectomy when follow-up is uncertain, not the plan for elective surgery.
whyNot.D: Vaccinating after surgery is reserved for emergency splenectomy; with elective surgery, preoperative vaccination gives better responses.
whyNot.E: Waiting 3 months leaves her unprotected during the period when post-splenectomy infection risk is highest.

items.objective: Time vaccination at least 2 weeks before elective splenectomy.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man underwent emergency splenectomy for a grade V splenic laceration after a fall from a ladder. He is seen in the surgical clinic 15 days after the operation. He has recovered well and has no fever. He received a tetanus booster in the emergency department and has had no other adult vaccines. Which of the following vaccines should he receive now?

options.label: D
options.html: Pneumococcal conjugate, MenACWY, MenB and Hib vaccines

items.explanationHtml:
After emergency splenectomy, vaccines are given about 2 weeks after surgery, when responses are better than in the immediate postoperative period. Asplenic adults should receive a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV20 or PCV21, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23), meningococcal ACWY conjugate (2-dose primary series, with boosters every 5 years), meningococcal B (primary series with boosters), Hib (1 dose if not previously vaccinated), and annual inactivated influenza vaccine.

Takeaway: after emergency splenectomy, give pneumococcal conjugate, MenACWY, MenB and Hib vaccines about 2 weeks postoperatively.

whyNot.A: Hib and influenza are part of the plan but leave him unprotected against pneumococcus and meningococcus, the main OPSI pathogens.
whyNot.B: These live vaccines are not contraindicated by asplenia, but they do not protect against the encapsulated bacteria that cause post-splenectomy sepsis.
whyNot.C: Pneumococcal vaccine alone leaves him unprotected against meningococcal and Hib disease.
whyNot.E: A polysaccharide vaccine alone gives weaker, T-cell-independent responses and omits meningococcal and Hib protection.

items.objective: Select the vaccines indicated after emergency splenectomy.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman who had a splenectomy for trauma 10 years ago comes to the emergency department because of fever, chills and myalgias that began 6 hours ago. She is not sure whether her vaccines are current. Temperature is 39.6°C (103.3°F), pulse 124/min, respirations 24/min and blood pressure 94/56 mm Hg. She is alert. There is no neck stiffness or rash. Lungs are clear. Two sets of blood cultures have been drawn, and laboratory studies and a chest radiograph are pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Abdominal CT with IV contrast before antibiotics

options.label: D
options.html: Withhold antibiotics until the leukocyte count is available

options.label: E
options.html: Withhold antibiotics until blood culture results are known

items.explanationHtml:
Fever in an asplenic patient may be the start of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection, which can progress to septic shock and DIC within hours. After blood cultures, empiric IV antibiotics are given immediately: ceftriaxone for pneumococcus, meningococcus and Hib, plus vancomycin because she is hypotensive and resistant pneumococci are possible. Fluids and evaluation for the source proceed alongside.

Takeaway: fever in an asplenic patient is an emergency: cultures, then immediate IV ceftriaxone (with vancomycin if septic) without waiting for tests.

whyNot.A: Imaging may be needed later but must not delay antibiotics in suspected post-splenectomy sepsis.
whyNot.C: Standby oral amoxicillin-clavulanate is for patients who cannot reach care; she is hypotensive and needs IV therapy and admission.
whyNot.D: A normal or low leukocyte count does not exclude overwhelming sepsis, and waiting delays treatment.
whyNot.E: Culture results take a day or more; waiting can be fatal.

items.objective: Give immediate empiric IV antibiotics for fever in an asplenic patient.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man who had a splenectomy 6 years ago for hereditary spherocytosis is bitten on the hand by his neighbor's dog. He comes to an urgent care clinic 2 hours later. He has two small puncture wounds over the dorsum of the left hand without tendon involvement. He is afebrile. The dog is vaccinated against rabies and is available for observation. His tetanus vaccination is current. The wound is irrigated. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional management?
items.explanationHtml:
Asplenic patients are at risk of fulminant sepsis from Capnocytophaga canimorsus, a gram-negative rod in dog and cat mouths. Every dog or cat bite in an asplenic patient warrants prompt antibiotic prophylaxis; amoxicillin-clavulanate covers Capnocytophaga, Pasteurella, streptococci, staphylococci and anaerobes. Hand wounds are also high-risk independent of asplenia.

Takeaway: give amoxicillin-clavulanate after a dog or cat bite in an asplenic patient to cover Capnocytophaga and Pasteurella.

whyNot.B: Cephalexin lacks reliable activity against Pasteurella and anaerobes, so it is not appropriate for bite prophylaxis.
whyNot.C: Doxycycline is an alternative only with penicillin allergy, usually combined with anaerobic coverage.
whyNot.D: Observation is inappropriate because a hand bite in an asplenic patient carries a high risk of serious infection.
whyNot.E: Rabies prophylaxis is not needed for a vaccinated domestic dog that can be observed for 10 days.

items.objective: Prescribe antibiotic prophylaxis after an animal bite in an asplenic patient.

items.stemHtml: A 22-month-old boy with sickle cell anemia (HbSS) is brought to the emergency department because he has been pale, sleepy and refusing to walk since this morning. He had a mild upper respiratory infection 3 days ago. Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse 178/min and blood pressure 72/40 mm Hg. Capillary refill is 4 seconds. The spleen is firm and palpable 7 cm below the left costal margin; at a clinic visit 1 month ago it was 1 cm. Hemoglobin is 3.9 g/dL (his baseline is 8.2 g/dL), reticulocytes 14% and platelet count 86,000/mm3. Blood cultures are drawn and IV ceftriaxone is given. A fluid bolus is started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
A sudden fall in hemoglobin with a rapidly enlarging spleen, preserved reticulocytosis, thrombocytopenia and hypovolemic shock in a toddler with HbSS is acute splenic sequestration. Restoring circulating red cells is urgent: give a simple packed red cell transfusion, in modest aliquots, because the spleen releases trapped cells as it shrinks and over-transfusion can raise viscosity. Caregivers are taught to palpate the spleen, and recurrent episodes lead to splenectomy or chronic transfusion.

Takeaway: acute splenic sequestration is treated with prompt, modest-volume simple red cell transfusion.

whyNot.A: Splenectomy is considered after recurrent episodes, not during acute shock.
whyNot.B: Hydroxyurea reduces vaso-occlusive events over months and does not correct acute sequestration.
whyNot.C: IVIG treats immune thrombocytopenia, which does not cause this splenic enlargement with severe anemia.
whyNot.E: Exchange transfusion is used for stroke or acute chest syndrome; in profound anemia from sequestration the need is to add red cells, not exchange them.

items.objective: Manage acute splenic sequestration crisis in a child with sickle cell disease.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after his car struck a tree at moderate speed. He was restrained. He has left upper quadrant tenderness and abrasions over the left lower chest. On arrival, pulse is 118/min and blood pressure 98/62 mm Hg; after 1 L of crystalloid, pulse is 92/min and blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg, and these values stay stable over 30 minutes. A FAST examination shows fluid in the left upper quadrant. Hemoglobin is 12.6 g/dL. Chest radiography shows fractures of the left 9th and 10th ribs without pneumothorax. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the abdomen with IV contrast

items.explanationHtml:
He has responded to resuscitation and is hemodynamically stable, so the next step is CT of the abdomen with IV contrast to grade the splenic injury, look for active contrast extravasation and identify other injuries. Most stable patients with splenic injury are managed nonoperatively, with angioembolization for a contrast blush or pseudoaneurysm. Laparotomy is for instability despite resuscitation or failure of nonoperative management.

Takeaway: in a hemodynamically stable patient with a positive FAST, CT with IV contrast guides nonoperative management of splenic injury.

whyNot.B: Diagnostic peritoneal lavage has been largely replaced by FAST and CT and adds nothing once FAST is positive.
whyNot.C: He has a solid-organ injury with hemoperitoneum and needs admission and imaging, not discharge.
whyNot.D: Laparotomy is indicated for hemodynamic instability despite resuscitation, but he has stabilized.
whyNot.E: Angioembolization is guided by CT findings such as a contrast blush; it is not performed blindly.

items.objective: Choose CT with contrast for a hemodynamically stable patient with suspected splenic injury.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old high-school football player comes to the clinic 10 days after the onset of fever, sore throat and fatigue. A heterophile antibody test 5 days ago was positive. His fever has resolved, and he feels much better. The tonsils are enlarged without exudate, and there is posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. The spleen tip is palpable on deep inspiration. He asks when he can return to full-contact practice. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice about when he can return?

options.label: B
options.html: In 1 more week, if he remains well

options.label: C
options.html: At least 3 to 4 weeks after symptom onset, once well

options.label: D
options.html: No sooner than 6 months after symptom onset

options.label: E
options.html: After ultrasound shows a normal spleen size

items.explanationHtml:
Splenic rupture in infectious mononucleosis is uncommon but most likely in the first 3 weeks of illness, and it can follow minor blows. Athletes should avoid contact and collision sports and heavy lifting for at least 3 to 4 weeks from symptom onset, and until they are asymptomatic and the spleen is no longer palpable. Routine ultrasound is not required to clear return.

Takeaway: after mononucleosis, avoid contact sports for at least 3 to 4 weeks from symptom onset and until the spleen is no longer enlarged.

whyNot.A: Resolution of fever does not reduce splenic fragility, which peaks in the first weeks.
whyNot.B: One more week brings him only to about day 17, still within the highest-risk period, and his spleen remains palpable.
whyNot.D: Six months is far longer than needed; most athletes can return within 1 to 2 months.
whyNot.E: Ultrasound is not routinely required; clinical recovery, time from onset and a nonpalpable spleen guide return.

items.objective: Advise on return to contact sports after infectious mononucleosis.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman underwent laparoscopic splenectomy 4 years ago for chronic immune thrombocytopenia, after which her platelet count normalized. For the past month she has had easy bruising and gum bleeding. Platelet count is 14,000/mm3; hemoglobin and leukocyte count are normal. The peripheral smear shows large platelets, and no Howell-Jolly bodies or target cells are seen. HIV and hepatitis C tests are negative. Which of the following is most likely to identify the cause of her relapse?
items.explanationHtml:
After splenectomy, Howell-Jolly bodies are expected; their absence implies functioning splenic tissue. A hypertrophied accessory spleen can resume clearing antibody-coated platelets and cause ITP relapse. Scintigraphy with heat-damaged radiolabelled red cells, which splenic tissue avidly removes, localizes accessory spleens; laparoscopic removal can restore remission.

Takeaway: ITP relapse after splenectomy with no Howell-Jolly bodies suggests an accessory spleen; locate it with heat-damaged red-cell scintigraphy.

whyNot.A: ADAMTS13 is tested for TTP, which would cause schistocytes and hemolysis rather than isolated thrombocytopenia.
whyNot.B: Marrow examination would show normal or increased megakaryocytes in ITP and would not explain the missing Howell-Jolly bodies.
whyNot.D: H pylori testing is reasonable in ITP, but it does not explain the absence of Howell-Jolly bodies after splenectomy.
whyNot.E: Platelet antibody tests have poor sensitivity and would not identify retained splenic tissue.

items.objective: Investigate ITP relapse after splenectomy for an accessory spleen.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who takes warfarin is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after she developed sudden left-sided weakness and became drowsy. Blood pressure is 172/94 mm Hg. CT of the head shows a 30-mL right basal ganglia hemorrhage. INR is 3.4, and platelet count is 210,000/mm3. Warfarin is held, and blood pressure lowering is started. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Fresh frozen plasma plus oral vitamin K

options.label: E
options.html: Protamine sulfate plus IV vitamin K

items.explanationHtml:
Warfarin-associated intracerebral hemorrhage needs immediate reversal to limit hematoma expansion. 4-factor PCC supplies factors II, VII, IX and X and corrects the INR within minutes in a small volume; IV vitamin K is given at the same time so that the liver can make new factors and the correction lasts after PCC wears off. Plasma is a fallback only when PCC is unavailable.

Takeaway: for warfarin-associated major bleeding, give IV vitamin K plus 4-factor PCC.

whyNot.A: Plasma needs thawing, large volumes and longer correction time and is a fallback only if PCC is unavailable; oral vitamin K acts too slowly for an intracranial bleed.
whyNot.B: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran and adds nothing to warfarin reversal.
whyNot.D: Oral vitamin K takes many hours and is used for a high INR without bleeding.
whyNot.E: Protamine reverses heparin and has no effect on warfarin; vitamin K alone is too slow.

items.objective: Reverse warfarin with IV vitamin K and 4-factor PCC for intracranial hemorrhage.

items.stemHtml:
A 78-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after passing large amounts of maroon stool and nearly fainting. He has atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease and benign prostatic hyperplasia. His medication list:

MedicationDoseLast taken
Dabigatran150 mg twice daily4 hours ago
Metoprolol succinate50 mg dailythis morning
Tamsulosin0.4 mg nightlylast night
Omeprazole20 mg dailythis morning

Pulse is 112/min and blood pressure 86/52 mm Hg despite 2 L of crystalloid and 2 units of red cells. Laboratory results:

TestResultReference
Hemoglobin6.8 g/dL13.5-17.5 g/dL
Platelets188,000/mm3150,000-400,000/mm3
Creatinine2.0 mg/dL0.6-1.2 mg/dL
aPTT62 s25-40 s
Thrombin timemarkedly prolongednormal

Urgent endoscopy is planned. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment to reverse his anticoagulation?
items.explanationHtml:
He has life-threatening bleeding while taking dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, and reduced kidney function slows its elimination; the prolonged thrombin time and aPTT confirm drug effect. Idarucizumab, a Fab fragment that binds dabigatran, reverses it within minutes. If unavailable, 4-factor PCC or hemodialysis are alternatives. His dabigatran dose should also be reviewed given his kidney function once he recovers.

Takeaway: reverse dabigatran in life-threatening bleeding with idarucizumab; kidney impairment prolongs its effect.

whyNot.A: Andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors, not a direct thrombin inhibitor.
whyNot.B: Plasma does not neutralize dabigatran and adds volume without reliable correction.
whyNot.D: Vitamin K reverses warfarin and has no effect on dabigatran.
whyNot.E: Protamine neutralizes heparin, not dabigatran.

items.objective: Choose idarucizumab to reverse dabigatran in life-threatening bleeding.

items.stemHtml:
A 56-year-old woman with stage II breast cancer comes for a scheduled check 9 days after her second cycle of adjuvant docetaxel and cyclophosphamide. She received pegfilgrastim the day after each cycle. She feels tired but well and has no fever, chills, cough, dysuria or diarrhea. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse 84/min and blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg. Her implanted port site is clean. CBC results:

TestResultReference
Leukocytes1,400/mm34,500-11,000/mm3
Segmented neutrophils28%54-62%
Band forms4%3-5%
Lymphocytes58%25-33%
Hemoglobin10.9 g/dL12.0-16.0 g/dL
Platelets132,000/mm3150,000-400,000/mm3

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Fever precautions with home temperature monitoring

items.explanationHtml:
Her absolute neutrophil count is 1,400 x (0.28 + 0.04) = about 450/mm3, severe neutropenia at the expected nadir. She is afebrile and well, so she does not have febrile neutropenia and needs no antibiotics. The appropriate plan is education: check her temperature, avoid sick contacts, and come in immediately for a temperature of 38.0°C (100.4°F) or higher or any symptoms of infection. Counts should recover within days.

Takeaway: afebrile neutropenia in a well patient needs fever precautions, not empiric antibiotics or extra G-CSF.

whyNot.A: Empiric IV antipseudomonal therapy is for febrile neutropenia; she has no fever.
whyNot.B: She already received pegfilgrastim; adding therapeutic G-CSF for afebrile neutropenia is not recommended.
whyNot.D: Granulocyte transfusion is reserved for rare refractory infections in profound, prolonged neutropenia.
whyNot.E: Oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate is outpatient therapy for low-risk febrile neutropenia, which she does not have.

items.objective: Calculate the ANC and manage afebrile chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman with Graves disease started methimazole 6 weeks ago. She calls the clinic because of a temperature of 38.9°C (102.0°F) and a severe sore throat that began this morning. She has no cough or rash. Her palpitations have improved. She is not pregnant. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue methimazole and obtain a rapid streptococcal antigen test

options.label: B
options.html: Continue methimazole and start oral penicillin

options.label: C
options.html: Stop methimazole and obtain a CBC with differential today

options.label: E
options.html: Stop methimazole and schedule radioactive iodine therapy next week

items.explanationHtml:
Fever and sore throat in the first months of thionamide therapy may signal agranulocytosis. The drug is stopped immediately and a CBC with differential is obtained the same day. If the absolute neutrophil count is below 500/mm3, the drug is discontinued permanently, febrile patients are admitted for broad-spectrum antibiotics, and definitive therapy (radioactive iodine or surgery) is planned once she is well, with beta-blockade for symptoms.

Takeaway: fever or sore throat on a thionamide: stop the drug and check a CBC with differential immediately.

whyNot.A: Continuing methimazole risks worsening agranulocytosis; neutrophil count must be checked first.
whyNot.B: Treating presumed pharyngitis while continuing the drug misses a potentially fatal agranulocytosis.
whyNot.D: Switching to propylthiouracil risks cross-reactive agranulocytosis and should not be done if agranulocytosis is confirmed.
whyNot.E: Definitive therapy may be needed, but the immediate priority is to determine whether she is neutropenic and needs urgent treatment.

items.objective: Respond to fever and sore throat in a patient taking a thionamide.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man becomes short of breath and confused 40 minutes after bronchoscopy during which his airway was sprayed repeatedly with benzocaine. He has no history of anemia or hemolysis, and his G6PD activity was normal when tested last year before dapsone was considered. Pulse is 116/min, respirations 26/min and blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg.
