He has gray-blue lips. Pulse oximetry reads 84% on 15 L/min oxygen by nonrebreather mask. Arterial blood is dark brown; PaO2 is 245 mm Hg. Co-oximetry shows methemoglobin 34%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Symptomatic methemoglobinemia (confusion, dyspnea) at a level of 34% after benzocaine requires prompt treatment. With normal G6PD activity, IV methylene blue is first-line: it is reduced by NADPH-dependent methemoglobin reductase to leukomethylene blue, which converts ferric hemoglobin back to ferrous hemoglobin, usually within an hour. Stopping the agent and giving oxygen continue alongside.

Takeaway: give IV methylene blue for symptomatic acquired methemoglobinemia when G6PD activity is normal.

whyNot.A: Hyperbaric oxygen is a rescue for patients who cannot receive or do not respond to methylene blue.
whyNot.B: Ascorbic acid acts slowly and is reserved for G6PD deficiency or when methylene blue is unavailable.
whyNot.C: Hydroxocobalamin is the antidote for cyanide poisoning, not methemoglobinemia.
whyNot.E: Exchange transfusion is reserved for severe cases refractory to methylene blue or with contraindications to it.

items.objective: Treat symptomatic benzocaine-induced methemoglobinemia with methylene blue.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy with newly diagnosed T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and a mediastinal mass is to begin induction chemotherapy tomorrow. Leukocyte count is 168,000/mm3. Serum potassium is 4.6 mEq/L, phosphorus 5.4 mg/dL, calcium 9.0 mg/dL, uric acid 9.1 mg/dL and creatinine 0.6 mg/dL. Urine output is good. He had acute hemolysis after eating fava beans at age 5, and G6PD testing at that time showed severe deficiency. IV hydration has been started. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional measure to prevent tumor lysis syndrome?

options.label: E
options.html: Sodium bicarbonate infusion to alkalinize the urine

items.explanationHtml:
He is at high risk of tumor lysis syndrome (lymphoblastic leukemia with a very high count and bulky disease, and an already raised uric acid). Rasburicase would ordinarily be preferred, but it produces hydrogen peroxide and can cause severe hemolysis and methemoglobinemia in G6PD deficiency, so it is contraindicated. He should receive aggressive hydration plus allopurinol (which prevents new uric acid formation), with close electrolyte monitoring and early nephrology involvement in case dialysis is needed.

Takeaway: in G6PD deficiency, prevent tumor lysis with hydration and allopurinol; rasburicase is contraindicated.

whyNot.B: Colchicine treats gouty inflammation and does nothing to prevent uric acid nephropathy.
whyNot.C: Probenecid increases urinary uric acid excretion and would raise the risk of tubular crystal deposition.
whyNot.D: Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency because the hydrogen peroxide it generates causes hemolysis.
whyNot.E: Urine alkalinization is no longer recommended; it can promote calcium phosphate and xanthine precipitation.

items.objective: Choose allopurinol over rasburicase for tumor lysis prevention in G6PD deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman is hospitalized for MRSA bacteremia from a septic knee joint. She has received IV vancomycin for 9 days, with clearance of her blood cultures. Today she has new petechiae on her legs and oozing from her intravenous site. Platelet count is 6,000/mm3, down from 240,000/mm3 3 days ago. Hemoglobin and leukocyte count are unchanged. PT, aPTT and fibrinogen are normal. The smear shows no schistocytes or platelet clumps. She has received no heparin during this admission, and her line is flushed with saline. She has no signs of sepsis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Start intravenous immune globulin and continue vancomycin

options.label: D
options.html: Stop vancomycin and change to daptomycin

options.label: E
options.html: Stop vancomycin and continue without antibiotics

items.explanationHtml:
An abrupt, isolated fall to a very low platelet count about a week after starting vancomycin, with normal coagulation tests and no heparin exposure, suggests vancomycin-induced immune thrombocytopenia. The drug must be stopped; continued exposure keeps the drug-dependent antibodies active. Her bacteremia still needs treatment, so she should switch to an unrelated anti-MRSA agent such as daptomycin. Platelets can be transfused for bleeding, and counts usually recover within about a week.

Takeaway: suspected drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia: stop the drug and substitute an unrelated agent.

whyNot.A: Transfused platelets are destroyed rapidly while the drug is still present; the culprit must be stopped.
whyNot.B: Argatroban treats heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, but she has had no heparin exposure and is bleeding, not clotting.
whyNot.C: IVIG may help severe bleeding, but continuing vancomycin would sustain the thrombocytopenia.
whyNot.E: MRSA bacteremia needs a full course of therapy; stopping all antibiotics is unsafe.

items.objective: Manage drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia by stopping the drug and substituting an alternative.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man is receiving a continuous intravenous infusion of unfractionated heparin for a pulmonary embolism. Because of a pump programming error, he received ten times the intended infusion rate over the past 2 hours. He now has hematuria and bleeding from his arterial line site. Pulse is 104/min and blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg. aPTT is above 150 seconds. The infusion has been stopped. Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to give?
items.explanationHtml:
Unfractionated heparin is a highly negatively charged polysaccharide; protamine sulfate, a positively charged protein, binds and neutralizes it immediately. The dose is calculated from the heparin given over the last few hours, and protamine is infused slowly because of the risk of hypotension and anaphylaxis. Heparin's short half-life also helps, but protamine is indicated for active bleeding with a very high aPTT.

Takeaway: protamine sulfate reverses unfractionated heparin.

whyNot.A: Andexanet alfa reverses oral factor Xa inhibitors, not unfractionated heparin.
whyNot.B: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran only.
whyNot.D: Tranexamic acid inhibits fibrinolysis but does not neutralize heparin.
whyNot.E: Vitamin K reverses warfarin; heparin does not affect vitamin K-dependent factor synthesis.

items.objective: Reverse unfractionated heparin with protamine sulfate.

items.stemHtml: A 3-day-old boy born at 39 weeks' gestation is evaluated for yellow skin that his parents first noticed yesterday. He is breastfeeding 9 times daily and has 5 wet diapers and 4 yellow stools daily. He has lost 6% of his birth weight. He appears well. Examination shows jaundice to the mid-abdomen; the liver and spleen are not palpable. Serum total bilirubin is 11.2 mg/dL and direct bilirubin is 0.3 mg/dL. Maternal and infant blood types are both O, Rh-positive, and a direct antiglobulin test is negative. Which of the following best explains the main reason for his limited ability to clear bilirubin?

options.label: C
options.html: Impaired canalicular secretion of conjugated bilirubin

options.label: D
options.html: Maternal IgG antibodies against fetal red cells

items.explanationHtml:
This well, feeding, term infant has physiologic jaundice: onset after 24 hours, an unconjugated pattern and no evidence of hemolysis. Hepatic UGT1A1 activity is low at birth and matures over the first weeks, so conjugation cannot keep up with the higher bilirubin load produced by a large, short-lived neonatal red cell mass. Enterohepatic recirculation adds to the load.

Takeaway: physiologic newborn jaundice is unconjugated, appears after 24 hours and reflects immature UGT1A1 plus increased bilirubin production.

whyNot.A: Beta-glucuronidase is active in the newborn gut and increases deconjugation and reabsorption; a deficiency would lower bilirubin.
whyNot.C: A canalicular defect causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia; his direct bilirubin is normal.
whyNot.D: Mother and infant are both group O, Rh-positive, and the antiglobulin test is negative, so there is no isoimmune hemolysis.
whyNot.E: Biliary obstruction causes a rise in direct bilirubin and pale stools; his stools are yellow and direct bilirubin is normal.

items.objective: Explain the mechanisms of physiologic unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in a term newborn.

items.stemHtml: A 5-month-old girl born at 38 weeks' gestation is brought for a well-child visit. She has had two upper respiratory infections that resolved without treatment. Growth and development are normal. As part of a research study, serum immunoglobulins are measured; IgG is lower than it was in her cord blood sample and below the adult reference range, while IgM and IgA are low but rising compared with birth. Blood count and lymphocyte subsets are normal. Which of the following best explains her IgG concentration?

options.label: A
options.html: Catabolism of transplacental maternal IgG before her own synthesis has risen

options.label: B
options.html: Defective class switching due to absent CD40 ligand

options.label: C
options.html: Failure of B-cell maturation from absent Bruton tyrosine kinase

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of IgG through the gut from protein-losing enteropathy

options.label: E
options.html: Transfer of IgG into breast milk from the infant's serum

items.explanationHtml:
Maternal IgG crosses the placenta by FcRn-mediated transcytosis, mostly in the third trimester, so cord IgG is near adult levels. Its half-life is about 3–4 weeks. The infant's own IgG production rises slowly, so total IgG reaches a physiologic nadir at about 3–6 months. IgM and IgA do not cross the placenta and rise steadily from low levels after birth.

Takeaway: the 3–6-month IgG nadir is physiologic: maternal IgG has been catabolised and infant synthesis is still low.

whyNot.B: CD40 ligand deficiency gives high or normal IgM with low IgG and recurrent opportunistic infections; her IgM is low and rising and she is well.
whyNot.C: Bruton agammaglobulinemia affects boys and causes absent B cells; her lymphocyte subsets are normal.
whyNot.D: She is growing normally with no diarrhea or edema, and the pattern fits normal infant immunoglobulin kinetics.
whyNot.E: Antibody moves from mother to infant in milk (mainly secretory IgA), not from infant serum into milk.

items.objective: Explain the timing of the physiologic IgG nadir in infancy.

items.stemHtml: A 10-month-old boy is brought to the clinic because his legs have looked bowed since he started pulling to stand. He was born at term and has been exclusively breastfed without supplements; he eats few solid foods. The family lives in a northern city and he spends little time outdoors. Examination shows widened wrists, bead-like swellings along the costochondral junctions and bowing of both legs. Serum calcium is 8.5 mg/dL, phosphorus is 2.6 mg/dL, and alkaline phosphatase is markedly increased. Which of the following would most likely have prevented this condition?

options.label: A
options.html: Daily oral iron supplementation from 4 months of age

options.label: B
options.html: Daily oral vitamin D supplementation from the first days of life

options.label: C
options.html: Early introduction of whole cow's milk at 6 months of age

options.label: E
options.html: Oral fluoride supplementation from 6 months of age

items.explanationHtml:
Human milk contains little vitamin D, and this infant had limited sun exposure. Vitamin D deficiency reduces intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, secondary hyperparathyroidism lowers phosphate further, and growth-plate cartilage fails to mineralize: widened metaphyses, a rachitic rosary and bowing, with a high alkaline phosphatase. 400 IU of vitamin D daily, started in the first days of life, is recommended for every breastfed or partially breastfed infant.

Takeaway: breastfed infants need 400 IU of vitamin D daily from the first days of life to prevent nutritional rickets.

whyNot.A: Iron prevents iron deficiency anemia; it does not affect bone mineralization.
whyNot.C: Whole cow's milk is not recommended before 12 months and is not the preventive standard for rickets.
whyNot.D: Vitamin K at birth prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding, not rickets.
whyNot.E: Fluoride prevents dental caries and has no role in preventing rickets.

items.objective: Identify vitamin D supplementation as the measure that prevents nutritional rickets in breastfed infants.

items.stemHtml: A 22-month-old girl is brought to the clinic because of pallor and fatigue. She drinks about 40 oz (1.2 L) of whole cow's milk daily from a bottle and eats little else. Examination shows pale conjunctivae and no hepatosplenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL, MCV is 62 fL, and red cell distribution width is increased. Stool is positive for occult blood. Which of the following best explains how her diet has caused this anemia?

options.label: A
options.html: Cow's milk calcium and casein reduce iron absorption, and milk displaces iron-rich foods

options.label: B
options.html: Cow's milk lacks folate and causes impaired DNA synthesis in erythroid precursors

options.label: C
options.html: Cow's milk protein causes immune-mediated hemolysis of red cells

options.label: D
options.html: Cow's milk raises hepcidin and traps iron in macrophages

options.label: E
options.html: Cow's milk vitamin B12 is poorly absorbed from the toddler intestine

items.explanationHtml:
Excessive cow's milk intake is a classic cause of toddler iron deficiency. Cow's milk is low in iron, its calcium and casein inhibit non-heme iron absorption, the volume displaces iron-rich foods, and in some young children it causes occult intestinal blood loss. The microcytic, hypochromic anemia with a high RDW fits iron deficiency. Intake is best kept below about 24 oz a day after 12 months, and whole milk is not introduced before 12 months.

Takeaway: excess cow's milk causes toddler iron deficiency by low iron content, inhibited absorption, food displacement and occult blood loss.

whyNot.B: Folate deficiency gives a macrocytic anemia; her MCV is low.
whyNot.C: Milk protein does not cause hemolysis, and the low MCV with high RDW fits iron deficiency.
whyNot.D: Raised hepcidin is the mechanism of anemia of inflammation; she has no inflammatory illness and has dietary iron deficiency.
whyNot.E: B12 deficiency is macrocytic, and cow's milk is a good source of B12.

items.objective: Explain how excessive cow's milk intake causes iron deficiency anemia in a toddler.

items.stemHtml: A 9-month-old boy born at 29 weeks' gestation is evaluated because he cannot sit without support. When his head is turned to one side, the arm on that side extends while the opposite arm flexes; a sudden backward drop of the head produces arm abduction and extension. Muscle tone is increased in the legs, deep tendon reflexes are brisk, and the legs cross when he is held upright. Which of the following best explains the persistence of these infant reflexes?

options.label: A
options.html: Anterior horn cell degeneration in the spinal cord

options.label: C
options.html: Failure of descending cortical inhibition from upper motor neuron injury

options.label: D
options.html: Impaired acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction

options.label: E
options.html: Primary myopathy with loss of muscle fibres

items.explanationHtml:
The asymmetric tonic neck and Moro reflexes are normally suppressed by about 4–6 months as cortical and corticospinal pathways mature and inhibit brainstem reflex patterns. Persistence at 9 months with spasticity, hyperreflexia and scissoring indicates an upper motor neuron lesion; in a very preterm infant, periventricular white-matter injury causing spastic cerebral palsy is the likely cause.

Takeaway: primitive reflexes that persist beyond 6 months with spasticity point to an upper motor neuron lesion such as cerebral palsy.

whyNot.A: Anterior horn cell disease (spinal muscular atrophy) causes hypotonia and absent reflexes, not spasticity.
whyNot.B: A peripheral neuropathy lowers tone and reflexes; it does not release primitive reflexes.
whyNot.D: A neuromuscular junction disorder causes weakness and hypotonia without hyperreflexia.
whyNot.E: Myopathies cause weakness with low tone and depressed reflexes.

items.objective: Relate persistence of primitive reflexes to loss of descending cortical inhibition.

items.stemHtml: A child is brought to a clinic for a routine visit. Her parents report that she pedals a tricycle, walks upstairs placing one foot on each step, and speaks in three-word sentences that a stranger understands most of the time. During the visit she copies a circle but cannot copy a cross. She plays pretend games and takes turns with her older brother. Which of the following is the most likely age of this child if her development is typical?
items.explanationHtml:
Riding a tricycle, alternating feet on the stairs, copying a circle, three-word sentences understood by strangers about three quarters of the time and imaginative, turn-taking play together place this child at about 3 years. The inability to copy a cross (about 4 years) caps the estimate.

Takeaway: a typical 3-year-old pedals a tricycle, copies a circle and speaks in three-word sentences that strangers mostly understand.

whyNot.A: At 18 months a child runs stiffly and uses single words; tricycle riding and copying a circle come later.
whyNot.B: A 2-year-old uses two-word phrases, about half understood by strangers, and copies a line rather than a circle.
whyNot.D: A 4-year-old hops on one foot, copies a cross and is fully intelligible to strangers.
whyNot.E: A 5-year-old skips and copies a triangle.

items.objective: Estimate a child's age from milestones across motor, language and social domains.

items.stemHtml: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because her parents have noticed that her feet point inward when she walks and she trips occasionally when running. She sits comfortably on the floor with her knees together and her feet out to the sides. She is at the 50th percentile for height. When she stands, both kneecaps face inward. Internal rotation of both hips is markedly increased and external rotation is reduced; thigh–foot angles are neutral and the feet are normally shaped. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her gait?
items.explanationHtml:
In-toeing at 3–8 years with inward-facing kneecaps, W-sitting and increased hip internal rotation is typical of increased femoral anteversion. It is a normal rotational variant that usually improves by about 8–10 years; braces and special shoes do not alter its course.

Takeaway: in-toeing at 3–8 years with inward-pointing kneecaps and excess hip internal rotation is femoral anteversion.

whyNot.A: Hip dysplasia limits abduction and causes a limp or leg-length difference, not symmetric increased internal rotation.
whyNot.C: Tibial torsion turns the thigh–foot angle inward and presents earlier, at 1–3 years; her thigh–foot angles are neutral.
whyNot.D: Metatarsus adductus is a forefoot deformity of infancy with a curved lateral border; her feet are normally shaped.
whyNot.E: Slipped epiphysis occurs in adolescents, causes pain and loss of internal rotation, the opposite of her finding.

items.objective: Distinguish the causes of in-toeing by age and examination findings.

items.stemHtml: A male newborn delivered at 39 weeks' gestation is examined at 2 hours of age. He is pink, breathing comfortably, and has a soft continuous murmur at the left upper sternal border. Echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart with a small left-to-right shunt through the ductus arteriosus. Repeat echocardiography at 3 days of age shows that the ductus has closed. Which of the following changes after birth most directly caused closure of the ductus?

options.label: A
options.html: Fall in arterial PO<sub>2</sub> and rise in circulating bradykinin

options.label: B
options.html: Fall in left atrial pressure below right atrial pressure

options.label: C
options.html: Rise in arterial PO<sub>2</sub> and fall in circulating prostaglandin E<sub>2</sub>

options.label: D
options.html: Rise in pulmonary vascular resistance above systemic resistance

options.label: E
options.html: Rise in umbilical venous return to the right atrium

items.explanationHtml:
In fetal life the ductus is held open by low PO2 and by prostaglandin E2 made mainly by the placenta. After birth, oxygenated blood constricts ductal smooth muscle, and PGE2 falls because the placenta is gone and the perfused lungs clear it. Functional closure usually occurs within the first days in a term infant; fibrosis later forms the ligamentum arteriosum.

Takeaway: the ductus closes after birth because arterial oxygen rises and prostaglandin E2 falls; PGE1 infusion reverses this, COX inhibitors promote it.

whyNot.A: Arterial PO2 rises after birth; a fall would tend to keep the ductus open.
whyNot.B: Left atrial pressure rises above right after birth; this closes the foramen ovale, not the ductus.
whyNot.D: Pulmonary resistance falls after birth; a persistently high value is the mechanism of persistent pulmonary hypertension.
whyNot.E: Umbilical venous flow stops when the cord is clamped.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of postnatal ductus arteriosus closure.

items.stemHtml: A 4-month-old girl, exclusively breastfed, attends a daycare centre where several children have had rotavirus diarrhea over the past month. She has remained well. Researchers studying the outbreak find that her mother's milk contains antibody that binds rotavirus. This milk antibody is mostly produced by plasma cells located in which of the following sites, and in which form?

options.label: A
options.html: Infant intestinal lamina propria, as monomeric IgG

options.label: B
options.html: Infant mesenteric lymph nodes, as pentameric IgM

options.label: C
options.html: Maternal bone marrow, as monomeric IgG

options.label: D
options.html: Maternal mammary gland, as dimeric secretory IgA

items.explanationHtml:
Plasma cells primed in the mother's gut-associated lymphoid tissue home to the lactating breast (the enteromammary link) and secrete dimeric IgA joined by J chain. Epithelial polymeric immunoglobulin receptor carries it into milk, leaving the secretory component attached. In the infant gut it binds pathogens without being absorbed, giving protection matched to the mother's environment.

Takeaway: breast milk protects the infant gut mainly with secretory IgA from mammary plasma cells primed in the mother's gut.

whyNot.A: Infant plasma cells make little antibody at 4 months, and the antibody in milk is maternal.
whyNot.B: The antibody comes from the mother, and IgM is a minor component of milk.
whyNot.C: Marrow plasma cells make serum IgG, which reaches the fetus by the placenta; milk antibody is mainly secretory IgA.
whyNot.E: IgE is not a protective milk antibody against enteric viruses.

items.objective: Describe the source and structure of the protective antibody in human milk.

items.stemHtml: A 10-hour-old girl born at 38 weeks' gestation is noted to be jaundiced. Pregnancy was uncomplicated. The mother's blood group is O, Rh-positive; the infant is group A, Rh-positive. Serum total bilirubin is 9.8 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL and reticulocytes 9% (reference for newborns 3–7%). The direct antiglobulin test is weakly positive, and the peripheral smear shows spherocytes. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of her jaundice?

options.label: A
options.html: Deficient hepatic uptake of bilirubin from low ligandin

options.label: B
options.html: Inherited defect of the red cell membrane protein spectrin

options.label: C
options.html: Maternal anti-A IgG crossing the placenta and coating fetal red cells

options.label: D
options.html: Maternal anti-A IgM crossing the placenta and fixing complement

options.label: E
options.html: Red cell oxidant injury from glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

items.explanationHtml:
Jaundice in the first 24 hours is never physiologic. A group O mother has naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B; some is IgG, which crosses the placenta by FcRn and coats group A or B fetal red cells. Splenic macrophages remove membrane, making spherocytes, and hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin. ABO disease can occur in a first pregnancy because no prior sensitization is needed, and the antiglobulin test is often only weakly positive because fetal cells carry few A or B antigens.

Takeaway: jaundice before 24 hours with an O mother, an A or B infant and a positive antiglobulin test is ABO isoimmune hemolysis from maternal IgG.

whyNot.A: Low ligandin contributes to physiologic jaundice, which appears after 24 hours and lacks hemolysis.
whyNot.B: Hereditary spherocytosis causes spherocytes but a negative antiglobulin test; the positive test and ABO mismatch point to antibody.
whyNot.D: IgM does not cross the placenta; only IgG does.
whyNot.E: G6PD deficiency causes hemolysis with a negative antiglobulin test and bite or blister cells rather than spherocytes.

items.objective: Identify ABO hemolytic disease as a cause of jaundice in the first day of life.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl has had breast development for 6 months and a growth spurt; her bone age is 10 years. Basal LH is in the pubertal range, and LH rises sharply after GnRH stimulation. Brain MRI is normal. She is started on a long-acting GnRH agonist given as a depot injection every 3 months. After a brief rise in gonadotropins during the first weeks, LH and estradiol fall to prepubertal levels. Which of the following best explains this suppression?

options.label: A
options.html: Competitive blockade of estrogen receptors in the breast and growth plate

options.label: B
options.html: Desensitization and downregulation of pituitary GnRH receptors

options.label: E
options.html: Negative feedback from increased circulating inhibin

items.explanationHtml:
Gonadotrophs respond to GnRH only when it arrives in pulses. Continuous exposure to a long-acting agonist first stimulates release (the flare), then uncouples and downregulates GnRH receptors, so LH and FSH fall and the gonads return to a prepubertal state. This is the treatment for central precocious puberty.

Takeaway: continuous GnRH agonist exposure downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors after an initial flare; pulsatile GnRH stimulates.

whyNot.A: A GnRH agonist acts on the pituitary; estrogen receptor blockade describes a selective estrogen receptor modulator.
whyNot.C: Aromatase inhibitors block estrogen synthesis in tissue; the agonist lowers LH itself.
whyNot.D: The drug acts at the pituitary GnRH receptor, downstream of kisspeptin signalling.
whyNot.E: Inhibin selectively suppresses FSH; it does not explain the fall in LH and estradiol.

items.objective: Explain why continuous GnRH agonist therapy suppresses the reproductive axis.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because of body odour and a few dark pubic hairs over the past 4 months. She has no breast development, and her height has tracked the 60th percentile since infancy. Blood pressure is normal and there is no clitoromegaly. Bone age is 8 years. Serum DHEA-sulfate is mildly increased for age but in the range typical of early puberty; LH, FSH and 17-hydroxyprogesterone are prepubertal or normal. Which of the following structures is the most likely source of the hormone responsible for her findings?
items.explanationHtml:
Pubic hair and body odour without breast development, normal growth and a near-normal bone age fit premature adrenarche. Maturation of the zona reticularis raises DHEA and DHEA-S independently of gonadotropins. A normal 17-hydroxyprogesterone and normal blood pressure argue against congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and the absence of rapid virilization and growth acceleration argues against a tumor.

Takeaway: adrenarche reflects zona reticularis DHEA/DHEA-S production and is independent of the gonadotropin axis.

whyNot.A: The zona fasciculata makes cortisol; adrenal androgens come mainly from the zona reticularis.
whyNot.B: The zona glomerulosa makes aldosterone and lacks the 17-alpha-hydroxylase activity needed for androgens.
whyNot.D: Granulosa cells make estradiol under FSH; she has no breast development and gonadotropins are prepubertal.
whyNot.E: Theca androgen production is LH-driven and accompanies gonadarche; her gonadotropins are prepubertal.

items.objective: Distinguish adrenarche from gonadarche by its hormonal source.

items.stemHtml: An 11-year-old boy is seen for a sports physical examination. He has no pubic or axillary hair and his penis is prepubertal in size. Each testis measures 5 mL by orchidometer (prepubertal volume is under 4 mL), and the scrotal skin is slightly thinner and redder than before. Which of the following cell populations accounts for most of the increase in testicular volume at this stage?
items.explanationHtml:
Testicular enlargement to about 4 mL or more is the first physical sign of puberty in boys (SMR 2). Most testicular volume is seminiferous tubules, so the enlargement reflects FSH-driven proliferation of Sertoli cells and the start of germ-cell expansion, with testosterone from Leydig cells acting locally. Pubic hair and penile growth come later.

Takeaway: testicular enlargement is the first sign of male puberty and mostly reflects growth of the seminiferous tubules.

whyNot.A: Interstitial stroma contributes little to testicular volume.
whyNot.B: Leydig cells sit between the tubules and are a small fraction of testicular volume, although they make testosterone.
whyNot.C: Myoid cells form a thin layer around each tubule and do not account for the volume increase.
whyNot.E: Vascular growth contributes negligibly to testicular volume.

items.objective: Identify the first sign of male puberty and the tissue that produces it.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old man is evaluated for continued growth in height; he has grown 4 cm over the past 2 years. He is 204 cm tall with long arms and genu valgum. He has normal secondary sexual characteristics. Radiographs show open epiphyses and low bone mineral density. Serum testosterone is increased, estradiol is undetectable, and LH and FSH are increased. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his findings?
items.explanationHtml:
Estrogen, not testosterone, is the main signal for growth-plate fusion in both sexes. In aromatase deficiency testosterone cannot be converted to estradiol, so epiphyses stay open, linear growth continues into adulthood, and bone density is low. Loss of estrogen feedback raises LH and FSH and testosterone rises. Estrogen replacement closes the epiphyses.

Takeaway: estrogen made by aromatase drives epiphyseal fusion in both sexes; its absence in men leads to tall stature with open growth plates.

whyNot.A: Androgen insensitivity causes undervirilization and a female or ambiguous phenotype; he has normal male sexual development.
whyNot.C: Excess GH after puberty causes acromegaly; it would not explain undetectable estradiol.
whyNot.D: Kallmann syndrome causes low LH, FSH and testosterone with absent puberty.
whyNot.E: Klinefelter syndrome gives low testosterone with small testes and often gynecomastia; his testosterone is high.

items.objective: Explain the role of estrogen in pubertal growth-plate closure in males.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because of a tender lump under his left nipple for 3 months. He is otherwise well and takes no medications or supplements; he does not use cannabis or anabolic steroids. He has SMR 3 pubic hair and genitalia, and his testes are 10 mL each with no masses. Examination shows a 2-cm firm, mobile, mildly tender disc of tissue directly beneath the left areola. Which of the following best explains this finding?

options.label: A
options.html: Excess prolactin secretion from a pituitary microadenoma

options.label: B
options.html: Primary testicular failure with loss of testosterone

options.label: C
options.html: Production of human chorionic gonadotropin by a germ cell tumor

options.label: D
options.html: Proliferation of fat without glandular tissue

options.label: E
options.html: Transient increase in the estradiol-to-testosterone ratio during puberty

items.explanationHtml:
Pubertal gynecomastia is common in mid-puberty. Estradiol (partly from aromatization of rising androgens) increases relatively earlier than free testosterone, and the transient higher ratio stimulates ductal and stromal breast tissue. It is firm, subareolar and sometimes tender, may be unilateral, and usually regresses within about 6 months to 2 years.

Takeaway: pubertal gynecomastia reflects a temporary rise in estrogen relative to androgen and usually regresses without treatment.

whyNot.A: Prolactinoma causes hypogonadism and galactorrhea, not isolated tender subareolar tissue in a normally progressing puberty.
whyNot.B: His testes are normal in size for his stage; gonadal failure would give small firm testes.
whyNot.C: The testes are normal and without masses, and the presentation fits a common benign variant.
whyNot.D: Fatty enlargement (pseudogynecomastia) is soft and not a firm, tender subareolar disc.

items.objective: Explain the hormonal basis of normal pubertal gynecomastia.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because she has been falling asleep in her first-period class. Over the past year she has been unable to fall asleep before about 1 AM, although she goes to bed at 10 PM. On school days she wakes at 6:30 AM with difficulty; on weekends she sleeps until about 11 AM and wakes refreshed. Her mood, appetite and school performance are otherwise good. She does not snore. Which of the following best explains her sleep pattern?

options.label: A
options.html: Increased slow-wave sleep from pubertal growth hormone secretion

options.label: B
options.html: Intrusion of REM sleep into wakefulness from hypocretin loss

options.label: C
options.html: Later evening melatonin onset from a pubertal shift in circadian timing

options.label: D
options.html: Obstruction of the upper airway during sleep

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced total sleep need after the growth spurt

items.explanationHtml:
During puberty the circadian clock shifts later: evening melatonin onset moves later and homeostatic sleep pressure builds more slowly, so adolescents cannot fall asleep early. Fixed early school start times then cut sleep short, causing daytime sleepiness and weekend catch-up sleep. Sleep is normal in quality when timing is free.

Takeaway: adolescent sleep-phase delay reflects a later circadian rhythm (later melatonin onset), not reduced sleep need.

whyNot.A: Slow-wave sleep actually declines across adolescence, and it does not explain the late sleep onset.
whyNot.B: Hypocretin loss causes narcolepsy with cataplexy or sleep paralysis; she sleeps well when allowed to choose her timing.
whyNot.D: She does not snore and wakes refreshed after unrestricted sleep, which argues against sleep-disordered breathing.
whyNot.E: Adolescents still need about 8–10 hours of sleep; her sleepiness reflects a shortfall.

items.objective: Explain the physiology of sleep-phase delay in adolescence.

items.stemHtml: In a functional MRI study, 14-year-olds and 25-year-olds perform a task in which they choose between a safe option and a risky option with a larger possible reward. When peers are watching, the 14-year-olds choose the risky option on more trials than when alone, while the adults' choices do not change. During risky choices in front of peers, the adolescents show greater activity in the ventral striatum than the adults. Which of the following developmental patterns best explains this result?

options.label: A
options.html: Completed prefrontal myelination with immature reward circuits

options.label: B
options.html: Early pubertal reward sensitivity with later-maturing prefrontal control

options.label: C
options.html: Increased synapse formation in the prefrontal cortex throughout adolescence

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of amygdala responsiveness at the onset of puberty

options.label: E
options.html: Regression of white matter volume during the teenage years

items.explanationHtml:
Reward and emotional circuits (ventral striatum, amygdala) become more reactive early in puberty, while the prefrontal control network matures more slowly, with pruning and myelination continuing into the mid-20s. This mismatch favours sensation-seeking and peer-influenced risk-taking, most visible in emotionally charged or social settings.

Takeaway: adolescent risk-taking reflects early reward-system sensitivity outpacing the slower maturation of prefrontal control.

whyNot.A: Prefrontal myelination continues into the mid-20s, and reward circuits are highly reactive in adolescence.
whyNot.C: Adolescence is marked by net synaptic pruning of cortical grey matter, not net synapse gain.
whyNot.D: Limbic responsiveness rises in early adolescence rather than falling.
whyNot.E: White matter volume rises through adolescence with continued myelination.

items.objective: Describe the mismatch in brain maturation that underlies adolescent risk-taking.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl who runs 70 km per week is evaluated because she has not had a menstrual period. Breast development began at 12 years and has reached SMR 3. Her BMI is 16.5 kg/m2 and body fat is low. She eats a restricted diet but does not wish to lose weight. Serum LH, FSH and estradiol are low; prolactin, TSH and a pregnancy test are normal. Which of the following hormonal changes most directly links her low energy stores to her reproductive findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Decreased leptin reducing hypothalamic GnRH pulse activity

options.label: B
options.html: Excess adrenal androgen suppressing pituitary FSH release

options.label: C
options.html: Increased inhibin B blocking FSH synthesis

options.label: D
options.html: Increased thyroid hormone accelerating estrogen clearance

options.label: E
options.html: Primary ovarian failure from autoimmune oophoritis

items.explanationHtml:
Adipose tissue signals energy reserve through leptin, which acts on hypothalamic kisspeptin and related circuits as a permissive signal for GnRH pulsatility. With low energy availability, leptin falls, GnRH pulses slow, LH and FSH fall and estradiol stays low: functional hypothalamic hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. This is part of relative energy deficiency in sport and threatens bone mass.

Takeaway: low leptin from low energy stores slows GnRH pulses and causes functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

whyNot.B: Adrenal androgen excess causes hirsutism and acne, and does not explain the low-energy context.
whyNot.C: Inhibin B is low when the gonads are quiet; it would not lower LH.
whyNot.D: Her TSH is normal, and energy deficiency tends to lower thyroid hormone activity.
whyNot.E: Ovarian failure raises FSH and LH; hers are low, indicating a central cause.

items.objective: Explain how energy deficiency suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.

items.stemHtml: In a study of children followed through puberty, blood is sampled every 20 minutes for 24 hours at yearly intervals. In one boy aged 10 years, at a time when his testes are still prepubertal in size and his daytime gonadotropin values are low, a new change in LH secretion is detected for the first time. Which of the following is the most likely change?

options.label: A
options.html: A continuous, non-pulsatile rise in LH throughout the day

options.label: B
options.html: A fall in LH pulse frequency during the night

options.label: C
options.html: An increase in daytime LH pulse amplitude with no night change

options.label: D
options.html: An increase in LH pulse amplitude during sleep

options.label: E
options.html: Loss of LH response to GnRH from the pituitary

items.explanationHtml:
The first detectable hormonal event of gonadarche is a sleep-associated increase in LH pulse amplitude, which precedes physical signs. As puberty advances, daytime pulses increase too and the day–night difference fades. This is why a morning (soon-after-waking) LH sample is most informative when assessing early central puberty.

Takeaway: gonadarche begins with sleep-entrained increases in LH pulse amplitude, before any physical change.

whyNot.A: Normal gonadotropin secretion is pulsatile; continuous exposure would suppress the axis.
whyNot.B: Early puberty brings an increase, not a fall, in nocturnal LH activity.
whyNot.C: Daytime pulses rise later; the earliest change is sleep-related.
whyNot.E: Pituitary responsiveness increases at puberty rather than being lost.

items.objective: Identify the earliest hormonal change of gonadarche.

items.stemHtml: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because she had her first menstrual period 2 months ago. Breast development began when she was 10 years old and is now SMR 4. Over the past 2 years she grew rapidly, but her growth has slowed during the past 6 months. Her parents ask how much taller she will grow. Which of the following is the most accurate counsel about her remaining growth?

options.label: A
options.html: Her growth has ended because menarche marks epiphyseal fusion

options.label: B
options.html: She has most of her growth spurt still ahead of her

options.label: C
options.html: She will grow a limited amount more, as her growth spurt has peaked

options.label: D
options.html: She will grow at her peak velocity until about 16 years of age

options.label: E
options.html: Her remaining growth depends mainly on adrenal androgen output

items.explanationHtml:
In girls the growth spurt comes early: peak height velocity occurs at about SMR 2–3, before menarche. Menarche usually follows thelarche by about 2–2½ years, when growth is already decelerating; most girls gain only a few more centimetres as rising estrogen closes the epiphyses. In boys, by contrast, the spurt comes late (SMR 3–4).

Takeaway: menarche occurs after peak height velocity, so girls have only limited growth left once periods begin.

whyNot.A: Growth plates are not yet fused at menarche; girls typically gain a few more centimetres.
whyNot.B: In girls peak height velocity comes before menarche, around SMR 2–3.
whyNot.D: Height velocity falls after the peak; it does not continue at its maximum for years.
whyNot.E: Remaining growth depends on how much growth-plate cartilage remains before estrogen-driven fusion.

items.objective: Relate menarche to the timing of the female pubertal growth spurt.

items.stemHtml:
A 28-hour-old boy born at 39 weeks' gestation after an uncomplicated pregnancy is screened in the newborn nursery before discharge. Prenatal ultrasonography was normal. He is feeding well, and vital signs are normal. Examination shows no murmur, normal femoral pulses and no respiratory distress. Pulse oximetry results are shown.

TimeRight hand SpO2Foot SpO2
Screen 1 (28 h)94%92%
Screen 2 (29 h)93%92%
Screen 3 (30 h)94%91%

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Discharge with a routine visit in 2 days

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat pulse oximetry at 48 hours of age

items.explanationHtml:
Critical congenital heart disease screening is done after 24 hours on the right hand and a foot. A pass needs 95% or more in either site with a hand–foot difference of 3 points or less. Values of 90–94% in both sites are repeated; if they persist, the screen is failed even in a well-appearing infant. A failed screen calls for a full evaluation, including echocardiography, while also considering pulmonary and infectious causes of hypoxemia.

Takeaway: persistent newborn saturations below 95% at both sites on repeat screening are a failed CCHD screen: obtain an echocardiogram.

whyNot.A: A chest film does not exclude critical heart disease; a failed oximetry screen needs an echocardiogram.
whyNot.B: Persistent saturations below 95% in both sites are a failed screen, and discharge risks missing a duct-dependent lesion.
whyNot.D: He is well and stable; alprostadil is started when a duct-dependent lesion is diagnosed or the infant deteriorates, after urgent evaluation.
whyNot.E: Further repeats are not part of the algorithm once the screen has failed.

items.objective: Interpret a newborn pulse oximetry screen and choose the next step after a failed result.

items.stemHtml: A 3-week-old girl is brought for follow-up after not passing her newborn hearing screen. Otoacoustic emission testing in the nursery did not pass in the right ear, and an outpatient rescreen last week also did not pass in the right ear. She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and has no family history of hearing loss. Her parents say she startles when a door slams. Otoscopic examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Reassurance because she startles to loud noise

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat otoacoustic emission screening at 12 months

items.explanationHtml:
Newborn hearing programs aim to screen by 1 month, diagnose by 3 months and intervene by 6 months. An infant who has not passed the screen and a rescreen needs a diagnostic audiologic evaluation with diagnostic auditory brainstem response testing before 3 months. Parental impressions and startle responses do not exclude hearing loss. Congenital CMV testing is also considered early when hearing loss is suspected.

Takeaway: an infant who fails the hearing screen and rescreen needs a diagnostic audiology evaluation (ABR) before 3 months of age.

whyNot.A: Imaging may follow once hearing loss is confirmed; it does not establish whether she can hear.
whyNot.C: A startle to loud sounds can occur with significant unilateral or partial hearing loss.
whyNot.D: Implant candidacy needs a confirmed diagnosis, degree of loss and a trial of amplification.
whyNot.E: Waiting a year misses the goal of diagnosis by 3 months and intervention by 6 months.

items.objective: Choose diagnostic audiologic evaluation after a failed newborn hearing rescreen.

items.stemHtml: A 6-month-old boy is brought for his scheduled well-child visit and vaccinations. He has had a runny nose and mild cough for 3 days. Two days ago he was diagnosed with acute otitis media and started on amoxicillin. He is feeding well and playful. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 130/min and respirations are 32/min. Examination shows clear rhinorrhea and a mildly bulging right tympanic membrane; the lungs are clear. His vaccinations are up to date. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding his vaccines?

options.label: A
options.html: Defer all vaccines until 2 weeks after the fever resolves

options.label: B
options.html: Defer all vaccines until the amoxicillin course is complete

options.label: C
options.html: Give half of the due vaccines today and the rest in 4 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
Mild acute illness, low-grade fever, otitis media and current antibiotic treatment are false contraindications. Vaccines are safe and immunogenic in this setting, and deferral creates a missed opportunity. Only moderate or severe acute illness is a precaution that justifies waiting.

Takeaway: mild illness, low-grade fever and current antibiotics are not reasons to defer vaccination.

whyNot.A: Mild illness with low-grade fever is not a reason to defer, and delay leaves him unprotected.
whyNot.B: Antibiotic use is a false contraindication; it does not change vaccine safety or response.
whyNot.C: Splitting doses adds visits and delays protection without improving safety.
whyNot.E: Laboratory testing is not needed to judge a mild illness; the decision is clinical.

items.objective: Recognize false contraindications to routine infant vaccination.

items.stemHtml: A 4-month-old girl is brought for her well-child visit. At 2 months she received all scheduled vaccines. At 11 weeks of age she had episodes of inconsolable crying with drawing up of her legs and a currant-jelly stool; ultrasonography showed an ileocolic intussusception, which was reduced with an air enema. She has been well since. Examination is normal. Which of the following vaccines should be withheld today?
items.explanationHtml:
A history of intussusception is a contraindication to further rotavirus vaccine, as is severe combined immunodeficiency. Rotavirus vaccines carry a small increased risk of intussusception, mostly in the week after the first dose. The other scheduled inactivated vaccines are given as planned.

Takeaway: history of intussusception (or SCID) contraindicates rotavirus vaccine; other vaccines proceed.

whyNot.A: There is no link between intussusception and DTaP; it should be given.
whyNot.B: Hib vaccine is inactivated and has no relation to intussusception.
whyNot.C: IPV is inactivated, given by injection and is not contraindicated.
whyNot.D: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine is not contraindicated by a history of intussusception.

items.objective: Identify the true contraindications to rotavirus vaccine.

items.stemHtml: A 10-month-old girl who recently moved to the area is brought for her first visit at the clinic. Her records show that she received her first doses of DTaP, inactivated poliovirus, Haemophilus influenzae type b and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines at 2 months of age; she has received no vaccines since because of a gap in insurance. She is healthy, and examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan for her DTaP series?

options.label: A
options.html: Check pertussis antibody titers before deciding

options.label: B
options.html: Give dose 2 today, then continue the series

options.label: C
options.html: Give Tdap today in place of DTaP

options.label: D
options.html: Restart the DTaP series from the first dose

options.label: E
options.html: Wait until 15 months of age to resume the series

items.explanationHtml:
The central catch-up rule is that a series is never restarted, whatever the interval since the last dose. Give the next dose now and complete the series using the minimum intervals in the catch-up schedule, giving all other vaccines she is eligible for at the same visit.

Takeaway: in catch-up immunization, give the next dose and continue at minimum intervals; never restart a series.

whyNot.A: Serologic testing is not used to guide routine DTaP catch-up.
whyNot.C: Tdap contains reduced antigen amounts and is not the vaccine for an infant's primary series.
whyNot.D: Doses already given count; a long gap never requires restarting a series.
whyNot.E: Waiting adds more months without pertussis protection; catch-up starts at this visit.

items.objective: Apply catch-up immunization principles to an interrupted infant series.

items.stemHtml:
A 9-month-old boy is brought for a well-child visit. He was born at term weighing 3.4 kg. His mother returned to full-time work when he was 4 months old, and several relatives now care for him during the day. He takes formula and some pureed foods. He has no vomiting, diarrhea, cough or recurrent infections. He sits without support, babbles and is wary of strangers. Examination shows a thin, alert infant with reduced subcutaneous fat and no other abnormalities. His growth measurements are shown.

AgeWeight percentileLength percentileHead circumference percentile
2 months50th50th50th
4 months45th50th50th
6 months15th45th50th
9 monthsbelow 3rd30th50th

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
items.explanationHtml:
Weight that falls first, with length following and head circumference preserved, indicates inadequate energy: most often too little intake. With no symptoms pointing to malabsorption or chronic disease, the highest-yield step is a detailed feeding history (amount and preparation of formula, who feeds him, solids offered) with a diet record and, ideally, an observed feed. The change in caregivers after 4 months is a clue. Broad laboratory testing without clinical leads rarely finds a cause.

Takeaway: in growth faltering with weight falling first and head growth preserved, start with a detailed feeding and diet history.

whyNot.B: Growth hormone deficiency causes falling length with relatively preserved weight, the opposite of this pattern.
whyNot.C: Hypothyroidism slows linear growth first; his weight fell first, with head growth preserved.
whyNot.D: Cystic fibrosis is on the newborn screen and he has no steatorrhea, cough or infections; testing without such clues is low-yield.
whyNot.E: Celiac disease needs gluten exposure and usually causes diarrhea or distension; he has neither.

items.objective: Use the pattern of growth curves to direct the evaluation of growth faltering.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old girl is brought for a well-child visit. She is otherwise healthy and takes no medications. She watches about 4 hours of videos daily and drinks two cans of soda most days. Her BMI is at the 97th percentile for age and sex; at her visit 2 years ago it was at the 91st percentile. Blood pressure is at the 70th percentile. Examination shows no acanthosis nigricans and is otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Brief advice and recheck BMI in 1 year

items.explanationHtml:
A BMI at or above the 95th percentile is obesity. The USPSTF recommends that children 6 years and older with high BMI be offered or referred to comprehensive, intensive behavioural interventions (at least 26 contact hours), and the AAP advises prompt, family-centred intensive health behaviour and lifestyle treatment rather than watchful waiting. Pharmacotherapy is considered from age 12 and surgery evaluation from age 13 for severe obesity.

Takeaway: children 6 years and older with obesity should be offered intensive, family-based behavioural treatment (26+ contact hours) now.

whyNot.A: Watchful waiting is no longer advised; obesity is treated promptly with intensive support.
whyNot.C: Metformin is not first-line weight treatment for a 9-year-old without diabetes.
whyNot.D: Weight-loss drugs are considered from 12 years of age, alongside lifestyle treatment.
whyNot.E: Metabolic surgery evaluation is for adolescents 13 years or older with severe obesity.

items.objective: Choose first-line management for obesity in a school-age child.

items.stemHtml: The parents of a healthy 2-year-old boy ask whether they can now turn his car seat to face forward, as his cousin's seat was turned at this age. He weighs 12.5 kg and is 86 cm long. He rides in a convertible car seat installed rear-facing in the back seat; the seat's label allows rear-facing use up to 18 kg and 100 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

options.label: A
options.html: Belt-positioning booster seat in the back seat

options.label: B
options.html: Continued rear-facing seat in the back seat

options.label: C
options.html: Forward-facing harnessed seat in the back seat now

options.label: D
options.html: Forward-facing harnessed seat in the front passenger seat

options.label: E
options.html: Lap-and-shoulder seat belt in the back seat

items.explanationHtml:
Rear-facing seats spread crash forces across the back, head and neck. Current advice is to keep a child rear-facing as long as possible, until the child reaches the highest weight or height allowed by the seat for rear-facing use, then move to a forward-facing harnessed seat, later a booster, and keep children in the back seat until 13 years.

Takeaway: keep toddlers rear-facing until they reach their seat's rear-facing height or weight limit, not until a fixed age.

whyNot.A: Boosters are for older children who have outgrown a harnessed seat; a toddler needs a harness.
whyNot.C: He has not yet reached his seat's rear-facing limits, so turning him now gives up protection.
whyNot.D: Children under 13 years should ride in the back seat, away from front air bags.
whyNot.E: A seat belt alone fits only once a child is about 4 ft 9 in tall.

items.objective: Give current car-seat guidance for a toddler.

items.stemHtml: A 15-month-old girl is brought for a well-child visit. She has six erupted teeth. She has not yet seen a dentist. Her parents brush her teeth with plain water, and she falls asleep with a bottle of milk most nights. The family's home receives fluoridated municipal water. Examination shows no visible caries. Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive measure at this visit, in addition to dental home referral and counselling?

options.label: D
options.html: Fluoride varnish applied to the teeth

items.explanationHtml:
The USPSTF recommends that primary care clinicians apply fluoride varnish to the primary teeth of all infants and children starting at tooth eruption through age 5. Oral fluoride supplements from 6 months are for children whose drinking water is low in fluoride. Counselling covers brushing with a smear of fluoride toothpaste and avoiding bedtime bottles.

Takeaway: apply fluoride varnish in primary care from first tooth eruption through age 5; oral fluoride only if water is deficient.

whyNot.A: Chlorhexidine rinse is not used as routine caries prevention in toddlers.
whyNot.B: Varnish is recommended from the eruption of the first tooth, not deferred.
whyNot.C: Radiographs are not a primary-care preventive measure and she has no visible caries.
whyNot.E: Supplements are for children whose water supply is low in fluoride; her water is fluoridated.

items.objective: Choose fluoride varnish as routine caries prevention in primary care.

items.stemHtml: A 10-year-old boy is brought for a well-child visit. He is healthy and active and takes no medications. He has no history of heart, kidney or endocrine disease. His parents are 40 and 42 years old and well; there is no known family history of early cardiovascular disease or high cholesterol. His BMI is at the 55th percentile and blood pressure is at the 50th percentile. Examination is normal. He has had no laboratory tests since infancy. Which of the following screening tests is recommended at this visit?

options.label: C
options.html: No laboratory screening until 17 years of age

items.explanationHtml:
Universal lipid screening is recommended once between 9 and 11 years and again between 17 and 21 years, in addition to risk-based screening from age 2. A nonfasting sample (non-HDL cholesterol or a full panel) is acceptable for the universal screen; abnormal results are confirmed with a repeat fasting panel. Universal screening finds familial hypercholesterolemia that family history alone would miss.

Takeaway: screen all children for dyslipidemia once at 9–11 years (nonfasting is acceptable) and again at 17–21 years.

whyNot.A: Diabetes screening is risk-based, starting around puberty in children with overweight plus risk factors; he has none.
whyNot.B: Diabetes screening is risk-based (for example with overweight and risk factors), and he has none.
whyNot.C: Universal lipid screening is done once between 9 and 11 years and again between 17 and 21 years.
whyNot.E: ALT is used to screen for fatty liver disease in children with obesity; his BMI is normal.

items.objective: Identify the age and method of universal pediatric lipid screening.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old girl is brought by her mother for a preventive visit before the school year. She has no medical problems and takes no medications. Her mother says she has been "moody" and spends a lot of time in her room on her phone. The girl answers questions briefly and looks at her mother before responding. Vital signs and growth are normal. The physician plans to take a psychosocial history. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to proceed?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask the mother to complete a written questionnaire about her daughter's behaviour

options.label: B
options.html: Defer the psychosocial history until the girl raises a concern herself

options.label: C
options.html: Explain confidentiality and its limits to both, then interview the girl alone

options.label: D
options.html: Interview the girl with her mother present to keep information shared

options.label: E
options.html: Promise the girl that nothing she says will be shared with anyone

items.explanationHtml:
Adolescents should have time alone with the clinician at each preventive visit. Setting expectations at the start, with both parent and adolescent present, matters: what the adolescent shares stays confidential unless there is a serious risk of harm to self or others, or abuse. The interview then moves from less to more sensitive topics: home, school, activities, substances, sexuality, mood and safety.

Takeaway: explain confidentiality and its limits to parent and adolescent, then interview the adolescent alone.

whyNot.A: The mother's view is useful, but it cannot replace the adolescent's own account of sensitive behaviours.
whyNot.B: Adolescents rarely volunteer risk behaviours; screening is routine at every preventive visit.
whyNot.D: Adolescents disclose far less with a parent present, and the interview loses most of its yield.
whyNot.E: Unconditional secrecy cannot be promised; serious risk of harm or abuse must be disclosed.

items.objective: Set up a confidential adolescent psychosocial interview.

items.stemHtml: During the confidential interview, the 15-year-old girl says she has had one male sexual partner for the past 4 months and that they use condoms "most of the time." She has no vaginal discharge, pelvic pain or dysuria. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. She has had no previous testing for sexually transmitted infections. Which of the following tests is most appropriate for her today?

options.label: D
options.html: Speculum examination with wet mount microscopy

options.label: E
options.html: Vaginal swab NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhea

items.explanationHtml:
Sexually active females under 25 years should be screened yearly for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The preferred specimen is a vaginal swab NAAT, which can be self-collected; urine NAAT is an alternative. HIV screening is also recommended from age 15. A pelvic examination is not required, and cervical cytology waits until age 21.

Takeaway: screen sexually active females under 25 yearly for chlamydia and gonorrhea with a vaginal swab NAAT; no cytology before 21.

whyNot.A: Cervical cancer screening starts at 21 years whatever the age of sexual debut.
whyNot.B: Routine HSV serology is not recommended in people without symptoms.
whyNot.C: HPV testing is part of cervical cancer screening, which does not begin until 21 years.
whyNot.D: Wet mount evaluates vaginitis symptoms, which she does not have; STI screening needs no speculum examination.

items.objective: Choose the appropriate STI screening test for an asymptomatic sexually active adolescent.

items.stemHtml: The girl's screening tests return negative. She wants to avoid pregnancy for the next several years and says she forgets to take her acne medication on many days. She has no history of venous thromboembolism, migraine with aura or hypertension, and she has not been pregnant. Blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. A urine pregnancy test today is negative. In addition to counselling about condom use, which of the following contraceptive methods is most appropriate to recommend?
items.explanationHtml:
Long-acting reversible contraception (implant or intrauterine device) is recommended as first-line for adolescents: it does not depend on daily or monthly action and has the lowest typical-use failure rate. The etonogestrel implant is the most effective reversible method and is safe in adolescents who have never been pregnant. Condoms are still needed for STI prevention.

Takeaway: LARC, such as the etonogestrel implant, is first-line contraception for adolescents; pair it with condoms for STI prevention.

whyNot.A: A daily pill depends on adherence, which she reports is difficult, so typical-use failure is much higher.
whyNot.B: The injection needs visits every 3 months and is less effective in typical use than an implant.
whyNot.D: The patch needs weekly changes and has a typical-use failure rate similar to the pill.
whyNot.E: The ring needs monthly user action and is less effective in typical use than long-acting methods.

items.objective: Recommend long-acting reversible contraception as first-line for an adolescent.

items.stemHtml: A 14-year-old boy completes an adolescent depression questionnaire in the waiting room before his annual visit. His score is in the moderately severe range, and he marked that on several days in the past 2 weeks he had thoughts that he would be better off dead. He says school has been "hard" since his parents separated 3 months ago. He has no medical problems. Vital signs and examination are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask him directly about suicidal thoughts, plans and access to means

options.label: B
options.html: Prescribe fluoxetine and arrange follow-up in 4 weeks

options.label: C
options.html: Refer him for outpatient counselling and review at the next annual visit

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat the questionnaire in 2 weeks before acting

options.label: E
options.html: Tell his parents about the result before speaking with him

items.explanationHtml:
The USPSTF recommends screening adolescents 12–18 years for major depression. A positive screen, particularly with thoughts of death, is followed by a direct, private assessment of suicide risk: thoughts, intent, plan, prior attempts and access to lethal means (firearms, medications). Asking does not increase risk. The result determines the level of care, the safety plan and whether parents must be informed.

Takeaway: after a positive adolescent depression screen, ask directly about suicidal ideation, plan and means before anything else.

whyNot.B: Treatment decisions follow a diagnostic and safety assessment; starting a drug first skips the urgent risk evaluation.
whyNot.C: A positive screen with death-related thoughts needs assessment today and close follow-up, not a year's wait.
whyNot.D: Repeating the screen delays the essential step of assessing his current suicide risk.
whyNot.E: The first step is to talk with him; parents are informed when safety requires it, after the risk is assessed.

items.objective: Choose suicide risk assessment as the next step after a positive adolescent depression screen.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl is seen alone for a confidential visit at the start of which the limits of confidentiality were explained. She reports low mood for 2 months, and she says she has been saving her mother's sleeping pills and plans to take them all this weekend. She asks the physician not to tell her parents, who are in the waiting room. She has no psychiatric history. Vital signs are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Arrange an outpatient psychiatry appointment within 2 weeks

options.label: B
options.html: Ask her to sign a no-suicide contract and send her home

options.label: C
options.html: Begin an antidepressant and schedule a phone check in 1 week

options.label: D
options.html: Inform her parents and arrange an emergency psychiatric evaluation today

options.label: E
options.html: Keep the disclosure confidential as she has requested

items.explanationHtml:
Adolescent confidentiality has limits that were set out at the start of the visit: a serious risk of harm to the patient or others, or abuse. An active suicide plan with access to a lethal method is imminent risk. She needs an emergency psychiatric evaluation today with continuous supervision, and her parents must be told so that the means can be removed and she can be kept safe. Explain to her what will be shared and why.

Takeaway: an adolescent with an active suicide plan needs emergency evaluation and parental notification; imminent risk overrides confidentiality.

whyNot.A: An active plan with available means needs same-day emergency evaluation, not a delayed appointment.
whyNot.B: No-suicide contracts do not prevent suicide and are not a substitute for an emergency evaluation.
whyNot.C: Medication does not address imminent risk, and SSRIs take weeks to work.
whyNot.E: A serious and imminent risk of self-harm is a recognised limit of adolescent confidentiality.

items.objective: Recognize when imminent risk of harm overrides adolescent confidentiality.

items.stemHtml:
A 14-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because he is the shortest boy in his class and has no signs of puberty. He is healthy, eats well and plays soccer. His father was a "late bloomer" who grew until 19 years of age; his mother had menarche at 13. His sense of smell is normal. Testes are 3 mL bilaterally, the penis is prepubertal and there is no pubic hair. Height data and test results are shown.

Age (years)Height percentileHeight velocity
1025th5.5 cm/year
1212th5.2 cm/year
144th5.0 cm/year
TestResult
Bone age11.5 years
LH, FSH, testosteronePrepubertal
TSH, free T4Normal
Blood count, ESR, tissue transglutaminase IgANormal
IGF-1Low for chronological age, normal for bone age

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A healthy boy with normal prepubertal growth velocity, a height percentile that drifts down only as peers enter their spurt, a delayed bone age, prepubertal gonadotropins and a parent with late puberty has constitutional delay of growth and puberty. Chronic disease and hypothyroidism have been screened out. Management is reassurance and follow-up; a short course of low-dose testosterone can be offered if he is distressed. Persistent absence of puberty would prompt evaluation for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

Takeaway: constitutional delay shows normal growth velocity, delayed bone age, prepubertal gonadotropins and often a family history of late puberty.

whyNot.B: In familial short stature bone age matches chronological age and puberty starts on time.
whyNot.C: GH deficiency gives subnormal height velocity; his prepubertal velocity is normal and IGF-1 fits his bone age.
whyNot.D: Kallmann syndrome is a permanent GnRH deficiency usually with anosmia; his sense of smell is normal and the family history favours a timing variant.
whyNot.E: Klinefelter syndrome raises FSH and LH, and puberty usually begins; his gonadotropins are prepubertal.

items.objective: Diagnose constitutional delay of growth and puberty from growth data and laboratory results.

items.stemHtml: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because she has not started breast development. She has been the shortest in her class since early childhood; her height is below the 3rd percentile and her growth velocity over the past year was 3.5 cm. Her parents are of average height. She had recurrent ear infections as a young child. Examination shows SMR 1 breasts and SMR 2 pubic hair. Serum FSH is 82 mIU/mL (prepubertal reference under 5) and LH is increased; estradiol is low. TSH is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Reassurance and repeat hormone tests in 1 year

items.explanationHtml:
Absent breast development at 14 with high FSH and LH means primary ovarian insufficiency (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism). In a short girl, Turner syndrome is the leading cause, and the next step is a karyotype. A confirmed diagnosis leads to cardiac and renal imaging, hearing assessment, growth hormone discussion and planned estrogen replacement to induce puberty.

Takeaway: delayed puberty with high FSH means gonadal failure; in a short girl obtain a karyotype for Turner syndrome.

whyNot.A: MRI evaluates hypothalamic or pituitary causes, which give low gonadotropins; hers are high.
whyNot.C: A progestin challenge assesses estrogen status in amenorrhea after breast development; it adds nothing when FSH is high and breasts are undeveloped.
whyNot.D: High gonadotropins indicate gonadal failure, not a benign delay, and waiting postpones diagnosis and treatment.
whyNot.E: Hyperprolactinemia suppresses gonadotropins; it does not cause high FSH.

items.objective: Choose karyotype in a girl with delayed puberty and elevated gonadotropins.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because of pubic hair and enlargement of his penis over the past 6 months. He has grown 9 cm in the past year. He has no headaches or vision changes, and there is no exposure to topical testosterone in the home. Examination shows SMR 3 pubic hair and penile enlargement; both testes are 8 mL. Neurological examination is normal. Bone age is 10.5 years. Morning ultrasensitive LH is in the pubertal range and testosterone is increased. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: CT scan of the adrenal glands

options.label: E
options.html: Start a GnRH agonist without further testing

items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral testicular enlargement with pubertal LH, rapid growth and advanced bone age establish central precocious puberty (onset before 9 years in a boy). In boys an underlying CNS lesion, such as a hypothalamic hamartoma or a tumor, is found more often than in girls, so brain MRI is obtained in every boy with central precocious puberty. Treatment is a long-acting GnRH agonist plus management of any lesion.

Takeaway: every boy with central precocious puberty needs a brain MRI to look for a CNS lesion.

whyNot.B: Adrenal sources give gonadotropin-independent puberty with small testes; his testes are enlarged and LH is pubertal.
whyNot.C: Ultrasonography helps with a unilateral testicular mass; both testes are enlarged symmetrically.
whyNot.D: Adrenal hyperplasia causes peripheral puberty with prepubertal testes and suppressed LH.
whyNot.E: A CNS lesion must be excluded before or alongside treatment, particularly in a boy.

items.objective: Choose brain imaging in a boy with central precocious puberty.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy comes for a pre-participation evaluation before the basketball season. He reports that twice during sprint drills last season he felt lightheaded and had to sit down, which he attributed to dehydration. His paternal uncle died suddenly at 34 years of age while jogging. He takes no medications or supplements. Pulse is 64/min and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border; it becomes louder when he stands from a squat and softer when he squats. Femoral pulses are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: Clear after a normal exercise stress test

options.label: B
options.html: Clear after a normal resting ECG alone

options.label: C
options.html: Clear for all sports with advice on hydration

items.explanationHtml:
Exertional presyncope, a family history of sudden death before age 50, and a systolic murmur that increases with standing or Valsalva (reduced preload worsens dynamic outflow obstruction) suggest hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes. He should not be cleared until ECG, echocardiography and cardiology assessment are complete.

Takeaway: exertional syncope or presyncope, family history of early sudden death or a dynamic murmur means no sports clearance until cardiac evaluation.

whyNot.A: A stress test does not exclude hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; structural imaging is required.
whyNot.B: A normal ECG does not exclude cardiomyopathy when history and examination are this suggestive.
whyNot.C: Exertional presyncope with this murmur and family history is a red flag for cardiomyopathy, not dehydration.
whyNot.D: The risk is sudden death from exertion, which contact restriction does not address.

items.objective: Recognize pre-participation findings that require cardiac evaluation before sports clearance.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her parents because she has lost 9 kg over 4 months. She runs daily and eats mostly vegetables; she says she feels "fat" despite her weight loss. Her last menstrual period was 3 months ago. Supine pulse is 40/min and rises to 72/min on standing; blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg supine. Temperature is 35.4°C (95.7°F). BMI is 15.8 kg/m2. Serum potassium is 3.2 mEq/L, phosphorus 2.7 mg/dL and glucose 68 mg/dL. ECG shows sinus bradycardia. A pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Hospital admission for medical stabilization and supervised refeeding

options.label: B
options.html: Oral contraceptive to restore menses and protect bone

options.label: C
options.html: Outpatient family-based treatment with weekly weight checks

options.label: D
options.html: Referral to a dietitian and review in 1 month

options.label: E
options.html: Start olanzapine and review in 2 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
This adolescent with restrictive eating, weight loss, body-image distortion and amenorrhea most likely has anorexia nervosa. Marked bradycardia, orthostatic change, hypotension, hypothermia and electrolyte abnormalities indicate medical instability and require admission for cardiac monitoring and cautious refeeding with close monitoring of phosphate, potassium and magnesium to avoid refeeding syndrome.

Takeaway: an adolescent with an eating disorder and bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia or electrolyte disturbance needs inpatient medical stabilization.

whyNot.B: Hormonal therapy does not treat the malnutrition and masks the return of menses as a recovery marker.
whyNot.C: Family-based treatment is the outpatient standard, but she is medically unstable and needs inpatient care first.
whyNot.D: Her bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia and electrolyte changes make a month's delay unsafe.
whyNot.E: Medication is not first-line and does not address her immediate medical instability.

items.objective: Identify medical instability requiring hospital admission in an adolescent eating disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 13-year-old girl with nephrotic syndrome diagnosed 4 weeks ago is seen in follow-up. She has been taking prednisone 60 mg daily (about 1.5 mg/kg) since diagnosis; proteinuria has resolved and a taper over the next 4 weeks is planned, after which prednisone will stop. She has no history of chickenpox, and her family declined varicella vaccine when she was younger; they now wish her to receive it. Varicella IgG is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate timing for varicella vaccination?

options.label: C
options.html: At least 1 month after prednisone is stopped

options.label: D
options.html: At least 1 year after prednisone is stopped

options.label: E
options.html: After 5 years without a nephrotic relapse

items.explanationHtml:
Varicella vaccine is live attenuated. Systemic corticosteroids at 2 mg/kg/day or 20 mg/day of prednisone or more for 14 days or longer count as significant immunosuppression, and live vaccines are deferred until at least 1 month after the steroids are stopped. Until then, she should be counselled about exposures; post-exposure varicella-zoster immune globulin may be needed while she is immunosuppressed.

Takeaway: after high-dose steroids for 14 days or more, wait at least 1 month after stopping before giving a live vaccine.
