whyNot.A: Prednisone at 20 mg/day or more for 14 days or longer is significant immunosuppression, which contraindicates live vaccines.
whyNot.B: One week is too short for immune function to recover after high-dose steroids.
whyNot.D: A year's delay leaves her susceptible without benefit; 1 month is sufficient.
whyNot.E: Remission off high-dose steroids is enough; a long delay leaves her susceptible during future relapses and steroid courses.

items.objective: Time live vaccine administration after high-dose corticosteroid therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy is seen alone during his annual preventive visit. On a validated adolescent substance-use questionnaire he reports drinking 4–5 beers at parties about once a month for the past 6 months, and he once rode home with a friend who had been drinking. He uses no other substances, his grades are stable, and he has had no legal problems or blackouts. The screen is positive for risky use. He says drinking is "no big deal." Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Brief intervention using motivational interviewing, with follow-up

options.label: B
options.html: Immediate disclosure of his drinking to his parents

options.label: C
options.html: Reassurance that this is normal experimentation

options.label: D
options.html: Referral to a residential treatment program

options.label: E
options.html: Urine drug testing without his knowledge

items.explanationHtml:
Adolescents should be screened for substance use at preventive visits with a validated tool. Risky use without features of a severe disorder is managed with a brief intervention: nonjudgemental feedback, motivational interviewing to explore his own reasons for change, specific safety plans (never riding with an impaired driver, a safe-ride agreement) and follow-up. Higher-risk patterns lead to referral.

Takeaway: screen-positive risky adolescent substance use is managed with a motivational brief intervention, a safety plan and follow-up.

whyNot.B: Substance use without imminent danger does not by itself override confidentiality, and disclosure may end his openness.
whyNot.C: Binge drinking and riding with an impaired driver are serious risks that call for intervention, not reassurance.
whyNot.D: Residential treatment is for severe substance use disorders; his pattern is risky use without dependence.
whyNot.E: Covert testing of a competent adolescent is not appropriate and damages trust.

items.objective: Manage risky adolescent alcohol use found on screening.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of hot flashes and night sweats for 9 months. Her last menstrual period was 14 months ago; before that, her cycles had become irregular over 2 years. She takes no medications. Body mass index is 24 kg/m2. Serum FSH is markedly elevated, LH is elevated to a lesser degree, and estradiol is low. Which of the following is the most likely primary cause of the disproportionate rise in her serum FSH?

options.label: B
options.html: Decreased ovarian inhibin B and estradiol production

options.label: D
options.html: Increased hepatic sex hormone–binding globulin synthesis

items.explanationHtml:
Depletion of ovarian follicles removes the granulosa-cell products that feed back on the pituitary. Inhibin B selectively suppresses FSH, and estradiol suppresses both gonadotropins, so losing both raises FSH more than LH.

This pattern (high FSH greater than LH, low estradiol) after 12 months of amenorrhea at age 52 is the expected postmenopausal profile.

Takeaway: Postmenopausal FSH rises more than LH because the failing ovary loses both inhibin B and estradiol feedback.

whyNot.A: Kisspeptin neurons become more active, not less, after estrogen withdrawal; less kisspeptin would lower gonadotropins.
whyNot.C: Adrenal androgens decline gradually with age and do not drive gonadotropin secretion.
whyNot.D: Changes in SHBG alter free sex-steroid fractions but are not the cause of the selective FSH rise.
whyNot.E: Dopamine regulates prolactin, not FSH; it does not explain her gonadotropin pattern.

items.objective: Explain why FSH rises more than LH after menopause.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old woman has had 12 hot flashes a day for the past year, which wake her several times each night. She does not want hormone therapy. Her physician prescribes an oral drug that blocks a receptor on neurons in the preoptic thermoregulatory area of the hypothalamus. These neurons receive increased input from arcuate nucleus neurons that become hyperactive when estrogen levels fall. Baseline liver enzymes are measured before treatment. Which of the following endogenous ligands normally activates the receptor this drug blocks?
items.explanationHtml:
The drug is an NK3 receptor antagonist (fezolinetant). Arcuate neurons that co-express kisspeptin, neurokinin B and dynorphin hypertrophy and become overactive after estrogen withdrawal. Their neurokinin B signals through NK3 receptors to the thermoregulatory center, narrowing the thermoneutral zone so small temperature rises trigger flushing and sweating.

Blocking NK3 receptors reduces vasomotor symptoms without hormonal effects; liver enzymes are monitored because of reports of hepatotoxicity.

Takeaway: Postmenopausal hot flashes are driven by neurokinin B signalling through NK3 receptors, the target of fezolinetant.

whyNot.A: Dynorphin is co-released by the same arcuate neurons but acts on κ-opioid receptors and restrains, rather than drives, their firing.
whyNot.B: Kisspeptin from these neurons acts on GnRH neurons (KISS1R) to drive gonadotropins; it is not the thermoregulatory signal targeted here.
whyNot.D: Neuropeptide Y is an arcuate orexigenic peptide involved in appetite, not the target of this therapy.
whyNot.E: Orexin regulates wakefulness; orexin antagonists treat insomnia, not hot flashes.

items.objective: Identify neurokinin B and the NK3 receptor as the mechanism of menopausal vasomotor symptoms.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old woman had bilateral oophorectomy at age 44 for endometriosis and has not taken hormone therapy. She has no other medical conditions and takes no medications. Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry shows a lumbar spine T-score of −2.1. Serum calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone, alkaline phosphatase and 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentrations are within the reference ranges. Which of the following best explains her accelerated bone loss?

options.label: A
options.html: Decreased intestinal calcium absorption from vitamin D deficiency

options.label: B
options.html: Decreased osteoblast collagen synthesis from glucocorticoid excess

options.label: C
options.html: Increased osteoclast activity from more RANKL relative to osteoprotegerin

options.label: D
options.html: Increased parathyroid hormone secretion from low serum calcium

options.label: E
options.html: Increased renal phosphate wasting from excess FGF23

items.explanationHtml:
Estrogen normally lowers RANKL expression by osteoblast-lineage and T cells, raises osteoprotegerin (the RANKL decoy receptor), and shortens osteoclast lifespan. Surgical menopause removes estrogen abruptly, so osteoclastogenesis and resorption outpace formation, a high-turnover loss that falls hardest on trabecular bone such as the lumbar spine.

Normal calcium, phosphorus, PTH, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D argue against metabolic bone disease.

Takeaway: Estrogen deficiency causes bone loss by raising the RANKL-to-osteoprotegerin ratio and boosting osteoclast activity.

whyNot.A: Her 25-hydroxyvitamin D level is normal, so impaired calcium absorption from deficiency is not the explanation.
whyNot.B: She takes no glucocorticoids and has no features of Cushing syndrome.
whyNot.D: Her calcium and PTH are normal; secondary hyperparathyroidism is not present.
whyNot.E: FGF23 excess causes hypophosphatemia and osteomalacia; her phosphorus is normal.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of bone loss after estrogen withdrawal.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman has been postmenopausal for 11 years and has not taken hormone therapy. Her body mass index is 39 kg/m2. As part of a research study, her serum estrogens are measured. Estradiol is low, and the predominant circulating estrogen is estrone. Which of the following is the main site of production of this estrone?
items.explanationHtml:
After menopause, the ovary no longer has follicles with granulosa cells to aromatize androgens. Estrone is formed in peripheral tissues, mainly adipose stromal cells, by aromatase acting on androstenedione supplied by the adrenal cortex and ovarian stroma. Women with more adipose tissue therefore have higher postmenopausal estrone levels.

Takeaway: Postmenopausal estrogen is mainly estrone made by aromatase in adipose tissue from adrenal and ovarian androstenedione.

whyNot.B: The zona reticularis supplies the androgen precursor (DHEA, androstenedione) but has little aromatase.
whyNot.C: There is no corpus luteum without ovulation; it makes progesterone and estradiol in cycling women.
whyNot.D: Granulosa cells are the main estradiol source in cycling women but are absent after follicle depletion.
whyNot.E: Theca cells make androstenedione, which needs aromatization elsewhere; they are not the estrone source.

items.objective: Identify peripheral aromatization in adipose tissue as the source of postmenopausal estrone.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman has a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan because her mother had a hip fracture. Her Z-scores are −2.3 at the lumbar spine and −2.0 at the femoral neck. Between ages 15 and 23 she had a restrictive eating disorder with amenorrhea; she has maintained a normal weight with regular menses since then. Serum calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone, TSH and 25-hydroxyvitamin D are within the reference ranges. Which of the following best explains her low bone density?

options.label: B
options.html: Failure to attain normal peak bone mass

options.label: C
options.html: Hypercalciuria from a renal tubular defect

options.label: D
options.html: Impaired mineralization from vitamin D deficiency

items.explanationHtml:
Bone mass accrues rapidly in adolescence and peaks by the late twenties to about 30. Low energy intake and hypoestrogenic amenorrhea during those years reduce bone accrual, and the deficit is only partly recovered once weight and menses return. A low Z-score (compared with age-matched peers) in a premenopausal woman with this history reflects a low peak rather than later loss.

Takeaway: Peak bone mass is set by about age 30; adolescent hypoestrogenism and undernutrition lower it permanently.

whyNot.A: She is 41 with regular menses, before the late-transition phase of rapid bone loss.
whyNot.C: Nothing suggests stones or a tubular disorder, and secondary causes were screened.
whyNot.D: Her 25-hydroxyvitamin D and phosphorus are normal, so osteomalacia is unlikely.
whyNot.E: Her calcium and PTH are normal, excluding primary hyperparathyroidism.

items.objective: Relate low adult bone density to failure to reach peak bone mass after adolescent amenorrhea.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man has run competitively since college and has trained 50 km per week for 40 years. His maximal oxygen uptake measured on a treadmill is 20% lower than a measurement made when he was 30. Hemoglobin concentration, resting heart rate and resting ejection fraction are unchanged from that time, and arterial oxygen saturation stays at 97% at peak exercise. Which of the following changes most likely accounts for the decline in his maximal oxygen uptake?

options.label: C
options.html: Decreased left ventricular contractility at rest

items.explanationHtml:
By the Fick principle, VO2max equals maximal cardiac output times the maximal arteriovenous O2 difference. With age, maximal heart rate falls because sinoatrial and β-adrenergic responsiveness decline, which lowers maximal cardiac output. This happens even in lifelong endurance athletes, whose training preserves stroke volume and peripheral extraction but not maximal heart rate.

Takeaway: The age-related fall in VO2max is driven mainly by a falling maximal heart rate, which training does not prevent.

whyNot.A: His arterial saturation is preserved at peak exercise, so diffusion is not limiting.
whyNot.B: His hemoglobin is unchanged, so oxygen-carrying capacity is not the explanation.
whyNot.C: His resting ejection fraction is unchanged; resting contractility is preserved with healthy aging.
whyNot.E: More mitochondria would increase extraction and raise, not lower, VO<sub>2</sub>max.

items.objective: Explain the main physiologic cause of declining maximal oxygen uptake with age.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old man is evaluated 6 months after a pelvic fracture from a motorcycle crash. Since the injury he has been unable to achieve an erection, although he can still ejaculate with manual stimulation. Testosterone and prolactin concentrations are normal. Imaging and electrophysiologic testing indicate injury to the sacral (S2–S4) pelvic splanchnic nerves, with intact thoracolumbar outflow and an intact pudendal nerve. Loss of which of the following most directly explains his erectile dysfunction?

options.label: A
options.html: Nitric oxide release in the corpora cavernosa

options.label: B
options.html: Norepinephrine release from hypogastric nerve terminals

options.label: C
options.html: Pudendal activation of the bulbospongiosus muscle

options.label: E
options.html: Vasopressin release from the posterior pituitary

items.explanationHtml:
Erection is a parasympathetic event. Pelvic splanchnic (S2–S4) fibres release nitric oxide (with endothelial NO), which activates guanylyl cyclase; cGMP relaxes cavernosal arterioles and trabecular smooth muscle so the sinusoids fill and compress the outflow veins.

His emission (sympathetic, hypogastric) and ejaculation (somatic, pudendal) are preserved, consistent with isolated parasympathetic injury.

Takeaway: Erection depends on parasympathetic nitric oxide and cGMP; emission is sympathetic and ejaculation is pudendal.

whyNot.B: Sympathetic norepinephrine drives emission and detumescence; its loss would not prevent erection.
whyNot.C: Pudendal-mediated bulbospongiosus contraction produces ejaculation, which he retains.
whyNot.D: His testosterone is normal, and androgen loss mainly reduces desire rather than abolishing reflex erection.
whyNot.E: Vasopressin has no established role in penile erection.

items.objective: Identify the autonomic pathway and mediator responsible for erection.

items.stemHtml: A healthy 70-year-old man asks whether he is "going through male menopause." He fathered a child at age 66. He exercises regularly and has a body mass index of 25 kg/m2. He reports slightly less frequent morning erections than in his 40s but no other symptoms. Compared with when he was 30 years old, which of the following findings is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Abrupt cessation of Leydig cell function

items.explanationHtml:
Men have no abrupt equivalent of menopause. Total testosterone falls slowly from middle age while SHBG rises, so free (bioavailable) testosterone falls more than total testosterone. Spermatogenesis continues into old age, as his recent paternity shows, and LH is normal or mildly elevated.

Takeaway: Male reproductive aging is a gradual fall in free testosterone with rising SHBG and preserved spermatogenesis.

whyNot.A: Leydig cell output declines slowly over decades; there is no abrupt cessation in men.
whyNot.B: Spermatogenesis persists into old age; he fathered a child at 66.
whyNot.C: SHBG rises with age (it falls with obesity and insulin resistance, which he lacks).
whyNot.E: Falling testosterone feedback leaves LH normal or modestly raised, not suppressed.

items.objective: Contrast male reproductive aging with female menopause.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man comes to the clinic 3 weeks after his wife died of a stroke. He cries daily, has trouble falling asleep and has lost his appetite. Twice he briefly heard her voice calling his name from the kitchen and knew she was not there. He has returned to work part time, spends evenings with his brother, and says he "feels lost without her" but that his life is still worth living. He has no history of psychiatric illness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Within weeks of a death, sadness, crying, insomnia, poor appetite and yearning are typical. Brief, recognized perceptions of the deceased's voice are common in normal grief and are not psychosis. His self-worth is intact, he has no suicidal thinking, and he is resuming work and social contact.

Takeaway: Early grief with intact self-worth and returning function is normal bereavement; it needs support and follow-up, not psychiatric diagnosis.

whyNot.A: Adjustment disorder is not diagnosed when the reaction is an expected response to bereavement.
whyNot.B: He lacks pervasive worthlessness, suicidal ideation, psychomotor change or loss of function out of proportion to the loss.
whyNot.D: Prolonged grief disorder needs at least 12 months since the death in adults.
whyNot.E: He recognizes the experiences are not real, and he has no disorganization or other psychotic symptoms.

items.objective: Distinguish normal bereavement from depression and prolonged grief disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of 1 year of vaginal dryness and pain with intercourse. Her last menstrual period was at age 51. She has had two urinary tract infections in the past 6 months. Pelvic examination shows pale, thin vaginal mucosa with loss of rugae and no discharge. Vaginal pH is 6.0. Saline microscopy shows many small, round parabasal epithelial cells, few lactobacilli, no clue cells and no motile organisms. Which of the following best explains the elevated vaginal pH?

options.label: A
options.html: Decreased glycogen in vaginal epithelial cells

options.label: E
options.html: Overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria producing amines

items.explanationHtml:
Estrogen stimulates maturation of the vaginal epithelium and glycogen storage in its superficial cells. Lactobacilli ferment that glycogen (via host-derived sugars) to lactic acid, keeping the pH low. After menopause the epithelium thins (parabasal cells predominate), glycogen falls, lactobacilli decline and pH rises, which also favours colonization by uropathogens.

Takeaway: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause raises vaginal pH because estrogen loss depletes epithelial glycogen and lactobacilli.

whyNot.B: Bartholin gland secretion lubricates the introitus but does not set vaginal pH.
whyNot.C: Cervical mucus falls rather than rises after menopause and does not explain the epithelial atrophy.
whyNot.D: Postmenopausal mucosa thins rather than keratinizes, and androgen excess is not present.
whyNot.E: Amine-producing anaerobic overgrowth (bacterial vaginosis) would show clue cells and a discharge.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of raised vaginal pH in genitourinary syndrome of menopause.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old woman who weighs 46 kg is started on gabapentin 300 mg three times daily for postherpetic neuralgia. Five days later she is brought to the clinic because of drowsiness, unsteadiness and a near-fall. Serum creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL, unchanged from 1 year ago. Gabapentin is not metabolized and is excreted unchanged in the urine. Which of the following best explains her toxicity despite a normal serum creatinine?

options.label: A
options.html: Decreased creatinine production masking low GFR

options.label: B
options.html: Decreased hepatic glucuronidation of the drug

options.label: C
options.html: Decreased plasma protein binding of the drug

options.label: D
options.html: Increased renal tubular secretion of creatinine

options.label: E
options.html: Increased volume of distribution of the drug

items.explanationHtml:
GFR declines with age, but creatinine production falls with muscle mass, so serum creatinine can remain in the reference range despite a markedly reduced GFR. An estimate that uses age and weight (Cockcroft–Gault: (140 − 84) × 46 × 0.85 / (72 × 1.0) ≈ 30 mL/min) shows she needs a much lower dose of a renally cleared drug.

Takeaway: In small, older adults a normal creatinine can hide a low GFR; dose renally cleared drugs by estimated clearance.

whyNot.B: Gabapentin is not metabolized by the liver, so hepatic conjugation is irrelevant.
whyNot.C: Gabapentin is minimally protein bound, so changes in binding do not alter its free level.
whyNot.D: More tubular creatinine secretion would lower creatinine, but this is not an age-related change that explains toxicity.
whyNot.E: Gabapentin is hydrophilic; with less body water its volume of distribution falls rather than rises.

items.objective: Explain why serum creatinine overestimates kidney function in older adults.

items.stemHtml: An 86-year-old man with mild dementia who lives alone is brought to the emergency department during a heat wave because of 2 days of lethargy. He did not complain of thirst to his daughter. Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 104/min, and blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg. Mucous membranes are dry. Serum sodium is 158 mEq/L, and urine osmolality is 520 mOsm/kg H2O. Which of the following age-related changes most contributed to his electrolyte abnormality?

options.label: B
options.html: Decreased thirst in response to hyperosmolality

items.explanationHtml:
Older adults have a blunted thirst response to rising plasma osmolality, lower total body water and reduced maximal urine concentrating ability. When free-water losses rise (heat, fever) and access to water or the drive to drink falls (dementia, living alone), hypernatremia follows. His urine is concentrated, showing intact ADH action but not enough water intake.

Takeaway: Reduced thirst and lower body water make older adults prone to hypernatremia when water losses rise.

whyNot.A: Lower aldosterone with age promotes sodium loss and hyperkalemia, not hypernatremia.
whyNot.C: ADH release is preserved or increased with age and works to retain water, opposing hypernatremia.
whyNot.D: Maximal concentrating capacity falls, not rises, with age.
whyNot.E: Total body water falls with age, which reduces the buffer against water loss.

items.objective: Explain why older adults develop hypernatremia during dehydrating illness.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old man comes to the clinic because of light-headedness for a few seconds when he stands up from a chair. He has not fainted. He takes no medications and has no diabetes or neurologic disease. Supine blood pressure is 138/76 mm Hg with a pulse of 72/min; after 3 minutes standing, blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg with a pulse of 76/min. Plasma norepinephrine concentration is higher than the average for young adults. Which of the following best explains the minimal rise in heart rate on standing?

options.label: E
options.html: Increased cardiac vagal tone on standing

items.explanationHtml:
Standing pools blood in the legs and lowers arterial pressure; carotid and aortic baroreceptors normally trigger vagal withdrawal and sympathetic activation to raise heart rate and vascular tone. With aging, stiffer arteries deform less, baroreflex gain falls, and cardiac β-adrenergic responsiveness declines, so the compensatory tachycardia is blunted and orthostatic hypotension results even though circulating norepinephrine is high.

Takeaway: Blunted baroreflex sensitivity is a normal age-related change that predisposes older adults to orthostatic hypotension.

whyNot.B: Plasma norepinephrine rises with age; the problem is reduced end-organ and reflex responsiveness.
whyNot.C: Arteries stiffen (compliance falls) with age, which reduces baroreceptor stretch signalling.
whyNot.D: β<sub>1</sub>-receptor responsiveness falls with age; more responsiveness would increase the heart rate rise.
whyNot.E: Standing normally withdraws vagal tone; increased vagal tone would suggest a vasovagal reflex with syncope, not this pattern.

items.objective: Explain the physiologic basis of orthostatic hypotension in older adults.

items.stemHtml: A healthy 78-year-old woman who is a lifelong nonsmoker takes part in a study of lung aging. She walks 3 km daily and has no respiratory symptoms. Her pulmonary function tests are compared with tests she had at age 30 in an earlier study. Which of the following values is most likely to have increased?
items.explanationHtml:
Aging reduces lung elastic recoil and stiffens the chest wall. Small airways close at higher lung volumes during expiration (higher closing volume), so residual volume and functional residual capacity rise. Total lung capacity is roughly unchanged, so vital capacity (TLC − RV) falls. FEV1, FVC and the ratio drift down, and V/Q mismatch widens the A–a gradient.

Takeaway: With aging, loss of elastic recoil raises residual volume while total lung capacity stays about the same.

whyNot.A: Diffusing capacity declines with age as alveolar surface area and capillary volume fall.
whyNot.B: FEV<sub>1</sub> falls slightly faster than FVC, so the ratio declines modestly rather than rising.
whyNot.D: TLC is about unchanged because lower recoil and stiffer chest wall offset each other.
whyNot.E: Vital capacity falls because residual volume takes up more of an unchanged TLC.

items.objective: Predict the effect of normal aging on lung volumes.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man comes to the clinic because he has had increasing difficulty following conversations in restaurants over the past 3 years; he hears voices but cannot make out words. He has no tinnitus, vertigo or ear pain and no history of noise exposure or ototoxic drugs. Otoscopy is normal. The Weber test does not lateralize, and air conduction exceeds bone conduction on both sides. Audiometry shows a symmetric loss that is greatest at high frequencies. Degeneration of which of the following structures most likely explains his hearing loss?

options.label: A
options.html: Hair cells at the apex of the cochlea

options.label: B
options.html: Hair cells at the base of the cochlea

options.label: E
options.html: Vestibular hair cells of the utricle

items.explanationHtml:
Presbycusis is bilateral, symmetric sensorineural loss of high frequencies. The basilar membrane near the cochlear base (by the oval window) is narrow and stiff and responds to high frequencies; its hair cells (especially outer hair cells) are lost first with age. Losing high-frequency consonant sounds makes speech hard to understand, especially with background noise.

Takeaway: Presbycusis is high-frequency sensorineural loss from hair cell loss at the cochlear base.

whyNot.A: Apical hair cells encode low frequencies, which are relatively spared in his audiogram.
whyNot.C: Ossicular disease causes conductive loss, with bone conduction exceeding air conduction.
whyNot.D: Tympanic membrane changes cause conductive loss; his otoscopy and Rinne tests are normal.
whyNot.E: Utricular hair cells sense linear acceleration; their loss causes imbalance, not hearing loss.

items.objective: Localize the lesion in age-related hearing loss.

items.stemHtml: A 77-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of a painful band of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the left side of her chest for 2 days. She had chickenpox as a child. She has no known immunodeficiency and takes amlodipine and no other medications. Complete blood count, serum immunoglobulin concentrations and complement levels are within the reference ranges. Which of the following age-related changes most directly underlies this reactivation?
items.explanationHtml:
Varicella-zoster virus stays latent in dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia and is held in check by virus-specific cell-mediated (T-cell) immunity. Immunosenescence, beginning with thymic involution and narrowing of the naive T-cell pool, lets this immunity wane, so zoster incidence rises steeply with age. Boosting it is the rationale for recombinant zoster vaccination from age 50.

Takeaway: Zoster in older adults reflects waning virus-specific cell-mediated immunity, part of immunosenescence.

whyNot.A: Her blood count is normal, and neutrophils do not control latent herpesviruses.
whyNot.B: Her immunoglobulins are normal; antibodies do not prevent reactivation from latency.
whyNot.C: Splenic macrophages clear encapsulated bacteria; their function does not govern VZV latency.
whyNot.E: Her complement levels are normal, and complement deficiency predisposes to bacterial, not herpesvirus, infections.

items.objective: Link immunosenescence of T-cell immunity to herpes zoster in older adults.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman is given oral diazepam 5 mg nightly for 4 nights during a hospital stay for anxiety-related insomnia. She remains drowsy and unsteady for 5 days after the last dose. Her serum albumin, liver enzymes and creatinine clearance are within the reference ranges for her age. Compared with a 30-year-old, she has a higher percentage of body fat and lower total body water. Which of the following pharmacokinetic changes best explains her prolonged sedation?

options.label: A
options.html: Decreased volume of distribution of the drug

options.label: B
options.html: Increased hepatic glucuronidation of the drug

options.label: C
options.html: Increased plasma protein binding of the drug

options.label: D
options.html: Increased renal tubular secretion of the drug

options.label: E
options.html: Increased volume of distribution of the drug

items.explanationHtml:
Diazepam is highly lipid-soluble. With more body fat, its volume of distribution rises; because t½ = 0.693 × Vd/CL, a larger Vd prolongs half-life. Reduced phase I (oxidative) metabolism of diazepam and its active metabolite desmethyldiazepam slows clearance further, so the drug accumulates and effects persist for days.

Takeaway: Lipophilic drugs have a larger volume of distribution and longer half-life in older adults.

whyNot.A: A smaller volume of distribution applies to water-soluble drugs (lithium, digoxin), not lipophilic diazepam.
whyNot.B: Diazepam is cleared mainly by oxidation; more glucuronidation would shorten, not prolong, its effect.
whyNot.C: Greater protein binding would reduce the free, active fraction; albumin is normal here.
whyNot.D: More renal secretion would speed elimination; diazepam is not cleared unchanged by the kidney.

items.objective: Explain how age-related body composition changes prolong the half-life of lipophilic drugs.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old man is admitted for a hip fracture. On hospital day 2 he develops tremor, sweating, tachycardia and agitation; his family reports that he drinks 6 to 8 beers daily. He has compensated cirrhosis with an albumin of 3.2 g/dL. The team wants a benzodiazepine whose clearance depends on direct conjugation, without oxidative metabolism or long-acting active metabolites. Which of the following drugs best meets this requirement?
items.explanationHtml:
Aging and liver disease reduce phase I (cytochrome P450) oxidation much more than phase II glucuronidation. Lorazepam (like oxazepam and temazepam) is glucuronidated directly to inactive products, so its clearance is relatively preserved and it does not accumulate active metabolites.

Takeaway: When a benzodiazepine is needed in older or cirrhotic patients, choose one cleared by glucuronidation, such as lorazepam.

whyNot.A: Chlordiazepoxide is oxidized to long-acting active metabolites that accumulate with reduced phase I capacity.
whyNot.B: Clonazepam depends on hepatic nitroreduction (a phase I step) and has a long half-life.
whyNot.C: Diazepam is oxidized to desmethyldiazepam, a very long-acting active metabolite.
whyNot.D: Flurazepam has an extremely long-acting active metabolite and is avoided in older adults.

items.objective: Choose a benzodiazepine whose clearance is preserved when phase I metabolism is reduced.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old retired accountant comes to the clinic because she worries about her memory. Over the past 2 years she has had more trouble recalling the names of acquaintances, although the names come to her later in the day. She takes longer to learn new software than she used to. She still manages her own finances and medications, drives without getting lost, and volunteers weekly. Her husband has noticed no change. Montreal Cognitive Assessment score is 28/30. Physical and neurologic examinations are normal. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her symptoms?
items.explanationHtml:
Slower retrieval of names that are recalled later, slower learning of new material, preserved crystallized knowledge, normal objective testing and full independence in instrumental activities are typical of normal aging. Mild neurocognitive disorder requires objective decline below age norms; dementia requires loss of independence.

Takeaway: Normal cognitive aging slows retrieval and learning but leaves testing within norms and daily function intact.

whyNot.A: Dementia requires impairment that interferes with independence; she manages finances, medications and driving.
whyNot.B: Delirium is acute and fluctuating with inattention; her course is gradual and her attention is intact.
whyNot.C: Mild neurocognitive disorder requires objective decline beyond age norms, and her test score is normal.
whyNot.E: She reports no depressed mood, anhedonia or vegetative symptoms.

items.objective: Distinguish normal cognitive aging from mild and major neurocognitive disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old man reports that he becomes sleepy at about 8:30 PM and wakes at 4:30 AM, earlier than when he was working. He wakes briefly two or three times each night and takes a 30-minute nap after lunch. He feels rested, has no snoring or witnessed apneas, and does not act out dreams. Polysomnography is performed as part of a research study. Compared with a 25-year-old, which of the following findings is most expected?

options.label: E
options.html: Loss of muscle atonia during REM sleep

items.explanationHtml:
Normal aging reduces slow-wave (N3) sleep markedly, increases brief awakenings, lowers sleep efficiency and total nocturnal sleep, and advances circadian phase (earlier sleep and wake times). REM sleep is relatively preserved. Without daytime impairment, his pattern is normal.

Takeaway: Aging decreases slow-wave sleep and sleep efficiency and advances circadian phase.

whyNot.A: Sleep latency tends to lengthen, not shorten, with age.
whyNot.C: More awakenings reduce sleep efficiency in older adults.
whyNot.D: Total nighttime sleep decreases with age.
whyNot.E: Loss of REM atonia defines REM sleep behavior disorder, a disease, and he does not act out dreams.

items.objective: Describe normal age-related changes in sleep architecture.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man comes for a health maintenance visit. He feels well. He has no medical conditions and takes no medications. He does not smoke and drinks two beers on weekends. His father developed type 2 diabetes at age 60. Blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg, and body mass index is 29 kg/m2. Physical examination is normal. Which of the following tests is most appropriate to offer at this visit?
items.explanationHtml:
Adults 35–70 years old with overweight or obesity should be screened for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes with HbA1c, fasting glucose or an oral glucose tolerance test. An abnormal result leads to confirmation and, for prediabetes, referral to an intensive lifestyle program.

Takeaway: Screen adults 35–70 with a BMI of 25 or more for prediabetes and diabetes.

whyNot.A: A resting ECG has no screening role in asymptomatic low-risk adults.
whyNot.C: Vitamin D screening in asymptomatic adults is not recommended.
whyNot.D: Thyroid screening of asymptomatic adults is not recommended.
whyNot.E: Urinalysis is not a recommended screening test in healthy adults.

items.objective: Identify the indication for diabetes screening in overweight adults.

items.stemHtml:
A 62-year-old woman comes for a health maintenance visit. She has hypertension treated with lisinopril. She is a nonsmoker and does not have diabetes. She has no history of cardiovascular disease and no family history of premature coronary disease. Blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg, and body mass index is 27 kg/m2. Fasting laboratory results are shown.

TestResult
Total cholesterol232 mg/dL
LDL cholesterol150 mg/dL
HDL cholesterol46 mg/dL
Triglycerides180 mg/dL
Glucose, fasting94 mg/dL
Calculated 10-year ASCVD risk12%

In addition to lifestyle counselling, which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Adults 40–75 with at least one cardiovascular risk factor (here, hypertension and dyslipidemia) and a 10-year ASCVD risk of 10% or more benefit from statin therapy for primary prevention; a moderate-intensity statin is the usual starting choice.

Takeaway: Offer a statin for primary prevention to adults 40–75 with a risk factor and 10-year risk of 10% or higher.

whyNot.A: Starting aspirin for primary prevention is not recommended at age 60 or older because bleeding risk offsets the benefit.
whyNot.B: Ezetimibe is an add-on when statins are insufficient or not tolerated, not first-line primary prevention.
whyNot.D: Niacin does not reduce cardiovascular events when added to modern therapy and has adverse effects.
whyNot.E: Omega-3 supplements do not replace statins for lowering LDL-driven risk.

items.objective: Apply risk-based criteria for statin primary prevention.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman comes for a health maintenance visit. Two years ago she had a total abdominal hysterectomy, including removal of the cervix, for symptomatic uterine leiomyomas; pathology showed benign leiomyomas and a normal cervix. Her cervical screening tests before surgery were all normal, and she has had no cervical dysplasia. She has one male sexual partner. Which of the following is the most appropriate cervical cancer screening plan?

options.label: A
options.html: Annual pelvic examination with vaginal cytology

options.label: B
options.html: Cytology of the vaginal cuff every 3 years

options.label: C
options.html: HPV testing of the vaginal cuff every 5 years

items.explanationHtml:
Women who have had a total hysterectomy with removal of the cervix for a benign reason, and who have no history of high-grade precancer (CIN 2 or worse) or cervical cancer, no longer need cervical cancer screening. Vaginal cancer is rare, and vaginal cuff testing produces false positives without benefit.

Takeaway: Stop cervical screening after total hysterectomy for benign disease without a history of high-grade dysplasia.

whyNot.A: Routine vaginal cytology after benign hysterectomy is not recommended.
whyNot.B: Cuff cytology is not indicated without a history of high-grade cervical disease.
whyNot.C: Cuff HPV testing is not indicated without a cervix or prior high-grade disease.
whyNot.E: Colposcopy is a diagnostic procedure after an abnormal result, not a screening test.

items.objective: Recognize when cervical cancer screening is no longer indicated after hysterectomy.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman comes to discuss weight loss. Her weight has increased by 12 kg over 6 years. She has tried diets on her own without lasting success and has not joined a structured program. She has no hypertension, diabetes, sleep apnea or joint disease, and she takes no medications. Body mass index is 32 kg/m2. Blood pressure is 126/80 mm Hg. Fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids and TSH are within the reference ranges. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
items.explanationHtml:
Adults with a BMI of 30 or more should be offered or referred to intensive, multicomponent behavioral interventions (many sessions over a year addressing diet, physical activity, self-monitoring and barriers). These produce clinically meaningful weight loss and reduce progression to diabetes. Medication is added if lifestyle measures alone are insufficient.

Takeaway: First-line management of obesity is an intensive multicomponent behavioral intervention.

whyNot.A: Surgery is considered at higher BMI thresholds or with obesity-related disease, and after a structured nonsurgical attempt.
whyNot.C: She is euthyroid; thyroid hormone for weight loss is harmful.
whyNot.D: Medication is an adjunct to, not a substitute for, a structured lifestyle program, and phentermine is for short-term use.
whyNot.E: Very-low-calorie diets need medical supervision, are not first-line, and are followed by high rates of regain.

items.objective: Choose first-line management for adult obesity without comorbidity.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman comes for a health maintenance visit. Her mother was diagnosed with ovarian cancer at age 56, and her maternal aunt had breast cancer at age 41. No relatives have had genetic testing. She has no breast symptoms, and breast examination is normal. A brief familial risk assessment tool gives a positive result. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Women with a personal or family history of breast, ovarian, tubal or peritoneal cancer, or an ancestry linked to BRCA founder variants, should have a familial risk assessment. When it is positive, the next step is genetic counseling, which refines risk, chooses the right test (ideally starting with an affected relative if possible) and prepares her for results. Management (enhanced imaging, risk-reducing surgery) depends on what testing shows.

Takeaway: A positive familial risk assessment leads to genetic counseling, then BRCA testing if indicated.

whyNot.A: Imaging decisions depend on her genetic status, which is not yet known.
whyNot.B: Risk-reducing surgery is considered only after a pathogenic variant is confirmed and counseling is done.
whyNot.C: High-risk MRI screening depends on confirmed mutation status or calculated lifetime risk after counseling.
whyNot.E: CA-125 is not an effective screening test for ovarian cancer.

items.objective: Apply BRCA risk assessment and referral for genetic counseling.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man comes for his first health maintenance visit in many years. He feels well. He has been in a monogamous heterosexual relationship for 20 years, has not used injection drugs, has had no blood transfusions, and has not been incarcerated. He was born in the United States. He has had HIV testing in the past, which was negative, and he received hepatitis B vaccine as an adult. Physical examination is normal. Which of the following screening tests is most appropriate?

options.label: E
options.html: Urine chlamydia nucleic acid amplification test

items.explanationHtml:
All adults should be screened at least once for hepatitis C, regardless of risk factors, because many infected people are unaware and curative direct-acting antivirals are available. A positive antibody test is followed by HCV RNA testing to confirm current infection.

Takeaway: Offer one-time hepatitis C antibody screening to all adults.

whyNot.B: Hepatitis A immunity testing is not a screening test; vaccination is offered by risk or on request.
whyNot.C: Latent tuberculosis screening is for adults at increased risk, which he is not.
whyNot.D: Syphilis screening is for those at increased risk, and he has none.
whyNot.E: Chlamydia screening is not recommended for low-risk men.

items.objective: Apply universal one-time hepatitis C screening in adults.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man who moved to the United States from Vietnam 10 years ago comes to establish care. He feels well. He does not know whether he received hepatitis B vaccine, and he has not been tested for hepatitis B. He drinks alcohol about once a month and takes no medications. Examination shows no stigmata of liver disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial hepatitis B test?
items.explanationHtml:
Adults born in regions of intermediate or high hepatitis B prevalence should be screened, and the CDC recommends screening all adults at least once. The triple panel in one draw separates chronic infection (HBsAg positive), resolved infection (anti-HBc positive, HBsAg negative), vaccine immunity (anti-HBs alone) and susceptibility (all negative, so vaccinate).

Takeaway: Screen for hepatitis B with HBsAg, anti-HBs and total anti-HBc, which together define infection, immunity or susceptibility.

whyNot.A: HBV DNA is measured after infection is found, to stage disease and guide treatment.
whyNot.B: HBeAg status assesses replication in known chronic infection; it is not a screening test.
whyNot.D: IgM anti-HBc identifies acute infection and misses chronic infection and immunity status.
whyNot.E: ALT can be normal in chronic infection and does not establish infection or immunity.

items.objective: Select the recommended hepatitis B screening panel.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man who smokes 1 pack of cigarettes daily says he wants to quit within the next 2 weeks. He has tried quitting without medication twice. He has a seizure disorder controlled with levetiracetam and has had no seizures for 3 years. He has no psychiatric history. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. In addition to behavioral counselling, which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Nonpregnant adults who smoke should receive behavioral support plus FDA-approved pharmacotherapy. Varenicline, an α4β2 nicotinic receptor partial agonist, is the most effective single agent; combination nicotine replacement is a comparable alternative. Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in a seizure disorder.

Takeaway: Varenicline plus counselling is first-line for smoking cessation; avoid bupropion with a seizure disorder.

whyNot.A: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in his epilepsy.
whyNot.B: Evidence is insufficient to recommend electronic cigarettes for cessation.
whyNot.C: Naltrexone is used for alcohol and opioid use disorders, not smoking cessation.
whyNot.D: Nortriptyline is a second-line option with anticholinergic and cardiac adverse effects and also lowers the seizure threshold.

items.objective: Choose smoking-cessation pharmacotherapy considering contraindications.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old woman comes for a health maintenance visit. On a standard alcohol screening questionnaire she reports drinking two to three glasses of wine on most weeknights and four or five glasses on Saturdays, about 14 drinks weekly. She has had no withdrawal symptoms, blackouts, legal problems or failed attempts to cut down, and she meets no criteria for alcohol use disorder. Examination is normal, and liver enzymes are within the reference ranges. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: E
options.html: Referral to a 12-step program as the sole intervention

items.explanationHtml:
She exceeds low-risk limits for women (no more than 3 drinks on any day and 7 per week) but has no alcohol use disorder. Adults who screen positive for unhealthy use should receive a brief behavioral counseling intervention: feedback on risk, advice, goal setting and follow-up.

Takeaway: Unhealthy alcohol use without a use disorder is managed with brief behavioral counseling.

whyNot.B: Disulfiram is a treatment for established alcohol use disorder in motivated patients.
whyNot.C: She has no physiologic dependence or withdrawal risk requiring detoxification.
whyNot.D: Imaging is not indicated with normal examination and liver enzymes.
whyNot.E: Mutual-help groups suit alcohol use disorder; she first needs brief counseling, and a referral alone omits it.

items.objective: Manage a positive screen for unhealthy alcohol use.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman comes for an annual examination and is seen alone. In response to routine screening questions about relationship safety, she says that her boyfriend has pushed her against a wall twice in the past 3 months and checks her phone and bank account. She has no injuries today. She lives with him, has no children, and says she feels safe going home tonight. She does not want the police involved. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Advise immediate separation from her partner

options.label: C
options.html: Report to police without her consent

options.label: D
options.html: Safety assessment and referral to advocacy services

items.explanationHtml:
Women of reproductive age should be screened for intimate partner violence, and those who disclose it should be offered or referred to ongoing support. The clinician acknowledges the disclosure, assesses immediate danger (weapons, escalation, strangulation, threats), documents, develops a safety plan, and connects her with advocacy resources, while respecting her decisions as a competent adult.

Takeaway: After disclosure of intimate partner violence, assess safety, document, safety-plan and refer to advocacy; respect autonomy.

whyNot.A: Directing a patient to leave can increase danger and ignores her autonomy; leaving is often the most dangerous period.
whyNot.B: Couples counseling can expose her to retaliation and is not recommended in abusive relationships.
whyNot.C: Reporting adult intimate partner violence without consent is generally not required and breaks confidentiality.
whyNot.E: Deferring action to next year fails to offer the support that makes screening worthwhile.

items.objective: Respond appropriately to a disclosure of intimate partner violence.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman comes for preconception counseling. Her first pregnancy 2 years ago was terminated at 18 weeks' gestation after ultrasonography showed anencephaly. She plans to stop contraception next month. She has no medical conditions, takes no medications, and eats a varied diet. Which of the following daily folic acid doses is most appropriate to begin now?
items.explanationHtml:
All people who could become pregnant should take 0.4–0.8 mg of folic acid daily. After a pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect, the recurrence risk is higher, and 4 mg daily is recommended, starting at least 1 month before conception and continuing through the first trimester.

Takeaway: Prior neural tube defect pregnancy: 4 mg folic acid daily from before conception; everyone else who could conceive: 0.4–0.8 mg.

whyNot.A: 0.1 mg is below the dose shown to prevent neural tube defects even in low-risk women.
whyNot.B: 0.4 mg is the dose for women without a prior affected pregnancy.
whyNot.C: 1 mg is above the standard dose but below the recommended high-risk dose.
whyNot.E: 10 mg exceeds any recommended dose and can mask vitamin B<sub>12</sub> deficiency.

items.objective: Select folic acid dosing for a woman with a prior neural tube defect pregnancy.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man comes to the emergency department 3 hours after stepping on a nail while working in his garden; the nail went through his shoe and was covered with soil. The puncture wound is on the sole of the foot and is irrigated. He completed the childhood tetanus series, received Tdap at age 25, and received a Td booster 7 years ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate tetanus prophylaxis?
items.explanationHtml:
For a contaminated or puncture wound in a person with 3 or more documented prior tetanus toxoid doses, a booster is given if 5 or more years have passed since the last dose. His last dose was 7 years ago, so he needs Td or Tdap. Tetanus immune globulin is reserved for patients with fewer than 3 documented doses or an unknown history.

Takeaway: Dirty wound plus complete series: booster if 5 or more years since the last dose; immune globulin only if the series is incomplete or unknown.

whyNot.B: Immune globulin is not needed because he has had more than 3 documented doses.
whyNot.C: The 10-year interval applies to clean minor wounds; for a dirty wound, 7 years is too long.
whyNot.D: He completed the primary series in childhood, so it is not repeated.
whyNot.E: Passive immunization alone is not indicated, and he needs an active booster.

items.objective: Apply tetanus wound prophylaxis rules.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman comes for a health maintenance visit. She has not received any HPV vaccine doses. She has had three male sexual partners and had cervical cytology at age 22 showing a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, which resolved on follow-up. She is not pregnant and is not immunocompromised. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding HPV vaccination?

options.label: A
options.html: Defer vaccination until HPV testing is negative

options.label: B
options.html: No vaccination because of her age

options.label: C
options.html: No vaccination because of prior sexual activity

items.explanationHtml:
Catch-up HPV vaccination is recommended for everyone through age 26, regardless of sexual history or prior abnormal cytology, because it protects against types not yet acquired. A series started at age 15 or older uses 3 doses (at 0, 1–2 and 6 months).

Takeaway: Vaccinate everyone through age 26 against HPV; start at 15 or older means 3 doses, and no HPV test is needed first.

whyNot.A: HPV testing before vaccination is not recommended and does not change the decision.
whyNot.B: Routine catch-up extends through age 26; she is 24.
whyNot.C: Prior sexual activity and past HPV-related changes do not cancel the benefit against other types.
whyNot.E: The 2-dose schedule applies only when the series starts before the 15th birthday.

items.objective: Apply HPV catch-up vaccination recommendations.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man comes for follow-up 3 weeks after an emergency splenectomy for a splenic laceration sustained in a car crash. He has recovered well. Before discharge he received a dose of PCV20, a dose of Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine and the first dose of quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate (MenACWY) vaccine. His other routine vaccines are up to date. Which of the following additional vaccines is indicated because of his asplenia?
items.explanationHtml:
People with anatomic or functional asplenia are at risk of overwhelming infection by encapsulated organisms. They need pneumococcal vaccination, a one-time Hib dose, a 2-dose MenACWY primary series with boosters every 5 years, and a meningococcal serogroup B (MenB) series.

Takeaway: Asplenia: pneumococcal, Hib, MenACWY (with boosters) and MenB vaccines.

whyNot.A: BCG is not used for asplenia and is not routinely given in the United States.
whyNot.B: Hepatitis A vaccine is for travel, liver disease and other risk groups, not asplenia.
whyNot.D: Typhoid vaccine is for travel to endemic regions.
whyNot.E: Yellow fever vaccine is for travel to endemic areas and is not indicated by asplenia.

items.objective: Identify vaccines indicated after splenectomy.

items.stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman is starting work as a phlebotomist. She has no record of hepatitis B vaccination, and HBsAg, anti-HBs and anti-HBc are all negative. She completes a hepatitis B vaccine series. She is healthy and takes no medications. Which of the following is the most appropriate follow-up after the final dose?

options.label: B
options.html: Booster dose every 5 years without testing

options.label: C
options.html: HBsAg testing every year while employed

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat the full series in 10 years

items.explanationHtml:
Health-care personnel at risk of blood exposure should have anti-HBs measured 1–2 months after completing the series. A level of 10 mIU/mL or more confirms long-term protection, and no boosters or further testing are needed. A lower level prompts revaccination and retesting.

Takeaway: Health-care workers need post-vaccination anti-HBs testing 1–2 months after the hepatitis B series.

whyNot.B: Routine boosters are not recommended for immunocompetent people with a documented response.
whyNot.C: Yearly HBsAg testing is not needed for vaccinated workers; exposures are handled case by case.
whyNot.D: Without post-vaccination testing, her response is unknown, which matters for managing needlestick exposures.
whyNot.E: Responders keep immune memory; repeating the series is not recommended.

items.objective: Apply post-vaccination serologic testing for health-care personnel.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man comes for a health maintenance visit. On a two-item depression screen, he reports feeling down and having little interest in activities on more than half the days over the past 2 weeks. He denies thoughts of self-harm when asked. He has no medical conditions and takes no medications. Physical examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Adults should be screened for depression in settings that can confirm the diagnosis and arrange treatment. A positive two-item screen is followed by a full assessment, such as the nine-item questionnaire plus a clinical interview to confirm criteria, severity, suicide risk, bipolar history and contributing conditions, before choosing treatment.

Takeaway: A positive brief depression screen requires a full diagnostic assessment before treatment.

whyNot.A: Treatment should follow confirmation of the diagnosis and severity, not a screen alone.
whyNot.C: He has no suicidal ideation or danger requiring admission.
whyNot.D: A positive screen needs evaluation now, not in a year.
whyNot.E: Nothing suggests Cushing syndrome; cortisol testing is not part of depression screening.

items.objective: Respond to a positive depression screen.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman comes for preconception counseling. She and her partner plan to start trying to conceive this month. She takes no medications. Her vaccination records cannot be found. Rubella IgG is negative; varicella IgG is positive. A urine pregnancy test today is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: Defer rubella vaccination until after her first pregnancy

options.label: B
options.html: MMR vaccine now and avoid conception for 4 weeks

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat rubella IgG measurement in 6 months

options.label: E
options.html: Varicella vaccine now and avoid conception for 4 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
Nonimmune women who are not pregnant should receive MMR before conception, because rubella in early pregnancy causes congenital rubella syndrome. MMR is a live vaccine, so pregnancy should be avoided for 4 weeks after vaccination; inadvertent vaccination in pregnancy is not an indication for termination. Folic acid supplementation should also start now.

Takeaway: Vaccinate rubella-nonimmune women with MMR before conception and advise avoiding pregnancy for 4 weeks.

whyNot.A: Deferring leaves her pregnancy unprotected against congenital rubella; she can be vaccinated now because she is not pregnant.
whyNot.C: Retesting does not create immunity and delays protection.
whyNot.D: Immune globulin does not provide lasting protection and is not used for preconception prevention.
whyNot.E: She is already immune to varicella, and this does not address rubella.

items.objective: Provide preconception rubella vaccination correctly.

items.stemHtml: The woman described in the previous visit received MMR vaccine and conceived 3 months later. She now comes for a prenatal visit at 28 weeks' gestation in early October. The pregnancy has been uncomplicated. She received Tdap during a previous visit to the emergency department for a laceration 2 years ago. She has not had an influenza vaccine this season. Which of the following is the most appropriate vaccination plan at this visit?

options.label: C
options.html: Live attenuated influenza vaccine and Tdap

options.label: E
options.html: Postpone all vaccines until after delivery

items.explanationHtml:
Tdap is recommended during every pregnancy, ideally at 27–36 weeks' gestation, regardless of prior Tdap, so that maternal antibodies cross the placenta and protect the newborn against pertussis. Inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended in any trimester during influenza season. RSV vaccination, when chosen, is given later, at 32–36 weeks during the season.

Takeaway: Give Tdap in every pregnancy at 27–36 weeks and inactivated influenza vaccine during the season.

whyNot.B: A previous Tdap does not replace the dose needed in each pregnancy to protect the infant.
whyNot.C: Live attenuated influenza vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy.
whyNot.D: MMR is a live vaccine contraindicated in pregnancy, and one documented dose after a negative titer suffices before pregnancy.
whyNot.E: Delaying vaccines leaves mother and newborn unprotected; these vaccines are recommended during pregnancy.

items.objective: Select the vaccines recommended during pregnancy.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man comes for a health maintenance visit. He smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 15 years and quit at age 45. Three years ago, at age 65, a screening abdominal ultrasound showed an infrarenal aortic diameter of 2.4 cm. He has hypertension controlled with amlodipine and no symptoms. Pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Abdominal examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding abdominal aortic aneurysm?

options.label: C
options.html: CT angiography of the abdomen now

items.explanationHtml:
Men 65–75 who have ever smoked should have a one-time ultrasound screen for abdominal aortic aneurysm. A normal aortic diameter (under 3.0 cm) makes clinically important aneurysm development unlikely, so repeat screening is not recommended.

Takeaway: AAA screening is a single ultrasound; a normal aorta at 65 needs no repeat.

whyNot.A: Annual imaging is for surveillance of known aneurysms, not after a normal screen.
whyNot.B: No repeat interval is recommended after a normal screening ultrasound.
whyNot.C: CT angiography adds radiation and contrast without indication.
whyNot.E: D-dimer has no role in aneurysm screening.

items.objective: Apply the one-time nature of AAA screening.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman comes for a health maintenance visit. Menopause occurred at age 52. She has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. She has not had a fracture, does not smoke, and drinks one glass of wine weekly. She has not had bone density testing. Height is unchanged from her prior record, and body mass index is 23 kg/m2. Which of the following is the most appropriate screening test for osteoporosis?

options.label: A
options.html: DXA of the hip and spine

items.explanationHtml:
All women 65 and older should be screened for osteoporosis. Central DXA of the hip and lumbar spine is the standard test; it defines osteoporosis by T-score and feeds fracture-risk calculation and treatment decisions.

Takeaway: Screen women 65 and older for osteoporosis with central DXA.

whyNot.B: Radiographs detect vertebral fractures but are insensitive for low bone density.
whyNot.C: Heel ultrasound can predict fracture risk but is not the diagnostic standard for treatment thresholds.
whyNot.D: Alkaline phosphatase is normal in postmenopausal osteoporosis.
whyNot.E: Bone turnover markers do not diagnose osteoporosis.

items.objective: Select the recommended osteoporosis screening test.

items.stemHtml:
An 81-year-old woman is brought to the clinic by her son because she has become more forgetful over the past 3 months; she has missed two appointments and repeats questions. She also reports constipation and a dry mouth. She lives alone and still cooks and manages her bills. Vital signs are normal. She is oriented and attentive; she recalls 1 of 3 words at 5 minutes. Neurologic examination is otherwise normal. Serum electrolytes, glucose, TSH and vitamin B12 are within the reference ranges. Her medication list is shown.

MedicationUseStarted
Lisinopril 10 mg dailyHypertension8 years ago
Atorvastatin 20 mg dailyHyperlipidemia8 years ago
Omeprazole 20 mg dailyReflux2 years ago
Oxybutynin 5 mg three times dailyUrge incontinence4 months ago
Acetaminophen as neededKnee pain3 years ago

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Oxybutynin is a strongly anticholinergic antimuscarinic that crosses the blood–brain barrier. Older adults have reduced cholinergic reserve, so it can cause memory impairment, constipation and dry mouth, exactly the triad that began after it was started. The next step is to stop it and reassess cognition; urge incontinence can be managed with bladder training and, if needed, a β3 agonist.

Takeaway: New cognitive decline after starting an anticholinergic drug is an adverse effect: stop the drug before working up dementia.

whyNot.A: Starting a cholinesterase inhibitor while giving an anticholinergic is a prescribing cascade; the reversible cause must be removed first.
whyNot.B: Statins have not been shown to cause progressive cognitive decline and do not explain her anticholinergic symptoms.
whyNot.C: Long-term PPI use can lower B<sub>12</sub>, but her B<sub>12</sub> is normal and the timing points to oxybutynin.
whyNot.E: Imaging may be part of a dementia work-up but should follow removal of an obvious drug cause.

items.objective: Recognize and deprescribe an anticholinergic causing cognitive impairment in an older adult.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old man comes to the clinic after two falls in the past 6 months while walking in his garden; he tripped and could not recover his balance. He had no dizziness, palpitations or loss of consciousness, and he was not injured. He takes amlodipine. Blood pressure is 134/78 mm Hg supine and 130/76 mm Hg standing. Visual acuity is 20/30 bilaterally. He takes 15 seconds to rise from a chair, walk 3 meters, turn and sit down. Strength is 4/5 in hip flexors. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 34 ng/mL (sufficiency at least 20–30 ng/mL). Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention to reduce his risk of further falls?

options.label: B
options.html: Exercise program for balance and gait

items.explanationHtml:
His falls are mechanical, with slow Timed Up and Go and proximal weakness, and he has no orthostatic hypotension. Exercise interventions that train gait, balance and strength (supervised physical therapy, group programs, tai chi) are the best-supported way to prevent falls in community-dwelling older adults at increased risk.

Takeaway: For an older adult at increased fall risk from gait and strength deficits, prescribe balance and strength exercise.

whyNot.A: His neurologic examination and history give no indication for brain imaging.
whyNot.C: Hip protectors may reduce fractures in institutional settings but do not prevent falls, and adherence is poor.
whyNot.D: His vitamin D is sufficient; high-dose vitamin D does not prevent falls and may increase them.
whyNot.E: Immobilization accelerates deconditioning and sarcopenia.

items.objective: Choose the evidence-based intervention to prevent falls.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman comes for her annual wellness visit. On the standard falls screening questions, she reports that she fell once in her kitchen 8 months ago without injury and that she has felt unsteady when walking outdoors since then. She has hypertension and osteoarthritis of the knees. She takes lisinopril and acetaminophen. Blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg seated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
items.explanationHtml:
A positive falls screen (a fall in the past year, unsteadiness or fear of falling) leads to a multifactorial risk assessment that begins with an objective gait, strength and balance test such as the Timed Up and Go (12 seconds or longer suggests increased risk), along with orthostatic vital signs, a medication review, vision, feet and home safety.

Takeaway: A positive falls screen leads to a gait and balance assessment such as the Timed Up and Go, as part of a multifactorial evaluation.

whyNot.A: Bone density addresses fracture risk, not the cause of falling; it does not replace the falls assessment.
whyNot.B: Imaging is not indicated without focal neurologic findings or head injury.
whyNot.C: Echocardiography is for suspected structural heart disease or syncope, which she does not have.
whyNot.D: Ambulatory rhythm monitoring is for unexplained syncope or palpitations, which she does not report.

items.objective: Begin the multifactorial falls assessment after a positive screen.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, heart failure and mild dementia lives with her daughter. She takes glyburide 5 mg twice daily, metoprolol and furosemide. Her daughter has found her sweaty and confused on three mornings in the past month; each episode resolved with orange juice. She has lost 4 kg over 6 months because of poor appetite. HbA1c is 6.2%, and estimated GFR is 38 mL/min/1.73 m2. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Add a bedtime snack and continue glyburide

items.explanationHtml:
Glyburide is a long-acting sulfonylurea with active metabolites cleared by the kidney, and it causes prolonged hypoglycemia in older adults, especially with reduced GFR and poor intake. In a frail older adult with dementia, a reasonable HbA1c target is below about 8.0%; her HbA1c of 6.2% with recurrent hypoglycemia shows overtreatment. Stopping glyburide is the priority, then monitoring glucose and adding a low-hypoglycemia agent only if needed.

Takeaway: Recurrent hypoglycemia with a low HbA1c in a frail older adult calls for deprescribing the sulfonylurea and relaxing targets.

whyNot.A: A snack does not remove the cause of hypoglycemia, and her glucose control is already tighter than needed.
whyNot.C: A higher dose would worsen hypoglycemia.
whyNot.D: Insulin adds hypoglycemia risk, and her HbA1c does not justify more treatment.
whyNot.E: Another sulfonylurea keeps the hypoglycemia risk when no glucose-lowering intensification is needed.

items.objective: Deprescribe a sulfonylurea causing hypoglycemia in a frail older adult.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old man has taken lorazepam 1 mg nightly for insomnia for 10 years. He fell in his bathroom at night last month and bruised his hip. He asks whether he should stop the medicine; he is worried about not sleeping. He has no history of seizures or alcohol use disorder and no psychiatric symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?

options.label: C
options.html: Gradual taper plus CBT for insomnia

items.explanationHtml:
Benzodiazepines in older adults increase falls, fractures, cognitive impairment and motor vehicle crashes. After long-term use, they should be tapered gradually (for example, a 10–25% dose reduction every 2–4 weeks, slower near the end) to avoid withdrawal and rebound insomnia. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia improves sleep and raises taper success.

Takeaway: Deprescribe long-term benzodiazepines in older adults with a slow taper supported by CBT for insomnia.

whyNot.A: Abrupt cessation after years of use risks withdrawal, rebound insomnia and, rarely, seizures.
whyNot.B: Continuing exposes him to further falls and cognitive harm after a fall has already occurred.
whyNot.D: Diphenhydramine is strongly anticholinergic and causes confusion, retention and falls in older adults.
whyNot.E: Zolpidem carries similar fall, fracture and complex-sleep-behavior risks in older adults.

items.objective: Plan benzodiazepine deprescribing in an older adult.

items.stemHtml: A 75-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his daughter, who says that over the past year he has missed bill payments, repeated stories, and once got lost driving to a familiar store. He reports no depressed mood. He takes amlodipine. Vital signs are normal. He is alert and attentive. Montreal Cognitive Assessment score is 19/30, with deficits in delayed recall and executive tasks. Neurologic examination shows no focal deficits. Which of the following tests is most appropriate as part of the initial evaluation?
items.explanationHtml:
Progressive decline affecting instrumental activities with an abnormal cognitive test suggests a neurocognitive disorder. The initial evaluation includes an informant history, depression screen, medication review, laboratory tests for treatable contributors (vitamin B12 and TSH, plus a blood count and metabolic panel) and structural neuroimaging.

Takeaway: Initial dementia evaluation includes vitamin B12 and TSH to identify reversible contributors, with structural imaging.

whyNot.A: Amyloid PET is a specialized test, for example when considering anti-amyloid therapy, not an initial test.
whyNot.B: APOE genotyping does not diagnose dementia and is not recommended in routine evaluation.
whyNot.C: EEG is reserved for suspected seizures, prion disease or fluctuating encephalopathy.
whyNot.D: CSF testing is used in atypical, rapidly progressive or early-onset cases, not routinely first.

items.objective: Select initial laboratory tests in the evaluation of cognitive decline.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of urine leakage for 8 months. She has a sudden, strong urge to void several times a day and on some days cannot reach the toilet in time; she wakes twice nightly to void. She does not leak with coughing or lifting. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine and mild cognitive impairment. Pelvic examination shows mild vaginal atrophy without prolapse. Urinalysis is normal, and post-void residual volume is 40 mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
items.explanationHtml:
Urgency, frequency and nocturia without stress leakage, a normal urinalysis and a low post-void residual indicate urge incontinence from detrusor overactivity. First-line treatment is behavioral: bladder training with scheduled voiding and urge suppression, pelvic floor exercises, and managing fluid and caffeine. A β3 agonist is preferred over antimuscarinics if medication is needed, given her cognitive impairment.

Takeaway: Urge incontinence is treated first with bladder training; avoid anticholinergic drugs in older adults with cognitive impairment.

whyNot.B: Indwelling catheters cause infection and are reserved for retention that cannot be managed otherwise.
whyNot.C: A midurethral sling treats stress incontinence, which she does not have.
whyNot.D: Oxybutynin is strongly anticholinergic and can worsen her cognition; behavioral therapy comes first.
whyNot.E: A pessary treats prolapse or stress incontinence, not detrusor overactivity.

items.objective: Manage urge urinary incontinence in an older woman.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman comes for a health maintenance visit. She has well-controlled hypertension and no other conditions. She does not smoke. She has received no pneumococcal vaccines. She received the influenza vaccine this season and the recombinant zoster series last year. Which of the following is the most appropriate pneumococcal vaccination plan?
items.explanationHtml:
All adults 50 and older who have not received a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine should be vaccinated. A single dose of PCV20 (or PCV21) completes the series. If PCV15 is used instead, it is followed by PPSV23 at least 1 year later.

Takeaway: Pneumococcal vaccination for older adults: one dose of PCV20 or PCV21, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23 a year later.

whyNot.A: PCV15 must be followed by PPSV23 at least 1 year later (8 weeks is allowed only for certain high-risk conditions), not 1 week.
whyNot.C: Repeated PPSV23 every 5 years is not the current schedule.
whyNot.D: PPSV23 alone gives a weaker, T-cell–independent response and is no longer the recommended initial vaccine.
whyNot.E: Pneumococcal vaccine is recommended for all adults in her age group regardless of health.

items.objective: Apply the current adult pneumococcal vaccination schedule.

items.stemHtml: A 77-year-old man comes for a health maintenance visit in September. He is healthy apart from treated hypertension and walks 5 km daily. He received a single dose of an RSV vaccine last October. He asks which vaccines he needs this autumn. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding RSV vaccination?

options.label: B
options.html: Monoclonal antibody against RSV each season

options.label: D
options.html: Second RSV vaccine dose 1 month after the first

items.explanationHtml:
A single dose of RSV vaccine is recommended for all adults 75 and older (and for adults 60–74 at increased risk). It is not an annual vaccine; protection from one dose extends across more than one season, and revaccination is not currently recommended.

Takeaway: RSV vaccine in older adults is a single dose, not an annual vaccine.

whyNot.A: RSV vaccination is not repeated each year under current recommendations.
whyNot.B: RSV monoclonal antibodies are for infants, not for vaccinated older adults.
whyNot.D: The adult RSV vaccines are given as a single dose.
whyNot.E: Serologic testing is not used to guide RSV vaccination.

items.objective: Apply RSV vaccination recommendations for older adults.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman comes for a health maintenance visit. She had shingles on her right flank 2 years ago, which resolved with valacyclovir. She received the live attenuated zoster vaccine at age 62. She has no immunocompromising conditions. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding zoster vaccination?

options.label: C
options.html: No vaccine because of prior shingles

options.label: D
options.html: No vaccine because of prior live zoster vaccine

items.explanationHtml:
Recombinant (adjuvanted glycoprotein E) zoster vaccine is recommended as 2 doses, 2–6 months apart, for all adults 50 and older. It is given regardless of a prior episode of zoster (once the acute episode has resolved) and regardless of prior live zoster vaccine (at least 8 weeks later), because live-vaccine protection wanes and zoster can recur.

Takeaway: Give two doses of recombinant zoster vaccine from age 50, even after prior shingles or prior live zoster vaccine.

whyNot.A: Serologic testing is not needed; nearly all older adults are seropositive, and testing does not change the recommendation.
whyNot.B: The live zoster vaccine is no longer available in the United States and is less effective.
whyNot.C: Shingles can recur, and vaccination after an episode is recommended.
whyNot.D: Protection from the live vaccine wanes; recipients should receive the recombinant vaccine.

items.objective: Apply recombinant zoster vaccine recommendations after prior zoster or live vaccine.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man comes to the clinic in October for his influenza vaccine. He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and no other conditions. He has no egg allergy and has tolerated influenza vaccines in previous years. The clinic stocks several influenza vaccine formulations. Which of the following is the most appropriate choice for him?

options.label: D
options.html: No vaccine because he was vaccinated last year

items.explanationHtml:
Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for everyone 6 months and older. For adults 65 and older, high-dose inactivated, recombinant, or adjuvanted inactivated vaccine is preferred, because immunosenescence blunts the antibody response to standard-dose vaccine and these products give better protection. If none is available, any age-appropriate inactivated vaccine should be given rather than delaying.

Takeaway: For adults 65 and older, prefer high-dose, recombinant or adjuvanted influenza vaccine every year.
