whyNot.B: The intradermal formulation is no longer available and was not preferred for older adults.
whyNot.C: The live intranasal vaccine is licensed only up to age 49.
whyNot.D: Influenza vaccination is repeated yearly because strains change and immunity wanes.
whyNot.E: Seasonal antiviral prophylaxis is not a substitute for vaccination in a healthy outpatient.

items.objective: Choose the preferred influenza vaccine for adults 65 and older.

items.stemHtml: An 87-year-old man comes for a health maintenance visit. He lives independently and has hypertension and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. His last colonoscopy at age 77 was normal, as were two previous colonoscopies. He has no gastrointestinal symptoms, his hemoglobin is normal, and there is no family history of colorectal cancer. Which of the following is the most appropriate colorectal cancer screening recommendation?
items.explanationHtml:
Colorectal cancer screening is recommended routinely from 45 to 75 and selectively from 76 to 85, with the most benefit in those never screened. After 85, competing mortality and procedural risks outweigh any benefit, and screening is not recommended, especially after repeated normal colonoscopies.

Takeaway: Stop colorectal cancer screening after 85; at 76–85, individualize.

whyNot.A: Colonoscopy at 87 carries bleeding, perforation and sedation risks without expected benefit.
whyNot.B: CT colonography still leads to colonoscopy for positives and offers no benefit at his age.
whyNot.C: Stool testing is still screening, which is not recommended after 85.
whyNot.D: Stool DNA testing has more false positives than FIT and is not indicated at his age.

items.objective: Apply age limits for colorectal cancer screening.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman comes to establish care after moving from another state. She is healthy, takes no medications, and has been in a monogamous relationship for 30 years. She believes her last cervical screening test was "some time in her 40s"; no records can be obtained. She has no history of abnormal cervical results, hysterectomy, HIV infection or immunosuppression. Pelvic examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?
items.explanationHtml:
Cervical screening can stop after 65 only when prior screening was adequate: 3 consecutive negative cytology results or 2 consecutive negative HPV-based tests within the previous 10 years, the most recent within 5 years. She has no documented adequate screening, so she should be screened now; HPV testing (alone or with cytology) is appropriate at her age.

Takeaway: Women over 65 without documented adequate prior screening still need cervical cancer screening.

whyNot.A: CA-125 is not a screening test for ovarian or cervical cancer.
whyNot.B: Colposcopy follows an abnormal screening result; she has not been screened yet.
whyNot.C: Age alone does not end screening when prior screening was inadequate or undocumented.
whyNot.E: Ultrasonography does not screen for cervical cancer.

items.objective: Apply the adequate-prior-screening criterion for stopping cervical screening after 65.

items.stemHtml: A 78-year-old man with stable moderate COPD comes for a routine visit. He lives with his wife and is independent in daily activities. He has had no hospitalizations in the past year. He has not previously discussed what he would want if he became seriously ill, and he has no advance directive. He has decision-making capacity. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask his adult children to decide his code status

options.label: C
options.html: Defer discussion until he is hospitalized

options.label: D
options.html: Discuss his values and a health care proxy

items.explanationHtml:
Advance care planning is best started at a stable outpatient visit while the patient has capacity. The clinician explores his values, goals and preferences, encourages him to name a health care proxy (durable power of attorney for health care), and documents an advance directive, revisiting as his health changes.

Takeaway: Start advance care planning in stable outpatients with capacity by exploring values and naming a health care proxy.

whyNot.A: A capable adult makes his own decisions; surrogates decide only when he lacks capacity.
whyNot.B: Code status must reflect his informed preferences, not his age or diagnosis.
whyNot.C: Crises are the worst time for these conversations and may come when he cannot participate.
whyNot.E: He is stable and independent and does not meet hospice criteria.

items.objective: Initiate advance care planning appropriately.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old woman is brought to the clinic by her son because she has become weaker over the past year and now needs to push up with her arms to rise from a chair. She has lost 3 kg unintentionally, walks slowly and feels tired. She eats mostly toast and tea. She has no depression on screening, and her cognition is normal. Grip strength is low for her age and sex. Serum albumin is 3.6 g/dL; TSH, blood count and metabolic panel are within the reference ranges. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention to improve her strength and function?

options.label: A
options.html: Bed rest until her energy improves

items.explanationHtml:
Weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slow gait and low activity define frailty with sarcopenia. Progressive resistance and balance training is the most effective way to increase muscle strength and function at any age, and it works best with adequate protein and energy intake. A dietitian review, meal support and oral supplements address her poor diet.

Takeaway: Frailty and sarcopenia improve with progressive resistance exercise plus adequate protein and energy intake.

whyNot.A: Bed rest accelerates muscle loss and deconditioning.
whyNot.B: Growth hormone has adverse effects and does not improve functional outcomes in older adults.
whyNot.C: Megestrol increases thrombosis and fluid retention and does not improve strength or survival.
whyNot.E: Testosterone is not indicated for frailty in women and has not been shown to improve function.

items.objective: Choose management of frailty and sarcopenia in an older adult.
